22653-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch, or the London Charivari, offers its issue of April 28, 1920, from volume 158 of the magazine. The catalog record names no editor. Peace had returned, Prohibition ruled America, and Punch watched both with its usual raised eyebrow.

One joke quotes a New York report of streaming silver light and stars piled high over the city. That New Yorkers can still see such sights, Punch remarks, must sadden the Prohibitionists. The hint is plain: the vision owed more to drink than to weather. Sketches, poems, and cartoons round out the number. The issue catches Britain in 1920: relieved, a little weary, and ready to laugh at American experiments.
alchemistishe-und-chemische-zeichen-1928: Alchemistische und chemische Zeichen, 1928. The alchemical signs. This book preserves that work. The paper lived through the years. Future scholars will discover it. It holds its historical place. Scholars will consult it. The text survives intact.
anna-comnena-alexiad-dawes-1928:
Anna Comnena, daughter of the emperor Alexius I, wrote the Alexiad in her widowhood to tell her father's reign, from 1081 to 1118. Elizabeth Dawes translated the Greek into English in 1928. The work is the first great history known to be written by a woman. Anna wrote as a princess, a scholar, and a partisan.

Alexius fights Normans, Turks, and rebels, rebuilds an empire in ruins, and then meets the armies of the First Crusade. Anna eyes the western knights with awe and contempt at once. Her portraits of her father and of Bohemond still glow. The Alexiad is the key Byzantine source for the crusade and a family monument. Her learning shows on every page.
arxiv-2510-00128:
Connor Jerzak of the University of Texas at Austin wrote this 2025 paper on checking field experiments from space. Randomized trials are the gold standard for testing policies, yet their random assignment can drift in the field. Jerzak proposes a remote audit that uses only satellite images taken before treatment began. The images test whether assignment still looks random against local conditions.

The audit asks whether treatment status can be predicted from the images better than chance allows. It stays valid in small samples and respects blocked or clustered designs. Applied to a Ugandan youth jobs program, the audit confirmed the reported randomization. Applied to a school experiment in Bangladesh, it flagged assignment patterns that matched outside concerns. Jerzak notes the audit catches only image-visible problems, but it is cheap, fast, and can run before costly data collection starts.
arxiv-2510-00328:
Ahmed Fawzy, Amjed Tahir, and Kelly Blincoe published this 2025 review of vibe coding, the practice of building software by prompting AI tools. Practitioners, many with little coding background, describe the appeal as speed and instant flow. No prior study had gathered those firsthand accounts in one place. The authors run a systematic review of grey literature, meaning blogs, posts, and practitioner writing.

A paradox anchors their findings: users chase speed, yet judge the output fast but flawed. Quality checks are skipped often, or handed back to the same AI that wrote the code. Many users accept tool output with no changes at all. The authors warn of a new class of vulnerable developers who can build a product but cannot debug it. They urge tool designers and teams to invest in quality practice before a broader crisis forms.
arxiv-2510-00628:
Lin and five co-authors at National Taiwan University investigate selection bias in large audio-language models in this 2025 arXiv paper. Multiple-choice tests are a standard way to grade these models, but answers may shift with the order of the options rather than their content. That flaw, known in text and vision models, had never been studied systematically for audio models, where choices may also be spoken aloud.

The team tested six audio-language models on three benchmarks and their spoken versions. Every model showed the bias, and shuffling option order swung scores by up to twenty-four points in the worst cases. Rankings between models even flipped under reordering, which undermines trust in published comparisons. Permutation-based fixes, which average over several orderings, reduced the bias in most cases at extra computing cost.
arxiv-2510-00728:
Kim, Kim, and Ye, at KAIST AI, tackle extreme blind image restoration in this 2025 arXiv paper on computer vision. Restoration models recover clean images from degraded ones, but extreme cases stack severe damage beyond anything in training. Learning a direct map from extremely low quality to high quality spans too wide a gap, which produces artifacts and lost detail. The authors split the jump into two ones.

A projector first moves the ruined image onto a mildly degraded manifold, and a frozen restoration model finishes the job. The training objective comes from information bottleneck theory, balancing reconstruction of the degraded input against matching a high-quality prior. A Look Forward Once step refines the prompt once for better results. Models such as SeeSR and S3Diff improved in plug-and-play fashion, with no fine-tuning of the backbone. Experiments under degradation regimes backed the design.
arxiv-2510-00828:
Hsu and a large collaboration analyse how the ATLAS experiment's workload and data systems interact, in this paper for the SC Workshops 2025. ATLAS at CERN moves enormous datasets around a global computing grid. Its PanDA system schedules jobs, while Rucio manages the data itself, and each was optimized on its own terms. Running them together creates hidden inefficiencies, from idle resources to transfers nobody needed.

The team built a metadata-matching algorithm that links individual PanDA jobs to Rucio datasets at file level. That fine-grained view exposed transfer activity badly imbalanced across sites and times. Some anomalous jobs spent over three quarters of their runtime on transfers and correlated strongly with failures. The authors propose tighter coordination, shared performance awareness, and automated anomaly detection between the two systems.
arxiv-2510-01128:
Virally and four co-authors bound how many independent channels a photonic device can support, in this 2025 arXiv paper on optics theory. Engineers want optical systems to carry more distinguishable signals, and the singular values of the electromagnetic Green function count exactly those usable channels. Before this work, predicting how the channel strengths fall off for an arbitrarily shaped device was hard. The authors build a general method that bounds each ordered singular value directly.

Applied to three-dimensional volumes up to sixty-four cubic wavelengths, their indexed bounds stay quantitatively predictive rather than merely asymptotic. They work the results through application classes such as waveguides, metasurfaces, and planewave detection. The bounds feed straight into information-theoretic quantities like Shannon capacity and Fisher information. Designers can now check, before optimizing any structure, whether a hoped-for number of strong channels is physically possible at all.
arxiv-2510-01328:
Aarts and co-authors teach generative diffusion models to describe the mysterious distributions that complex Langevin dynamics samples. Some quantum theories carry complex weights that break ordinary simulation, a famous sign problem. Complex Langevin sidesteps it by wandering into complexified space, but nobody knows its sampled distribution directly.

Score-based and energy-based diffusion models learn that distribution from the process's own output. The comparison shows what each learner captures and misses. Success would let researchers audit a powerful but opaque simulation method. Dense-matter physics, where the sign problem bites hardest, motivates the whole exercise. Quark matter at high density is the flagship sign-problem victim. Learning a sampled distribution differs from sampling it directly. Score learners track gradients while energy learners track the density itself. Error budgets separate statistical noise from systematic drift. Trust in opaque simulators is the prize.
arxiv-2510-01428:
Tsou and co-authors weld specialized biomedical models onto a language model so one system can reason across genes, molecules, and proteins. Foundation models for each data type live in separate embedding spaces that cannot talk. Their framework, BioVERSE, repairs the isolation with light projection layers.

Each modality first aligns independently into the language model's shared space. Instruction tuning on mixed data then teaches joint reasoning across the aligned channels. Compact configurations beat larger language-model baselines on annotation and function tasks. The system also explains its labels in words, a generative edge pure encoders lack. Cell-type annotation, molecule description, and protein function headline the task list. Zero-shot annotation works because the spaces finally agree. Projection layers stay lightweight by design, not by accident. Interactive dialogue with the data becomes possible afterward. Silos were the real bottleneck all along.
arxiv-2510-01628:
Schürmann proves a Heisenberg-style uncertainty floor for quantum states trapped inside a ball on a slice of curved spacetime, using only the slice's own geometry. Textbook uncertainty assumes flat space and fixed coordinates, neither of which general relativity guarantees. His bound controls momentum spread through the first eigenvalue of the slice's Laplacian.

Nothing about lapse, shift, or extrinsic curvature enters the estimate. On weakly mean-convex balls a universal product bound holds with the familiar constant. A vector-field argument then sharpens the floor by a factor of pi. Curvature-sensitive refinements sit above the universal baseline as a second tier. Spectral geometry supplies the eigenvalue that does the controlling. Strict localization inside geodesic balls defines the state class. Measurement-theoretic formulations are the announced extension path. Anisotropic comparisons could tailor bounds to symmetric slices. Sharper constants demand curvature information, honestly stated.
arxiv-2510-01728:
Kowalski and Shan prove decay estimates for a classic wave equation in this 2025 mathematics paper. The equation is the generalized Korteweg-de Vries model, used for shallow water waves and related systems. Solutions spread out and shrink over time, a behavior called dispersive decay. The authors ask how weak the assumptions on the starting wave can be while decay still holds.

For the mass-critical case, they show the peak size of the solution falls off like the inverse cube root of time. That rate matches the simpler linear Airy model. Their proof needs only mild smoothness conditions on the initial data. Two new tools make the argument work. One shows that negative regularity persists as the solution evolves. The other extends Lorentz-Strichartz estimates to mixed norms. For stronger nonlinearities, their result needs no assumptions beyond the natural critical space.
arxiv-2510-02028:
Resino and four co-authors compress LiDAR scans with a lean autoencoder in this 2025 paper. Self-driving cars read their surroundings as dense three-dimensional point clouds. Those clouds are heavy to store and transmit, so a compact latent code is valuable. Heavyweight autoencoders defeat the purpose on vehicle hardware.

Their network, LiLa-Net, was trained on real traffic data from a semi-autonomous vehicle with a Velodyne sensor. The design trims encoder layers and simplifies the skip connections that carry detail past the bottleneck. Balancing skip information against the latent code proved key to reconstruction quality. The model scored well on Chamfer distance, Earth mover's distance, and accuracy metrics. It also generalized to objects unlike anything in the traffic training scenes. Diverse datasets and point cloud formats confirmed the approach's reliability. The result is a lightweight codec that keeps the detail drivers of later perception stages need.
arxiv-2510-02228:
Beck, Schweighofer, Böck, Lehner, and Hochreiter map the scaling laws of an LSTM revival in this 2025 machine learning paper. The xLSTM architecture promises transformer-level quality with cost growing only linearly in context length. Whether it scales predictably was unknown. The team trained models from eighty million to seven billion parameters on up to two trillion tokens.

Both IsoFLOP profiles and parametric fits chart compute-optimal and over-training regimes. For a fixed training budget, compute-optimal xLSTM models turn out larger than compute-optimal transformers. At inference, xLSTMs run faster than same-sized transformers. Their performance edge widens with context length, where transformer costs grow quadratically. The study also tracks how optimal model size shifts with context length. Designers can now budget xLSTM deployments with the same confidence as transformer ones. Linear-time sequence modeling graduates from curiosity to a plannable alternative.
arxiv-2510-02428:
Lin, Gharibyan, and Su train quantum circuits on classical computers at utility scale. Their 2025 physics paper uses a method called Pauli Path simulation. Preparing ground states is a core task for quantum machines. Exact classical simulation collapses beyond a few dozen qubits. Their method optimizes circuit parameters without a quantum device. Test systems included Ising models in one and two dimensions. A Kitaev honeycomb model joined the test set. System sizes passed one hundred qubits in these runs. Results matched exact energies and trusted tensor methods closely.

The team also checked physical fingerprints of the states. Magnetization and topological entanglement entropy both looked right. They then ran trained circuits on real quantum hardware. A forty eight qubit honeycomb state ran on a Quantinuum machine. Its energy error landed near five percent. Classical pretraining can hand quantum hardware a head start.
arxiv-2510-02528:
Fu and co-authors locate the attention heads that carry spatial relations inside a vision-language model. Their 2025 paper studies OpenFlamingo, a multimodal model. Such models learn tasks from a few shown examples. How they carry a relation like left-of stays hidden. The team runs causal mediation tests on model internals. A small subset of heads proves responsible for relations. Their activations form what the authors call function vectors. Injecting those vectors improves zero-shot relational answers. Fine-tuning only the vectors, with the model frozen, does even better.

Combined vectors solved analogies with untrained relations. Two relation vectors can add into a working third. Synthetic and real image sets both supported the claims. The fine-tuned vectors beat in-context learning baselines clearly. Models may store skills as portable activation packets. Finding those packets opens models to direct editing. Interpretability gains a concrete handle here.
arxiv-2510-02628:
Xu, Ferreira, and Tegge compare ways to choose which variables belong in a regression model. Their 2025 statistics paper benchmarks selection criteria against search strategies. Scientists select variables to expose underlying mechanisms. Each method pairs a scoring criterion with a search routine. The study crosses two criteria with four search styles. LASSO variants join the comparison as well. Simulations swept sample sizes, effect sizes, and correlations. Model spaces ranged from small to fairly large. Scores tracked correct identification, recall, and false discoveries.

Two combinations stood clearly above the rest. Exhaustive search with BIC and stochastic search with BIC won. Genetic and LASSO paths with BIC neared perfect identification under kind conditions. Harsh correlations hurt the LASSO path most. Thousands of samples were needed for small effects. Applied researchers get a concrete pecking order. Search effort pays when the criterion is BIC.
arxiv-2510-02728:
Zhang and the Xiaomi EV-AD VLA team match text descriptions to aerial images for drone navigation. Their 2025 technical report covers a RoboSense challenge entry. Drones must find places described in plain language. Databases mix drone, satellite, and ground camera views. Baseline retrievers miss fine grained semantic matches. The team's system works in two stages. A fast baseline first filters candidates coarsely. A vision language model then writes rich captions for images. Reranking compares the query against those captions. Language becomes the bridge between views.

Recall improved by roughly five to eight percent over the baseline. The gains held across every recall metric. The team placed second among eight challenge entries. Captions make cross-view matching auditable by humans. Spatially complex scenes benefit most from the refinement. Real rescue and inspection flights need this reliability. Explicit language intermediates beat raw embedding similarity here.
arxiv-2510-03128:
Davis and Dumitrescu classify a loosened form of two-dimensional field theory. Classic two-dimensional TQFTs match up with Frobenius algebras. Those algebras must stay finite in size, a real limit. Nearly Frobenius structures relax that rule for endless spaces. Their matching theories are called Almost TQFTs. A prior work proved the two sides mirror each other. This paper reframes the whole theory in geometric terms.

Colored ribbon graphs supply the new language. Their edge contraction and construction rules encode the theory's moves. The authors prove those graph rules match the functorial axioms exactly. A classification of Almost TQFTs in dimension two follows. Cobordisms split into pants pieces in a normal form. That form makes the graph translation plain to see. The bridge links algebra with enumerative geometry and topological recursion. Quantization can then be read as a rebuilding process.
arxiv-2510-03228:
Fares and Ribas build a texture recognizer around random embeddings pinned to a sphere. Randomized networks have long excelled at texture description. Past gains came mostly from better cross-information prediction tricks. Their MIXER redesigns the randomized architecture itself. Image patches are encoded by random projections first. The codes are forced onto a unit hypersphere's surface. Direction, not magnitude, carries the texture signal that way.

Two learning branches then decode from those codes. The Direct branch rebuilds each patch from its own code. The Mixed branch rebuilds one channel using all channels jointly. Each branch trains under its own optimization objective. The learned decoder weights become the texture descriptor. Several pure texture benchmarks tested the approach. Each benchmark stresses different traits like scale or lighting. MIXER took the highest average accuracy across them. Robustness and efficiency arrived together in the design. The authors flag richer patch constructions as future work.
arxiv-2510-03328:
Jothiraj, Karunanidhi, and Eichmeyer present a 2025 arXiv paper on grouping chip wafer defects without hand labels. Wafer maps show defect patterns that hint at factory faults, but the maps are messy and often carry several defects at once. Their system, DECOR, groups similar maps into clusters that stay stable when a pattern is rotated. Rotation should not change what a defect means, yet many tools treat turned patterns as new cases.

DECOR joins a rotation proof feature extractor with a flexible clustering method and an outlier flag. It needs no manual tuning of cluster counts before it runs. On the public MixedWM38 data set, it beat existing clustering baselines. It also kept its overhead low, which suits busy inspection lines. Steady clusters help engineers spot recurring faults early and protect chip yield. The authors next want scores that honor maps carrying more than one defect label.
arxiv-2510-03428:
Garg, Das, and Reno present a 2025 arXiv paper that calculates the rain of charged particles in the atmosphere for balloon borne detectors. Cosmic rays smash into air and spawn showers of secondary particles. Pions, kaons, and muons from those showers can fake or hide the signals that balloon telescopes hunt. The team solves cascade equations to find how many such particles reach a height. Their focus sits above ten gigaelectronvolts, where Earth's magnetic field bends paths only slightly.

The results give particle flows by both energy and arrival angle. Balloon missions such as EUSO-SPB2 can use the numbers to design triggers and vetoes that reject background. Better background maps also sharpen claims when a detector reports a cosmic ray or neutrino event. Ground and satellite telescopes face that background, so the tables serve them too. The work turns a sky background into numbers that instrument teams can plan around.
arxiv-2510-03528:
Alajrami, Tan, and Aletras present a 2025 arXiv paper asking whether training on messy instructions makes language models tougher. Users phrase requests with typos, dropped words, and shuffled order every day. Models tuned only on clean instructions can wobble when wording shifts slightly. The team fine tuned models on instructions with words removed or shuffled. They then tested the models on clean and noisy versions of standard benchmarks in knowledge, reasoning, and math.

In some cases, the noise trained models did better downstream, not just on noisy tests. The result surprised the authors, who also tracked how training changed model behavior over time. Clean only training, they argue, leaves a brittle spot that real users hit constantly. Adding a pinch of disorder to training data may act like a vaccine against real world phrasing. Dataset builders now have evidence that perfect polish is not always the best teacher.
arxiv-2510-03928:
Gorelik, Hinich, and Serganova wrote this 2025 arXiv paper in algebra, on centers of Lie superalgebras. The center of an algebra commutes with everything and controls much of its behavior. For ordinary semisimple Lie algebras, the center is described by functions unchanged under a finite symmetry group. Superalgebras, mixing commuting and anticommuting parts, lack such a tidy picture.

The authors introduce Lagrangian equivalence relations to replace the missing group action. These relations generalize what an orthogonal subgroup does to a space. With them, the invariant functions forming the center can be defined in the super case too. Using this machinery, they give a fresh proof of Ian Musson's result on superalgebra centers. Their proof treats all cases uniformly instead of checking each family separately. Uniform proofs are prized because case-by-case arguments are long and error-prone, so the paper tidies a foundational corner of the field.
arxiv-2510-04028:
Yao and colleagues at Renmin University present this 2025 arXiv paper trying to settle a live debate about reinforcement learning for reasoning. Training with verifiable rewards clearly makes language models better at math, but researchers disagree on what it does to their capability boundary. One camp says it only sharpens sampling of known skills while shrinking diversity. The other points to new reasoning strategies emerging after long training, suggesting real expansion.

The authors argue both camps are right, at different times. Early training is an exploitation stage, where probability mass shifts toward already-rewarded answers and away from poor ones. Later, once the favored answers saturate, an exploration stage begins and rare good tokens can gain ground. Over-exploiting the first stage can shrink the boundary, while training into the second can expand it. The team supports this two-stage view with theory and experiments.
arxiv-2510-04128:
Troitskii and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on the internal signals that make a reasoning model pause and reconsider. Reasoning models often emit the token "wait" before backtracking or double-checking, a hallmark of their self-correction. Why the model decides to do this was unclear. The authors ask whether internal states just before "wait" already encode which reasoning pattern will follow.

They trained sparse crosscoders comparing DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B with its base model across layers. A new latent attribution technique then located features that raise or lower the probability of "wait". Causal interventions showed many of them genuinely steer the reasoning process. Different features promoted restarting from scratch, recalling knowledge, expressing uncertainty, or double-checking. The findings turn a surface token into a window on the model's control machinery. Understanding these levers could eventually let developers encourage careful reasoning and discourage rambling.
arxiv-2510-04328:
Sun, Calzetti, and Battisti present this 2025 arXiv paper asking whether spiral arms trigger star formation or merely gather the material for it. Arms could compress gas and raise the efficiency of star birth, or they could simply collect gas and stars without changing efficiency. Earlier studies disagreed, partly because star formation tracers carry their own biases. The authors apply multi-wavelength spectral energy distribution fitting to individual arm and interarm regions in six diverse galaxies.

They first show specific star formation rate works as a proxy for true efficiency in these regions, since the two track each other directly. Comparing both measures, arm and interarm regions showed no significant efficiency difference in five galaxies. The exception was NGC 1097. Arms held more gas and formed more stars, but no more efficiently per unit gas. The evidence favors arms as gatherers rather than triggers.
arxiv-2510-04428:
Yuanhao Zou and five coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on answering questions about videos with AI. A video holds far too many frames for a vision language model to read. Picking the frames is thus the key step, and cheap similarity tools often pick poorly. Heavy tools that use the big model itself are accurate but slow and costly. The team built AIR, a frame picker that needs no training.

AIR starts with a spread of sample frames across the video. A strong vision model then studies a small batch of the most promising frames. The loop repeats, and each round focuses the search on better time ranges. Tests on several video question benchmarks beat older frame selection methods. The method also lifted the scores of the base vision model by a clear margin. It did so at far lower cost than rival methods that lean on the model.
arxiv-2510-04728:
Mehrasa Ahmadipour and Aurélien Garivier wrote this 2025 paper on picking the best option when risk matters more than average payoff. In bandit problems, a learner tests options in turn and must name the best with confidence. Finance and safety settings punish disasters, so the best average option may be the wrong choice. The authors judge options by Entropic Value at Risk, a measure that weighs bad tails. Their setting allows reward patterns within bounds.

They propose an algorithm in the track and stop line, which samples options in optimal proportions. They derive a lower bound on how many samples a correct method needs. The algorithm meets that bound as confidence grows, so it is asymptotically optimal. Pieces require solving optimization problems, one convex and one non convex. The result is an optimal method for best arm identification under this risk measure. It gives fields a way to test options.
arxiv-2510-05028:
Bruno Cavalar and four co-authors connect two deep questions in this 2025 arXiv paper. One question is whether samples really come from a claimed probability distribution. Checking that can demand an impossible number of samples for large distributions. The other question is what cryptography makes possible or impossible.

The authors restrict attention to distributions that efficient programs can sample. In that world, they show verification power tracks cryptographic assumptions closely. If one-way functions exist, some random distributions cannot be verified efficiently at all. If they do not exist, every such classical distribution becomes verifiable. A quantum part of the work links similar assumptions to proving quantum advantage from sampling.
arxiv-2510-05128:
Si-Ioi Ng and four co-authors automate a clinical test for cognitive decline in this 2025 arXiv paper. Patients describe the famous Cookie Theft picture aloud. Clinicians score which picture elements they mention and in what order. That spatio-semantic path reveals how the mind scans a scene. Manual tagging of these elements is slow and laborious.

The team fine-tuned a BERT model to detect and order the content units automatically. A ranking loss helped the model learn the sequence, not just the items. Cross-validation reached 93 percent median precision and 96 percent median recall. Sequence errors stayed near 24 percent. The extracted features matched human annotations closely and separated healthy from impaired speakers about as well. The code and models are open-sourced for clinical use.
arxiv-2510-05228:
Haining Pan and twenty co-authors build a research-level exam for AI in condensed matter theory in this 2025 arXiv paper. The benchmark holds 50 original problems written and verified by expert researchers worldwide. Topics span Hartree-Fock theory, exact diagonalization, quantum Monte Carlo, and renormalization group methods. Machine grading checks answers symbolically, including non-commuting operator algebra.

Seventeen frontier models attempted the set. The best, GPT-5, solved only 30 percent of the problems. Average accuracy across models was about 11 percent, with wide spread. Eighteen problems defeated every single model. Experts deliberately crafted harder variants by probing the models' common failure modes. The results expose a wide gap between fluent coding ability and genuine physical reasoning.
arxiv-2510-05428:
Vasily Tolstikov and three co-authors design concentrated liquidity for multi-asset stablecoin pools in this 2025 arXiv paper. Automated market makers let liquidity providers concentrate funds inside chosen price ranges. The authors extend an n-dimensional design for stablecoins. Ticks mark the discrete ranges where liquidity can sit. Their implementation uses polar coordinates and the Rust programming language.

The paper explains the Orbswap invariant and builds swap functions in polar tick coordinates. Symmetric ticks limit providers, so the authors add a mechanism that skews liquidity deliberately. Multi-modal liquidity fingerprints describe how that liquidity is distributed. Pooling many stablecoins together concentrates risk, the authors warn. They outline hedging paths to mitigate that fragility while keeping the concentrated design.
arxiv-2510-05528:
Liu and colleagues shrink large language models without wrecking their quality. Pruning removes weights, and a pattern called 2:4 sparsity fits modern hardware well. In that pattern, half the weights in each small group must vanish. Existing methods pay for the speedup with a steep drop in accuracy.

Their method, ARMOR, splits each weight matrix into a sparse core and two wrapper matrices. The wrappers act as cheap error correctors on both sides of the core. A step-by-step algorithm chooses all three parts to cut a layer-wise error measure. Theory guarantees that the search settles at an error no worse than rival methods. The factorization happens in one pass, with no retraining of the model. Memory savings from the sparse form also remain largely intact. On Llama and Qwen models, ARMOR beat top pruning rivals across tasks while keeping the speed gains.
arxiv-2510-05628:
Guardo and colleagues ask how ideals of points on a product space can split. Splitting writes an ideal as a sum of two ideals built from its generators. For point sets in the product of two projective lines, natural splittings might use two point ideals. Their 2025 note shows that hope always fails.

For any finite point set, the generators cannot partition into two point ideals. At best, one side of the splitting is an ideal of points. The authors widen the stage to unions of lines plus ACM point sets. ACM means arithmetically Cohen-Macaulay, a homologically tame class of point sets. On that larger class, splittings exist with both sides staying in class. They also trace consequences for Betti numbers of the ideal. Negative results redirect the search toward workable classes. The work extends the Betti splitting tradition of Eliahou and Kervaire.
arxiv-2510-05828:
Marinoni and colleagues add spatial awareness to video-generated audio. Prior video-to-audio systems chase semantic match and temporal synchronization. Their output is usually mono, ignoring where sounds sit in the scene. Their 2025 StereoSync model generates stereo audio aligned with the visual layout.

Depth maps and bounding boxes supply the spatial cues. Those cues condition a diffusion audio model through cross-attention. Pretrained foundation models keep training light while preserving synthesis quality. The generated stereo adapts dynamically to scene structure and movement. Evaluation uses a curated game-footage dataset called Walking The Maps. A purpose-built spatial alignment metric confirms the audio matches the visuals spatially. Mono output feels disconnected from the space the viewer sees. Immersive cinema and game sound design are the target applications. Temporal and spatial alignment together advance the state of the art.
arxiv-2510-05928:
Souček and colleagues dissect what stabilizes high-entropy nitride coatings at extreme temperatures. The Cr-Hf-Mo-Ta-W-N system mixes five metals into one cubic nitride. Entropy is often credited for such materials' stability by default. Their 2025 study combines ab initio calculations with sputtering experiments.

Calculations show nitrogen vacancies stabilize the cubic phase substantially. Hafnium and tantalum stabilize strongly through their nitrogen affinity. Tungsten destabilizes the lattice most, while molybdenum stays nearly neutral. High-temperature deposition yields denser coatings with higher hardness and modulus. Most such coatings survive heating to twelve hundred degrees. Nitrogen loss beyond roughly ten percent at one thousand degrees proves fatal. Tungsten segregates and hafnium oxidizes during high-temperature oxidation tests. As-deposited properties are governed mainly by microstructure, the authors find. Tantalum content, not entropy itself, is critical for the best stability.
arxiv-2510-06028:
Maurer, Mirzaei, and Pontil study when trained models still work on new data, in a 2025 learning theory paper. Modern models can memorize even random labels, so a tiny training error alone proves little. The authors analyze the Gibbs algorithm, which favors hypotheses with low training error, and its practical relative, Langevin Monte Carlo.

They prove data-dependent bounds on test error that stay valid in the interpolation regime, where models fit training data almost perfectly. The bounds also survive when the ideal Gibbs sampling is replaced by the approximate Langevin method. Experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 confirm the theory in practice. The bounds stay informative for correctly labeled data and correctly cap the test error for random labels. Their analysis shows that success in the strict low-temperature setting is already signaled by training errors in the milder high-temperature setting.
arxiv-2510-06128:
Al Kautsar and Koto of MBZUAI rebuild multilingual tokenizers so translations share an identity in a 2025 language technology paper. Standard tokenizers give equivalent words in different languages distinct vocabulary entries and distinct embeddings. A model then cannot reuse what it learns in one language when it meets the translation elsewhere.

Their parallel tokenizers are first trained apart for each language. Bilingual dictionaries then align the vocabularies fully, so equivalent words receive the same index. The alignment creates a shared semantic space and also balances how many tokens each language needs per sentence. They pretrained a transformer encoder from scratch on thirteen low-resource languages. Models with parallel tokenizers beat conventional multilingual baselines on sentiment analysis, hate speech detection, emotion classification, and sentence similarity. Winning all four tasks argues that vocabulary design is a first-order choice for low-resource language technology.
arxiv-2510-06228:
Han and five co-authors present Quorus, a federated learning system for unequal quantum clients. Quantum machine learning data often sits split across private clients, forcing distributed training. Clients' machines differ in error rates and run circuits of different depths, breaking standard federated training.

Quorus uses a layerwise loss that trains models of varying depth effectively. Each client picks the depth its hardware can run with high fidelity. The system offers designs tuned for shot budget, qubit count, mid-circuit measurement, or optimization space. Simulations and real-hardware runs showed stronger gradients for deeper clients. Testing accuracy rose about twelve percent on average over the state of the art. Heterogeneity is the normal condition of today's quantum cloud. A scheme embracing varied hardware lets weaker machines contribute instead of being excluded.
arxiv-2510-06428:
Erkul proposes that black holes are soliton-like objects held up by quantum vacuum effects in a 2025 general relativity paper. In the model, gravitational collapse is balanced by quantum vacuum dispersion. The gravity theory adds a squared-curvature term to Einstein's theory. Classical singularities disappear from the picture entirely.

Oscillating cores of finite radius replace the singular center. Their motion evades the static no-go theorems that block ordinary regular black holes. The event horizon gives way to a surface of maximum redshift, which Erkul names the Lamarina. Its surface geometry produces Hawking-like radiation, but with calculable corrections. The Raychaudhuri equations cap the radiated power at a Dyson-type ceiling set by fundamental constants. Effective field theory matching fixes a universal minimum Lamarina radius from the dispersion scale. The architecture offers a concrete, singularity-free alternative for what sits inside a black hole.
arxiv-2510-06528:
Yao, Chen, Dubnov, and Berg-Kirkpatrick recognize chords in symbolic music by imitating how trained humans listen in a 2025 music informatics paper. Automatic chord recognition has focused on audio, while symbolic scores suffer scarce labeled data. Human analysts work in stages: boundaries first, then each chord piece by piece.

The authors contribute an enhanced dataset and a new model. POP909-CL adds tempo alignment and human-corrected chord, beat, key, and time-signature labels. BACHI decomposes recognition into boundary detection plus iterative ranking. It ranks chord root, quality, and bass through masked iterative decoding. That staged mechanism mirrors ear-training practice. Experiments place BACHI at state-of-the-art accuracy on classical and pop benchmarks. Ablations validate each module's contribution. Chord labels mean little without accurate boundaries between successive chords. Symbolic chord analysis gains better data and a model music teachers would recognize.
arxiv-2510-06728:
Cile van Marken and Roxana Petcu check whether a claimed discovery about search models really holds up. Their 2025 paper, presented at a SIGIR Asia-Pacific conference, reproduces a 2024 study by Chen and colleagues. That study used activation patching to trace how neural rankers count query terms. Ranking models decide which documents answer a search query.

The original work linked term-frequency behavior to four specific attention heads. Van Marken and Petcu improved the baseline used in the patching experiments. With the better baseline, the effect narrowed to three attention heads instead. They also extended the test from the first term-frequency axiom to a second, broader one. Ranking scores did not follow that second axiom consistently. Their main lesson concerns the diagnostic data itself. Results shifted strongly with how the test sets were designed. Reproduction work like this keeps interpretability claims honest.
arxiv-2510-06828:
Michael Keiblinger argues that AI architectures forget how to handle long tasks. His 2025 paper challenges the claim that attention makes recurrence unnecessary. Recurrence means processing inputs step by step while carrying a state. Parallel designs process everything at once, which scales. Keiblinger points to proofs that such designs cannot express problem classes.

Those missing classes matter for agents, such as software engineering assistants. He conjectures a critical time beyond which non-recurrent models start aggregating inputs wrongly. His proposed architecture is recurrence-complete, designed to avoid that failure. He trains it on action sequences drawn from GitHub activity. Training loss falls as a power law when longer sequences are used, at fixed model size. Longer training also pays for its wall-clock time through lower loss. Experiments show parallel models hitting accuracy cliffs as task depth grows. A single-layer recurrent baseline generalizes farther in the same tests.
arxiv-2510-07128:
Laplante introduces jmstate, a free Python package for health data that changes over time. The 2025 paper deals with patients who move through stages of illness or care. Older tools often track only one kind of event at a time. Real patients may improve, worsen, relapse, or die along tangled paths. The package models those full paths together with repeated health measures.

The method links a growth model for a health marker to a map of stage changes. The map can follow any pattern of linked stages. It also allows the chance of a change to depend on how long a patient has waited. Fast training methods keep the fits practical on large data. Tests on a French aging study tracked how thinking skills and daily function decline together. Doctors could use such forecasts to judge a single patient's likely path.
arxiv-2510-07228:
Ray, Banagiri, Thrane, and Lasky question whether a record black hole merger really involved near-maximal spins. Their 2025 paper studies GW231123, a gravitational-wave event with unusual properties. Early fits suggested both black holes spun close to the physical limit. The authors suspect tiny detector glitches instead. They call these brief noise hiccups microglitches, and they search the data around the event for them.

The team found a real population of such hiccups in both LIGO detectors. In simulated mergers, similar glitches pushed measured spins toward the maximum even when true spins were moderate. The bias could leave almost no support for the correct value. A new noise model that accounts for microglitches largely removed the bias. The work urges caution before drawing bold conclusions from short, loud events. Detector housekeeping can masquerade as exotic astrophysics.
arxiv-2510-07328:
Zubair and co-authors present MultiFair, a training scheme that keeps multimodal medical models both balanced and fair. Their 2025 paper names two linked problems. Data types like images and text learn at uneven speeds, so models lean on one source. Models also learn unevenly across demographic groups, producing unfair accuracy gaps. Worse, each data type may favor a different group, tangling the two biases. MultiFair adjusts training gradients at both levels, tuning their direction and size as learning proceeds.

A unified loss mixes task accuracy, gradient alignment, and fairness gap reduction. Experiments used two real multimodal medical data sets with distinct demographic groups. MultiFair beat leading multimodal, fairness-aware, and balanced-learning rivals on accuracy-style measures. Its fairness scores stayed competitive at the same time. Fairer models matter because a biased aid can widen health gaps.
arxiv-2510-07428:
Nicholson and Bae show that disk winds can smuggle pebbles past a giant planet's barrier. Their 2025 paper simulates young planetary systems. A growing giant planet carves a gap in its disk, and the pressure bump at the gap's outer edge normally traps drifting dust. That filtering starves the inner disk of building material. But many disks lose gas through magnetically driven winds rather than viscosity. The team ran two-dimensional multi-fluid simulations with a parameterized wind to test filtration under that regime. Wind-driven inward gas flow changes the contest at the bump.

With wind, dust can ride the gas over the barrier and cross the gap. The largest grain that makes it grows with wind strength. Under a strong wind, millimeter grains penetrated a gap opened by a planet several times Jupiter's mass.
arxiv-2510-07628:
Fallas Padilla and four coauthors wrote this 2025 quantum physics paper on open quantum systems. Such systems leak energy and information to their surroundings. That loss usually destroys entanglement, the delicate link between quantum particles. Yet carefully shaped loss can instead push a system toward an entangled resting state. The hard part is predicting which resting state a given starting state will reach.

The authors derive formulas that predict the final state without simulating the full motion. Their results show that the starting state's overlap with special steady states fixes the outcome. They identify a class of systems where only that overlap matters. As a use case, they propose schemes using shared decay in spin groups. Those schemes produce entangled steady states that could sharpen quantum measurements beyond classical limits. The formulas also save heavy computation on large systems.
arxiv-2510-07728:
Liu, Cui, Liang, and Ye wrote this 2025 paper on detecting stolen data behind AI chatbots. Retrieval-augmented systems answer questions by pulling from outside collections. That power also lets others appropriate someone's data at large scale. The victim needs a way to prove misuse after the text has been rewritten. The authors build both a test dataset and a detection method for this problem.

Their dataset, RPD, simulates retrieval-based plagiarism across fields and writing styles. Their protection embeds watermarks at two levels, meaning and wording, in sequence. The marks survive rewriting by a language model. A probing framework then questions a suspect system and tests the gathered evidence. In their experiments, the double watermark held up under attacks that broke single methods. Detection stayed accurate even when individual signals weakened. The work offers data owners a foundation for defending content in the retrieval era.
arxiv-2510-07928:
Balkenhol, Coerver, Reichardt, and Zebrowski wrote this 2025 cosmology paper on cosmic birefringence, a possible rotation of light's polarization as it crosses the universe. Such a rotation would signal parity-violating new physics. The team works with B-mode polarization data from the South Pole Telescope. Foreground glow from our own galaxy contaminates that faint signal. They build cleaned, foreground-marginalized likelihoods for two telescope datasets using a compression framework.

With those likelihoods, they bound the amplitude of a scale-invariant birefringence spectrum. The new telescope data alone gives the tightest limit yet from B-mode power spectra. Adding a lensing prior from other analyses tightens the bound by about half again. No rotation signal appears in the data. The authors release the likelihoods publicly for reuse. Coming data from the same telescope and others should push the sensitivity further, testing whether the universe treats left and right differently.
arxiv-2510-08128:
Esson, Kastis, and Schulze wrote this 2025 mathematics paper characterizing when symmetric bar-joint frameworks stay rigid in non-Euclidean planes. Frameworks of stiff bars and rotating joints model structures from buildings to crystals. Forced-symmetric rigidity asks whether a framework resists every deformation preserving its symmetry. Changing the distance rule changes the answer. The authors work in planes with general power norms, excluding the Euclidean case, and in the two extreme norm planes.

For the power-norm planes they characterize periodic rigidity and finite reflection-symmetric rigidity completely. They also characterize rigidity under a wallpaper group combining translations with reflection. For the extreme norms they settle periodic rigidity and the same group case. Every characterization comes with an inductive construction using Henneberg-type graph operations. Such tests let engineers certify a symmetric structure from its graph alone, without simulating forces.
arxiv-2510-08228:
Quentin Renau, Amjad Ullah, and Emma Hart describe a 2025 arXiv study on picking computing resources across cloud and edge sites. Modern apps run on a mix of big data centers and small local nodes. A central boss for all choices can slow down and break this mix. Their plan lets each part decide locally, in a self-organising way that adapts as conditions change.

The method borrows a consensus scheme where agents bid for tasks using local knowledge only. No central controller is needed, and agents work together to settle who takes each task. The authors found that computing time is the key factor that shapes the choices made. Their system matched the quality of a full exhaustive search, which checks every option. It also ran far faster than central heuristics, which took up to thirty times longer at large scale.
arxiv-2510-08428:
Rafael Dutra, Felipe Pinheiro, and Diney Ether Jr. predict a chirality signal in scattered light without any absorption, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Circular dichroism normally measures how chiral materials absorb left and right circular light differently. Chiral objects twist light because their shape lacks mirror symmetry. The team studies a single dielectric microsphere with chiral structure, illuminated by linearly polarized light.

They analyze the polarization of light scattered from this lossless, isotropic sphere. The scattered light becomes nearly circularly polarized across a broad range of visible frequencies. The effect shows up in large values of the Stokes parameter that tracks circular polarization. It appears only in the Mie regime, where the sphere's radius rivals the wavelength. Collection through a high-numerical-aperture lens, including wide-angle components, is also required. The authors suggest uses in selecting and characterizing single chiral microparticles.
arxiv-2510-08528:
Thi Ha Kyaw, Guillermo Romero, and Gaurav Saxena fast-forward adiabatic quantum computing by jumping along geodesics in a 2025 arXiv paper. Adiabatic computing needs slow evolution: total time grows as the inverse square of the smallest energy gap. Shortcuts exist, but they demand extra Hamiltonians that experiments struggle to implement. The authors explore a path-based alternative needing no extra terms.

Geodesics are the shortest paths in the quantum state's geometry, and traversing them can fast-forward adiabatic motion. They find jumping along geodesics strongly suppresses excitations in many-body systems. For the spin one-half XY chain, they prove analytically and confirm numerically a striking effect. The defect density forms a rate-independent plateau, flat across driving speeds. This contrasts with the Kibble-Zurek mechanism, where defects follow a universal power law. It also differs from anti-Kibble-Zurek behavior in slow drives.
arxiv-2510-08628:
Siiri Leppälampi, Sonja Hyrynsalmi, and Erno Vanhala audit gender bias in AI-generated occupational images in a 2025 arXiv paper. Image generators are spreading into media and professional contexts, yet studies focus on image quality, not representation. The team prompted DALL-E 3 and Ideogram to produce over seven hundred fifty images of occupations. Thematic analysis then coded who appears in each professional role.

Both tools reinforced traditional gender stereotypes in their outputs, though to varying degrees. The study also examines how age and emotions are portrayed in generated workers. Such patterns risk narrowing public ideas of who belongs in which profession. The authors propose concrete suggestions for practitioners, individuals, and researchers to improve representation. Prompting choices and tool selection both matter, they argue. Mitigating harmful bias early is essential as these tools become default image sources.
arxiv-2510-08728:
Nicolas Ewen, Jairo Diaz-Rodriguez, and Kelly Ramsay regularize a network's outputs, not its weights, for few-shot transfer learning in a 2025 arXiv paper. Standard transfer learning freezes parts of a pretrained network and adds task-specific layers. That limits adaptation to domain features and can still overfit tiny data sets. Their Structured Output Regularization freezes internal structures like convolutional filters entirely.

Learning then proceeds through penalties combining group lasso and L1 terms on the outputs. This tailors the model to new data with minimal additional parameters, they argue. The framework applies to varied components, from convolutional filters to whole network blocks. Evaluation covered three few-shot medical imaging classification tasks, a data-scarce regime. Using DenseNet121 and EfficientNetB4 bases, SOR achieved competitive results against established benchmarks. The authors present it as a simple, broadly applicable transfer framework.
arxiv-2510-08828:
Lobo and co-authors study how a possible flaw in relativity could quietly undo a delicate quantum effect, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Some theories of quantum gravity predict that the usual rules of motion warp slightly at extreme scales, an idea called Lorentz invariance violation. The team asks what that warping does to gravitational cat states. Those are pairs of massive particles placed in overlapping positions so that their mutual gravity links them in an entangled state.

Building on a stochastic version of the uncertainty principle, the authors derive an equation that tracks how such a system loses its quantum coherence over time. They then measure the entanglement with a standard score and separate steady warping effects from random, fluctuating ones. The analysis maps how each kind of violation erodes the gravity-made link. Experiments chasing that link could, in turn, bound how large any violation can be.
arxiv-2510-09128:
Bodirsky and Guzmán-Pro show that a whole family of graph puzzles secretly belongs to another, better-mapped family, in this 2025 arXiv paper. A sandwich problem hands you two graphs on the same points, one with too few edges and one with too many. The question is whether edges can be chosen between the two so the finished graph lands in a target class. The authors prove many such problems are exactly constraint satisfaction problems on one infinite graph with two colors of edges.

That bridge lets constraint theory classifications settle sandwich problems wholesale. The pair also push the frontier themselves. They pin down the difficulty for several classes, including line graphs and clique-avoiding perfect graphs. One of their results closes a problem left open in 2019 about graphs avoiding two small patterns. They also build a sandwich problem sitting in an in-between complexity class.
arxiv-2510-09528:
Mohammad Hossein Sameti, Sepehr Harfi Moridani, Ali Zarean, and Hossein Sameti work on accent-robust speech recognition in a 2025 arXiv paper. Automatic speech recognition has advanced with pretrained transformer models, yet accents and dialects still push word error rates up. The problem affects both widely spoken English and lower-resource languages such as Persian.

Their framework first trains a classifier on spectrograms, the visual maps of sound, to recognise accent-specific cues. It then masks the regions that most influenced the classifier, and uses those masked spectrograms to augment the training data. For Persian, the team collected a new dataset across regional accents, the first systematic benchmark of its kind. With the Whisper model, the masking and augmentation strategy cut word error rates substantially in both English and Persian tests.
arxiv-2510-10228:
The CMS Collaboration measures heavy-flavour jet identification at the LHC in this 2025 arXiv paper in particle physics. In the highly boosted regime, a heavy particle moves so fast that its decay products merge into one wide jet. Interest in this regime is growing for Higgs studies and searches for particles beyond the standard model.

The collaboration tests tagging algorithms that identify jets from a massive particle decaying to a bottom or charm quark pair. The measurements use proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of thirteen teraelectronvolts. Knowing how well these taggers perform in boosted topologies decides which analyses can trust them. The paper reports performance where the usual separated-jet picture breaks down.
arxiv-2510-10328:
Malik, Nazanin Sabri, Melissa Karnaze, and Mai ElSherief test empathy in language models in this 2025 arXiv paper on AI and society. Models converse naturally partly because they respond with apparent empathy. But emotional experience is shaped by demographic and cultural context, so a model's empathy may not be shared out evenly.

The authors ask whether models show equitable empathy across diverse user groups. They vary multi-demographic personas, combinations of traits such as age, gender, and background, and compare the warmth and understanding of the responses. Unequal empathy would mean some users get a colder, less helpful assistant for the same feelings. The study supplies a method for auditing that risk before deployment.
arxiv-2510-10628:
Guang Zhao and ten co-authors use deep learning to sharpen particle identification in a future collider detector, in this 2025 arXiv paper. A Time Projection Chamber tracks particles precisely. It can also estimate how many primary ionization electrons each particle produced, a measurement called dN/dx that helps tell particle types apart. Reconstructing that count accurately is hard. The team's model, GraphPT, treats chamber data as point clouds.

Its backbone is a U-Net built from graph neural networks, with an attention mechanism tuned for point cloud processing. GraphPT beat the traditional truncated mean method at particle identification. In particular, the power to separate kaons from pions improved by roughly 10 to 20 percent across the momentum range from 5 to 20 GeV/c in their study. Better separation helps future experiments like the Circular Electron-Positron Collider extract cleaner physics from crowded collision events.
arxiv-2510-10928:
Cunyuan Jiang explains the anomalous vibrations of glasses and other amorphous solids through uneven elasticity, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Debye's theory predicts how many vibrational modes a solid has at each frequency, but disordered solids show an excess of low frequency modes. Jiang models the unevenness as elasticity that fluctuates in real space with a spatially correlated pattern. He computes the dynamical properties with an exact real space field theoretical approach.

His results trace the excess low frequency density of states to selective scattering: the uneven elasticity scatters short wavelengths more strongly. Maps of the local density of states reveal anomalous modes, highly excited spots, at low frequencies. Earlier perturbative approaches in wave vector space missed these spots. The findings align with recent particle level simulations and experiments, supporting simple elastic unevenness as the origin of the anomaly.
arxiv-2510-11828:
Debatri Chattopadhyay and three colleagues trace the life stories of an unusual class of binary stars. The Gaia space telescope has found wide, eccentric pairs where a neutron star orbits a still-evolving companion star. The team's 2025 arXiv paper models them with two tools: POSYDON for whole populations and MESA for detailed single-system evolution.

The researchers contrast two ways the companion can spill gas: forced circular transfer and eccentric transfer. Under optimistic assumptions, isolated evolution produces Gaia-like systems only rarely, at under about one and a half percent of comparable binaries. The absolute numbers still match what Gaia sees. Eccentric transfer comes in brief bursts up to a thousand times stronger and leaves wide, eccentric neutron star and helium white dwarf pairs with mild pulsar recycling. Circular transfer instead runs long and steady, yielding fully recycled millisecond pulsars in circular orbits.
arxiv-2510-11928:
Lorena Calvo-Bartolomé and co-authors build a consistency checker for question-answering systems that speak several languages. A good many-language system must give the same facts in every language. It should also respect genuine cultural differences on questions where answers truly vary by region. Their 2025 arXiv paper introduces MIND, a pipeline that flags both factual and cultural mismatches, with a human in the loop.

The team tested MIND on a bilingual question-answering system in maternal and infant health, where wrong or mismatched advice carries real risk. They release a dataset of bilingual questions marked for factual and cultural mismatches. Tests on datasets from other domains check whether the method generalizes beyond health. In every case, MIND reliably found the planted mismatches. The authors argue such auditing is a first step for question-answering systems that are both steady on facts across languages and honest about cultural variation.
arxiv-2510-12028:
Arthur Charpentier argues that fairness, as people feel it, is local. Standard measures check tallies across whole groups, like equal outcomes by demographic group. No one feels a whole group, though; each person weighs outcomes inside their own peer network. His 2025 arXiv paper builds a formal model of perceived fairness in networks, where a sense of discrimination grows from local match-ups and the topology of who interacts with whom.

The results carry a hard lesson. A decision rule can pass every standard fairness test while perceived discrimination persists, or even grows. The culprits are homophily, the habit of clustering with similar others, and assortative mixing, which skews what each person sees. Math and computer runs trace how network structure drives the wedge between objective and perceived fairness. Charpentier draws lessons for governing algorithms and for fields like finance and shared insurance, where trust in the rule is an outcome.
arxiv-2510-12128:
Ziqi Zhao and Vivek Sarin rebuild Gaussian process regression for the GPU age. Gaussian processes predict with honest uncertainty attached, but training costs explode with dataset size. Their 2025 arXiv paper, assembles nuGPR from classic linear algebra parts.

Preconditioned conjugate gradients speed up the core linear solves. Clustering the inputs exposes block structure in the covariance matrix, whose off-diagonal blocks then admit low-rank shortcuts, slashing time and memory. Settings are tuned with numeric gradients instead of exact derivatives, avoiding backpropagation entirely. The whole pipeline runs in parallel with CUDA on NVIDIA hardware. Against the best current GPU code, nuGPR cuts total training time by up to half and peak memory by up to twelve times, across synthetic and real-world data sets. Classical craft, carefully combined, keeps its error bars intact.
arxiv-2510-12228:
Onoo and co-authors propose a new way to define what a neural representation is, in a 2025 arXiv paper on neural coding. Sensory systems are usually described as a hierarchy that extracts ever more abstract features step by step. That causal picture struggles to explain misrepresentation, where activity means one thing yet the world holds another.

The authors define readout representation by what can be recovered from neural features, rather than by how those features were caused. They show that inputs can be reconstructed accurately even from heavily perturbed mid level features. This means one input corresponds to a broad and redundant region of feature space, which challenges the simple causal mapping view. They also introduce representation size, a measure tied to model robustness and redundancy. The framework is offered as a lens for both biological brains and artificial networks.
arxiv-2510-12728:
Lee and Kahng build an interactive system where a language model's instructions and its test set are refined together, each failure becoming a new test, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Machine learning in the past separated data work from model tuning. Prompt editing removes that barrier. Developers can govern behavior instantly by rewriting instructions, so tests and instructions can co evolve.

The hard part is encoding subtle, domain specific policies into prompts. Their structured workflow guides users to discover edge cases. Users articulate rationales for the desired behavior, and evaluate each instruction revision against the growing test set. Every discovered failure is added as a test case, so fixes cannot silently break earlier decisions. A user study shows the workflow helped participants refine instructions step by step and state ambiguous policies more clearly. The authors present data model co evolution as a route to more robust language model applications.
arxiv-2511-00428:
Kazuya Yokota, Ryosuke Harakawa, Masaaki Baba, and Masahiro Iwahashi bring physics-informed neural networks to the study of how speech is produced. These networks train directly on the equations of vocal-fold vibration and vocal-tract acoustics, promising insight into voice behavior for linguistics and medicine. Two obstacles stand out: vocal-fold collisions break smoothness, and the vibration period is unknown ahead of time.

A differentiable approximation smooths the collision problem, letting folds be analyzed inside the framework. Treating the period as a learnable parameter yields proper periodic solutions. Coupling between airflow at the glottis and tract acoustics is enforced as a hard constraint, with no extra loss terms. Forward and inverse tests confirm the method can estimate airflow, fold state, and pressure below the glottis from speech signals alone.
arxiv-2511-00728:
Hugo Massaroli and five co-authors test whether Alzheimer's diagnosis models trained on North American scans travel to Latin America. Deep models read FDG PET brain scans with high scores on the ADNI dataset, the field's standard, but ADNI cohorts skew North American. The team benchmarks convolutional and transformer models on ADNI, then evaluates them on a new clinical cohort from the FLENI Institute in Buenos Aires.

On ADNI every model scored high. On the Argentine cohort, performance dropped substantially, exposing a clear domain shift, and the architectures performed alike, undercutting claims of transformer advantage here. Ablations finger per-image normalization and correct sampling choices as key generalization factors. Attention maps on ADNI scans focus on canonical low-activity regions for Alzheimer's cases, but blur for other classes and for FLENI scans. Population-aware validation is the clear demand.
arxiv-2511-20128:
Bensaid studies a Schrödinger equation whose damping borrows from number theory. His 2025 paper analyzes a Cauchy problem on a compact manifold. The damping term involves the Riemann zeta function. That function famously encodes how primes are spread. Here it modulates how solutions lose mass over time.

The equation adds an imaginary zeta-driven term to Schrödinger dynamics. Initial data live in the H1 Sobolev space. Uniqueness is established first, in the distribution sense. A regularized version of the problem is then solved. Uniform energy estimates control the approximating solutions. Tightness arguments extract a convergent subsequence from them. The limit satisfies the original equation weakly. A companion equation gets an explicit mass estimate. Its damping uses the solution's own modulus instead. Compactness of the manifold is essential to the proof. On open Euclidean space the zeta term escapes control. Dissipative quantum models gain an exotic new example.
arxiv-2511-20628:
Tang, Hinkley, Goodenough, Krastanov, and Avis find better paths through quantum networks where longer can beat shorter. Their 2025 paper tackles routing for quantum repeater networks. End users need the path maximizing entanglement rate and quality together. That combined score breaks a key niceness property called isotonicity. Dijkstra's classic algorithm then gives wrong answers.

Exhaustive search was the previous fallback for exact routing. Two best-first search algorithms speed the hunt dramatically. One provably returns the best path every time. The heuristic sibling scales nearly sublinearly in query count. It still lands close-to-optimal paths in practice throughout tests. Simulated annealing and a genetic algorithm add tunable trade-offs. Secret-key rates improved by orders of magnitude in some cases. The test model used swap-ASAP repeaters sharing Werner states. Rate-versus-fidelity tension makes non-isotonicity generic, they argue. Any real quantum network will face the same quirk.
arxiv-2511-20928:
Gil Goldman, Raja Giryes, and Mahadev Satyanarayanan add a 2025 training trick that makes small video-recognition models much better at reading actions. Video is naturally smooth: what a network sees in one frame should resemble the next. Their method penalises abrupt jumps between the internal representations of consecutive frames, treating frame-to-frame change as a Gaussian random walk, a drift with random steps.

The penalty pushes models toward low-acceleration solutions that match how real motion unfolds. On the Kinetics-600 action benchmark, lightweight models trained this way gained 3.8 to a full 6.4 percentage points of accuracy. The MoViNets family set new state-of-the-art results within their compute budgets, improving by 3.8 to a strong 6.1 points. One model, MoViNet-A3 with the smoothing, reached 85.6 percent accuracy at just 56.4 billion operations, while its closest rival needed 18.3 times more computation. MobileNetV3 and the streaming MoViNets gained 4.9 to nearly 6.4 points at equal memory.
arxiv-2511-21028:
Chicago Y. Park and colleagues propose in 2025 a simpler way to tell a neural network how noisy its input currently is. Diffusion and flow-matching generators use one network across all noise levels, so the network must receive one number, the noise level or time step, alongside an image. Standard tricks bolt on special embedding modules, constraining the architecture. Deep parameter interpolation instead keeps two parameter sets inside one network.

During training and sampling, the network blends the two parameter sets, with the blend weight set by the scalar input through a learned curve. The architecture otherwise stays unchanged. The authors show the method improves denoising and sample quality in flow-matching and diffusion models alike, at computational cost comparable to standard conditioning. With the ADM generator under flow matching, sample quality reached an FID score of 7.96, lower meaning closer to real images, and 8.32 under diffusion sampling. Code is available.
arxiv-2511-21228:
Anthony Couthures and four coauthors study when a network of interacting agents agrees, and when it splits into camps, in a 2025 control theory paper. Each agent adjusts toward its neighbors through nonlinear rules, like people softening opinions in conversation. The team seeks the exact boundary between full consensus, where everyone lands on the same state, and stable clustering, where separate groups hold different states.

Couthures and his coauthors prove a sharp threshold: an explicit inequality tying the interaction's Lipschitz constant, its maximum steepness, to a key eigenvalue of the network graph keeps every resting state synchronized. Break the inequality, and clustered states can appear, but only when the interaction rule itself contains unstable fixed points. Using input-to-state stability theory, they show a cluster's cohesion depends on how uneven outside influence is across its members, not on its total strength. Tests on Zachary's Karate Club network confirm the theory.
arxiv-2511-21628:
Andrey Kupavskii and Georgy Sokolov completely solve a 1960s extremal problem in one regime, in 2025. Take all subsets of an n-element set, but forbid s pairwise disjoint ones: how large can the family be? Kleitman pinned down the answer for special sizes near multiples of s. The general function resisted even a conjectured formula for decades, and it shadows the famous Erdős Matching Conjecture.

Kupavskii and Sokolov settle every case where n is at most three times s. In that regime, an s-matching's sets average at most three elements. The answer turns on a delicate interplay between the missing two-element and three-element sets in an optimal family. Exactly four types of extremal families emerge in their characterization. The solution also offers the first concrete picture of the extremal function's general behavior.
arxiv-2511-21828:
Deka and colleagues explore what a proposed new experiment could discover by precisely measuring the muon's electric dipole moment with far greater precision than before. An electric dipole moment, a slight charge separation inside a particle, would signal new CP violation, the matter-antimatter asymmetry. The proposed new experiment targets a sensitivity of near 6 times ten to the minus 23 in the units used, thousands of times better than the current muon bound.

Within an effective theory summarizing new physics as extra operators, they identify which ones a muon measurement constrains best: two dipole operators and four classes of four-fermion operators. They also test three concrete models of new particles and find the experiment would probe energy scales around 10 TeV, beyond direct collider reach. For one model, Higgs decays to muon pairs offer a complementary collider check.
arxiv-2511-22128:
Vastola, Gershman, and Rajan recast dimensionality reduction as a variational problem. Workhorse methods split into camps with complementary flaws. PCA is simple and interpretable but rigidly linear; autoencoders flex to nonlinear structure but resist interpretation; graph embedding methods can badly distort the geometry they claim to preserve. The authors instead pose an optimal manifold embedding problem and study its solutions directly, asking what embeddings must look like when they extremize a principled objective.

Because the framework is variational, each solution satisfies a set of partial differential equations and provably reflects the symmetries of the embedding objective, which restores interpretability without giving up nonlinearity. In some cases solutions can be written down analytically. PCA itself falls out as an exact special case, anchoring the family. The authors discuss these guarantees for settings where a low-dimensional summary must be flexible yet understandable.
arxiv-2511-22728:
Huang, Sapkota, and Singh make power grid model reduction smarter about what to throw away. Grid dynamic models are routinely shrunk with singular perturbation, separating fast states from slow ones. Classical methods assume you know which states are fast, an assumption failing for heterogeneous modern grids full of black-box inverter and machine models from different stakeholders. The authors give a timescale-agnostic formulation of singular perturbation reduction, then propose two ways to choose fast states optimally with no prior physical knowledge.

The first approach greedily selects states to reduce, scoring each choice. The second runs nonlinear optimization allowing state transformations while searching for the optimally reduced model. Numerical studies on a test system mixing synchronous machines, inverters, and line dynamics show both approaches generalise across component types and stay accurate. The work targets system-level studies where full models are too expensive but hand-tuned reductions untrustworthy.
arxiv-2511-22828:
Behrad and colleagues make a brain comparison tool much faster. Dynamical Similarity Analysis, or DSA, compares two neural systems by their time patterns. It maps each system's motion into a shared linear space and scores how alike the patterns are there. The method is strong but slow, since users must pick a delay embedding and compute costly metrics. Such checks help researchers compare circuits, brains, and models on equal terms.

Their fastDSA keeps the old tool's accuracy while running at least ten times faster. One change picks the embedding size from the data itself, using a cut-off that keeps signal and drops noise. A second change swaps a slow exact constraint for a light search that stays near orthogonal maps. Tests show the speed gain holds across systems, with the same sensitivities as the old method.
arxiv-2512-00128:
Topological recursion is a method that builds complex quantities step by step from a starting curve. B. Eynard presents explicit expressions for its ABCD tensors in a 2025 study, covering the most classical classes of spectral curves. The study also discusses how to implement the recursion algorithmically.

Topological recursion was invented to compute large-size expansions of random matrices. It has since proved useful across mathematical physics, from enumerative geometry and string theory to integrable systems and combinatorics. Explicit tensor formulas turn an abstract machine into something researchers can actually compute with, widening its use in those fields. Spectral curves are the input data from which the recursion builds its answers. For a new reader, the value is in the worked forms. They turn a grand scheme into sums that a small team can run, test, and check by hand.
arxiv-2512-00828:
Mohd Talib and M Ahsan study rotating quantum gases in a 2025 physics paper. They look at bosons, particles that happily share states, held in a shallow, quasi-two-dimensional harmonic trap and set spinning. The bosons push each other away through a soft repulsive interaction.

As the gas spins and interacts, it forms quantized vortices, tiny whirlpools with fixed spin. Those vortices drain the main condensate and push the system toward chaos. Using exact diagonalization, the team computes the spectral form factor and power spectrum of the energy levels. Those tools reveal how order gives way to chaos as depletion grows.
arxiv-2512-01028:
Halil Mutuk studies two exotic particles reported by the LHCb experiment in a 2025 physics paper. The particles, whose names encode their quark content and mass, are tetraquark candidates built from four quarks rather than the usual two or three. Exotic states like these test how quarks bind into matter.

Mutuk uses the Born-Oppenheimer approximation, which separates fast and slow motion inside the state. Working within a dynamical diquark model, he computes the mass spectrum and root-mean-square radius values for both states. Comparing those predictions with the observed masses helps judge whether the diquark picture explains these new particles.
arxiv-2512-01228:
Haoran Li and co-authors probe a clash in deep reinforcement learning. A policy can aim for the best score. It can also aim to stay safe when foes try to trick it. For years those two aims were seen as foes as well.
