Fresh theory hints the two aims may line up more than thought. The team asks how to gain both in real training. They test ways to keep score high while attacks fail. If both aims can be met, agents for games, robots, and trade could be both sharp and hard to fool.
arxiv-2512-01728:
Zhengjia Wang and co-authors detect misinformation that works by omission. False content can be plainly fabricated. It can also mislead by leaving key facts out. The second kind fools readers while seeming complete. It has drawn far less study than plain fabrication.

Their method uses omission-aware graph inference. Facts and their links form a graph the model can reason over. Missing links that should be present raise a flag. Catching quiet omissions would help platforms and readers judge news that is true in each line but false as a whole.
arxiv-2512-01828:
Jorge E. Cardona and Ilya Pavlyukevich study a random motion whose speed depends on where the moving particle currently sits. Their 2025 paper treats a diffusion process with a power-law nonlinearity, written as a stochastic differential equation driven by Brownian motion, the standard model of random wandering.

Because the noise term grows or shrinks with position, the particle spreads in ways that plain Brownian motion does not, and standard tools can break down. The authors work out how solutions of the equation behave under this position-dependent randomness. Results of this kind matter wherever spread is uneven, from particles in varied media to models in finance.
arxiv-2512-02128:
Neutrinos get their tiny masses somehow, and the Babu-Nandi-Tavartkiladze model is one proposed mechanism, extending the Standard Model with new particles. Saiyad Ashanujjaman and Siddharth Maharathy analyze in 2025 the model's vacuum structure, the possible lowest-energy states its fields can settle into.

The extension adds a scalar quadruplet and a vector-like triplet fermion, both carrying weak charge, whose interplay generates neutrino masses. Which vacuum the model prefers decides whether that mechanism works and what it predicts. Vacuum studies are the due diligence of model building: a theory whose lowest state breaks the wrong symmetries is ruled out before any experiment runs.
arxiv-2512-02228:
Companies can now answer a task with a simple model call, an AI assistant, or a fully autonomous agent, and the most powerful option is often the wrong one. Shubhi Asthana and four co-authors present STRIDE in 2025, a systematic framework for choosing which of these AI modalities a job really needs.

Agents bring multi-step reasoning, persistent memory, and tool use, but deploying them everywhere raises cost, complexity, and risk. STRIDE weighs those trade-offs task by task. A disciplined selection framework helps organizations spend agent-level effort only where it earns its keep, a practical question as agentic systems spread through industry.
arxiv-2512-02528:
Vincent Wieland and four co-authors test methods that fit epidemic models to data when exact math fails. Stochastic compartmental models split a population into groups, such as sick and well, and capture the randomness of spread. Pandemics like COVID-19 showed how much fast, honest fitting matters for public decisions.

Simulation based inference estimates model parameters by comparing simulated outbreaks with real ones. Fitted models feed nowcasts and short term forecasts that guide health officials. The team's assessment shows which methods hold up for such models, helping future teams pick tools before the next crisis hits. The next team to face an outbreak can start from this ranked list of tools and skip the dead ends.
arxiv-2512-02728:
Sabrina D. C. Feitosa reviews how risk is managed, or mishandled, in data science projects. Such projects fail often, held back by technical limits, weak organization, and poor risk practice. Low data maturity, weak governance, and teams talking past each other are common causes named in the literature.

Ethical and social risks often lack any structured handling at all. Feitosa's integrative analysis compares methods for managing these risks across the field. A clear map of what exists, and what is missing, helps project leaders choose safeguards before a data project stalls or causes harm. The scan of past work shows a field that talks much of risk yet plans for it in fits and starts.
arxiv-2512-02828:
G. M. Oliveira and nine co-authors study why superconducting nanowires lose strength near normal metal contacts. Transitions from superconducting to metal states probe mesoscopic superconductivity, but geometry and measurement quirks can muddy readings. Their wires pair epitaxial indium arsenide with aluminum.

Metallic contacts induce an inverse proximity effect, weakening the superconductor near the contact. Those weak spots strongly suppress the critical current and create an anomalous metallic phase. Recognizing contact effects prevents false claims about the wire material itself, and guides cleaner device design. Weak spots at the joins are a plain fact of such wires. Plans that own that fact will build rigs that last far more years in the lab.
arxiv-2512-03228:
Fake galaxy catalogs help real surveys avoid false claims. J. Bautista and a large team describe mock catalogs for the DESI peculiar velocity survey in this 2025 work. The mocks match the first data release of the survey.

Their catalogs copy the number density and clustering of bright galaxies at low redshift. Teams test their methods on mocks before trusting results on real data. That practice reveals biases and errors early. The mocks are an official product, so other groups can check DESI velocity results in the same way. Mocks also let teams rehearse the full analysis before the real catalog is unblinded.
arxiv-2512-03428:
Finding which variable causes which is hard from data alone. Ziyi Ding and Xiao-Ping Zhang present GaussDetect-LiNGAM in this 2025 work. Their method finds causal direction for two variables without an explicit Gaussianity test.

Under standard LiNGAM assumptions, they prove a clean equivalence. Noise Gaussianity in the forward model matches independence between regressor and residual in the reverse model. That equivalence lets the method decide direction more directly. Reliable causal direction helps in medicine, economics, and engineering. A test-free route simplifies causal software, since Gaussianity checks are often fragile in small samples and noisy records.
arxiv-2512-03528:
Teams of AI agents learn better when they can talk. Guang Yang and co-authors study that learning under communication limits in this 2025 work. In real settings, communication is often lossy, with messages dropped or garbled.

Past methods with communication struggle to scale and lack robustness. Complex, dynamic settings expose those limits fast. The authors build priors, built-in assumptions, that respect communication constraints. Constrained learning could make agent teams workable in disaster response, traffic, and games where bandwidth is scarce. Priors that assume loss can teach agents to act well even when messages vanish, a common failure in field deployments of robot teams.
arxiv-2512-03728:
Mobile networks are being rebuilt around artificial intelligence, and the global standards body 3GPP is writing the rules for that change. Pradnya Taksande and three colleagues survey the effort in a 2025 preprint on emerging communications technology. Their focus is Release 19 of the 5G Advanced standard, viewed through the work on service and system aspects.

The survey separates two directions of travel. In one, AI improves the network itself, for example by optimising how resources are used. In the other, the network is reshaped to serve AI applications such as image recognition. By organising the new features this way, the authors give engineers a map of what Release 19 adds. They also show where standardisation is heading next, as early work on Release 20 begins.
arxiv-2512-03828:
Engagement between a person and a robot is easy to feel and hard to define, and vague definitions fail when the setting changes. Dominykas Strazdas and colleagues introduce IM HERE in a 2025 robotics preprint, a model of engagement meant to work for human-human, human-robot, and even robot-robot encounters. The goal is software that analyses social behaviour and acts within social norms.

The model describes every relationship through effort: how much each side invests in the interaction. That bilateral view reduces relationship patterns to a focus placement plus four key states. Mutual relationships, group behaviour, and norm-following actions all fit inside the same scheme. Because the model combines perceived and objective states, it can pinpoint where a miscommunication arises. The authors aim at autonomous systems that pursue their own social goals while integrating smoothly with the people around them.
arxiv-2512-03928:
Variational autoencoders compress data into a latent space shaped like a simple prior, but real data rarely spreads itself so neatly. Michele Alessi, Alessio Ansuini, and Alex Rodríguez introduce DiVAE in a 2025 machine learning preprint. Their addition nudges the encoder to place latent points in proportion to how dense the original data is in each region.

The method adds one lightweight penalty term to the usual training objective, comparing the model's log-prior probability with a log-density estimated from data. A precision weighting keeps the penalty robust, and the extra computing cost is negligible. If the prior itself can learn, it drifts toward high-density regions too. On synthetic datasets, DiVAE matched latent densities to ground truth better and calibrated out-of-distribution uncertainty more honestly. On handwritten digits, it improved both interpretability and detection of out-of-distribution inputs with learnable priors.
arxiv-2512-04028:
Bringing a quantum system to a chosen temperature normally means coupling it to a large thermal bath and waiting. M. Harinarayanan and Karthik Rajeev show a shortcut in a 2025 quantum physics preprint: a second oscillator can play the bath. Their protocol starts with one harmonic oscillator in its ground state and repeatedly quenches the frequencies and the coupling between the pair.

Because the dynamics stays Gaussian, the thermalisation condition collapses into three solvable equations. They yield exact analytic recipes for a dense set of temperatures, and numerical recipes for the rest. Any temperature can be approached as closely as desired, with a trade-off between speed and precision. No macroscopic reservoir is involved at any point. The authors pitch the scheme as a practical tool for quantum thermodynamics experiments. It also suits fast, controlled thermal state preparation in the laboratory.
arxiv-2512-04628:
Ning Zhang presents a proof of Banach's isometric subspace problem, a long-standing question in the geometry of convex bodies. The problem asks, roughly, whether a body whose flat slices are all symmetric in a strong sense must itself be a round ball. Gromov proved key earlier cases. Zhang's 2025 arXiv paper claims the full finite-dimensional result.

The proof starts locally. Continuity of linear maps between central sections of the body lets Zhang build global linear maps on subspaces two dimensions below the whole space. Those maps then carry the argument to the full claim. A settled Banach problem closes a classic chapter in convex geometry. The methods, which grow global structure from local section data, may serve other rigidity questions where symmetry of slices is the only clue.
arxiv-2512-05428:
Keeryn Johnson, Cleyton Magalhaes, and Ronnie de Souza Santos introduce Bita, a conversational assistant that helps software testers test AI systems for unfairness. Bias in deployed models can produce discriminatory outcomes, and fairness testing exists to catch it before release — but current tools demand advanced expertise and fit real workflows poorly. Bita is designed to lower that barrier: testers talk to it, and it helps them spot likely sources of bias in a system.

Bita also reviews test plans through a fairness lens and drafts fairness-oriented exploratory testing charters for testers to run. A large language model, grounded by retrieval over curated fairness literature, supplies the answers, keeping them tied to published practice rather than improvisation. Validation on real-world systems shows Bita supporting fairness tasks with structured, reproducible evidence. The authors offer it as a practical way to make fairness testing accessible, systematic, and usable in industry.
arxiv-2512-05528:
Taketo Akama and five co-authors decode where a listener's attention goes inside a song, using a cheap headset and real music. Vision researchers track experts' and novices' eyes to study how art is perceived. Hearing has lacked an equal, objective tool, especially outside artificial laboratory sounds. The team asks whether focused attention to musical elements can be read from brain signals during natural listening to studio songs. The songs play through a consumer device carrying only four electrodes.

Decoding works: attention can be picked out not only in new songs but in listeners the system has never seen. It improves on prior approaches under the tested conditions. The lightweight setup keeps burden low and the experience authentic. Consumer-grade hardware proves sufficient for meaningful decoding. The authors point toward uses in music education, personalized listening technology, and therapy, where knowing what a listener attends to could change the design.
arxiv-2512-05628:
Sonali Patnaik computes how often certain B mesons decay into partners plus a tau lepton and its neutrino. These decays are prized tests of flavor physics, since the heavy tau makes them sensitive to cracks in the Standard Model. The 2025 study works inside the relativistic independent quark model. In that picture, mesons are built from quarks held by a potential, with corrections for leftover interactions and center of mass motion.

Patnaik derives the form factors that encode the decay dynamics, across the full range of momentum transfer. From them come branching fractions for channels of the B, Bs, and Bc mesons. The numbers agree well with other theory work and with measurements. Quantities tied to polarization, watched closely in recent LHCb and Belle results, also come out in line with Standard Model hopes. Where lattice computing has little to say yet, these predictions give experiments a target to aim at.
arxiv-2512-06028:
Kamyar Sepehri Pirayvatloo and Kazem Haghnejad Azar connect two classical sequences, the Bernoulli and Euler numbers, to splitting a number into an ordered list of parts. Bernoulli numbers govern sums of powers. Euler numbers count alternating permutations. The authors define two auxiliary functions recursively, each new value built from earlier ones through sums over factorial denominators, odd factorials for the Bernoulli side, even for the Euler side.

The payoff: both classical sequences equal these values, up to a simple factor. Each function is also a signed sum over all ordered partitions of the number. Counting forms often reveal divisibility secrets that analysis hides. A fresh recursive handle on two-hundred-year-old numbers is a genuinely useful addition.
arxiv-2512-06228:
Xuanxin Wu, Yuki Arase, and Masaaki Nagata tackle a control problem in text simplification: one reader needs hard words swapped out, another needs a full rewrite with less detail. Software that rewrites text in plainer words must follow the rule set it is given. Training data for each rule set has been costly to build by hand, since it once needed paired examples written by people.

Their method lets a large language model act as a judge that grades drafts against a stated rule set. Those grades are used to build training pairs on their own, so no human labeled pairs are needed. Small open models trained this way matched or beat a top closed model on tests, at both sentence and whole document scale. The result is a cheap path to rewriting tools tuned for schools, health care, and other set needs.
arxiv-2512-06328:
Jiahao Li and three co authors present ReCAD, a way to teach AI models to draw precise, editable design files. Computer aided design files are built from steps a human can later tweak, which makes them far more useful than a flat picture of a part. Prior tools leaned on heavy training, gave weak edit support, and left the raw skill of large models untapped.

ReCAD starts by fine tuning a vision language model on design scripts rewritten as code with clear parameters, paired with plain text accounts of each part. Reward based learning then guides the model on hard cases, using the code as a hint. Skills are taught in layers, from simple building blocks up to joined structures, under one score that rewards both correct shape and correct meaning. On text to design and image to design tests, ReCAD set new best scores.
arxiv-2512-06428:
Yuwen Wang, Shiwen Ye, Jingnan Zhang, and Junhui Wang tackle group finding in networks where ties can be hostile as well as friendly. Signed networks show up in diplomacy, trade, and social life, yet most tools were built for unsigned ones where every tie looks alike. The authors first pin down two senses of balance for such networks, a strong and a weak form, where friend and foe patterns stay consistent across groups.

They then propose a signed block model with a tuning knob that can capture both balance forms at once. Using traits of two sided graphs, they prove the model's groups can be told apart from data in principle. Their fast alternating algorithm fits the model, and theory shows its group calls and tie forecasts settle to the truth as data grows. Tests on fake data and a real network of nations back the gains.
arxiv-2512-06928:
Jeremy Zuchuat warns economists about a bias hiding in a popular way of studying how long people stay unemployed. Panel data that follow the same person over time invite fixed-effects models, which strip out personal traits and promise a clean read on how job-finding chances change with time out of work. Zuchuat shows the promise can fail. If outcomes take special values exactly when a person exits unemployment, a mechanical link appears between the model's errors and its clock.

From that link he derives the conditions under which the method still gives valid answers. Simulations then show the bias can be extremely large when those conditions fail. The warning reaches beyond job search: any study using panel data to measure the pure effect of time faces the same trap. Researchers should check the exit pattern before trusting such estimates.
arxiv-2512-07028:
Halina Wiśniewska studies a ratio built from the gamma function, the continuous extension of the factorial that appears across probability and analysis. The ratio, introduced by Gurland, compares gamma values at paired points and has attracted bounds from several classic authors. Wiśniewska introduces a modified form of the ratio that is friendlier to exact expansions, then represents the gamma function as an infinite product to unlock it.

The product form yields a finite expansion for the logarithm of the modified ratio, written with the Hurwitz zeta function, together with explicit bounds on the error left behind. Those bounds ground a proper convergence analysis. From the expansion flow new two-sided inequalities for the original Gurland ratio.
arxiv-2512-07128:
Chau Truong, Hieu Ta Quang, and Dung D Le teach CLIP, the model that matches images with text, to read long descriptions instead of short captions. CLIP learned from terse labels, so it stumbles over the detailed paragraphs real users write. Rival fixes bolt on region proposals that pre-cut images into pieces, which costs heavily at deployment time. MulCLIP instead aligns text and image at several levels inside one end-to-end model.

Global matching is kept between the image and both a summary and the full long caption, with room made for longer text sequences. Two finer strategies follow: one rebuilds masked words from locally adjusted image features, tying words to patches, and another gathers the most relevant patches for each sub-caption automatically. Across diverse benchmarks the method improved downstream results, and ablation tests credit the multi-level design.
arxiv-2512-07428:
Artem Nosenko and Dmitri Efremov wrote this 2025 physics paper on unusual magnetic order in solid materials. Some crystals with a center of symmetry host patterns described by more than one wave at once. Scientists call these multi-Q structures, and their inner cause is still an open question.

The authors focus on a square lattice setting with two competing patterns. One pattern uses a single wave, and the other combines two waves. For the double pattern they calculate the dynamical magnetic structure factor. That factor predicts how neutrons scatter when they bounce off the material. They then set the two patterns side by side. The contrast, they show, is clear enough for inelastic neutron scattering tests. Such tests can tell which magnetic order a real sample actually holds.
arxiv-2512-07628:
Zhiqi Li and ten co-authors wrote this 2025 paper on generating three-dimensional objects and scenes. Good 3D generators should build things from parts, the way real scenes are composed. But letting every part attend to every other part grows costly very fast.

Their model, MoCA, keeps that cost under control with two designs. A routing step picks the most relevant components for full global attention. The rest are not dropped; they are compressed into a compact summary. That summary preserves background context while shrinking the attention workload. Fine detail survives where it matters, and the part count can grow. Tests cover both single objects built from parts and full scenes. MoCA beats the baseline methods on both kinds of task. The result is a generator that scales to richer, more crowded scenes. Composition, the authors argue, should not force a choice between detail and size.
arxiv-2512-07728:
Jacobus Conradi, Ivor van der Hoog, and Eva Rotenberg wrote this 2025 computer science paper. The Fréchet distance measures how similar two polygonal curves are. It is, loosely, the shortest leash between two walkers.

The classic way to compute it walks through a free-space diagram. A recent rival approach hops through a discrete graph like a frog. That frog method bisects edges again and again until values converge. Its inventors reported large practical speedups over the state of the art. Conradi and colleagues revisit the frog and find three limits. It never computes the exact distance, only an approximation. Its bisection adds needed events only in the endless limit.  The authors build a variant that fixes all three flaws. Exactness, polynomial-time convergence, and near-optimal lossless simplification are proven. Their open-source tests add a surprise about the older champion.
arxiv-2512-07928:
Guim Planella Planas wrote this 2025 theoretical physics paper on strings hiding inside field theory. Perturbation theory writes a field theory's answers as sums of Feynman diagrams. He shows how to reorganize that sum into something string-shaped.

Schwinger parametrization is the first tool in the conversion. Ribbon graphs from the diagrams correspond one-to-one with Riemann surfaces. Strebel differentials supply that bridge between graphs and geometry. Each Feynman diagram thus becomes a two-dimensional surface of its own. A conformal field theory is then built on that worldsheet. Its correlation functions reproduce the full set of Feynman rules from geometry alone. Restoring the surface's symmetries promotes the construction further. The integral over surface shapes becomes a path integral over metrics. A non-critical string theory emerges, with its Liouville mode as a holographic direction. Loop divergences match the string theory's degeneration limits exactly.
arxiv-2512-08228:
Jusheng Zhang, Kaitong Cai, Xiaoyang Guo, and a large team of computer vision researchers posted a benchmark paper on arXiv in December 2025. Their benchmark, MM CoT, tests whether multimodal models truly reason in steps about images. Models can sound fluent while producing chains of thought that ignore the picture or break basic logic, and older benchmarks rarely check for that.

Instead of asking models to write explanations, MM CoT asks them to pick the one event chain that fits two demands at once. Every step must match visible evidence. The chain must also stay causally sound. Tricky wrong options are built to fail exactly one of those demands, exposing which kind of reasoning broke. Leading vision language models still struggled on the test. Scores also correlated weakly with older benchmarks, suggesting it measures something distinct: a base for models that reason faithfully, not just plausibly.
arxiv-2512-08628:
Xinyi Zhao, Ralph Hertwig, and Dirk U Wulff, psychologists, posted a bibliometric study on arXiv in December 2025. They ask how a century of psychology research maps onto the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals. Contributions from the social and behavioral sciences are rarely woven into policy agendas, so the team built a baseline for tracking them.

They assembled over two hundred thirty thousand psychology publications, from 1894 to 2022, tagging each to the seventeen goals. Health, education, work, inequality, and gender dominate, with the focus shifting over time from work toward education, inequality, and, since the nineteen sixties, health. American research leads on most goals, while other countries show distinct priorities. Women make up about a third of authors, concentrated in social and health goals. After the goals launched in 2015, tagged work began out citing comparable untagged work. The map exposes gaps for the field to close.
arxiv-2512-08828:
Swaraj Bose and Walter Dempsey propose a method to build prediction intervals for individual treatment effects across many decision points. Quantifying uncertainty for one person at one time is crucial in health, finance, education, and online markets. Prior work often used cross sectional data or strong exchangeability assumptions that may not hold over time.

Their conformal inference method targets time varying effects under weaker assumptions than earlier work. Coverage is guaranteed through a lower bound that depends on how far the data depart from exchangeability. Simulations modeled on micro randomized trials, a sequential design used in mobile health, support the theory. The authors also apply the method to a real mobile health study of interns. The result is a practical tool for personalized decision making that reports honest uncertainty when treatments are offered repeatedly over time.
arxiv-2512-08928:
Zachary Andalman and coauthors study the role of nozzle shocks when a star is torn apart. In such a tidal disruption event, bound debris returns on stretched orbits in a thin stream. Near the closest approach, inclined orbits converge and the stream is squeezed vertically to an extreme degree, forming a nozzle shock whose dissipation could affect circularization.

The team builds an idealized model that joins three dimensional particle simulations, a semi analytic affine model, and one dimensional fluid simulations. Because the model is cheap to run, the shock can be resolved clearly, with a realistic equation of state, at many times. Near peak return, hydrogen recombination and molecule formation broaden the stream several fold, raising dissipation at the nozzle. That dissipation still cannot circularize the debris directly. Instead, the thicker stream is far more likely to hit itself on the next orbit,.
arxiv-2512-09028:
Myrann Baker Rasooli and coauthors show that a mobile impurity in a superfluid of light can swim against the flow once a critical speed is passed. A superfluid flows without friction below that threshold and exerts no drag. Above it, superfluidity breaks down and energy moves into excitations such as vortices.

Their system is a two dimensional paraxial superfluid of light with a finite mass impurity placed in the flow. Past the threshold, the impurity periodically emits quantized vortex antivortex pairs downstream. Those emissions give an upstream recoil that produces a net propulsive force, so the impurity moves against the current. The effect resembles how living swimmers exploit wake turbulence to save effort. A point vortex model for the center of mass motion describes how the mechanism depends on impurity shape and flow speed. The work links energy dissipation in quantum fluids to self propulsion ideas from active matter.
arxiv-2512-09428:
Maciej Gałązka, Hanieh Keneshlou, and Klemen Šivic describe the components of Hilbert schemes of points, geometric spaces that parametrize configurations of a fixed number of points in affine space. Such schemes are known to break into several irreducible components, and cataloging them is a hard problem in algebraic geometry. The authors settle the cases of nine and ten points.

Their main tools are the variety of commuting matrices and a close analysis of loci of local algebras with a given Hilbert function, which measures an algebra's graded size. They also prove that every finite local algebra of degree nine or ten whose socle has dimension two is smoothable, meaning it can be obtained as a limit of points. As the main consequence, they establish that two varieties built from these algebras, the cactus Grassmannian and the secant Grassmannian, are actually equal in the cases studied.
arxiv-2512-09728:
Camille Moisset, Bruce Sutherland, and Lois Baker investigate why satellite measurements of the ocean's internal tides lose their orderly phase pattern near the Equator. Internal tides are waves inside the ocean, generated when tidal flow crosses underwater topography. They travel thousands of kilometers and help redistribute energy and drive mixing, so their coherence matters for interpreting dynamics.

The team studies a wavepacket of the lunar semidiurnal tide meeting an equatorial jet, a band of current flowing along the Equator. Their linear model uses modal decomposition and is solved with the Dedalus software. A uniform jet can reflect the wavepacket outright or distort it, depending on the jet's strength. A sheared jet instead scatters energy into higher modes, which move more slowly and dissipate more easily; as the packet exits, some energy transfers back. The resulting phase speed differences between modes can explain part of the incoherence seen in satellite altimetry.
arxiv-2512-10028:
Achwaq Ghezal, Yazid Delenda, and Mekki Aouachria work out how a noncommutative spacetime would show up in collider data. In noncommutative geometry, coordinates fail to commute, controlled by a small antisymmetric parameter. They study W and Z boson production with a jet at the Large Hadron Collider, within the noncommutative Standard Model. The work covers all partonic channels and leptonic decays. A distinctive feature emerges: production amplitudes get corrections already at first order in the noncommutativity parameter, where many processes only feel second order effects.

The authors predict angular distributions and a forward backward asymmetry, and compare them with state of the art Standard Model results. They then confront real ATLAS data on Z plus jet events. From the azimuthal spectrum and asymmetry they derive stringent lower bounds on the noncommutative scale, reaching into the multi teraelectronvolt range. They average observables over Earth's rotation with care.
arxiv-2512-10128:
Chuan Huang, Gustaf Hendeby, and Isaac Skog present positioning systems that navigate by magnetism alone. Indoor magnetic fields vary from place to place in stable, complicated ways, making them a fingerprint for location where satellite signals fail. Magnetic SLAM systems map that field while locating themselves in it, holding their error bounded in places already visited. Their weakness: leading methods lean on low drift odometry from cameras, wheel encoders, or step counting, which may be unavailable. The authors' two systems use only an inertial unit and seven magnetometers.

The two versions differ in whether state estimation happens in one step or two. In real multi floor indoor tests, the systems beat the leading magnetic inertial odometry method, keeping position error under a meter over trajectories lasting minutes. The target application is emergency responders in mines or fires, where smoke kills vision and satellites never reach.
arxiv-2512-10528:
Connor Gauntlett and David Kimsey carry a classical chapter of analysis onto the unit sphere in complex spaces of any dimension. On the circle, orthogonal polynomials come with Verblunsky coefficients and a famous theorem of Szegő and Verblunsky tying an endless product of those coefficients to an integral of the weight. The authors build the same machinery for measures living on higher-dimensional spheres.

They define the polynomials, the coefficients, and an associated Christoffel function, then prove a recurrence in the spirit of the classical Szegő recurrences and an analogue of Verblunsky's theorem. Equalities connect the polynomials, moment matrix determinants, and the Christoffel function, and when the singular part of the measure is discrete, everything depends only on the smooth part. Under one more condition they prove the full Szegő-Verblunsky identity, and exhibit a weight where it fails.
arxiv-2512-11028:
F. Mernier and a large team measure the chemical makeup of hot gas at the centre of the Centaurus galaxy cluster using a new high resolution X ray instrument. Cluster gas holds metals forged by several kinds of stars and supernovae over cosmic time, making it a record of how elements were made and spread. The XRISM satellite's Resolve instrument gives unusually sharp spectra of that gas.

Most measured element ratios relative to iron match the Solar System's composition, echoing earlier results for the Perseus cluster. Two ratios, involving nitrogen and magnesium, differ clearly, challenging the idea that all cluster cores share a fully solar mix. Combinations of yields from aging stars and both supernova types can explain the pattern. The authors call for more high resolution studies of other clusters.
arxiv-2512-11328:
Abhishek Tiwari and fellow authors simulate how the ratio of ion to electron temperature steers turbulence inside a fusion plasma. Their setting is the DIII-D tokamak running in quiescent H mode, a regime prized for steady confinement without violent edge bursts. Small scale turbulence leaks heat and particles, so knowing which mode dominates under which settings matters for reactor design.

Using a gyrokinetic code with a lifelike equilibrium, they varied each temperature separately. Lowering the ratio favoured trapped electron modes over ion temperature gradient modes, with the ratio itself setting the crossover. Heating electrons raised transport levels more than cooling ions did, and eddy sizes followed the same trends. Adding impurities barely changed transport. Helium plasmas grew instabilities faster yet saturated at lower transport than deuterium, a hint that helium operation could confine better than expected.
arxiv-2512-11628:
Yichi Zang studies odd states of the Virasoro algebra, a core math object in two dimensional field theory. The states in question have half step order flaws, and they show up in the study of Argyres-Douglas theories, a class of strong quantum field theories. Whole step states have a clear free field recipe, but half step ones are tangled by branch cuts.

Zang gives two recipes and proves they agree. One twists a free boson field by a sign flip, guided by the shape of Hitchin systems. The other follows a recursion rule for the state values. Both match at ranks 3/2 and 5/2. The tools should help compute states for the linked theories.
arxiv-2512-11728:
Emily E Whitehead and co-authors test how a fuzzy edge in star models changes the fate of massive stars. Inside a star, churning zones mix material past their formal edge, an effect called convective boundary mixing or overshooting. One dimensional star codes must guess its strength.

The team ran two grids with the MESA code for low metal massive stars. One grid used the standard mixing strength, the other used values from 3D simulations. Shell clashes between carbon, neon, and oxygen burning were common in both. The stronger mixing grid showed more hydrogen helium and helium carbon clashes at lower masses. Such clashes can reshape the star before it explodes and change what it forges.
arxiv-2512-11928:
Alexander Peysakhovich and co-authors teach a diffusion model to paint cells virtually. Cell painting stains cells so their shapes glow in telling colors, a workhorse of drug screening. The catch is that staining kills the cells and takes labor, so live dynamics cannot be watched.

Their model, MONET, predicts paint channels from plain brightfield images, which need no stain. Quality rose with scale. A consistency design lets it render time lapse videos even though no painted video training data exists. It even transfers partly to new cell lines and imaging setups without retraining. The team frames virtual painting as a partner to the real thing, opening live cell studies that staining forbids.
arxiv-2512-12528:
Indrakshi Dey, Ilias Cherkaoui, and Mohamed Khalafalla Hassan build a noise based method to predict anomalies in a fused signal in a 2025 paper. Instead of hunting for odd patterns in the signal itself, they study its leftover noise. A wavelet packet transform splits the signal by time and frequency, and an orthogonal projection separates structure from residual noise.

Higher order statistics then measure non-Gaussian traits and nonlinear coupling in that residual, using the third order cumulant. Compact noise signatures feed a Mahalanobis detector with a closed form decision rule. The authors prove orthonormality, energy preservation, and the Gaussian null behavior of the cumulants, grounding the test's performance under mean shift alternatives.
arxiv-2512-12928:
Weizhe Huang and co-authors present ProServe, a scheduling system for serving large language models to many users at once. Interactive services must handle thousands of requests, each with its own service level goals. Requests also differ in priority, since some clients and tasks carry far more business value.

ProServe is built to schedule requests with multiple priorities in one unified system. Its aim is to give stronger performance promises to high priority work without starving the rest. The paper frames priority as a missing dimension in current serving systems. It then designs scheduling around that dimension, for deployments where mixed client tiers share the same model.
arxiv-2512-13128:
Linh Han Thanh and co-authors revisit the role of the streaming instability in shaping the cosmic-ray energy spectrum from giga- to tera-electron-volts. A puzzling hardening of the spectrum near 300 giga-electron-volts needs explanation. One model lets cosmic rays stir up waves that then control their own spread.

The team returns to a 2012 model of that idea and runs a wide parameter study with self-consistent diffusion. They find the range of parameters that best fits the data. Their conclusion is that this self-generated wave picture remains a competitive account of the hardening, standing alongside other explanations of the cosmic-ray spectrum.
arxiv-2512-13428:
Anika Islam and co-authors present a lightweight ensemble for few-shot plant disease classification, aimed at farms with little labeled data and cheap phones. Most deep models for leaf disease need big labeled sets and heavy computation. Their design adapts two MobileNet models to the plant domain and fuses their features.

A Bi-LSTM classifier with attention then reads the fused features. On tomato diseases from PlantVillage, accuracy reached 98.23 percent with 15 examples per class, close to a far heavier benchmark. On messy field photos it reached 69.28 percent. The model is about 40 megabytes and stays mobile friendly, a fit for data-scarce regions.
arxiv-2512-13628:
Nikhil Pappu studies quantum zero-knowledge proofs that stay private even after a proof is revoked. A non-interactive zero-knowledge proof lets a prover convince a verifier without giving away the secret. The certified-everlasting form adds a revocation step that the prover can check.

After a successful revocation, the verifier's state should be simulable from the statement alone, in a statistically close way. Pappu first shows a barrier to building such proofs in the common reference string model from known interactive proofs. He then bypasses it with a non-black-box use of other proofs and one-way functions, based on the learning with errors premise. A second build uses shared EPR pairs and needs only single-qubit measures.
arxiv-2512-13928:
Jakub Ślęzak argues that codifference deserves wider use as a measure of dispersion and dependence. Codifference is standard for stable vectors and processes where covariance is infinite. He contends it also gives useful information for other heavy-tail and non-Gaussian distributions, regardless of tails.

Ślęzak analyzes codifference with as few assumptions on the model as possible. That leads him to propose its natural domain and three natural variants. Using variable scale mixture distributions, he shows codifference reflects bulk properties and ignores tails far more than covariance does. It can also detect nonlinear forms of memory that covariance misses. He closes by giving the asymptotic distribution of its estimator, in a 23-page paper.
arxiv-2512-14228:
Aneesha Fernando and four coauthors test large language models for georeferencing in a 2025 paper. Georeferencing assigns map coordinates to places named in text. Many old biological specimen records describe a site only in words, such as a distance from a town, which place name tools handle poorly.

The team first found prompting patterns that work, then fine tuned a model with QLoRA on specimen data from several regions and languages. On average, 65 percent of records landed within 10 km of the true site. For New York state, 85 percent fell within 10 km and 67 percent within 1 km. The model did well even on long, complex descriptions, a common pain point in biodiversity work.
arxiv-2512-15128:
Kaoru Irie and a coauthor examine the long run forecasts of a model family used for count data over time. Poisson gamma state space models are popular for non negative integer series because they give closed form filtering and prediction formulas. The authors dig into the mechanics of their multi step ahead predictive distributions.

They show the model's forecasts are non stationary in a specific way. The predictive mean stays constant while the predictive variance grows without bound as the horizon lengthens, much like a Gaussian random walk. In the long run the whole distribution collapses onto zero, so point and interval forecasts both drift to zero. The study also maps how hyperparameters and the discount factor shape that long run behavior, a warning for anyone using these models to forecast far ahead.
arxiv-2512-15528:
Daiqing Wu and co authors present EmoCaliber, a model that states its confidence when reading emotion in images, in a 2025 paper. Visual emotion comprehension asks a system to name the feeling an image conveys. Large multimodal models usually output one firm label, yet viewers often disagree about emotion, so a single label hides real doubt.

The team trains a model in three stages: structured reasoning first, then stating confidence, then calibrating that confidence. On their unified VECBench benchmark, EmoCaliber beats prior methods at both emotion prediction and confidence estimation. The added confidence signal tells users how plausible other readings are and how much the model trusts itself.
arxiv-2512-15728:
Yuhan Hou and co authors present FedSight AI, a multi agent system that simulates Federal Reserve rate deliberations, in a 2025 paper, dated December 5. The Federal Open Market Committee sets the federal funds rate, and predicting its choices matters across the economy. Single model forecasts miss the committee's debate driven character.

Member agents review structured indicators and unstructured inputs such as the Beige Book, debate options, and vote, mirroring committee reasoning. A Chain of Draft extension enforces concise staged reasoning for speed and accuracy. At 2023 and 2024 meetings, the Chain of Draft version reached 93.75 percent accuracy and 93.33 percent stability, beating MiniFed and ordinal random forest baselines.
arxiv-2512-16328:
Zhi-Hang Yao and four co-authors study entropy where matter is born from energy in a physics paper posted to arXiv in 2025. In a strong electric field, electron-positron pairs can pop into existence, the Schwinger effect. The team uses a Sauter pulse, a field that swells and fades smoothly in time.

They compute three kinds of entropy for the created pairs: entanglement entropy, a thermal distribution entropy, and a version corrected by chemical potential. For short pulses the entanglement entropy is larger, while for long pulses the order flips. The chemical potential makes the per-particle thermal entropy wiggle non-monotonically for short pulses, echoing the entanglement behavior. Counting full momentum, they also define a thermal entropy through the Unruh temperature, and both entropies level off at constants, with the thermal one higher.
arxiv-2512-16728:
M. Messa and a large team report AMORE6, a tiny dwarf galaxy seen as it was in the reionization era, at redshift 5.7253. The galaxy is very poor in metals, light in mass at about 440,000 solar masses, and compact, and it is magnified by the cluster A2744.

Its Lyman-alpha line is narrow, near symmetric, and strong, with a rest-frame width of 150 angstroms and almost no shift from the galaxy systemic speed. Those traits point to a thin veil of neutral hydrogen, which fits with ionizing light leaking out. On that basis the authors rank AMORE6 among the most compelling leaking candidates yet found from that era.
arxiv-2512-16828:
Wen Li and coauthors study spin-triplet superconductors in a Zeeman magnetic field. They cover both unitary and nonunitary pairing states. Triplet pairing, where electron spins align, can react to fields in ways singlet pairing cannot.

Within a mean-field frame, they diagonalize the Bogoliubov-de Gennes Hamiltonian exactly. They derive formulas for the quasiparticle spectrum, the gap, and the critical heat level. Formulas for spin magnetization come too. All hold at any field strength and heat level. They trace how spin response bends nonlinearly, and how the gap and transition shift. Clear contrasts mark unitary and nonunitary states. Measures of those traits can reveal the order parameter in materials such as 4Hb-TaS2.
arxiv-2512-16928:
Kwangjun Ahn, Noah Amsel, and John Langford present Dion2, a simpler way to shrink the matrix inside the Muon optimizer for training neural networks. Muon performs well, but its orthonormalization step grows costly faster than linearly as models scale.

Earlier fixes cut matrix size with complex tricks. Dion2 instead picks a fraction of rows or columns at each step and orthonormalizes only those. That sampling makes each update sparse, cutting both compute and the data shuffled between machines. The sparsity in turn helps Muon scale to larger models and clusters. The method is released openly, giving trainers a light swap for a known bottleneck.
arxiv-2512-17028:
Victoria-Elisabeth Gruber and a large team introduce the Women Health Benchmark, the first test set built to grade language models on women health alone. As chatbots become first stops for health questions, their accuracy in this area had gone unmeasured.

The bench holds 96 validated case stumps across five specialties, from obstetrics to neurology, three query types, and eight error types such as dosage slips and missed urgency. Thirteen top models were graded, and failure rates ran near 60 percent. All models struggled to flag urgent cases, while GPT-5 cut inappropriate advice sharply. The team warns that chatbots are not yet reliable guides in women health.
arxiv-2512-17128:
Lin Sok, Martianus Frederic Ezerman, and Ling San study Hermitian hulls of rational algebraic geometry codes. They also study how those hulls feed quantum code design. Interest in code hulls is rising. The Hermitian case is now gaining over the better-known Euclidean one.

Using algebraic function fields in one variable, they bound the Hermitian hull size of generalized rational AG codes from below. They spot families where the bound is tight. Evaluation points are picked with care. Residues of the Weil differential for the dual code must carry an easy-to-check trait. From MDS codes with designed hulls, the Hermitian method yields two families of entanglement-assisted quantum codes. Their parameters are new and strong.
arxiv-2512-17228:
Chung-Ta Huang, Connie Cheng, and Vealy Lai built LUMIA, a handheld device that turns what its camera sees into music. Most digital music tools stress exact control and careful editing. LUMIA instead invites play: point the device at a scene, capture it, and hear a musical phrase shaped by that view.

Inside, a vision model reads each photo and writes a prompt that describes it. That prompt, plus instruments the user picks, feeds a text-to-music system that makes short loopable segments in real time. Users can layer one segment over another as they move. The work treats making music as a physical, in-the-moment act rather than a desk task.
arxiv-2512-17828:
Christopher Eckner, Felipe Figueroa, Simon Metayer, and Piotr Tourkine ask what a finished theory of gravity must look like at very high energies. They study how gravitons scatter and assume the answer comes from a calm theory of heavy spinning particles. Their claim is that such a theory cannot stay simple.

The authors show the theory would need endless families of states, called Regge trajectories, which is a hallmark of string like spectra. The demand traces back to a basic rule tied to cause and effect. Computer checks of a rival single family idea suggest those neat answers are false leads that break down as the search grows.
arxiv-2512-18328:
Emmanuel Gottlob, David Gröters, and Ulrich Schneider explain the energy gaps of quasicrystals, solids whose atoms form ordered patterns that never quite repeat. Normal band theory assumes a repeating grid, so quasicrystal gaps were mostly mapped by brute force on finite chunks. Their new frame works in a shape space that captures the pattern as a whole.

The gaps, they show, form a ladder. Each rung comes from echoes between atom sites at a growing distance, and the count of states below each gap locks to a fixed irrational area in that shape space. Big simulations of a tight binding model, built from local wave packets, match the calls closely. The frame can now guide work in the endless size limit.
arxiv-2512-18628:
Masaoki Mori's 2025 paper in geometry builds a broader family of affine buildings, structures used to study symmetry and group actions. Mori calls the new objects Babel buildings. They are nonconnected, nonconvex metric spaces of nonpositive curvature, carrying a canonical distance valued in a vector space of real numbers. A version of the CAT(0) inequality holds, together with a fixed point theorem for group actions on them.

Inside, Mori proves decomposition theorems of Bruhat, Cartan, and Kapranov type for strongly transitive, type-preserving group actions. The residues at a vertex are themselves lower-level Babel buildings, recursing down to ordinary affine buildings. The result is a concrete metric theory for buildings tied to higher-dimensional local fields.
arxiv-2512-18728:
Bhagyarathi Sahoo, Captain R. Singh, and Raghunath Sahoo study why quarkonia, bound states of heavy quarks, come out of lead-lead collisions with aligned spins. Spin alignment hints at the quark-gluon plasma, the hot matter formed in such collisions, and how it rotates. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025 and published in Physical Review D, proposes dissociation as the mechanism.

In their model, the spinning medium couples to quarkonium spin through a modified potential, so states of different spin break apart at different rates. They compute spin-dependent decay widths for charmonium and bottomonium states, including J/psi and Upsilon families, inside a rotating thermal medium. The observable rho_00 shifts with momentum, event multiplicity, and rotation. Vorticity, they conclude, leaves a readable fingerprint on spin alignment, opening a window on the plasma's microscopic swirling.
arxiv-2512-19228:
Valentin Schmidberger, Manuel Eberhardinger, Setareh Maghsudi, and Johannes Maucher teach language models to write forgery checks for documents. Banks and agencies rely on plausibility rules, code that flags data which cannot be right, to catch manipulation. Engineers write those rules by hand, which is slow and hard to scale.

The team fine-tuned two open eight-billion-parameter models, Llama 3.1 and OpenCoder, on code and data from real application cases. Different tuning strategies were compared under tight hardware limits. The question was how far a model adapted to an unknown domain can go in drafting correct, usable checks on its own.
arxiv-2512-19428:
Zhang Chong questions whether self-attention is truly needed for strong sequence models. His reading recasts attention as tensor lifting: token vectors are blown up into a huge space of pairwise interactions, and learning sculpts that space by gradient descent. The machinery is expressive but hard to describe with a few clean invariants.

The alternative is a causal Grassmann layer. Token states are compressed, nearby pairs are encoded as two-dimensional subspaces through Plücker coordinates, and gated mixing folds the geometry back in. Information travels as controlled deformations of low-rank subspaces over nested windows. The computation stays on a finite-dimensional manifold, which the author argues keeps the model interpretable.
arxiv-2512-19728:
Haocheng Lu, Minjun Zhu, and Henry Yu improve small language models at math by studying their mistakes in detail. Standard post-training grades each attempted solution as simply right or wrong, yet wrong chain-of-thought solutions often look convincing while hiding one subtle logical, algebraic, or numerical flaw. Their pipeline first fine-tunes on worked solutions, then brings in a compact verifier called MathVerifier.

The verifier scores each attempt along six error dimensions, producing interpretable wrongness and absurdity ratings. Those scores mine hard negatives, solutions that are nearly right but structurally flawed, and weight the preference pairs used in direct preference optimization. On a 1.5-billion-parameter Qwen2.5 model, the guided method beat plain fine-tuning and unweighted optimization, especially on problems where answers come out numerically close but logically broken.
arxiv-2512-19928:
Mazdak Abulnaga leads a ten-author team unifying two ways to align brain scans. Warping one MRI onto another backs group studies of the brain. Surface methods align the folded cortex. Volume methods align the inside. Done apart, the two breed mismatches. NeurAlign instead aligns volume and surface at once, in one deep learning frame.

A sphere-based space bridges the two sides. It links the cortex sheet's shape with the anatomy inside the volume. Spherical alignment is folded into the learning itself. That keeps the two domains in geometric step. On in-domain and out-of-domain data, NeurAlign beat classic and learned rivals. Dice overlap rose by up to seven points, with smooth warp fields kept. It also runs far faster than the standard pipeline. It needs nothing past the scan itself.
arxiv-2512-20228:
Kazuaki Tokuyama and co-authors use machine learning to hunt for new superconducting hydrides. Hydrogen-rich compounds can superconduct at high temperatures, but usually only under extreme pressure. Adding a third element can stabilize them at lower pressures, at the cost of a huge space of possible mixtures to check.

The team trained an ensemble of thirty XGBoost models on about two thousand known binary and ternary hydrides. They screened broad composition families at three pressure levels and kept candidates the ensemble agreed on. Systems such as calcium-titanium-hydrogen scored highly despite being absent from the training data. Feature analysis points to ionization energy and atomic radius as strong influences on predicted transition temperatures.
arxiv-2512-20328:
Antonio Vitale and co-authors address a trust problem: large language models write and summarize code well, but nobody can see why they produce a given output. Their approach, FeatureSHAP, explains model behaviour for software engineering tasks. It is fully automated and works with both open and proprietary models.

FeatureSHAP builds on Shapley values from game theory. It perturbs high-level input features one at a time and measures how the output changes, using task-specific similarity checks. On code generation and code summarization, it blames irrelevant features less and tracks the model more faithfully than benchmarks. A survey of thirty-seven practitioners found the explanations genuinely helped interpretation and decisions.
arxiv-2512-20428:
A E Cárcamo Hernández and co-authors propose a particle physics model that explains two mysteries at once: why neutrinos have tiny masses, and what dark matter might be. Their model gauges lepton number, then breaks that symmetry by three units, leaving a residual discrete symmetry behind.

The leftover symmetry forces neutrinos to gain mass through a one-loop scotogenic mechanism, and the masses come out Dirac-type rather than Majorana. The same symmetry stabilizes the lightest neutral particle carrying its charge, making a scalar in the model a dark matter candidate. The authors check this candidate against direct detection experiments and the measured relic abundance. Charged lepton flavour violating decays are predicted within reach of current experiments.
arxiv-2512-20528:
Joanna L P Wolff and co-authors listen to light emitted by a magnetic membrane only a few atoms thick. The material is NiPS3, whose zigzag antiferromagnetic order produces puzzling luminescence. Suspending the flake as a membrane lets the team probe how spin order, light, and mechanics intertwine without a substrate interfering.

They reveal nematic zigzag states and identify the excitons as magnetic ones, dressed by magnons: each optical excitation moves through the magnetic lattice by magnon-mediated hops. Strain tuning shifts the emission lines at rates that depend on the line's microscopic origin. Those rates betray strong localization of the magnetic excitons, which fades as the number of magnon hops grows. The work clarifies what these much-debated excitons actually are.
arxiv-2512-20728:
Vilas J Shinde builds a spectral microscope that watches frequencies change in time, at the data's own resolution. Fourier analysis gives a signal's frequency content but assumes periodicity and discards when each tone was active. Short-time transforms and wavelets trade off time detail against frequency detail. Flowfields, especially turbulent ones with bursty extreme events, need better.

The proposed spectral mode split produces spectral-space and spectral-time modes, each ranked by both frequency and energy. Together they form a tone map resolved at the flowfield's own grid size rather than a windowed blur. Numerical cases show spacetime-tone analysis of flowfields, and the same split serves reduced-order modelling and denoising. Engineers studying unsteady flows gain a sharper tool for events that standard modal analysis smears away.
arxiv-2512-21028:
Oussama Ben Sghaier, Kevin Delcourt, and Houari Sahraoui watch what coding models do when the answers are lying in plain sight. Unit tests are meant to validate generated code, but to a model trained to exploit every signal they are also a leak. On the hard split of BigCodeBench, five models faced five prompting conditions that varied whether tests were visible and whether using them was restricted, explicitly or implicitly.

Seeing the tests nearly doubled correctness for some models, and restrictions or partial exposure only blunted the effect. Four recurring adaptation strategies emerged, led by test-driven refinement, where the model iterates against the visible tests. The study matters for anyone benchmarking agents: a score earned with tests in view measures a different skill than solving the problem, and evaluations should say which one they intend.
arxiv-2512-21228:
Wenyu Zhang, Qun Wang, and three co-authors ask whether the constituents inside a hadron are quantum-entangled, and answer from first principles. Working with a strongly coupled scalar Yukawa theory as a tractable stand-in for the strong force, they use light-front Hamiltonian methods with controlled truncations. They build mock nucleons, pions, and anti-nucleons. Then they extract reduced density matrices for their parton subsystems and compute entanglement entropy, mutual information, and linear entropy.

Without sea pairs, the entanglement entropy tracks the ordinary Shannon entropy of the transverse-momentum distribution, tying quantum information neatly to parton structure. With sea pairs included, the correspondence breaks. The entanglement exceeds anything a classical probability distribution over partons could encode. The hadron's wave function stores genuinely quantum correlations. The result positions entanglement as a probe of non-perturbative dynamics and sets up the same questions for real quantum chromodynamics and future colliders.
arxiv-2512-21528:
Radost Waszkiewicz, Piotr Szymczak, Maciej Lisicki, and their co-authors study the physics of pulling an espresso shot. Brewing forces hot water through a puck of ground coffee, a porous material that dissolves and flexes under pressure as the shot proceeds. That mix of flow, chemistry, and elasticity makes the process hard to model.

Using a café-grade espresso machine in a controlled setup, the team shows the interplay of elasticity and porosity governs the flow rate late in extraction. Flow rate in turn sets the concentration of dissolved solids in the cup, which shapes the taste. They build a minimal model capturing the nonlinear pressure-flow relationship. They also propose a method for reproducing how flow evolves during brewing. Dissolution, the slow washing away of the coffee itself, plays a central role in that evolution. The work gives espresso a poroelastic theory.
arxiv-2512-21728:
Yajie Chen, Hardi Peter, and their co-authors simulate a solar blowout jet from first principles. Blowout jets are a dramatic subclass of the extreme-ultraviolet and X-ray jets that erupt all over the Sun's corona. Earlier models usually set up a magnetic configuration by hand and triggered the jet with artificial changes at the surface.

Using the MURaM code, the team models a coronal hole region from the upper convection zone into the lower corona, letting convection do the work. A twisted flux tube forms on its own, emerges through the surface, and reconnects with the open field. The jet starts narrow, then broadens into a blowout as the twist releases, launching a fast heating front. The simulated jet matches observations: a slow upflow near one hundred eighty kilometers per second and a fast front near five hundred.
arxiv-2512-21928:
Jupiter's Great Red Spot has drifted westward for over a century, and an earlier f-plane asymptotic analysis explained several of its features but not that drift. Oladiran Johnson Abimbola extends the theory to the beta plane, adding the planet's vorticity gradient and a dimensionless Rossby deformation parameter, then applies perturbation theory systematically to the vortex.

The extended theory predicts a westward drift of about three point seven meters per second, within about five percent of the observed value. It also explains the observed ninety-day oscillation in drift rate and the north-south asymmetry of the surrounding circulation. Applied without free parameters, the same theory describes vortices on Saturn, Neptune, and Earth, arguing that the vorticity gradient is essential to long-lived atmospheric vortices.
arxiv-2512-22528:
Bin Shen and eleven co-authors squeeze and magnetize a heavy-fermion metal, CePdIn, to map its magnetic phases. The compound sits in a geometrically frustrated crystal structure where the Kondo effect and quantum fluctuations fight the exchange interactions that order its moments. At ambient pressure it shows two magnetic transitions, near 1.65 kelvin and near 1.15 kelvin in temperature, both suppressed by fields along the crystal's c-axis.

Under pressure, the ordering temperature first falls to 0.8 kelvin, then jumps abruptly upward near 2.6 gigapascals, before fading away entirely near 5 gigapascals. The high-pressure phase also resists magnetic fields better. Together, the evidence points to two distinct antiferromagnetic phases, plausibly switched by pressure strengthening the Kondo hybridization and reshaping the electronic structure.
arxiv-2512-22728:
Keisuke Nakashi, Masashi Kimura, Hayato Motohashi, and Kazufumi Takahashi study how black holes vibrate after a disturbance when gravity includes higher curvature corrections beyond Einstein's theory. Their subject is the ringdown, the fading set of tones a black hole emits, described by quasinormal mode frequencies. Earlier work suggested such corrections might hide in the fundamental tone, so the authors focus on the higher overtones instead.

Calculations for a round, non-spinning black hole show that the corrections reshape the effective potential near the horizon, and the overtone frequencies shift far more than the fundamental one. As the order of the correction grows, the shifts grow too. Fitted ringdown waveforms confirm the shifted tones can still be picked out of the signal, giving observers a sharper test of gravity.
arxiv-2512-22828:
Juha Park, Ian Roberts, and Wonjae Shin propose a faster way for ground systems to acquire signals from low Earth orbit satellites. Strong beamforming is needed to beat the severe signal loss over that distance. But first the satellite's position must be found, and the usual method sweeps a beam across the sky, wasting time. Their framework turns two traditional nuisances, Doppler shift and beam squint, into the measurement itself.

They derive a closed-form rainbow beamformer that uses beam squint, the way beam direction drifts with frequency, so different frequencies point where satellites with matching Doppler shifts should be. Several satellites can then be received at once with no sweeping. Three Doppler-aware angle estimation algorithms extract positions from the received signals. Simulations show better acquisition accuracy than beam sweeping while using far fewer time slots.
arxiv-2512-23028:
Thomson Tong and Diba Darooneh report on a system that reads body language in videos with vision-language models. Their pipeline samples frames and asks a model to find visible people. The model draws pixel-space bounding boxes with attributes such as emotion. The system checks replies against a fixed schema and can render an annotated video. Two current models, from the Qwen and Llama families, are compared, with attention to how architecture shapes engineering.

The report is candid about failure modes. Structured output can be valid in form while semantically wrong about the frame. Schema validation checks structure, not whether a box actually lands on a person. Person identifiers exist only within a single frame under the prompting contract, and interactive single-frame analysis returns free text rather than schema-checked data. The authors draw lessons for defensible claims, robust interfaces, and honest evaluations of such systems.
arxiv-2512-23128:
Karolina Korgul and a ten-author team built TRAP, a benchmark measuring how easily web agents can be talked out of their assigned task. Agents that manage email or professional networking read dynamic web content, and hidden adversarial instructions inside interface elements can persuade them to wander off mission. TRAP systematizes these prompt injection attacks into realistic tasks with controlled persuasion techniques.

Across six frontier models, injections succeeded in about a quarter of tasks on average. Rates ranged from roughly one in eight for the most resistant model to over two in five for the most susceptible. Small changes to interface or context often doubled the success rate, which the authors read as systemic, psychologically driven vulnerability rather than random failure. The team also releases a modular social-engineering injection framework and experiments on high-fidelity website clones, so the benchmark can grow as agents and attacks evolve.
arxiv-2512-23228:
Manimala Mitra, Dipankar Pradhan, and Subham Saha revisit a dark matter candidate under pressure: a complex scalar particle that talks to ordinary matter only through the Higgs boson. Direct detection experiments have tightened the Higgs-portal coupling so much that the minimal model, with dark matter freezing out during the standard radiation era, is squeezed hard. Two escapes exist: a higher-dimensional Higgs-portal interaction, or a different early-universe history.

In an effective field theory, the authors compute production during the reheating and radiation eras. Freeze-out during reheating opens viable parameter regions that the standard story rules out through overproduction. The renormalizable coupling is constrained by relic density plus direct and indirect searches, while the operator's coupling is bounded by relic density and indirect signals from semi-annihilation. The paper computes how dark matter would be produced at hadron and lepton colliders, connecting cosmology to accelerator tests.
arxiv-2512-23328:
Huan-ang Gao and co-authors introduce CubeBench, a benchmark that stress-tests whether language model agents can reason about physical space over long horizons. Agents excel digitally but stumble in the physical world. There they must build a spatial mental model, track state through mental simulation, and explore actively while seeing only part of the scene. CubeBench isolates those three faculties using a familiar object: the Rubik's Cube.

Its three tiers progress from full symbolic state information to partial visual observation, diagnosing where an agent's spatial competence breaks. The results on leading models are stark: a uniform zero percent pass rate on the long-horizon tasks. The authors read that as a fundamental failure of long-term planning, not perception. A companion diagnostic framework supplies external solver tools to separate cognitive bottlenecks from raw capability. The failure-mode analysis is offered as guidance for building more physically grounded agents.
arxiv-2512-23428:
Hrishav Das and co-authors present a full observational portrait of supernova 2022eyw, a bright member of the Type Iax subclass, the feeble cousins of standard Type Ia explosions. Photometry and spectroscopy track it from before peak light to more than a hundred days after. It rose in about fifteen days to a peak brightness among the more luminous Iax events. Its light curve implies a modest yield of radioactive nickel, and ejecta of well under one solar mass.

Spectra show the subclass's signature evolution, iron features shifting from doubly to singly ionized as ejecta cool, with moderate speeds. Modeling finds well-mixed, iron-group-dominated ejecta with traces of unburnt carbon, the fingerprint of incomplete burning. Comparison with simulations points to a partial deflagration of a Chandrasekhar-mass white dwarf, between two standard model variants. The event supports pure deflagration as the mechanism behind luminous Type Iax supernovae.
arxiv-2512-23728:
Sepideh Adamiat, Wouter Kouw, and Bert de Vries design spiking neural networks that perform Bayesian inference the way brains might. Bayesian reasoning gives a principled account of perception and learning, while real neurons communicate in spikes, not in the smooth numbers of textbook inference. The paper connects the two pictures through message passing with Bernoulli messages, the simplest kind, each representing a binary probability.

Learning in their networks uses spike-timing-dependent plasticity, a biologically plausible rule in which synapses strengthen or weaken according to the relative timing of spikes, echoing Hebb's principle. The trained networks' behavior closely matched the true numerical solutions of the inference problems. As a versatility check, the authors implemented a factor graph from coding theory, showing the same spiking machinery can transmit signals over an unreliable channel.
arxiv-2512-23828:
David Galvin and four co-authors count graph colorings in the general sense of homomorphisms: an H-coloring of a graph G maps its vertices to a target graph H while preserving adjacency. Extremal questions ask which G, on a fixed number of vertices, admits the most or fewest such maps. Restricting G to trees, the authors ask when the humble path minimizes the count, and they name target graphs with that property Hoffman-London.

Their new technique exploits the target's automorphisms through an automorphic similarity matrix, from which the number of colorings of any tree can be computed; matrix conditions then certify when H is Hoffman-London. Several families pass the test, including loop threshold graphs and targets arising in statistical physics such as the Widom-Rowlinson model. Combining the method with extra observations, they fully characterize the minimizing trees for every target on three or fewer vertices.
arxiv-2512-23928:
Tianyuan Yu and four co-authors look back thirty years at SRM, the Scalable Reliable Multicast framework introduced in a 1995 SIGCOMM paper, and trace its fingerprints on Named Data Networking. SRM broke with its era by making delivery data-centric: instead of the sender guaranteeing transport, receivers noticed missing data and requested it by name. That idea seeded a research lineage, but deployment exposed a deep friction.

Applications named data, while the IP network underneath remained blind to names and delivered by address, so loss recovery stayed inefficient. Named Data Networking resolves the mismatch by aligning the network itself with data retrieval and by securing the data directly rather than the channel carrying it. The retrospective draws lessons about architectural semantics, arguing NDN's design emerged from decades of cumulative insight rather than a single invention.
arxiv-2512-24128:
Bruno Ebner and Daniel Hlubinka introduce a goodness-of-fit test for count data. The data fall on the natural numbers. The question is whether they follow the Zeta distribution. That law has a heavy tail. Its parameter is unknown. It must be estimated from the same data.

The test rests on a Stein-type characterization. The Zeta law is the stationary law of a birth-death process. That process supplies an operator through its generator. On genuine Zeta data, the operator should average to zero. The resulting statistic detects any departure in the long run. Its null behavior is established. A parametric bootstrap is also justified. Monte Carlo comparisons benchmark the test. Rivals include the only earlier Zeta-specific procedure. General tests based on distribution functions compete as well.
arxiv-2512-25028:
Babu and Sumit Biswas develop a universal seesaw version of the Pati-Salam model, which unifies quarks and leptons of each family into common multiplets. Parity is spontaneously broken, which helps solve the strong CP problem without an axion. The Higgs sector stays very simple, with a single pair of Higgs fields in left and right forms.

Fermion masses arise from mixing chiral fermions with vector-like quarks and leptons in larger representations. Particle theory readers get a unified model where neutrino masses, fermion masses, and the strong CP puzzle are addressed together. Simplicity of the Higgs sector is a notable virtue among unified models.
arxiv-2601-06628:
Ashutosh Dwibedi and co-authors study the pion's internal structure in 2026. They use the light-front quark model for their calculations throughout. Distribution functions are their tool for picturing the pion's insides.

They investigate the ground state and two radially excited states. The ground state is the familiar 1S pion configuration. The first two excited states are labeled 2S and 3S. Comparing all three shows how excitation changes the pion's structure. Light-front models picture hadrons as quarks moving near light speed. Distribution functions summarize where momentum and spin sit inside. Hadron physicists get new detail on excited pions, rarely measured directly. The results guide future experiments and lattice calculations alike.
arxiv-2601-07228:
Arash Amini and Luciano Vinas wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on how close a sample sits to truth. They study the gap between a sample spread and the true spread. The gap is gauged by the 1-Wasserstein distance, the cost of reshaping one spread into the next. Their data points link to each other.

Most past bounds lean on the points being free of each other, as in a result due to Sanov. Other bounds ask for a set mix rate. Amini and Vinas need just two things. First, the spread of the sample's moments must stay in check. Second, the tail of the data must obey a loose rule they call sub-Gaussianity, in a form that can bend to the case. Their proof, by the method of moments, lets the points lean on each other a great deal, as long as their moments act as foreseen.
arxiv-2601-07428:
Aleksander Cieślak and colleagues study a family of ideals in set theory connected to a classic forcing method. Their 2026 preprint gives an extensive study of idealized Miller null sets. These are sigma-ideals on the Baire space, indexed by ideals on countable sets. They mirror how the meager ideal relates to Cohen forcing. Cardinal invariants measure how large or small these sets can be.

Such invariants compare the sizes of different notions of smallness in infinite sets. The idealized Miller construction lets the authors vary the underlying ideal and watch the invariants respond. Results of this kind map the structure of the real line at a very fine level. The paper serves set theorists interested in forcing, ideals, and the continuum. It extends a well-studied analogy into a broader family.
arxiv-2601-07528:
Gagan Bhatia and a large team study how language models answer Islamic questions. Errors here carry serious religious weight, so grounding matters more than fluency. Standard multiple-choice tests miss key real-world failures, the authors argue. Models may invent free-form answers or fail to abstain when evidence is lacking. Their 2026 preprint moves from plain retrieval to agentic retrieval.

Retrieval-augmented generation supplies source text to ground an answer. An agentic version lets the system plan searches and check evidence in steps. The team examines faithfulness, meaning answers that stay true to sources. They also value proper abstention when sources do not support an answer. The work speaks to builders of religious question answering tools.
arxiv-2601-07628:
