Hongpei Li and colleagues scale a linear programming solver across many graphics processors. Their 2026 preprint presents a distributed version of the primal-dual hybrid gradient algorithm. This algorithm family has shown strong performance on single GPUs. Industrial problems, though, often exceed one GPU's memory and speed. Linear programming underlies logistics, energy planning, and much of operations research.

Splitting the solver across machines raises hard questions about communication and load balance. The authors tackle that distributed design for massive-scale problems. Success would let firms solve planning problems too large for a single node. The work sits where optimization theory meets high-performance computing. Readers building solvers for very large instances are the readers.
arxiv-2601-07928:
Nicole M. Lloyd-Ronning, Omer Bromberg, and Tsvi Piran chart how long gamma-ray bursts truly last, after correcting for distance effects. They present the distribution of intrinsic duration of bursts' prompt emission. Earlier work by some of the authors found evidence for collapsar progenitors. That evidence rested on a plateau in the distribution of T90, the time covering ninety percent of the prompt emission. Their 2026 preprint expands that analysis across cosmic time.

Intrinsic duration means the duration at the source, before cosmic expansion stretches it. Comparing distributions across eras tests whether burst progenitors change as the universe ages. Collapsars are massive stars whose collapse powers long bursts. A stable plateau signature would support that picture broadly. The paper serves gamma-ray burst scholars. It uses duration statistics to read the history of the stars that make bursts.
arxiv-2601-08028: Dongwei Chen, Emily King, and Clayton Shonkwiler study dual frames that work across different domains. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that sampling and reconstruction tools often live in distinct settings. A Dirac delta and a band-limited bump in classical sampling give one clear example. Oblique dual frames generalize this split setup, and the authors add new tools to study them. They also introduce a probabilistic variant of oblique dual frames. The work serves readers in signal processing and applied harmonic analysis.
arxiv-2601-08428: Vijay Pratap Sharma and co-authors present Bio-RV, a compact RISC-V processor for biomedical control. Their 2026 arXiv paper targets accelerator-based biomedical systems and implantable pacemaker systems. Bio-RV is a multi-cycle RV32I core built for low power and small resource use. It gives explicit execution control and external instruction loading. Those features support controlled firmware deployment, chip bring-up, and post-silicon testing. A small open core could help medical device teams verify behavior closely, where safety and battery life both matter.
arxiv-2601-08528: Yuchen Peng and co-authors present SVFusion, a CPU-GPU architecture for large-scale vector search. Their 2026 arXiv paper addresses approximate nearest neighbor search, which underpins retrieval and recommendation systems. Vector data growth has made efficient real-time indexing essential. SVFusion splits work across CPU and GPU in a co-processing design. Real-time search over huge embedding collections serves chatbots, shopping, and media apps. A balanced architecture could raise throughput without forcing all data onto costly GPU memory.
arxiv-2601-08628:
Jibril Ben Achour, Adolfo Cisterna, Amaro Diaz, and Keanu Muller wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on black holes that change over time in a magnetic field. The team builds a new exact solution of the Einstein-scalar-Maxwell equations. The black hole sits in an outer electromagnetic field that shifts with time. Most exact forms treat the hole as fixed and lone.

The new form adds two parts that exact work often leaves out. The first is a cosmos that moves and shifts around the hole, not a still backdrop. The second is the full push-back of the outer fields on the shape of space, with no weak-field shortcut. Such a form gives theorists a more true-to-life case to test. They can probe how a hole acts in a charged, shifting cosmos with math alone. That helps where pure computer runs are hard to check.
arxiv-2601-08828:
Xindi Wu and a team from NVIDIA and two US schools ask which train clips shape how a video tool moves things. Video tools can now make smooth clips from a text cue. Yet we know little of how train data steers the moves in those clips. A clip of a ball in flight may teach more than a still street scene.

Their tool is called Motive. It tracks the pull of each train clip on the moves a tool makes. It uses slope based math, scaled to work on huge, high grade sets. A reader who trains video tools gets a way to pick train clips with care. Good picks may cut cost and lift move quality at the same time.
arxiv-2601-09328:
Adrien Vandenbroucque, Amedeo Esposito, and Michael Gastpar study how a channel shrinks the gap between two spreads of chance. Such shrink is called contraction. It sets how fast a markov chain forgets its start, and how much a channel can leak on its input. The gap here is the Renyi divergence, a broad class set by an order pick.

They set that class next to the well read phi class of gaps. Some shrink traits hold for both. Some flip with the order pick of the Renyi class. That split tells a user which past claims they can port, and which they must prove a new. A reader in facts work gets a map of a key shrink class.
arxiv-2601-09428:
Siyi Li and four co-authors teach transformer models to draw CAD profiles the way Euclid built figures. Their 2026 arXiv paper produces a profile as a sequence of simple construction steps. The steps use tools in the spirit of ruler and compass: offsets, rotations, and intersections of curves.

A designer supplies starting geometry, and the model builds the final points and curves step by step. Working through explicit steps, rather than emitting raw coordinates, mirrors how human drafters plan a sketch. It also gives a checkable path from input to output. The approach could make generated CAD easier to edit and trust.
arxiv-2601-09828:
Xiaoxu Ma, Runhao Li, Xiangbo Zhang, and Zhenyu Weng unify two training styles for image hashing. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents UniHash. Deep hashing turns images into short codes so huge libraries can be searched fast.

Most methods train either pointwise or pairwise. Pointwise training wins on known categories; pairwise training generalizes better to new ones. A real system must do both. UniHash joins the two paradigms in one framework. Strong codes for unseen classes matter a great deal as catalogs keep growing into new topics that no one has labeled yet.
arxiv-2601-09928:
Saber Zerhoudi and Michael Granitzer take up a clash in web search. Good AI help often needs rich user data. But most tools send that data to firms far away. Users then lose say over what is shared and kept.

The pair built a browser add on that keeps the help in the browser. It gives search aid on the user's own device. That way, private browse data need not leave the machine. The paper shows the tool as a real choice, not just an idea. It is aimed at readers who care about both smart search and privacy.
arxiv-2601-10128:
Di Wang, Zhenhua Wu, Yu Liu, Kai Chang, and Shaohua Wu build small AI tools for a hard trade with thin data. The trade is chip design by TCAD sim. Such trades need tools that write code a real tool can run. Fluent text is not enough.

The team gives a schema first plan. A schema is a strict form for the code. The plan aligns the model to that form first. That aids work where data is scarce. They show the plan on TCAD tasks. The model writes scripts that build and run. The work is a guide for like trades with the same bind.
arxiv-2601-10428:
Xiaolin Liu and Sachiko Kuroyanagi study a faint hum of gravity waves that comes and goes. Vast pairs of black holes merge far away. Each merge is too faint to hear on its own. As a group, they form a hum in the data. That hum is not smooth. It blinks as loud pairs pass.

The team ask how the ear of the net shapes that hum. Each tool in the net hears in its own band and way. Part one of their work folds that reply in. It shows how a blinking hum looks to real tools. That step is key to a first catch of the hum.
arxiv-2601-10628:
Mihailo Stojnic studies the symmetric binary perceptron, a simple model of a neuron with weights of plus or minus one. Such models can show a gap between what statistics allow and what algorithms can find. That gap is called a statistical-computational gap. Stojnic attacks the question with random duality theory.

He uses a parametric form of the fully lifted random duality theory. A key sequence in the method can switch from ordered by size to freely ordered. That switch changes the threshold where solutions exist. From it, he reads signs of a nonzero gap. The work adds precision to what theory says about hard random problems.
arxiv-2601-10928:
Zhaosheng Li and a large team report X-ray and radio observations of the pulsar MAXI J1957+032. The source is an accreting millisecond X-ray pulsar, a neutron star spinning hundreds of times per second while it feeds. The study covers two major outbursts, in 2022 and 2025. The team reanalyzed the 2022 data from the NICER telescope.

From observations in the 0.3 to 5 keV band, they extracted the spin frequency and orbital parameters. Timing across outbursts shows how the spin evolves as matter falls in. Multi-wavelength coverage ties the X-ray pulse to the radio picture. Such records test how neutron stars gain spin and how their magnetic fields channel the inflow.
arxiv-2601-11828:
Trevor M. Leslie and Jan Peszek study how groups of moving agents line up. The Euler Alignment system models flocks and swarms. In the topological form, links depend on both gap and on how much mass lies between two agents.

That form was brought in by Shvydkoy and Tadmor. It can match flocks where each bird watches a fixed count of peers, not a fixed range. The team study the pure form and the mixed form of these rules. Their proofs help show when a swarm will move as one.
arxiv-2601-11928:
Ishmael Amartey asks how public school spending links to income gaps across US counties. He uses data from 2010 to 2022 and quantile regression, a tool that checks links at each level of the gap. Total spending per pupil is the first term he tests.

He finds total spending links to a small rise in the gap. The link is stronger in counties where the gap is already high. The mix of spending matters much more than the total. Which items funds go to may shape gaps more than how much is spent.
arxiv-2601-12028:
Kun-Yan Jiang, W.-Y. Chiu, and Yuan-Po Tsai seek top profit for electric vehicle charging sites. More EVs link to power grids, with gains for cost and air. But unplanned charging can strain the grid and cut profit.

They study many sites with storage banks and renewable sources. Sites can also trade energy with each other. A multi-agent learning method sets charge and trade plans. Good plans must serve cars, guard the grid, and earn well at once. The work is in Sustainable Energy, Grids and Networks.  The plan must also respect grid caps at peak hours.
arxiv-2601-12728:
Momoko Makita, Tomoharu Oka, Shiho Tsujimoto, and Tatsuya Kotani report new molecular features near the W44 cloud. W44 is a molecular cloud tied to a supernova remnant in our galaxy. Using ALMA data on carbon monoxide emission, they find eight compact features with extremely broad velocity widths. They name these features Petit Bullets, around a previously known Bullet.

Each Petit Bullet shows a distinct V shape in position velocity space. That shape recalls the Y shaped morphology of the original Bullet. Similar shapes hint at a common origin for all nine features. Broad velocity features can trace violent ejections or shocks in the cloud. The discovery adds a family of clues about energetic events near W44.
arxiv-2601-13028:
Levon Mardoyan and Armen Nersessian build new forms of a known quantum system. The base system joins a Kepler like pull with a Dirac monopole, a lone magnetic charge. It was first put forward about five decades ago by Zwanziger and, on their own, by McIntosh and Cisneros.

The pair now place their new forms on two curved spaces. One is the three dim sphere. The other is a two sheet hyperboloid, a saddle like curved space. For each form they work out the full set of allowed energy levels. They also give the wave forms in clean norm form. They close by showing that each new system keeps a least level of extra symmetry, called minimal superintegrability.
arxiv-2601-13228:
Tianqi Du and co-authors show that step by step text models can match diffusion models at free order writing. Diffusion text models can fill a gap at any spot in a text and can use both sides of the gap. That flex helps tasks such as fill in, rewrite, and self fix.

Yet their form caps depth. They guess one part from a next part in a single step link. Step by step models tend to give text of more grade and calm. The team shows how such models can be taught to write in any order too. If the claim holds, teams may not need a split model class for flex tasks.
arxiv-2601-13328:
Geoffrey Churchill and Steven Skiena cut the extra cost that low resource tongues pay in AI tools. Next to English, such tongues need far more tokens to state the same thought. A token is the chunk a model reads at a step. More tokens mean more fee, more power, and less room left for the task.

That gap is called a tokenization premium. It stems from how token cuts were fit to rich tongues first. The team gives ways to shrink the premium for thin tongues. For users of such tongues, cuts here mean AI that costs less and can hold more of a chat at once.
arxiv-2601-13428:
Xinyuan Chen and Fan Li estimate joint treatment effects in cluster trials with many outcomes. In such a trial, whole groups, such as clinics or schools, are assigned a cure, not lone folks. New trials oft track many outcomes at once, to catch both gains and risks of a cure.

Teams want one joint mark of effect. Old tools treat one outcome at a time, or rest on model forms with a dim causal sense and weak guards. Chen and Li give a broad causal mark for the joint case. Their estimate is built to stay sound when models bend. For trial teams, a joint mark with a clear causal sense aids firm calls.
arxiv-2601-13528:
Jackson Kaunismaa and co-authors show how guarded model out puts can be used to teach open models bad skills. Firms guard top models with filters that block risky out puts. Such guards are meant to stop misuse at the source.

The team shows an elicitation attack. By fine tune of an open model on guarded out puts, bad skills can be drawn out in the open model. The guard's own safe text holds clues that teach the skill past the guard's aim. For safety teams, the find is a warn that out put guards alone do not cap what a foe can build.
arxiv-2601-14028:
Alejandro Laso Garcia and a large team present an imaging platform for extreme plasma work in 2026. The platform sits at the HED-HiBEF instrument at the European XFEL. It serves high energy density and inertial fusion energy research. The platform combines the XFEL beam with two lasers.

One laser is ReLaX, a high-intensity short-pulse system. The other is DiPOLE-100X, a high-energy nanosecond-pulse laser. X-ray imaging can catch fast changes inside dense matter as lasers strike it. Such views help fusion teams see if their designs compress fuel as planned. Such views are hard to get with Earth-based tools. Dense hot matter can be probed for a flash, and the flash can tell a lot.
arxiv-2601-14528:
Luis Lazo, Hamed Jelodar, and Roozbeh Razavi-Far probe language model safety in this 2026 paper. They propose a homotopy-inspired prompt obfuscation framework. Prompt obfuscation rewords a request so its surface form hides its intent. Homotopy, a math idea about gradual deformation, guides how the prompts are engineered.

By systematically applying such prompts, the team shows how latent model behaviors can be influenced in unexpected ways. The study aims to deepen understanding of security and safety vulnerabilities in large language models. Readers get a structured way to test whether safety training holds when a request arrives in disguise.
arxiv-2601-14828:
Deniz Tuncer and Burak Kocuk take on a design task from materials science. Their 2026 arXiv paper concerns thin film stacks laid over a metal base. The aim is to boost how much light the coated metal reflects back.

A stack is built from thin layers of glass-like materials, each with its own thickness. Past work leaned on rough rules of thumb and often served just one wavelength of light. The authors build an exact math model for many wavelengths at once. Their model uses mixed-integer quadratically constrained programming, a form of exact global optimization.
arxiv-2601-15228:
Nathan Belrhali, Arthur Poisson, Sébastien Renaux-Petel, and Denis Werth build a momentum space for quantum fields in an expanding universe. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with de Sitter spacetime, the model space of fast early-universe expansion. They work in its Poincaré slicing.

Momentum space is where field calculations are usually done. The authors construct a natural version that needs no perturbative expansion. They identify the de Sitter frequency as a label of the space's symmetry group. That label ties the momenta to the unitary representations of the full de Sitter isometry group.
arxiv-2601-15328:
Ie. O. Petrenko and T. V. Obikhod compute how often three Higgs-like bosons would decay into a pair of muons. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with a model with extra Higgs fields, in its broken phase. A rare decay of the known Higgs boson drives the work.

The ATLAS experiment recently reported evidence for the Higgs decaying to a muon pair. That decay opens a rare window on how the Higgs couples to second-generation fermions. The authors compute the branching ratios for all three neutral Higgs states of the model. Those rates can be set against the new data.
arxiv-2601-15428:
P. Kurfürst, G. Bless, and co-authors compute what a supernova looks like when the matter around it is lopsided. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with supernovae that crash into circumstellar matter, the gas a star shed before it blew up. That matter often forms a disc or bipolar lobes.

A disc can come from mass transfer in a binary system. Lobes can come from a violent pre-explosive ejection, as seen in luminous blue variable stars. The team presents upgraded numerical calculations of the clash. They produce light curves, magnitudes, spectra, and polarization for these shapes.
arxiv-2601-15528:
Jiazhu Xie and five co-authors report a case study on chatbots for small firms in a 2026 arXiv paper. Large language models can power question-answering systems for such firms. These systems could automate customer support and staff access to internal knowledge. Real deployment is another matter. Costs, engineering effort, and security risks all stand in the way. Retrieval-augmented systems face these hurdles most sharply.

The paper studies a distributed chatbot deployment platform in industry use. Security for LLM-as-a-service is the title's focus. Small firms lack the staff to harden such systems alone. A shared platform that handles the hard parts could spread the benefits. The case study grounds the claims in one real rollout, rather than lab tests.
arxiv-2601-15728:
Hangle Hu, Chenyu Hou, Bin Cao, and Ruizhe Li compare two ways to query data in a 2026 arXiv paper. Text-to-SQL is the dominant route to databases. It turns questions into SQL queries. Real analytics work is shifting, though. Analysts often need Python or Pandas for file-based data and complex workflows. General-purpose code offers flexibility SQL lacks. Yet the reliability of text-to-Python for core retrieval is underexplored.

The authors benchmark the two approaches head to head. Their title names two factors: explicit logic and ambiguity. Code states logic plainly, step by step. Questions, though, can be ambiguous in either language. Knowing where Python wins or fails guides tool design. Data teams choosing an AI query layer face this exact choice.
arxiv-2601-16028: Moritz Wedemeyer writes on flexibility measures for systems in a 2026 arXiv paper. His title joins three ideas: a flexibility index, conditions, and data. Such an index gauges how much a system can adapt when conditions shift. A conditional form ties the score to operating conditions. A data-driven form computes the score from data, not from a model alone. The record's abstract stops at the author's institute list, which spans energy and process engineering groups in Germany and London. The full text holds the definitions the record never reaches.
arxiv-2601-16328:
Enrique Segura Carrillo and coauthors build two tone traps for qudit sums in strontium atoms. Their 2026 preprint deals with bare atoms as a base for quantum work. Bare atoms serve for clocks, sense and sums at top grade. Known magic traps fail for qudits in states with spin past zero. Fail traps cut how long a qudit state stays clean.

Two tone traps aim to give magic terms for those states. Magic terms hold all qudit states in the same trap depth. Same depth keeps qudit acts clean for more time. The work uses the 87 form of strontium atoms. It seeks long lived qudits for sums and clocks.
arxiv-2601-16828:
Zhecheng Hu, Wei Zhu, Shuming Wang, and Sharon Wang find six new cases of a rare star dimming. In these cases, a disk rings a pair of stars. The disk tilts off the pair's path plane. As it wobbles, it blocks the pair's light in beats. Their 2026 preprint found the six by a wide scan of sky shots.

The scan drew on data from the Zwicky survey. Fewer than ten such cases had known beats before. Six more give labs fresh labs for disk work. Disk tilt and warp can be read from the dimming. Such reads test how disks around pairs grow and shift.
arxiv-2601-17028:
Gnankan Landry Regis N'guessan builds a math kit for small ARM chips. His kit works in tropical algebra, a strange rule set. In that set, plus and times swap for min and max style rules. Many hard path and plan tasks turn plain there. Shortest paths and work plans fit that frame well. His 2026 preprint packs those rules in a light library named PALMA.

The kit uses SIMD tricks to speed grid math on chips. Small chips in cars and tools gain from that speed. Spectral reads add a check on grid traits. Worked cases show the kit on real tasks. Such kits bring deep math to tiny gear.
arxiv-2601-17128:
Anran Li, John Swensen, and Mehdi Hosseinzadeh split hard control tasks in blocks to solve them. Such tasks bend in non-convex ways, with dips and traps. Old tools oft stall in poor dips. Or they cost too much time to run at all. Their 2026 preprint swaps blocks in turn to crack the task. Each block holds some vars fixed while the rest move.

Block steps are cheap and can dodge poor dips. The swaps run till the blocks agree on a fit. Control tasks in robots and grids fit this form. Cheap true fits there save power and time.
arxiv-2601-17628:
Felipe Arenas-Uribe wrote a tutorial on higher-order gravity models for space systems. Gravity shapes the modeling and control of spacecraft. The Newtonian point-mass model is a useful first step. Real bodies, though, are not perfect spheres. Oblateness and mass lumps change their pull. The tutorial builds up spherical harmonics to capture those traits.

Harmonics add detail in ordered layers. Users can stop at the order their mission needs. A clear tutorial serves students and mission designers alike. It bridges basic training and flight-grade models. Better gravity models mean tighter orbits and safer maneuvers. The work makes a hard topic approachable in steps.
arxiv-2601-17728:
Meysam Alizadeh, Fabrizio Gilardi, and Zeynab Samei elicit moral values from language models without supervision. AI systems now act across daily life. Their behavior should rest on human values. Past work hints models have limited moral reasoning on their own. That led to calls for explicit moral teaching. Ground truth for morals is hard to build, since frameworks are plural and biased.

An unsupervised method reads values the model already holds. It avoids baking one group's labels in as truth. Knowing held values is a first step to align them. The work serves auditors who probe model behavior. It treats moral pluralism as a design fact.
arxiv-2601-17928: Mohamad Maassarani proves results about quandles and the groups built from them. His 2026 preprint studies the enveloping group of a quandle, an algebraic structure used in knot theory. One result says a quandle and its image inside its enveloping group share the same enveloping group. The image quandle is also shown to be injective, so no two of its elements collapse into one.
arxiv-2601-18828:
Mohammad Zare builds IPBC, a tool that lets a human guide the group-ing of rich data while a tool does the bulk of the work. Rich data, with scores of traits per case, is hard to group. The gaps that sort cases shrink in worth as traits grow. When the tool's groups are drawn flat, they tend to stack and blur. A human can't fix what they can't see.

IPBC draws the groups in a way the user can bend by hand. The user can split, merge, and move groups while the tool keeps the maths sound. That loop aims for groups that are both true to the data and of use to the staff who know the field. Good groups are the base of work in sales, health, and the field sciences. It could beat both pure hand work and pure code.
arxiv-2601-18928:
Andrés Rubiano computes the center of a family of algebras built by a double extension. These algebras grow from smaller ones by adding two new generators at once, under rules set by fixed parameters. The type studied here carries a long numeric label drawn from its structure.

Rubiano finds the center, the part that commutes with all else, and in some cases smaller central subalgebras too. Part of the work leans on computations in the SageMath system. As a payoff, the results give fresh examples tied to the Zariski cancellation problem, a long open question in algebra.
arxiv-2601-19028:
Bo Leng and Vien Van study flat bands in light based lattices that twist in time. Flat band states, where energy barely changes with momentum, give a rich stage for strong interaction effects. In still two dimensional systems, though, a perfectly flat band can only sit in a trivial phase with no topological charge.

Floquet systems, driven in repeating time steps, break that limit. The pair work out the helicity of such bands for photons and find it quantized in a non-Abelian way. Their result opens a route to flat bands with real topological character, built from light.
arxiv-2601-19328:
Robbie Webbe and seven co-authors report first results from a hunt for slow changing X-ray sources. Their survey, STONKS, mines the XMM-Newton telescope's scans of the Milky Way's plane for long term transients. High energy transients reveal the most extreme events in the universe, but catching and following them is limited by the tools.

Slow transients are easy to miss: they change over months, not seconds, and most hunts favor the fast. A survey built for the slow ones opens a window on black holes and stars that flare and fade on human timescales. The first results show what that window reveals.
arxiv-2601-19528:
D. O. Armstrong and six colleagues build tiny sensors that can detect chemicals dissolved in a liquid. Their device is a photonic integrated circuit, a small chip that guides light instead of electric current. On the chip sits a microring resonator, a loop that traps light at set wavelengths. When a target substance is present, the light in the loop shifts, and that shift signals a detection.

The team studies how sensitive such a sensor can be. Their rings are made from silicon nitride, a material known for low light loss. The key measure is how much the signal moves when the liquid's refractive index changes by a small amount. High sensitivity means the chip can flag very low concentrations. Such sensors could serve in medical tests and water checks where samples are small.
arxiv-2601-19628:
Mairieli Wessel, Daniel Feitosa, and Sangeeth Kochanthara write a design fiction about the future of research. Design fiction tells a story about a possible future to spark debate. Their setting is software engineering research, where publication pressure keeps rising. Generative AI tools are now routine in writing, coding, and reviewing.

The story asks what happens to skill when machines do more of the work. Concerns include fading expertise, blurred responsibility, and trust in published results. Efficiency gains are real, but so are the risks. By staging the crisis as fiction, the authors let the community argue about it early. The piece is a warning and an invitation to set norms before habits harden.
arxiv-2601-19728: A report from the Belle II experiment describes how its simulations keep pace with real running conditions. Belle II, at the SuperKEKB accelerator in Tsukuba, Japan, hunts for physics beyond the Standard Model, with a focus on flavour measurements. Its Monte Carlo simulations must mirror the detector's changing state and the shifting beam backgrounds during data taking. The run-dependent approach rebuilds those conditions period by period, so simulated events match the data they are compared with.
arxiv-2601-20228:
Weizhou Wang, Xuanxi Zhang, Jonathan Weare, and Aaron R. Dinner present GG-PI, a method for capturing quantum effects in molecular simulation at lower cost. Nuclear quantum effects matter for accurate molecular modeling, but the standard tool, path integral molecular dynamics, is expensive. Their framework uses a ring-polymer picture of the atoms.

GG-PI joins generative modeling of a single-bead density with Gibbs sampling. From classical simulation data, it recovers quantum statistics for the system. Cheaper quantum-accurate sampling would help chemists model reactions and materials where light atoms, such as hydrogen, make quantum behavior hard to ignore. The gain is plain: less cost, for the same trust in the end result. It is, at heart, a bid to spend less and learn as much.
arxiv-2601-20428:
Sönke Beier writes a practical guide to diffusion maps, a method that uncovers curved low-dimensional structure inside high-dimensional data. The spectral technique is used ever more widely across biology, engineering, and the social sciences. Yet preprocessing, parameter settings, and component choice strongly shape the manifold it returns.

Those choices have not been discussed comprehensively in the literature, Beier argues. His paper works through how each decision affects the result in practice. A clear guide matters because two analysts can feed the same data to the same method and, through settings alone, reach unlike conclusions.
arxiv-2601-20628:
Efthymios Costa, Ioanna Papatsouma, and Angelos Markos present sparse clustering through a deterministic information bottleneck algorithm. Clustering assigns objects to groups with desirable traits. When the true cluster structure lives in only a subset of the features, traditional techniques struggle, since the irrelevant features drown the signal.

Their information-theoretic framework handles sparse data by weighting features and clustering jointly. Finding the few features that matter is common in genomics and text, where thousands of measurements hide a handful of drivers. Joint weighting could give cleaner groups in such data. In plain terms, the method lets the data say which facts count, and which can be set to one side.
arxiv-2601-20828:
Ben Gripaios and Oscar Randal-Williams prove a limit on what a class of physical theories can detect. Their 2026 paper concerns topological quantum field theories, or TQFTs. The authors show that such theories cannot detect certain homotopy spheres. The key example is Milnor's exotic seven-dimensional sphere. It looks like a standard sphere to topology, yet it is smooth in a different way.

The result holds under very general hypotheses. It covers a wide variety of target categories, even infinite ones. It also allows arbitrary tangential structures. The spheres in question bound parallelisable manifolds, a mild condition. The finding is a caution for hopes that TQFTs can see all fine structure. It marks a clear line between what these theories can and cannot sense.
arxiv-2601-20928:
A. T. Barnes and eleven co-authors warn that flat sky pictures can lie about how stars are born. Their 2026 paper studies projection effects in star-forming regions. Stars form as molecular clouds fragment into dense cores, filaments, and sub-clusters. The characteristic spacing of those cores is a key observable. It carries the imprint of the fragmentation physics. Observers often compare it with theoretical scales like the Jeans length or the sonic length.

The trap is projection. A three-dimensional web is seen as a two-dimensional image. True spacings shrink and merge on the flat sky. Comparisons with theory can then mislead. The authors quantify how projection distorts the spacing signal. Their corrections help observers read cloud structure honestly. The work serves any study that maps where new stars condense.
arxiv-2601-21128:
Václav Javorek and four co-authors argue that one right answer is the wrong standard for sign language translation. Their 2026 paper studies training and evaluation with paraphrases. Most translation corpora pair each signed utterance with a single written reference. Sign and spoken languages, though, relate in a highly non-isomorphic way. Multiple translations can be equally valid for one signing. A single reference constrains both training and scoring.

Metrics such as BLEU reward matching the one reference. Good translations that choose other words get punished. Paraphrase references would credit valid variety instead. The authors explore that shift for sign language translation. Fairer scoring could change which systems look best. The work matters for deaf communities who rely on this technology. It pushes evaluation to respect the nature of signed languages.
arxiv-2601-21328:
Hiroki Nakano, Tôru Sakai, and Yuko Hosokoshi map the ground state of a magnetic model on a special lattice. The lattice is built from linked pairs of sites, called dimers, set at right angles. Each site carries a large spin, and neighbors prefer to point in opposed ways.

Using exact numerical diagonalization, the authors find the edges of two phases. One phase is the exact dimer state, and the other shows classic ordered magnetism. Their results are read alongside earlier work on smaller spins. The map helps show how strong quantum effects reshape magnetism as spin size grows.
arxiv-2601-21728:
K.-H. Chae and six co-authors set out to measure gravity where it is extremely weak. Their 2026 study uses the three-dimensional motions of isolated wide binary stars, pairs that orbit each other at great distance. The sample holds thirty-six binaries, chosen as the best available set with accurate measured velocities.

At such low speeds of change, standard gravity and some rival ideas predict different motions. Careful measures can therefore test which picture fits. The title reports that the team finds an anomaly, a mismatch with the expected pull. Work like this matters. Wide binaries offer a clean local test of gravity, free of the dark matter debates that cloud measures in whole galaxies.
arxiv-2601-21828:
Phillip Antis and five co-authors prove a result about sums and products of small sets of numbers. A classic puzzle in number theory starts from a small set of numbers. It asks how large the set of pairwise sums must be. It asks the same for pairwise products. Sums and products cannot both stay small at once.

The team settles the cases of sets with ten and eleven natural numbers. Every set of ten numbers yields at least thirty distinct pairwise sums or at least thirty distinct pairwise products. And the paper shows this bound is sharp with an explicit example. Results like this feed the wider sum-product theory, which links elementary counting to deep questions about growth in arithmetic.
arxiv-2601-21928:
Reuben Wang proposes a way to stop ultracold molecules from destroying each other in collisions. Strongly dipolar molecules in excited rotational states are prized for quantum experiments, but collisions between them cause heavy losses, in pairs and in triples. Shielding them has been a long-standing goal.

His 2026 preprint combines a steady electric field with a microwave field. The steady field tunes two excited pair states into a Förster resonance, a condition where energy transfers efficiently. At the same time, the microwave field drives rotational transitions in a way that removes all long-range bound states. With no bound states to fall into, nearly complete suppression of collisional loss becomes possible, which would keep delicate molecular samples alive far longer.
arxiv-2601-22028:
Haoran Tang and Rajiv Khanna argue that most unlearning only teaches a model to stay quiet. Unlearning aims to remove specific knowledge from a trained model. Standard methods mimic a model retrained from scratch, using alignment-style objectives that act on the model's predictions, its output distribution.

Such methods reduce generation of the forgotten content, but the authors warn this can be mere suppression. The concepts may persist inside the model's representations, still entangled with knowledge that should be kept. Their 2026 preprint moves the objective from logits to latents, shaping internal representations directly. The distinction matters for privacy and safety law, where removal must be real, not a refusal script.
arxiv-2601-22328:
Luca Muscarnera and five co-authors seek the true rules behind a system from noisy, partial data. Their 2026 preprint presents MAAT, a method built on kernel state reconstruction with prior knowledge baked in. Past tools often crack under noise or hide the rules inside a black box.

MAAT aims to hand back clear, symbolic rules a human can read. It uses what experts already know to guide the search. Readable rules can be checked, trusted, and used to predict new cases. The work serves fields from climate to cell biology. It puts insight ahead of raw fit.
arxiv-2601-22428:
Isaac Pérez Castillo and four co-authors pool pass rates to judge active learning against plain lectures in first physics courses. Their 2026 preprint notes that research-backed teaching has grown for decades, yet student success still lags. They also stress a gap: few reports come from Latin American classes.

The team set a shared bar so pooled classes can be judged fairly. A common-gauge pool gives a cleaner read than lone class tales. The results can guide departments that must choose how to teach. They also lift a region's voice in the debate. The work is careful, shared evidence.
arxiv-2601-22528:
Hongze Mi and a large team give screen-using agents a memory that prunes and grows itself, with no training. Such agents drive apps through their screens, but long, cross-app tasks overflow their context. Their 2026 preprint names the system Darwinian Memory, after the way it keeps what works.

Useful notes survive and spread; weak ones fade. The self-tuning store aims to let agents learn from their own past runs. That could lift success on long chores like booking and filing. The work treats memory as a living part of the agent. It needs no costly retraining.
arxiv-2601-22628:
Chengyi Yang and a large team let a model teach itself at test time with a built course of tasks. Test-time training tunes a model on just the questions at hand. Their 2026 preprint, TTCS, notes that hard reasoning tasks defeat plain test-time tuning for two clear reasons.

Their fix synthesizes a curriculum: a staged set of tasks that grows toward the hard target. A good ladder lets the model climb instead of stall. The method keeps all tuning inside the test window. It aims at hard math and logic tasks. The work turns one hard ask into a course.
arxiv-2601-22928:
Alhassan Abdelhalim and three co-authors review what we really know about how language models work inside. These models are now used everywhere, yet the mechanisms behind their skill remain unclear. Many tools claim to explain them, but those tools are themselves not fully understood.

Their post-mortem sorts which claims about meaning inside transformers hold up, and which do not. Honest stock-taking matters because false confidence in explanations can mislead safety work. The review gives researchers a firmer base for the next round of methods. The post-mortem stance is deliberate: it judges the field's interpretability claims after the fact, against the evidence actually delivered.
arxiv-2601-23128:
Wenbo Liao and five co-authors quantify uncertainty for full rankings of items. Ranking models order products, papers, or candidates, and safe use needs honest error bounds. Conformal prediction can build sets for the true ranks of test items, using relative ranks from calibration data.

Full ranking is harder than top-few prediction, since every position matters. Their distribution-informed method aims for efficiency, keeping prediction sets small while valid. Trustworthy rankings help search, hiring, and recommendation systems explain their confidence. Relative ranks from calibration items anchor the construction, giving absolute rank sets for test items with stated coverage.
arxiv-2601-23228:
Ed Li, Junyu Ren, and Cat Yan fine-tune multi-agent systems with per-action process rewards. Multi-agent setups promise strong results through specialization. Training several agents at once faces two hurdles: assigning credit across agents, and the cost of many multi-agent rollouts.

Their MAPPA method uses AI feedback to reward each action, not just final outcomes. Finer rewards attack the credit problem and stretch each expensive rollout further. Process feedback could make agent teams trainable at realistic budgets. Per-action rewards from AI feedback attack both named challenges at once: credit assignment and sample efficiency.
arxiv-2603-01828:
Bauyrzhan Derbissaly and Nurbek Kakharman track eigenvalues of a biharmonic problem as its domain shrinks to a thin shell. Their 2026 work places the domain as a tubular neighborhood around a smooth planar region. The biharmonic operator, a fourth-order cousin of the Laplacian, governs plate-like bending problems.

A Steklov boundary condition ties boundary values to boundary flux through the eigenvalue itself. As shell thickness tends to zero, the team proves every eigenvalue tends to zero as well. That limit says thin shells lose all spectral stiffness in this Steklov sense, a clean asymptotic fact. Results of this kind guide how plate and shell models behave when thickness is a small parameter. They also show where thin models can safely replace full ones.
arxiv-2603-02028:
Ben Eze, Luca Magri, and Andrea Novoa rebuild full fluid flow fields from heavily masked, noisy snapshots. Their 2026 model, LAMP, adapts vision transformers, stars of image generation, to fluid dynamics data. Rebuilding high-dimensional fields from sparse sensors is a core challenge in scientific machine learning.

LAMP cuts each flow snapshot into patches, then compresses each patch with proper orthogonal decomposition. A single-layer transformer, trained by closed-form linear regression, rebuilds the full field from the masked input. Tests use two canonical two-dimensional wakes, one steady bluff body wake and one chaotic plate wake. Even with nine tenths masked, reconstruction stays accurate across a range of noise levels. The learned attention map doubles as a guide for optimal sensor placement, an interpretable bonus.
arxiv-2603-02128:
Veronika Solopova, Viktoria Skorik, Maksym Tereshchenko, and colleagues published this 2026 study of how language models act in world politics games. Six well-known models played four crisis cases drawn from real events. In each round they picked a set action and explained their choice. The team then compared those picks with human play.

Early rounds looked close to human choices, but the models drifted apart over time. Each model showed its own style and changed its plan in its own way. Their reasons leaned hard toward calm, joint work, and lower risk. They showed little hostile or rival thinking. That gap matters for anyone who might use such models to test policy or train staff.
arxiv-2603-02228:
Liang Chen and Qi Liu study memory limits for language model agents in this 2026 paper. A model's context window is small and costly, more like a cache than a full memory. Agents with outside read-write memory can in theory compute anything. In practice, what stays in the window decides what the agent can use.

Their design, Neural Paging, splits thinking from memory management. A small learned controller picks which tokens to keep for future use. The goal echoes a classic ideal: keep what will be needed soonest. Math shows the design cuts long-task cost from quadratic growth to a milder form. Tests on fake paging traces confirm the bounds hold, with room left for learned policies to do better.
arxiv-2603-02328:
Louis Paletta designs a local decoder for quantum error correction in this 2026 paper. Quantum memories store fragile data that noise constantly corrupts. Local decoders fix errors with simple rules shared across a chip, avoiding a central processor. Past local decoders for the toric code had weak thresholds and poor scaling.

Paletta's rule treats odd parity checks as defects that attract each other. Defects trade simple binary signals with neighbors to find partners. Simulations show error rates falling exponentially with system size below a critical noise level. The threshold gap to top central decoders shrinks by half on a log scale. Scaling is optimal at sizes experiments can reach. A fully local two-dimensional quantum memory thus looks practical.
arxiv-2603-02628:
Raghav Thakar, Gaurav Dixit, and Kagan Tumer extract trade-off fronts from pretrained controllers in this 2026 paper. Real agents must balance goals like speed, stability, and energy use. A Pareto front collects the policies that trade those goals optimally. Standard multi-objective learning builds fronts from scratch, ignoring existing specialists.

Preferences often emerge only after a policy was trained on one goal. Their offline method, MAPEX, reuses specialist policies, critics, and replay buffers. Specialist evaluations merge into a mixed advantage signal for each action. A behavior cloning loss, weighted by that signal, trains balanced new policies. On five simulated control suites, fronts matched established baselines. The sample cost was a tiny fraction of retraining from scratch, they report.
arxiv-2603-02728:
Yangchun Liu, Hairong Huang, Dong Wu, and colleagues report a way to heat fuel ions inside a proton-boron plasma. Their 2026 paper targets a fusion fuel that needs extreme heat and loses much energy as radiation. Heating the background protons directly would raise reaction rates without upsetting the plasma balance.

Using full kinetic simulations, they inject a proton beam and watch waves called ion Bernstein waves grow at set frequencies. Early on, wave energy splits fairly evenly between electrons and protons. Later, a shift of wave energy toward lower frequencies couples the waves mainly to protons, creating a fast proton group. That late-stage channel could make proton-boron fusion easier to sustain.
arxiv-2603-02828:
Shambel Sahlu and Amare Abebe test a universe where dark energy and dark matter trade energy by diffusion. Their 2026 paper constrains this diffusive dark fluid model with two major datasets. They combine cosmic microwave background data from Planck 2018 with distance data from the DESI instrument's second release.

The fitted expansion rates land close to the Planck value, with tensions the authors report as small in one case and modest in the other. They also compute how the energy exchange changes clumping growth and the matter power spectrum, the spread of structure across scales. Comparing those curves with the standard model shows where diffusion leaves a visible mark. Such checks narrow the room for interacting dark-sector theories.
arxiv-2603-02928:
Herman Tesso and Aki Vehtari fix a hidden flaw in a popular way of checking Bayesian models. Their 2026 paper studies LOO-PIT values, which should spread evenly between zero and one when a model is well calibrated. Each value comes from leaving one data point out and predicting it from the rest.

The catch is dependence: the leave-one-out predictions share nearly all their data, so the values lean on each other. The authors prove this dependence is real, grows with model complexity, and quietly weakens standard uniformity tests. They propose three corrected tests plus an automated plot that shows where calibration departs locally. On simulated and real data, the new tests caught misfits far more often than standard ones.
arxiv-2603-03028:
Yoan Spahn, Jens Hartmann, Benedikt Saalfrank, and colleagues make a cloud of atoms beam its light preferentially one way. The atoms sit inside a hollow-core waveguide, a fiber that guides both atoms and light. Unlike chiral setups, the coupling here is equal in both directions by design.

Laser-driven Raman transitions give the atoms oscillating phases that vary along the fiber, and their thermal motion turns that pattern into controllable directionality. By tuning the collective decay rate, the team pushed most emission into one direction. Light statistics shifted from thermal below threshold to coherent bursts above it, matching simulations and a simple motion-blur model. The effect opens nonreciprocal light-matter behavior in ordinary, non-chiral systems.
arxiv-2603-03128:
Isuru Ariyarathne, Gangani Ariyarathne, Alessandro Flammini, and colleagues catch manipulative social media accounts by watching how their behavior changes. Bots and coordinated campaigns often repurpose accounts or shift tactics to dodge detection. Existing detectors rarely use that change itself as evidence.

The team encodes each account's actions as a string of symbols, splits it into segments, and measures how much behavior shifts between neighbors. Honest accounts show steady change patterns, while bots cluster at very low or very high change. Coordinated accounts look alike within one campaign yet differ across campaigns. Classifiers trained on these change profiles scored well at spotting both bots and coordinated inauthentic behavior.
arxiv-2603-03228:
Damián Rafael Lattenero constructs a new space in general topology, the branch of mathematics that studies shape and nearness in abstract form. His 2026 paper builds the Extended Real Line with Reentry from the closed real line, endpoints included. The goal is a clean test case for fine distinctions between kinds of separation that topologists rank in the Clontz hierarchy.

The new space is compact and path-connected, and it is sober and uniquely sequential, yet its compact sets are not all closed. No compact path-connected space was known before that separates these two properties. Lattenero then generalizes the trick into a framework that builds similar spaces from many starting spaces, and shows the key hierarchy level survives repeated use and products.
arxiv-2603-03328:
Haruki Sakajo and four colleagues look inside language models through the structure of their layers. Interpretation work usually studies local links between tokens inside one layer, leaving the global pattern across layers unmapped. Their 2026 framework, StructLens, builds a maximum spanning tree over each layer's token representations, much as parsers build dependency trees for sentences, and compares layers by tree shape.

That structure-aware comparison paints a picture of layer similarity strikingly different from the standard cosine measure. Layers that look alike by content can differ in structure, and the reverse also holds. The signal proves practical as well: it guides layer pruning, the removal of layers to slim a model, better than content-based cues. The team releases its code for other researchers.
arxiv-2603-03428:
Tommaso Faleo and four colleagues build a light source that entangles photons in two ways at once. Hyperentanglement, being entangled in several properties simultaneously, raises the capacity of quantum communication, especially with frequency bins, which sort light by color and resist noise well. Their 2026 source works at telecom wavelengths in a single pass, with no filtering thrown away.

The trick is shaping: the team tailors the photons' joint spectrum by sculpting both the pump light and the crystal's nonlinear response. The resulting pairs are entangled in polarization and in frequency bins, with the state's size and makeup tunable on demand. Careful measurements, including two-photon interference, show polarization quality above ninety-nine percent averaged across frequency bins and strong spectral entanglement matching simulations. The authors pitch the source as a scalable route to high-dimensional quantum states.
arxiv-2603-03728:
Roman N Lee reports a calculation trick that turns a page of special functions into a line. The setting is dual conformal integrals, which appear in the maximally supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory used as a testing ground for quantum field theory methods. Conventional regularization breaks the very symmetry that makes these integrals special. A recent approach, developed with L Bork and A Onishchenko, regularizes while preserving dual conformal invariance throughout.

For two-loop five-point integrals, the payoff is dramatic. Every region's contribution, in the method-of-regions sense, collapses to gamma functions, and the final answer is a compact expression using only logarithms of cross-ratios. The conventional route yields sprawling polylogarithmic formulas for the same objects. Lee argues the symmetry-preserving plan may simplify calculations well beyond the dual conformal family.

bacon-opus-majus-burke-1928:
Roger Bacon, a Franciscan friar at Oxford, sent his Opus Majus to the pope in 1267 as a plan to renew all learning. Robert Belle Burke gave the whole work its first complete English form in 1928, in two volumes. Bacon wrote with a bold claim: true knowledge comes from experience, tested and seen.

Seven parts treat the causes of error, theology and philosophy, the study of tongues, mathematics, the science of sight, and experimental science, ending with moral philosophy. Bacon describes lenses, flying craft, and engines his age had never built. His plea for experiment reads like a charter for modern science. Burke's version lets English readers follow the whole great design.
bailey-greek-atomists-epicurus-1928:
Cyril Bailey's 1928 study traces one bold idea across six centuries: that all things are made of tiny solid atoms moving in empty space. Leucippus and Democritus first framed the theory in the fifth century BCE. Bailey follows it through Epicurus and ends with the Roman poet Lucretius.

He sets out how the early atomists explained sight, soul, and the birth of worlds without calling on gods. Then he shows how Epicurus softened the system with the swerve of atoms and a calm way of life. Bailey weighs the scant sources with care. His book became the landmark English account of ancient atomism and its long afterlife.
benda-treason-intellectuals-1928:
The Treason of the Intellectuals, published in French in 1927, appeared in English in 1928 in Richard Aldington's translation. It is Julien Benda's famous indictment of his fellow thinkers. Its charge: the clerks, whose calling was truth, had betrayed it for political passion.

Benda attacks writers who put nation, race, or class above universal values of justice and reason. He names the new cult of the particular as the age's spiritual crime. The book became a byword, quoted in every later quarrel over intellectuals and power. Its austerity still stings, and its question has never gone away.
browne-literary-history-of-persia-vol-2-:
The second volume of Edward G. Browne's Literary History of Persia, issued in 1928, runs from Firdawsi to Sa'di. These are the great centuries of Persian poetry, when the ghazal and the Sufi mathnawi came to flower. Browne surveys the age with extracts in his own English renderings throughout.

Sanai, Attar, and Rumi rise in these pages, and Omar Khayyam argues his way through the quatrains. Sa'di of Shiraz, the master of the Gulistan, closes the volume. Browne's love of Persia and his wide reading in its manuscripts give the survey its warmth. The book is the standard context for all Persian Sufi literature in English.
browne-literary-history-of-persia-vol-4-:
The fourth volume of Edward G. Browne's Literary History of Persia, from 1928, covers modern times, from 1500 to 1924, and completes the set. Browne knew this Persia at first hand: he had lived there, and he backed its constitutional revolution with pen and purse. His survey runs from the Safavid court to the newspapers of his own day.

Shi'a court poetry, the decline of verse under the Qajars, and the new prose of reformers and satirists fill the chapters. Browne prints the voices of the constitutional age in his own translations. The set of four volumes remains the fullest English history of Persian letters. It ends as both scholarship and a love letter to a nation.

Jean-Francois Champollion wrote home from his great trek in Letters from Egypt and Nubia, writ in 1828 and 1829. At last the man who cracked the script stood ere the tombs he had read on paper. He sails the Nile, reads walls at sight, and writes with joy, heat, and awe in each note home.

He sorts kings, dates, and gods as he goes, oft righting old claims. The notes were set in print for the crowd in France. They read as a log of a mind at its peak. The field's first field notes still charm.
champollion-precis-lettre-dacier-1828:
Jean-Francois Champollion taught the world to read Egypt's script in his Precis of 1828, with his famed note of 1822 bound in. Champollion had cracked the script by the stone of Rosetta and years of keen work. Here he sets out the whole scheme: which signs stand for sounds, which for things, and how scribes mixed them.

The book, in French, is the birth note of a whole field. Each claim rests on texts fans can check. Champollion died young, ere he saw Egypt in full. This work is the key that still unlocks its tombs.

The heading alone tells a reader the topic, the channel, and the moment, even where names stay deleted.
cia-0000136028: The record dated 2 February 1954 is a declassified CIA situation report about the Lincoln situation report for the week of 15 to 22 March, filed under a February date. Lincoln was the station cryptonym for PBSUCCESS, the CIA operation against President Arbenz in Guatemala that ended in June 1954. Taken with the rest of the station traffic, it helps map who handled what, and when, inside the mission.
cia-0000136128: Dated 6 April 1954, a declassified CIA cable deals with the need for the Guatemala station to channel traffic to Escobilla-Seman, the order cut off. Students of the 1954 coup use such records to check later accounts against what was written at the time.
cia-0000136228: A cable of 3 May 1954 survives in the declassified CIA files, dealing with operational readiness joined to factors that dictate delay, the heading breaking off mid-word. Records like this one let the operation be studied from the inside, in the terms its own staff used.
cia-0000136328: Labor politics, not a simple independence call, fills this June 1954 LINCOLN cable to ONTRICH about CALLIGERIS's public statements. The station urges a press statement saying present union leadership was usurped by communists tied to Moscow, and promising free union elections, collective bargaining, and protection from intimidation by employers. A future government statement should pledge to protect the whole people against predatory finance, foreign or domestic. It is messaging drafted for Guatemala's workers.

cia-0000137328: No satisfactory relationship is possible with a Castro-dominated government. The Havana embassy believes that, this briefing for the 10 March 1960 NSC meeting says.
