The embassy reads a deliberate attempt to force a crisis. Drastic American measures would follow. Propaganda is whipping up feeling among Cubans once cool to Castro. An incident could spark violence against Americans. The embassy has invoked limited warning phases.
cia-0000139028: Russian activities abroad are the stated subject of document 0000139028, a 1946 item of military information in the declassified CIA files. It dates from the first year after the war. Former allies were fast becoming rivals, and reports on Soviet moves carried new weight in Washington. The title is broad, and the record gives nothing narrower. The page should be read for what it is: an early Cold War watch report from a world being divided.
coelum-philosophorum-seu-de-secretis-nat: Coelum philosophorum seu de secretis naturae liber, 1528. Another edition. The record holds it. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
coelvm-philosophorvm-sev-de-secretis-nat: Coelum philosophorum, seu De secretis naturae liber, 1528. The philosophers' heaven. This book preserves that work. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
coke-institutes-part1-1628:
Edward Coke published the First Part of the Institutes in 1628, built as a commentary on Littleton's old book on land tenures. Lawyers call it Coke upon Littleton, and it became the most famous law book in English history. Coke, once chief justice and later a leader of Parliament against the crown, poured a lifetime of learning into its notes.

Page by page, the commentary turns a short medieval text into a full course in property law. Coke explains estates, inheritances, and the duties of lords and tenants, citing cases old and new. For two centuries, law students learned their profession from this book, and its authority in court was nearly unmatched. It stands as the oracle of the common law in its classical age.
correspondence-relative-to-phrenology-be: Correspondence Relative to Phrenology, 1828. The Hamilton correspondence. This book preserves that correspondence. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
corti-reign-of-the-house-of-rothschild-1:
Egon Caesar Corti, an Austrian historian, wrote The Reign of the House of Rothschild from the family's own papers. The English edition came out at New York in 1928. It covers the banking house from 1830 to 1871, its years of greatest power in Europe.

Corti follows the five Rothschild houses as they lend to kings, fund railways, and move money across borders. Letters and deals show how the family turned credit into sway over states. The book stays a rich source on the age when private bankers stood beside thrones. His access to the family archives gave the book its lasting weight.
corti-rise-of-the-house-of-rothschild-19:
Egon Caesar Corti, an Austrian writer, made this full history of the rise of the Rothschild house in 1928. Brian and Beatrix Lunn turned it into English, and it came out in New York the same year. Corti worked from the family's own store of papers, a rare chance for a writer.

The book tells how Mayer Amschel Rothschild of Frankfurt and his five sons built a bank that spanned Europe. Wars, state loans, and swift news fill the years from 1770 to 1830 in his tale. Later books on the house all cite Corti as their chief source.
deutsches-theatrum-chemicum-auf-welchem-: Deutsches Theatrum Chemicum, 1728. The German chemical theatre. This book preserves that collection. History keeps its place secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Scholars will consult it.
dobie-tales-old-time-texas-1928:
J. Frank Dobie spent his life gathering the folk tales of Texas. His Tales of Old-Time Texas, from 1928, sets down tales heard from ranch hands and old-timers. Dobie wrote them in a warm, plain style. The book holds a firm place in Texas letters.

One tale stands out for fans of strange lore. The Wild Woman of the Navidad haunted river lands in the 1830s and later years. Dobie gives the hunts, tracks, and fears tied to her name. Other tales tell of lost gold, ghosts, and hard men. The set keeps a lost Texas alive.
doe-osti-3013852-sierra-sd-users-manual-: Sierra/SD got its 5.28 manual, and this DOE text covers the user instructions. The pages detail the guidance. The engineers get their reference. The version was 5.28. The reference was engineer. The manual was users. The version was DOE's. The instructions were DOE's.
doe-osti-3013853-sierra-sd-user-s-guide-: Sierra/SD NasGen got its 5.28 guide, and this DOE text covers the user manual. The pages detail the guidance. The engineers get their reference. The tool was NasGen. The reference was engineer. The guide was user's. The manual was DOE's.
doe-osti-3013855-sierra-sd-example-probl: Sierra/SD examples got their 5.28 manual, and this DOE text covers problem sets. The pages detail the guidance. The engineers get their reference. The problems were example. The reference was engineer. The manual was examples. The sets were problem. The guidance was DOE's.
doe-osti-3013856-sierra-sd-its2sierra-us: Its2Sierra got its 5.28 manual, and this DOE text covers the user instructions. The pages detail the guidance. The engineers get their reference. The tool was Its2Sierra. The reference was engineer. The manual was user's. The instructions were user.
drake-world-encompassed-1628:
The World Encompassed by Sir Francis Drake, printed in 1628, tells of the second voyage ever made around the whole earth. Drake sailed from England in 1577 and came home in 1580, having raided Spain's Pacific coast and crossed oceans no Englishman had crossed. His nephew gathered the account from the journals of the voyage, decades after the return.

The narrative follows the fleet through storms, straits, and rich prizes, down to one ship and a hard homecoming. It was the first full English telling of the feat, issued long after Drake's death. The delay kept its details scarce goods among readers of travel. The book still carries the pride of a small nation tasting global reach.
eddington-nature-physical-world-1928:
Arthur Eddington published The Nature of the Physical World in 1928, from his Gifford Lectures. Eddington was a leading astronomer who helped prove Einstein's theory. He explains relativity and quantum theory for general readers with rare skill. Physics, he argues, deals in symbols and pointer readings, not in the solid stuff of common sense.

His two tables, the familiar one and the scientific one, open the book famously. Later chapters turn to entropy, time's arrow, and the place of mind in nature. Eddington suggests the stuff of the world is mind-stuff at root. The book became a landmark of popular science. It shaped how a generation pictured physics.
elinor-wyllys-or-the-young-folk-of-longb: Volume two of Susan Fenimore Cooper's pioneering American novel: the story of Longbridge concludes. Domestic realism before it had a name, gentle and true. The completion of a landmark. The novel's gentle moralizing charmed its first readers.
eliot-for-lancelot-andrewes-1928:
Eliot named this 1928 essay collection for Lancelot Andrewes, the Jacobean bishop and preacher whose sermons he admired. The title signals the book's subject: the meeting of style and belief in prose and poetry.

The essays cover Andrewes, Machiavelli, and the problem of writing religious prose in a doubting age. In the preface Eliot famously declared himself a classicist in literature, a royalist in politics, and an Anglo-Catholic in religion. That sentence shocked readers and fixed his public image for years. The book marks his turn from restless experiment toward order, tradition, and faith. It gathers the criticism of his conversion years.
epictetus-discourses-enchiridion-oldfath:
Volume 2 of Oldfather's Loeb Epictetus appeared in 1928, completing the set. It holds Books 3 and 4 of the Discourses as reported by Arrian, then the Enchiridion, or Manual, and the Fragments. An index closes the volume for study use.

The Enchiridion distills Epictetus's teaching into short rules for daily life: control what you can, accept what you cannot, and act with justice. Soldiers, monks, and prisoners have carried it for centuries. It is the most influential Stoic handbook ever written. With the Discourses complete beside it, Oldfather's second volume finishes the standard English Epictetus of the Loeb Classical Library.
europmc-pmc10216928:
Zeng and colleagues review current strategies for loading cargo into exosomes and steering them to targets, in a 2023 paper. Exosomes are tiny natural parcels, wrapped in a fatty skin, that cells release into the body. Their natural origin makes them gentle carriers for drugs, genes, and other cargo.

The review covers ways to load cargo, from soaking and squeezing to building producer cells that pack the parcels themselves. It then surveys methods that add homing features to the surface. The authors weigh promise against the hard work of making uniform batches.
europmc-pmc10509828:
Guo and co-authors reviewed leaf ageing in 2021, the last stage of a leaf's life. In this stage, called senescence, a leaf shifts from taking in food to sending its stores to the rest of the plant. That shift keeps the plant fit and feeds seeds and new growth. Age, plant hormones, and stress all steer the timing.

Gene hunts in the test plant Arabidopsis have named hundreds of genes tied to this stage. Control acts at many levels, from gene packing to protein edits after a gene is read. Guo stresses why farmers care: leaf ageing sets yield and crop quality. Tricks that delay or speed the stage may lift harvests. Open puzzles include how a leaf knows its own age.
europmc-pmc10767828:
Varadi and co-authors updated the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database in 2024. The bank holds shapes predicted by AlphaFold2, an AI that folds proteins from their code. It began in 2021 with near 300,000 shapes. Other big banks, from UniProt to Ensembl, now draw on its stock.

Coverage now tops 214 million protein sequences, Varadi reports. Fresh releases added model organisms, health-linked proteomes, and curated sets. Users can pull files by FTP or query the bank through Google Cloud data sets. The team tuned the error viewer, which shows where a shape may be off. The 3D viewer gained custom views, and search runs faster.
europmc-pmc11316928:
Tang and colleagues present a Python toolkit that unifies the stages of a genome project in this 2024 paper. Building a genome spans assembly, annotation, and comparison with other genomes. Tools exist for each stage, but they rarely talk to each other. Comparisons can check assembly quality, and assembly can expose artefacts that distort comparisons, the authors note.

Their library, JCVI, offers modular utilities for parsing formats, drawing graphics, and editing assemblies and annotations. Two bundled algorithms, MCscan and ALLMAPS, are widely used to build genome releases. MCscan finds matching gene blocks across genomes, a pattern called synteny. The toolkit produces publication-ready figures for quality assessment and evolutionary inference. The authors stress collaborative development, quality, and reusability across projects.
europmc-pmc1156928:
Varni, Burwinkle, and Lane appraise quality-of-life measurement in children's clinical care in this 2005 paper. Health-related quality of life, or HRQOL, scores how illness and treatment affect daily life and wellbeing. In adult care, doctors report such measures as useful, some change treatment based on them, and patients generally welcome them. Evidence in paediatric practice, by contrast, was scarce.

The authors review the updated literature and propose a precept, a guiding rule, for applying these measures with children. Used well, measurement can facilitate child and doctor communication and improve parent satisfaction, they argue. It can identify hidden morbidities, meaning problems that routine visits miss. It can also assist clinical decision-making. Demonstrating those benefits in routine paediatric settings is posed as the field's next required step.
europmc-pmc1216328:
Rendl, Lewis, and Fuchs dissected how hair follicles form in 2005. Hair starts when a signal cluster called the dermal papilla cues skin stem cells. Those cells then wrap around the cluster. Together they build a niche that drives hair growth.

Sorting cells by glowing color tags let the team isolate pure groups. Five cell types from the niche were profiled. Each type carried its own gene signature. Some signature genes proved key for follicle function. Rendl gives hair biology a parts list with labels. That list helps trace how skin builds complex structures.
europmc-pmc1513328:
Fine dust in city air can stoke swelling inside the body. Dubowsky and co-authors studied 44 older adults in 2006, tracking blood markers of inflammation against air pollution levels. They asked whether chronic illness sharpens that response.

A week's higher fine particle levels brought a 5.5 percent rise in white blood cell counts. One marker, CRP, rose 14 percent with a five-day pollution rise. In people with diabetes, obesity, and high blood pressure, the same rise gave an 81 percent CRP jump. Dubowsky concludes that these common conditions may make people far more sensitive to dirty air.
europmc-pmc1831728:
Moher and colleagues took a census of systematic reviews in 2007 to see how the field was growing and reporting its work. Systematic reviews pool many studies on one question and now guide care and policy. Earlier checks had missed newer reporting issues.

They sampled reviews indexed in Medline during November 2004 and scored them with a 51-item form. The 300 reviews found imply a yearly output near 2,500 reviews covering more than 33,700 studies. Most appeared in specialty journals, and 71 percent tested treatments, with a median of 16 studies and 1,112 participants each. Funding went unreported in over 40 percent of reviews. A typical review searched three electronic databases, yet only about two thirds stated which years were covered.
europmc-pmc1888728:
Gilbert and colleagues compared in 2007 the many recipes for pulling DNA and RNA out of formalin-fixed, wax-embedded tissues. Museums and pathology archives hold vast collections preserved this way, a genetic archive for studying populations and diseases. Formalin cross-links molecules, which muddies extraction and blocks the copying enzymes used in analysis.

The team ran a test panel of fixed specimens through the published protocols side by side. They compared pre-treatments, extraction and cleaning methods, and a post-extraction enzyme repair step. Gains were measured rather than judged by eye, unlike most prior checks. Many methods improved some trait of the nucleic acids won back, yet benefits often came with trade-offs on other traits. Their results guide which method fits which job, from short fragments for old museum skins to fuller RNA recovery.
europmc-pmc1977628:
Griffiths questioned in 1991 a half-century-old dogma: that cancer cells are more acidic inside than normal cells. The belief grew from Warburg's finding that tumors convert glucose to lactic acid even when oxygen is plentiful. Acid output seemed bound to mean an acidic interior.

Cultured tumor cells and cell balls often did show low internal pH, but those setups are highly artificial. Fine electrodes pushed into living tumors measured significantly acidic readings, yet an electrode samples the fluid around cells and damaged tissue, not the interior of an intact cell. Griffiths weighs newer magnetic resonance methods that can read internal pH in a living tumor without breaking cells open. The editorial asks the field to separate the acidity of a tumor's surroundings from the acidity of the cancer cell itself.
europmc-pmc2033628:
Pyrhönen and colleagues ran a randomised trial in 1995 for stomach cancer that could not be removed by surgery. Forty-one patients received either a three-drug chemotherapy mix, called FEMTX, or supportive care alone. Both groups also got vitamins A and E. The trial ran from 1986 to 1992. Chemotherapy combined fluorouracil, epidoxorubicin and methotrexate in repeated cycles.

Six of 21 treated patients responded, a rate of 29 percent, including four complete responses. No control patient responded, and 80 percent worsened. Time before the cancer grew was 5.4 months with chemotherapy, against 1.7 months without, and median survival was 12.3 months against 3.1 months, a clear gain. Severe side effects were common, especially low white cell counts, but only one possible treatment death occurred.
europmc-pmc2124828: A medical paper on the effect of certain experimental procedures on the islands of Langerhans. The pancreatic islets. This article preserves that endocrinology. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2124928: A medical paper on the influence of heat on different sera as culture media. The warmed serums. This article preserves that cell culture. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
europmc-pmc2125328: A medical paper with observations on the etiology of goitre in brook trout, the effect of feeding. The fish goitre. This article preserves that veterinary endocrinology. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
europmc-pmc2125428: A medical paper with studies on Treponema pallidum and syphilis. The pox germ. This article preserves that venereology. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
europmc-pmc2128128: A medical paper on a cutaneous nematode infection in monkeys. The skin worms. This article preserves that parasitology. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
europmc-pmc2131228: A medical paper with experimental bone marrow reactions, polycythemia and normoblastosis. The busy marrow. This article preserves that hematology. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
europmc-pmc2131328: A medical paper with studies on bacterial enzymes, the maltase of the diphtheria bacillus. The diphtheria enzyme. This article preserves that biochemistry. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
europmc-pmc2131428: A medical paper on the regeneration of autoplastic lymph node transplants. The regrown nodes. This article preserves that immunology. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
europmc-pmc2140328: A biology paper on relation between metamorphosis and other developmental phenomena in amphibians. The changing frogs. This article preserves that developmental biology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2140428: A biology paper with studies on the organization of the starfish egg. The starfish egg. This article preserves that embryology. History keeps its place secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The paper lived through the years.
europmc-pmc2140628: A biology paper with observations on the transport of carbon dioxide in the blood of marine invertebrates. The sea creatures' CO2. This article preserves that physiology. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
europmc-pmc2140928: A biology paper on hydration of gelatin in solution. The wet gel. This article preserves that biophysics. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
europmc-pmc2409828:
Bamford and colleagues launched COSMIC in 2004, a single home for cancer mutation data. Somatic mutations are DNA changes acquired during life that can drive cancer, and reports of them were scattered across thousands of papers. The new database aimed to collect them in one searchable place.

The team started with four genes known to mutate often in cancer: BRAF, HRAS, KRAS2, and NRAS. At launch the database held records on 66,634 samples and reported 10,647 mutations in total. Web pages let users query the data, view it as figures or tables, and export it in several formats. About 300 cancer genes were then known, so four was only a start. The authors said the catalogue would keep growing as curators added more genes and studies.
europmc-pmc2438328:
Liu, Yu, Zack, Zhu, and Qian built a database of tissue-specific gene control in 2008. Most gene databases ignore where in the body a gene acts. Their resource, TiGER, focuses on human tissues: which genes switch on where, and which control switches drive them.

TiGER holds activity profiles for 19,526 genes across human tissues. It also stores combined control patterns for 7,341 pairs of transcription factors, the proteins that bind DNA to switch genes on. A third layer lists 6,232 candidate control modules, stretches of DNA where several factors bind together, covering 2,130 well-catalogued genes. The data came from new computer methods that predict tissue-specific control from binding site patterns. The authors made the database public so others can mine how tissues keep their distinct gene programs running.
europmc-pmc2443128:
Lotrakul, Sumrithe, and Saipanish validated a Thai version of a nine-question depression screen in 2008. The PHQ-9 asks about mood symptoms over two weeks and is scored in minutes. Thai primary care lacked a short, trusted tool, since existing ones were long and impractical for routine use.

The questionnaire was translated with back-translation and cultural checks, then given to 1,000 family practice patients. A subgroup of about 300 also took two established interview and rating tools as reference standards. Internal consistency was satisfactory, at a score of 0.79 on the standard alpha measure, and scores tracked the reference severity scale moderately well. Used with a cut-off of nine or more, the screen caught 84% of true depression cases while clearing 77% of non-cases. The overall accuracy curve scored 0.89, close to the top mark of 1.
europmc-pmc2626828:
Morse surveyed in 1995 the factors that make infectious diseases emerge, infections newly appearing or rapidly expanding in range or incidence. Fresh examples then included HIV/AIDS, Lyme disease, hantavirus pulmonary syndrome, and a foodborne E. coli syndrome causing kidney failure. Morse argues that in virtually every case, specific precipitating factors can be identified.

Most factors are ecological, environmental, or demographic changes that push people into contact with an unfamiliar microbe or its animal host, or that help it spread. Those pressures are growing, not shrinking. Combined with constant microbial evolution and selection for drug resistance, they imply infections will keep emerging and probably increase. Morse stresses that surveillance and control need urgent strengthening. He presents the piece as the opening of a journal series on unifying concepts for emerging infections.
europmc-pmc2631628:
Michlewski, Guil, Semple, and Cáceres explored in 2008 how a protein called hnRNP A1 helps produce one particular microRNA, and what that reveals about microRNA control generally. MicroRNAs start as longer precursors that an enzyme, Drosha, must cut. The team had found hnRNP A1 assists that cut for the precursor of miR-18a, and here they worked out how.

HnRNP A1 binds the loop at the precursor's tip and relaxes the stem below it, opening a better cleavage site for Drosha. Surveying all precursors, about 14 percent carry highly conserved loops, which the authors predict serve as landing pads for such helper factors. Blocking those loops with designer molecules, which they name LooptomiRs, abolished processing in the test tube. The results add a layer of regulation to how cells make specific microRNAs.
europmc-pmc2685828:
Judson and colleagues mapped in 2009 how much toxicity knowledge actually exists for the thousands of chemicals in daily use. Only a fraction had ever been well tested, leaving regulators to guess which of the rest deserve scarce testing first. The United States Environmental Protection Agency built a giant catalogue, ACToR, pulling data from over 200 public sources worldwide.

From that catalogue the team charted the evidence for 9,912 chemicals on a screening shortlist: industrial chemicals made in bulk, pesticide ingredients, and drinking water contaminants. For each, the catalogue holds structure, physical traits, cell-test results, animal data, and official hazard verdicts. The picture was patchy: rich files for a few famous chemicals, near silence for most. Making the gaps visible, the authors argue, is the first step to a rational testing queue.
europmc-pmc2688028:
Alstott and colleagues built a computer model in 2009 to predict what a brain injury does to the wider brain, not just the wounded spot. Damage at one site often disturbs distant, healthy areas, in ways that depend in hard-to-guess fashion on where the wound sits. Whole-brain wiring maps now let such effects be simulated before they are seen in patients.

The team placed virtual lesions in a model of resting brain activity and watched the fallout. Each site produced its own signature of changed connections between far-apart regions, often spanning both hemispheres. Wounds along the brain's midline and near the junction of the temporal and parietal lobes shook the network most. Wounds in primary seeing, hearing, or movement areas stayed local. The size of the effect could be partly read off the wiring importance of the site itself.
europmc-pmc2707628:
Shechter and co-authors tested in 2009 whether blood-borne immune cells help or harm recovery after spinal cord injury in mice. The cord sits in the central nervous system, a site long seen as shielded from immunity. Two kinds of macrophage, large cells that clear debris, gather at a lesion: resident cells and newcomers from blood.

Mice that lacked the newcomer cells recovered poorly, while adding those cells improved repair. The newcomers calmed swelling and needed interleukin 10, an anti-swelling signal, to do so. Resident cells alone did not give that benefit. The result splits a group once treated as all harmful into helpful and harmful parts.
europmc-pmc2725828:
Watson, Gayer, and Connolly reviewed in 2007 the true risk of epidemics after natural disasters such as earthquakes, floods, and tsunamis. A common fear links dead bodies to outbreaks, and media reports often warn of imminent epidemics. Evidence, they argue, does not support that fear in most cases.

Bodies of people killed by the disaster itself pose little outbreak risk, with narrow exceptions such as cholera deaths. Real risk comes mainly from population displacement, when crowding, unsafe water, poor sanitation, and lost health care combine with local disease patterns. Their review lists the infections most likely to matter and sets priorities for water, shelter, and care in disaster settings.
europmc-pmc2774328:
Han and Zmasek presented in 2009 phyloXML, a computer language for describing evolutionary trees together with the data attached to them. Trees sit at the center of many studies, and their nodes and branches carry labels: species names, branch lengths, support values, gene names, or events such as duplications. Older formats had no standard way to hold such varied annotations.

phyloXML supplies ready elements for the common items, from taxonomy to gene identifiers. Flexible property elements let users add new kinds of data the designers never foresaw. The language is defined by a complete formal schema, so files can be checked and exchanged reliably. The authors also built software tools to read, write, convert, and draw phyloXML data. They offer it as a shared standard for evolutionary biology and comparative genomics.
europmc-pmc2810828:
Chun and Keleş proposed a new statistics method in 2010 for studies where measured factors vastly outnumber samples, a common problem in gene research. The older method they build on, partial least squares, shrinks data into a few combined factors but keeps every variable in play, so results stay hard to read.

Their sparse version forces most variable weights to zero while it builds those combined factors, picking the useful variables and shrinking the data at the same time. They also showed the older method's reliability claims break down when variables hugely outnumber samples. Test runs against rival methods, plus a joint study of gene activity and DNA binding, showed the sparse version predicts well.
europmc-pmc2824828:
Crews and colleagues examined the cell's recycling system in 2010 in brains from patients with Lewy body disease, a group of disorders marked by clumps of a protein called alpha-synuclein. The recycling system, autophagy, is a main route for clearing that protein, so faults in it could let clumps build.

Compared with healthy and Alzheimer brains, patient brains showed more of a brake protein called mTor and less of a recycling gear called Atg7, while other gears stayed level. Neurons stuffed with alpha-synuclein held the most mTor and showed swollen, abnormal recycling sacs. Mice engineered to overproduce the protein showed the same pattern. In those mice, a brake-lifting drug or extra Atg7 cut the protein buildup and eased brain cell damage.
europmc-pmc2871128:
Meng and Yu reviewed in 2010 why muscle melts away with age, a condition called sarcopenia that leaves older people weak and frail. Two slow-burning processes stand behind much of the loss: oxidative stress, damage from reactive oxygen byproducts, and low-grade molecular inflammation inside the tissue. Both build up over years in aging muscle.

The two processes tip the balance between building muscle protein and breaking it down toward breakdown. They also harm the cell's energy factories and can push muscle cells into programmed death. The review traces the major signal pathways switched on or off along the way. Single fixes are unlikely to reverse the loss, the authors argue, so exercise, careful calorie limits, and nutrition may need to work together.
europmc-pmc2935128:
Bostock and co-authors assessed the global status of fish farming in a 2010 review, covering farmed fish, shellfish, and other aquatic animals raised for food. Farmed output already supplied a large share of aquatic food eaten by people and was still growing.

Contrary to common belief, pond fish and shellfish that feed partly on natural growth dominate the sector, though fast-growing salmon, shrimp, and catfish farms drive trade. Most farms lean on free environmental goods, so charging for them would reshape costs. Climate change, feed supply, and new breeding tools add further uncertainty about the path ahead.
europmc-pmc2943128:
Bansal and Bilaspuri reviewed how oxidative stress affects sperm and male fertility in a 2010 article. Trouble arises when reactive oxygen species, aggressive oxygen by-products, overwhelm the body's antioxidant defences.

Too much of these species drains sperm energy, damages fatty membranes, and cuts movement and survival, contributing to infertility. Yet small controlled amounts are needed for normal steps such as preparing sperm to fertilise an egg. The review covers where the species come from and how added antioxidants can protect sperm during freezing for breeding work. It also notes using oxidative stress itself as a possible contraceptive route.
europmc-pmc2978728:
McNeela and colleagues studied pneumolysin, a toxin of the pneumonia bacterium, in a 2010 immunology study. The toxin is a candidate ingredient for future subunit vaccines, and its effect on the cells that start immune responses needed clarifying.

Purified toxin matured dendritic cells without making them release signals alone, but paired with other bacterial cues it greatly boosted inflammatory messengers. Mice given toxin-primed cells mounted stronger responses to a test antigen. europmc-pmc2990028:
Crump and Sugarman, writing for a working group on ethics in global health training, set out guidelines in 2010 for students' field placements abroad. Such programmes were multiplying fast, and the trips could burden host communities even while helping trainees.

Built from published literature and members' experience, the guidelines address universities, trainees, and funders together, covering preparation, supervision, and benefit sharing. europmc-pmc3042628:
Perry, Sang, Yin, Zheng, and Morel reviewed in 2011 the mouse models that stand in for human lupus, an autoimmune disease in which the body attacks its own tissues. Mice that develop a lupus like illness on their own have revealed many gene regions that raise risk, and several candidate genes inside them. Other mice get the illness only after a trigger, which highlights environmental roles.

Together the models have clarified which immune cells drive the disease and how it starts and worsens. They also serve as test beds for possible lupus drugs before human trials. Because the human disease is so varied, the authors stress matching each targeted drug to what a model can actually show. Lessons from these mice keep shaping the search for safer, more precise treatments.
europmc-pmc3055228:
Wilken, Veena, Wang, and Srivatsan reviewed in 2011 the case for curcumin, the yellow pigment of turmeric, as an add on treatment for head and neck cancer. Curcumin has been used for centuries in Ayurvedic medicine and is known to be safe, with calming and pain easing effects. Lab work shows it also slows cancer growth through many pathways at once.

It blocks a master inflammation switch inside cells and the growth, survival, and spread genes that switch controls. It also interferes with receptors and adhesion molecules that tumors use to grow new blood vessels and invade tissue. Head and neck cancers are common worldwide and their standard treatments can be disfiguring and harsh. The authors argue a safe add on could let doctors cut those burdens without losing effect. They also flag the hurdles, chiefly getting enough curcumin into the body.
europmc-pmc3155828:
Meghan Baker and colleagues pooled evidence on diabetes worsening tuberculosis outcomes in a 2011 paper in BMC Medicine. The two epidemics are colliding as diabetes spreads in countries where tuberculosis stays common. From three decades of literature, thirty-three studies comparing treatment results in patients with and without diabetes survived screening.

Patients with diabetes faced a clearly higher risk of treatment failure and death combined, a higher risk of death alone, and a much higher risk of relapse after apparent cure. The death risk grew even larger in the few studies that adjusted for age and other confounders. Results on early germ clearance were mixed. The authors call for diabetes testing, tighter sugar control, and closer monitoring during tuberculosis treatment.
europmc-pmc3212228:
Kan Wang and colleagues tested whether graphene oxide is safe around living tissue in this 2011 paper in Nanoscale Research Letters. Graphene oxide, a water-friendly form of the carbon sheet material, was being explored for medical uses. The team exposed human fibroblast cells and mice to a range of doses and watched for harm.

Low doses left the cultured cells unharmed, but higher doses reduced cell attachment, triggered cell death, and let particles enter internal compartments including the nucleus. In mice, low and middle injected doses caused no obvious toxicity, while the highest dose killed several animals and produced lung granulomas. Particles collected in the lungs, liver, spleen, and kidneys and were barely cleared. The authors warn that dose-dependent toxicity must be weighed before body uses.
europmc-pmc3248128:
Inti Zlobec and Alessandro Lugli reviewed tumor budding in colorectal cancer in this 2010 paper in Oncotarget. At a tumor's invasive edge, pathologists often see single cells or tiny clusters that have shed their epithelial character, a change called epithelial-mesenchymal transition. Those buds are not a frozen picture but a snapshot of an aggressive tumor in the act of spreading.

The authors assemble strong, consistent evidence that budding predicts spread to lymph nodes and distant sites, local recurrence, and shorter survival, independent of other factors. International cancer authorities already recognize budding as a relevant extra prognostic sign. The review argues for putting budding counts into routine diagnostic reporting and patient management, and floats the buds themselves as a possible treatment target, an oncotarget.
europmc-pmc3322928:
Lau and co-authors described a SARS patient whose illness reached her brain and spinal cord, in a 2004 case report. SARS, the severe respiratory disease that emerged in 2002, mainly attacked the lungs. The patient was a thirty two year old woman whose breathing illness followed the usual course for about three weeks.

On the twenty second day of illness she suffered a major whole body seizure. Doctors sampled the fluid around her spinal cord and tested it for the SARS coronavirus using a sensitive genetic test. The test came back positive, showing the virus was present in the fluid bathing her nervous system. The authors conclude the virus likely infected her central nervous system directly, an unusual turn that broadened the picture of what SARS could do.
europmc-pmc3409228:
Wang and co-workers compared tiny regulatory RNAs in blood serum and plasma in 2012, a practical question for disease testing. These microRNAs circulate in blood and their levels track cancers and other conditions, making them promising markers. Matched serum and plasma came from the same donors.

Serum consistently held higher microRNA concentrations than the paired plasma. Part of the gap traced to microRNAs released from platelets, suggesting the clotting that makes serum reshapes the RNA mix. Readings also varied with the measurement platform used. The authors caution that studies mixing sample types or platforms may reach false conclusions. Marker hunters, they say, must standardize before comparing numbers.

Walter Evans-Wentz, an American scholar of Celtic and Eastern religion, published Tibet's Great Yogi Milarepa in 1928. fauset-plum-bun-1928:

She decides to pass as white to gain freedom and a chance at success. Her sister stays in the Black community they grew up in.

Angela finds that passing brings loneliness and fear of being found out. Love and ambition pull her in opposite ways. In time she questions the price of hiding who she is. The novel is praised for its clear-eyed view of race, gender, and the cost of ambition.
ford-last-post-1928:
Last Post, published in 1928, closes Parade's End on a single long country day after the war. The armistice is past, Tietjens's brother Mark lies dying and silent, and the family's great house passes out of their hands for good.

Tietjens now lives with Valentine Wannop, selling antiques, while Sylvia's last maneuvers fail to reclaim him. Ford views the aftermath largely through other minds, letting the old order's end arrive quietly. Some readers find the volume a falling-off; others prize its elegy. Either way, it completes modernism's broadest portrait of England at war and in uneasy peace.
fortune-esoteric-orders-and-their-work-1:

She sets out their grades, their methods of work, and the ends they claim to serve. The book sorts true training from sham and tells the seeker what to expect at each step of the road. Few English books of its time spoke so plainly on the subject. It opened the doors of the orders to the plain reader.
freud-future-illusion-robson-scott-1928:
Sigmund Freud published The Future of an Illusion in German in 1927. The English text here is W. D. Robson-Scott's translation of 1928. Freud calls religion an illusion born of human wishes. Helpless before nature and fate, people create father-like gods for comfort and control. Civilization, he argues, rests in part on this shared wish.

He predicts that education and science will slowly loosen religion's hold. His dialogue partner raises objections, and Freud answers them in turn. The book is his clearest atheist manifesto. It angered believers and pleased free-thinkers in equal measure. Its debate on faith and reason continues today.
frus-1861-d128:

Within days, France would declare its neutrality in the American war. Dayton's early June letter comes from the last stretch of doubt. It shows an envoy at work in the gap between a court's private lean and its public word. The gap between lean and word was where envoys like Dayton earned their pay. Pay of that sort was earned in the gap, and Dayton earned his in full.
frus-1861-d228:

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1861-d28:

Such feed stock let Seward test what the great capitals told him in formal terms. Brussels news often bore on France, whose border lay a short ride from Sanford's desk. News that bore on France bore also on Spain and Italy, and Seward knew it.
frus-1862-d128:

The date falls in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.

Letters written just before such a blow catch the last calm of an older picture. And they help explain why foreign policy shifted so fast that fall. frus-1862-d428:

Spain and the United States had live questions between them in 1862, from Cuba and the Gulf trade to the allied expedition in Mexico. Tassara's letters open the Washington side of the Spanish file. Seward's replies beside them show how the Union answered a proud power. It gave no ground and offered no insult.

In it, each government stated its position in formal terms. Each then waited for the other's answer across a very short distance.

The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the spring of 1863.

British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. A reader gets the feel of diplomacy done by hand: formal greetings, careful wording, and hard points pressed without open threats. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d528:
22 May 1863 is the date on a letter from Secretary William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily. Such notes moved by hand between the State Department and the British legation, a few streets apart in wartime Washington.

The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.

The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

Read with its neighbors, the note helps explain a fact of the war: Britain never stepped in, and the record shows the effort that took. The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d128: Minutes of the President's meeting with the Joint Chiefs of Staff, held at 2 p.m. on November 15, 1943 in the President's cabin aboard the battleship Iowa, form Document 128 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. At sea on the way to Cairo, Roosevelt and his chiefs settled the American line for the coming talks. Minutes like these, taken on the spot, are the spine of the official record. The volume prints them in full.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d228:
The United States Chiefs of Staff issued paper C.C.S. 398 aboard the Iowa on 18 November 1943, listing the specific operations proposed for the defeat of Germany and her satellites in 1943 and 1944. It is the American plan of work for the coming year, offered to the Combined Chiefs of Staff.

Azores facilities would support the fight against U-boats and air ferry routes. The combined bomber offensive keeps the highest priority, as a thing that must come before Overlord, the cross-Channel invasion set for 1 May 1944. Where resources run short, Overlord wins over the Mediterranean every time. The paper also covers the build-up in Britain and a standing readiness to cross the Channel early if a chance opens.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d28: Home from Quebec, Roosevelt wrote to Churchill on August 26, 1943, and the message is Document 28 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The Quebec talks had just set the alliance's course for the next year, and follow-up letters kept the decisions moving. The catalog record names the parties and the date, nothing more. In the published series the note belongs to the bridge between the August conference and the autumn summits.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d328: President Roosevelt sent Marshal Stalin a short secret telegram, marked operational priority, from Cairo on 26 November 1943. Carried by Navy channels through Harriman for delivery to Stalin, it thanks him for his message of 23 November announcing that he would reach Tehran on the 28th or 29th. Roosevelt replies that he expects to reach Tehran himself on the 27th, and closes with a single warm line: it will be good to see you.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d428:
President Roosevelt sent Ambassador Steinhardt a secret telegram from Cairo on 2 December 1943, giving the assurance Turkey's president had demanded before accepting the Cairo invitation. It answers Steinhardt's report of the same day.

Roosevelt directs Steinhardt to tell Inönü at once that he is delighted the Turkish president can come. Inönü is to be assured, in the words he had asked for, that he is being invited to a free discussion as between equals. Roosevelt adds that he is especially happy to have the occasion to talk with him. Transport planes will be waiting at Adana on the morning of 4 December, and the British are advising their ambassador in the same sense. Steinhardt is told to be sure to bring an adequate American interpreter with him.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d528:
President Roosevelt sent a message to Secretary of State Cordell Hull on December 23, 1943, two days before Christmas and a fortnight after his return from Tehran and Cairo. The State Department printed it in the Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

The weeks after a summit are when its promises meet the machinery of government. Roosevelt's messages to Hull in this period passed decisions and problems from the traveling President to the department that had to execute them. For readers, this cable belongs to the unglamorous but decisive phase of diplomacy: turning handshakes in Tehran into instructions, appointments, and orders in Washington.
frus-1944-quebec-d128:
From Moscow on September 10, 1944, Ambassador Harriman urgently summarized for Roosevelt and Hull the Soviet reply on Warsaw aid. The British ambassador had shown him the message Moscow sent London. Harriman called it an extremely shrewd statement for the record, one that shifted the decision, and the blame, onto the Western allies.

In paraphrase, Moscow said real aid would come from the Red Army's advance. Supply drops, it claimed, had repeatedly fallen into German hands. Still, the Soviets were prepared to join a drop operation under a prearranged plan. Harriman asked for urgent instructions on whether to open talks with the Red Army staff, and noted he lacked fresh word on how much of Warsaw the insurgents still held.
frus-1944-quebec-d228:
Hull cabled Harriman on September 12, 1944, with the president's instructions on Warsaw. Marshall was being directed to have General Deane explore the Soviet offer to cooperate in aid, working with his British colleagues. Harriman was to lend Deane every support and tell Molotov that America was prepared to do its utmost, jointly with the British and Russians, on immediate aid to the garrison.

Hull added a political warning. The Soviet decision might come too late if the garrison had shrunk too far for drops to be practical, but that question would emerge in negotiation. What mattered was that Washington show no hesitation in implementing the Soviet promise, so it could not be blamed if aid failed to arrive in time.
frus-1944-quebec-d28:
President Roosevelt wrote to Prime Minister Churchill on August 23, 1944, the day Paris rose against its occupiers. The message appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

The last week of August 1944 carried the alliance from campaigning to conferring: France was being liberated, and the Quebec meeting was three weeks off. Roosevelt's correspondence then had to ready the big unsettled questions, above all Germany's treatment and the terms of continued aid to Britain. For readers, this message stands at the turn of the season, written while the guns were still firing in Paris.
frus-1945-50-intel-d128:
Vandenberg wrote to Secretary Byrnes on 12 September 1946. The director of central intelligence reporting to the secretary of state shows the CIG working its board members one by one. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

By September, Vandenberg was looking past the summer's rulings to the group's growth: more money, more missions, and a firmer charter. A letter to Byrnes sought the support of the board's senior member. Readers can watch the director's method: win the secretaries singly, then move the board. The campaign that fills the volume's later pages, ending in the stronger agency of the 1947 law, begins in approaches like this one.
frus-1945-50-intel-d228:
A memorandum dated 16 October 1947 links two senior offices. The sender was the Secretary of State’s Acting Special Assistant for Research and Intelligence (Armstrong). The reader was Acting Secretary of State Lovett. The State Department prints it as document 228 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. It was the first autumn of the new system: a fresh CIA, a fresh Council, and piles of first-year business.

A memo of this kind was the basic tool of office work at the top. It put a matter before a senior man and asked for a choice, a signature, or a view. The note's brevity hides its weight: men at this level did not write to each other for practice. Read next to the papers around it in the volume, it helps show how the postwar intelligence system took shape step by step.
frus-1945-50-intel-d28:
Minutes of a meeting held on 16 October 1945 come next in the volume. Minutes fix who met, what was weighed, and what, if anything, was agreed. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

Meeting records punctuate the letters and memoranda of this collection, marking the moments when paper gave way to talk. By mid-October 1945 the intelligence question had enough rival plans on the table to need face-to-face sorting. Readers should use the minutes as hinges. What the letters before them proposed, the meeting tested. What the meeting left open, the letters after them fought over. That rhythm, paper and meeting in turn, drives the whole five-year story.
frus-1945-50-intel-d328:
A letter dated 5 November 1947 links two senior offices. The sender was the Acting Secretary of State’s Special Assistant for Research and Intelligence (Armstrong). The reader was the Executive Secretary of the National Security Council (Souers). Readers meet it as document 328 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The shift from the old group to the CIA was fresh. The Council was still learning how to run its side of the work.

Letters between senior men often carried the real weight of a matter, since a signed letter put the writer's name and office behind the words. A signed page also protected the writer: no one could later say the point had never been put. To read it in place is to watch the Cold War state being assembled at desk level.
frus-1945-50-intel-d428:
National Security Council Intelligence Directive No. 8, dated 25 May 1948, is document 428 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

The spring of 1948 brought crisis in Europe, with the blockade of Berlin weeks away. At home, the Council kept adding rules for its intelligence agencies. A new directive in May shows the system still taking shape under pressure, rather than resting on the plan drawn up the year before. The Berlin crisis that summer would soon test every line of these standing orders. Orders written in calm months had to serve in wild ones, and mostly they did.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d128:
One flaw in the Germany plan bothered the President: no tough civilian voice in Berlin. Leo Pasvolsky recorded the objection on 15 November 1944, after a White House talk on the treatment of Germany. His memorandum is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

Roosevelt had read the State Department's memorandum and found it satisfactory except on this point. As he saw it, Eisenhower and the British and Russian commanders would run their zones. A commission of lower-ranking soldiers would sit in Berlin. What it lacked was a strong civilian point of view. His fix: give a general's commission to some outstanding civilian and make him the American member of the Berlin commission.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d228:
Leave the Turkish Straits alone: that is the hope stated in a briefing paper of 21 October 1944. The “Memorandum Regarding the Question of the Turkish Straits” is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It gives three reasons for wishing the subject never came up.

First, the Montreux Convention of 1936 has worked well, and Moscow itself said so, jointly with Britain, in 1941. The Straits went unused as a supply road to Russia because the Axis held the lands around them, not because of the treaty. Second, large changes would likely violate Turkish sovereignty and upset the balance in the Balkans and the Near East. Turkey, the paper adds, has been a good custodian of the Straits. Minor changes from Moscow or London would still be weighed with care.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d28: Harriman reported from Moscow on 14 December 1944, sending Roosevelt word as document 28 in this volume. The Foreign Relations editors placed his report among the leaders' letters in the Malta and Yalta record. Ambassador reports like this one grounded summit planning in what the Soviet government was actually doing, rather than what Washington hoped it might accept at the conference table.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d328:
Charles Bohlen kept the record of the first Roosevelt-Stalin talk at Yalta, held at 4 p.m. on February 4, 1945. After warm thanks for the welcome, the President said the military picture had much improved since they last met. Stalin agreed, reporting that Soviet armies were moving with success toward the line of the Oder.

Roosevelt joked that he had bet aboard his cruiser on a race: Russians to Berlin, or Americans to Manila first. Stalin answered that Manila would likely fall first, given the hard fighting on the Oder. Bohlen's minutes catch two partners sounding each other out before the formal sessions began.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d428:
Four powers sign this early American draft of the Declaration on Liberated Europe, dated February 5, 1945. France stands among them, beside the United States, Britain, and the Soviet Union. The draft pledges the four governments to concert their action in helping peoples freed from Nazi rule. Former Axis satellite peoples are included too.

Their pressing political and economic problems, the draft says, are to be solved by democratic means. It speaks of the Nazi war machine in retreat and puppet regimes collapsing. Later texts at Yalta cut France from the declaration. This draft preserves the wider promise the Americans first imagined.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d128:
Ambassador Harriman confirmed his travel party to Secretary Byrnes in a telegram from Moscow on July 6, 1945. The short message is document 128 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Byrnes had invited him the day before and said the State Department party would reach Berlin on July 13.

Harriman writes that he will plan to be in Berlin when the State Department party arrives. Edward Page and his assistant, Lieutenant Meiklejohn, will travel with him. So will General Deane, Admiral Maples, and General Ritchie of the American military mission in Moscow, who had their own orders from the War and Navy Departments. The telegram completes the picture of the Moscow contingent joining the American delegation at Potsdam.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d228:
The State Department argued for a Council of Foreign Ministers in a briefing memorandum dated June 27, 1945. The paper is document 228 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It is the full statement of the proposal the President would lay before Stalin and Churchill.

Without some machinery for peace negotiations and territorial settlements, the paper warns, confusion, political uncertainty, and economic stagnation will drag on in Europe. Versailles does not encourage faith in a full formal conference: slow, heated, and hard to ratify. The Department's formula is a council of the foreign ministers of the five permanent members of the Security Council: Britain, Russia, China, France, and the United States. Limiting the council to those five would also block bids to pack it with client states. It should meet as soon after the summit as preparations allow.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d28:
Hopkins saw Stalin alone after dinner at the Kremlin on June 1, 1945. Only the interpreter Pavlov was present, and Hopkins's memorandum records the plea he made. He wanted to impress on Stalin, as earnestly as he knew how, the bad effect in America of the detaining of fourteen Poles inside Poland. He spoke specifically of those charged only with having illegal radio transmitters.

He made clear he was not talking about the others, charged with more serious crimes. If this business could be settled, he believed, the list of Polish names for consultation in Moscow would win approval without great difficulty. The memorandum shows the envoy spending his credit on prisoners.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d328:
A briefing memorandum dated June 27, 1945, makes the case for a four-power treaty to keep Germany disarmed for good. Under such a treaty, the United States, Britain, France, and the Soviet Union would pledge their own forces to hold Germany down. The memo lists the gains early action could bring.

A firm pledge, it argues, would strengthen trust among the allies and head off other quarrels. It would also cut Soviet fears that a rebuilt Germany might one day join the West against Russia. If Germany stayed disarmed by joint promise, no grouping of European powers could threaten the Soviet Union, and Moscow could afford a softer policy elsewhere.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d428:
Payment for exported German coal is Pauley's condition in his cable from Moscow of July 7, 1945. On the Potter-Hyndley report he agrees fully: action should be taken at once to export from Germany all coal above German needs, and to reach maximum production early. His telegram answers Washington's message of July 3.

But Pauley adds a warning from his reparations post. Countries that do not pay for coal they receive should be put on definite notice. Such deliveries may later count as part of reparations payments under the final plan, or stand as exports for which payment in acceptable currencies will be required. Free coal, he insists, must not slip off the books.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d528:
Ukrainian refugees in Germany are the subject of an airgram from Tittmann at Vatican City, dated July 5, 1945. He transmits a translation of a note received from the Holy See that same day. Several thousand Ukrainians are in Germany, the note says, and fear that they may be sent to Galicia, in Soviet-held territory.

On their behalf, the Holy See has been asked to use its good offices. The wish is that these poor refugees may soon be allowed to leave Germany and take refuge in France, Belgium, the Netherlands, or any other country. Anything, the note pleads, rather than being obliged to go to territories under Russian domination. A like appeal for Baltic peoples had reached the Department in May.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d628:
A top secret briefing paper on the withdrawal of Allied forces from Iran is dated June 23, 1945. It is document 628 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Iran had raised the question in formal notes to all three Allied powers on May 19.

The paper traces how foreign troops came to Iran. British and Russian forces moved in during August 1941, after the Shah failed to expel German agents. A treaty of January 1942 made their stay lawful. It set withdrawal no later than six months after all fighting with Germany and her associates had ended. That word associates matters, since Japan still fought on. The British, the paper says, intend to raise the issue at the conference themselves.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1028: John McCloy wrote to Assistant Secretary James Dunn on July 17, 1945, about a French sector for Berlin. General Clay had worked out a tentative deal with General Weeks, the British deputy governor. A French area in the city would be carved from the existing British and American areas. McCloy suggests telling Ambassador Winant that agreement looks likely. Winant should then clear the way in the European Advisory Commission to send the question to the Control Council. Clay planned to settle a firm scheme with Weeks and Koeltz that week.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1128:
The Acting Secretary of State wrote to Ambassador Winant in London on 21 July 1945. With the president and the secretary of state at Potsdam, the home team kept the London embassy briefed and tasked. Winant was Washington's eyes on the British government through the summit.

A message of this kind could carry news of the talks, fresh orders, or a request for word from London. The London post was the most vital American embassy of the war years. Keeping it in step mattered even while the leaders met face to face. This cable shows the home office running that link in the middle of the summit.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1228:
Sato cabled Togo on 20 July 1945, keeping up the Moscow reports. The exchange between the two men ran almost daily through the summit. Each Sato cable tested Soviet mood; each came back with less hope than Tokyo wanted.

Japan's bid rested on a false guess: that Moscow would help end the war on mild terms. Sato, on the spot, saw the guess failing. His duty was to report what he saw without breaking Tokyo's will to hear it. This dispatch is one link in that painful chain. It shows the peace feeler dying by inches, in an envoy's careful words.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1328:
Murray, the American ambassador in Iran, wrote to the Acting Secretary of State on 20 July 1945. Iran sat under joint Allied occupation, with Soviet troops in the north and a vital supply route to Russia running through it. Its file was quiet at Potsdam but never cold.

An envoy's report from Tehran carried the facts of that uneasy triangle: a young shah, foreign armies, and oil beneath it all. Washington watched Iran as a test of Soviet conduct after the war. This dispatch is the Tehran post's word during the summit. It shows the coming Cold War's map being sketched in side reports.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1428:
The Soviet delegation submitted a text on 29 July 1945, the first of a cluster of Soviet texts from the conference's final days. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Clusters matter: when a delegation tables paper after paper in the closing stretch, it is marking the points it refuses to leave unsettled. This text opens a run of four Soviet submissions dated within two days. Readers who line the run up against the final protocol can see the last Soviet push in full. Judge how much of it the other leaders absorbed before they signed. Few parts of the volume show bargaining pressure so plainly.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-128:
On July 28, 1945, the United States delegation added this memorandum to its Potsdam files. That was the day Attlee took his seat as prime minister and the talks resumed in full. Staff papers from the date catch the conference resetting around a changed British team. The memo was printed in the second Potsdam volume.

Delegation memoranda were the glue of a large mission. They kept dozens of officers reading from the same page. This one preserves the team's shared picture at a turning point. For readers, it is a dated snapshot: what the Americans thought, in writing, before the closing bargains began.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-28:
Thompson's minutes for the plenary session of July 19, 1945, record a frontier incident raised by Stalin. They are an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Churchill answered a point Stalin had made at the previous meeting, about the Bulgarian-Greek frontier.

Churchill said he had made inquiries and heard of no fighting. The peoples there did not like each other much, and some sniping was likely. No Greek field division stood in northern Greece, he stressed. Greece had seven thousand guards on its Albanian and Yugoslav frontiers for internal order. Across the line stood far larger forces: thirty thousand Albanians, thirty thousand Yugoslavs, and twenty-four thousand Bulgarians. The great powers, Churchill argued, should make clear that marauding attacks would not be tolerated. Frontier questions belonged to the peace conference, and violators would prejudice their own claims.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d728:
Document 728 is a working paper of the United States delegation, dated July 20, 1945. Staff built such papers to shape options for the talks. It circulated inside the team rather than across the table. The paper was kept with the conference files and printed in the second Potsdam volume.

Working papers preserve roads not taken. Options that leaders later cut still stand here in full. Readers can weigh them and guess why they fell. The document also shows drafting as teamwork: many hands, one text. In the mass of Potsdam paper, these drafts are where policy first took written shape.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d828:
The United States delegation tabled this proposal on July 31, 1945, as document 828. It was offered on the conference's last full day. Late American texts aimed at the final protocol's remaining gaps. The proposal was printed in the second Potsdam volume of the official record.

A last-day proposal is a bid for the record as much as for the deal. Even where it failed, it marked the American position. Readers can compare it with the protocol adopted hours later. The document shows a delegation still drafting at the wire. Potsdam's paper war ended only when the conference did.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d928: The American reparations team in Moscow sent this short telegram to Edwin Pauley on July 25, 1945. It corrects two figures in their East Prussia message of the day before. Livestock and farm equipment values should read 1,250 million Reichsmarks for East Prussia as a whole, and 435 million for the northern part. Farm output should read 1,200 million, about 9 percent of the old Reich, and 425 million for the north. The team also fixes a message number in the same cable.
galsworthy-swan-song-1928:
John Galsworthy closed the Forsyte chronicles with Swan Song, published in 1928. It ends both the second trilogy, A Modern Comedy, and Soames Forsyte's long story. Galsworthy had followed the family from Victorian wealth into the unsettled 1920s.

Fleur's unhappy love for Jon Forsyte burns on inside her marriage, while Soames grows old and oddly tender. The General Strike of 1926 shakes London in the background. A fire at Soames's house brings the saga's themes of property and love to a final test. Galsworthy gives his most possessive character a strangely moving end, and an age closes with him.
gao-gaoreports-b-296228: Grove Resource Solutions doubled its July 2005 protest — two case numbers, one resources fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Two dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-304228: A No Child Left Behind video news release got a fiscal ruling in this September 2005 GAO call, which tests the Education Department's media buy. The decision reads the money law. The ruling decides whether the release was legal. The law had the final word.
gao-gaoreports-b-308128: Abstinence education funding got a legal ruling in this October 2006 GAO call, which tests the law's applicability to the program. The decision reads the statute. The ruling decides whether the federal dollars could legally flow. The law had the final word.
gao-gaoreports-b-309928: This 2007 GAO ruling is about agency Implementation of Ten Provisions of Law at Presidential Signing Statements. GAO's legal decisions tell agencies what federal funding law allows. Agencies follow these rulings when spending federal funds. Its full text is kept in the library next to this description.
gao-gaoreports-b-310928: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Data Integrators, Inc. The January 31, 2008 ruling examines how the agency evaluated the bids. The ruling sets ground rules for future federal contract contests. It is kept here as part of the lasting public record.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-328: Army LOGCAP contract management needed coordination in 2005, and GAO's report says high-level DOD teamwork was required. The review calls for the huddle. The wartime contractors deserved the watch. The coordination had to improve. The wartime contractors deserved the watch.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-528: Crop insurance fraud vulnerability needed reducing in 2005, and GAO's report says actions were needed to cut the program's exposure. The findings demand the safeguards. The report warns that the farm safety net should not be gamed. The actions had to be taken.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-628: Health IT strategy was taking shape in 2005, and GAO's report says HHS was building a national approach. The findings give the credit. The report shows the digital health plans were being drafted. The strategy had to be developed. The digital health plans were being drafted.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-728: FAA technical training was mostly effective in 2005, and GAO's report says management practices worked, though further actions could help. The findings balance credit and need. The report warns that the technicians deserved good training. The actions had to come. The technicians deserved good training.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-828: Nuclear projects in Russia needed better controls in 2005, and GAO's report says DOE management controls were required for the programs. The findings demand the discipline. The report warns that the bomb material deserved tight oversight. The controls had to be better.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-28: Performance budgeting engaged Congress too little in 2005, and GAO's report says PART focused attention on results, though more could engage lawmakers. The findings balance credit and need. The report warns that the budget grades deserved an audience. The engagement had to grow.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-328: The IRS's computer controls needed strengthening in 2006, and GAO's report says continued progress was required to harden the systems. The findings target the gaps. The report warns that the tax agency's vault needed locking. The controls had to be strengthened.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1128: GAO's 2007 report turns the audit lens on the China-watching commission — the small congressional shop tracking Beijing's rise. Its books, buys, and back-office habits needed tightening, GAO found. The report applies plain good-housekeeping rules to the very panel Congress built to keep an eye on America's top rival.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-28: Eminent domain's human cost was poorly measured in 2007, and GAO's report says information on its uses and effects was limited. The findings flag the blind spot. The report warns that the takings power deserved a closer look. The homeowners deserved the data.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-528: Congress wrote cyber homework for the agencies — and GAO's 2007 report says several flunked it outright. The findings show departments stumbling over the law's data-defense chores, from patching to planning. The report's message is blunt: statutes do not secure servers; only people following them do.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-828: The Guard and Reserve were flying without a flight plan in 2007 — GAO's report says the Pentagon needed a real strategy and honest numbers for the citizen force. The findings demand transparency on the part-time troops. The report treats the reserve bargain as too big to run on autopilot.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-128: This 2007 GAO report takes a hard look at toxic Chemical Releases: EPA Actions Could Reduce Environmental Information Available to Many Communities. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-28: In 2007, the Government Accountability Office published this report on national Flood Insurance Program: Greater Transparency and Oversight of Wind and Flood Damage Determinations Are Needed. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
h-e-j-1928-review-rasa-jala-nidhi-or-oce: H, , e, j. (1928), Review of Rasa-Jala-Nidhi, the book review. This book preserves that review. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
hall-well-of-loneliness-1928: Radclyffe Hall's 1928 The Well of Loneliness follows Stephen Gordon's lesbian life. Britain banned it for obscenity. The Tower library holds the full text. It spoke the unspeakable. Courts banned. Readers wept. Truth persisted. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
hawthorne-fanshawe-1828:
Nathaniel Hawthorne published Fanshawe in 1828, his first novel, issued anonymously at his own cost. He later tried to destroy every copy of the college romance he could find and burn. The book survives as the seed of the canon, essential to the origins of his art.

Fanshawe, a frail scholar at Harley College, wastes in study while a villain plots around him. Dr. Melmoth's ward Ellen is pursued by a scoundrel who lures her toward a cliff and death. Fanshawe saves her, renounces his hopeless love, and dies young of his scholar's ruined health in college. The plot is stock Gothic, but the gloom and guilt point straight to the later Hawthorne of Salem. He disowned the book so hard that his wife learned of it only late.
hurston-how-it-feels-to-be-colored-me-19:
How It Feels to Be Colored Me, published in 1928 in the magazine World Tomorrow, is Zora Neale Hurston's best-known essay. Hurston recalls growing up in Eatonville, Florida, where she first felt simply herself. She says she became colored when she moved to Jacksonville at age thirteen and felt set apart.

Rather than plead or boast, Hurston meets race with wit and self-assurance. She refuses pity and declares she does not feel tragically colored. Everyday images carry her points: colored bags of odds and ends, the feel of music, the shock of being watched. The essay became the most quoted personal statement of the Harlem Renaissance.
hutcheson-essay-passions-illustrations-1:
Hutcheson's Essay on the Nature and Conduct of the Passions and Affections, from 1728, is the first edition of his psychology of feeling. Its second half, the Illustrations on the Moral Sense, defends his central idea against two critics, Gilbert Burnet and John Balguy. Francis Hutcheson taught at Glasgow, where he shaped a generation of Scottish thinkers.

The essay sorts our passions and affections: calm desires, violent storms, and the steady pull of benevolence. Hutcheson asks how reason should govern feeling without killing it. The Illustrations then argue that our approval of virtue comes from a moral sense planted in our nature. The book completes the system begun in his Inquiry of 1725.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-28:
War returns in full force in Volume 28, from 1898. Thwaites covers the Hurons and Iroquois across 1646 and 1647, as peace fails. The annual report turns into a chronicle of slow disaster for Huronia.

Raids burn towns, scatter families, and close the river routes again. Priests write on, steady as ever, while their world crumbles. They bury the dead, guard the fleeing, and keep the chapels open. Each letter home carries grief, grit, and unshaken purpose at once. The volume shows a mission in its last years, still at work each day. Its writers refuse despair even as towns fall.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-maas-myrtil-102:
Myrtil Maas, a French mathematician turned insurance leader, is profiled in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born in France in 1792, he showed an early gift for mathematics. In 1813 he entered the Ecole Normale at Paris. Two years later a stray shot during a drill in the Champ de Mars wounded his leg. The wound never healed fully.

The article explains how prejudice bent his career. Being Jewish, he could not win a university chair in mathematics. He worked in a porcelain factory, then as a private tutor. An insurance company hired him as actuary in 1818 and later made him vice-president. In 1828 he became president of a new life and fire company founded by the Foulds. Maas also served the Jewish community, joining the Central Consistory in 1830. His old schoolfellows struck a medal in his honor before his death in 1865.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-malchus-cleodem:
Malchus, called Cleodemus the Prophet, is treated in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. He was a Hellenistic writer of the second century before the common era. His Semitic name was common in Phoenicia and Syria but not among Jews. Scholars have argued ever since over what he was: Phoenician, Syrian, Samaritan, or Jew.

The article tells what his lost history contained. Cleodemus wrote a history of the Jews in Greek, mixing Jewish tradition with Greek myth.
