Josephus preserves a scrap of it through Alexander Polyhistor. In his telling, three sons of Abraham and Keturah gave their names to a town, to Assyria, and to Africa. Those sons also helped Hercules fight in Libya, and Hercules married into their line. From that marriage came Didorus, ancestor of the Sophacians. The entry shows how Bible genealogy was once rewoven to fit Greek heroic myth.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meal-offering-1:
The meal-offering is every sacrifice drawn from the vegetable world. Emil G. Hirsch and Eduard König treat it in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. In the Bible it is called “minhah,” a word the article traces to an Arabic verb meaning “to give”: the offering is a gift. The impulse to bring God grain and flour, the authors hold, is as old and as general as the impulse to bring animals. Cain's offering from his field is its first example.

After noting scattered mentions in the early histories, bread laid before God and the loaves at Nob among them. Then the article turns to the rules of Leviticus. The material must be fine flour, oil, salt, and incense. Leaven and honey are strictly kept out, the article suggests, because they ferment. The one exception named is the jealousy-offering of Numbers, which breaks the fine-flour rule.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-menahem-ben-jai:
Menahem ben Jair, leader of the Sicarii in the first revolt against Rome, is given a compact biography in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by Gotthard Deutsch and S. J. Levinson. A grandson of Judas of Galilee, founder of the Zealot party, he first checked his men's lawlessness, then led them in 66 C.E. to storm Masada and kill its Roman garrison. In Jerusalem his followers entered the Antonia fortress and murdered the helpless wounded the Romans had left behind.

Success undid him. Swollen with victory, Menahem demanded command of the whole revolt and recognition as the Messiah, and his men turned to still crueler violence. Eleazar ben Ananias, seeing the Sicarii as a menace, turned the Zealots against him; Menahem fled to Ophla, was captured, and was executed, Eleazar succeeding him. The entry rests on Josephus and Grätz.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-messer-leon-jud:
Judah ben Jehiel Rofe, known as Messer Leon, was an Italian rabbi, physician, and philosopher who flourished in Mantua in the later fifteenth century. Gotthard Deutsch wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The article says he was born, by report, in Naples, and explains that Leon was the usual name for Judah while Messer was a title given to physicians.

As rabbi in Mantua, Leon clashed with his colleague Joseph Colon, and both men were expelled from the city in 1475. He wrote books on logic and grammar and commentaries on Aristotle, but his rhetoric text Nofet Ẓufim was the only work printed, at Mantua before 1480. In it he argued that Judaism welcomed secular learning, following Cicero and Quintilian.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-milan-latin-med:
Milan, capital of Lombardy and Italy's largest commercial city, had Jews from Roman times, and its Jewish Encyclopedia history by Richard Gottheil and Ismar Elbogen opens in conflict. Saint Ambrose, the city's patron, was their inveterate enemy and hoped for martyrdom over a destroyed synagogue. In 388 he shamed the emperor Theodosius out of ordering one rebuilt.

Later centuries show Lombard Jews as large landowners and a probable Jewish mintmaster named Gideon in tenth-century Milan. As the Italian cities rose, Jews were squeezed out, the article argues, because Lombard Christians themselves mastered commerce and banking. A heresy persecution in 1320 forced the podestà to promise their expulsion, and the long entry follows the community through many such turns.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mortara-case-11:
The Mortara case was the 1858 seizure of a Jewish child, Edgar Mortara, by papal guards in Bologna. Gotthard Deutsch tells the story in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. A servant, Anna Morisi, had secretly baptized the boy during an illness years before. When the Inquisition learned of it, it ordered the six year old taken from his parents.

The entry recounts the protests that followed across Europe and America. Sir Moses Montefiore traveled to Rome to plead with the pope, but he was never received. Kings and statesmen wrote, petitions circulated, and nothing moved Pius the Ninth. Edgar was raised Catholic, joined the Augustinian order, and preached as a missionary. The case hastened the fall of the Papal States and spurred the founding of the Alliance Israélite Universelle.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-mizorodi-:
Moses Mizorodi ben Judah Maruli was a Karaite scholar at Constantinople in the second half of the sixteenth century. Joseph Jacobs and Isaac Broydé wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He was a younger contemporary of Judah Poki, and he wrote a eulogy on Poki's Sha'ar Yehudah. He was a prolific writer in his day.

Almost everything he wrote is lost. Only a fragment of his Pentateuch commentary, Yemin Mosheh, survives in the Firkovich collection at St. Petersburg. The titles of the rest come from Simhah Luzki's list: works on Lamentations, Proverbs, Ruth, sermons, and the calendar. The entry is a small memorial to a library that vanished.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nashim-women-11:
Nashim, meaning Women, is the third order of the Mishnah, on betrothal, marriage, and divorce. Wilhelm Bacher and S. Mendelsohn mapped it for the Jewish Encyclopedia. Its seven tractates cover the whole legal relation of woman to man. Their sequence varies between codifiers and publishers, the article notes.

Yebamot treats the childless widow and the levirate duty; Ketubot, marriage contracts and a wife's civil rights. Nedarim handles vows a husband or father may annul, and Nazir the Nazirite's abstinence. Sotah covers the suspected wife's ordeal, Gittin the forms of divorce. Kiddushin closes the order with betrothal law and ethics between the sexes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nicopolis-bulga:
Nicopolis is a Bulgarian city on the Danube. Gotthard Deutsch and M. Franco wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews likely settled there at its founding under Trajan. Byzantine Jews came in numbers in 967. Merchants followed from Ragusa, Venice, and Genoa.

Hungary's expelled Jews found asylum there in 1367. Tirnova's Jews fled to Nicopolis a year later. The Spanish exiles of 1492 swelled the community greatly. Joseph Caro himself served as its chief rabbi. War in the 1590s burned Jewish homes and their library. Isaac Vega, an eyewitness, recorded that bitter loss. By 1904 only 189 Jews remained in Nicopolis. Caro's bath, his Torah copy, and his study hall survive.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nunez-maria-116:
Maria Nuñez was a Portuguese Marano who fled the Inquisition. Gotthard Deutsch and Meyer Kayserling wrote her entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Gaspar Lopez Homem was her father. She lived across the 1500s into the 1600s. Holland was the refuge she chose about 1590.

Her brother Manuel and uncle Miguel sailed with her. An English ship captured theirs on the way. Its captain, a nobleman, fell for her beauty. He proposed marriage, which she firmly refused. London buzzed at her looks in that season. Queen Elizabeth summoned her and drove her through London. Still she asked only passage onward to Holland. Amsterdam received her safely at last. Her mother and more kin joined her there. She wed her cousin Manuel Lopez Homem there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oppenheim-asher: Asher Anshel Oppenheim was a scholar of the Talmud at Dessau. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote his short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived at Dessau at the start of the eighteen hundreds. He wrote a work named Dibre Asher, or Words of Asher. Its first part bore a name that means letter of sharp swords. The work treats the rite of circumcision, the cutting of a male child. It came out at Dessau in the year 1804.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-paschkis-heinri:
Heinrich Paschkis was an Austrian pharmacologist born in Nikolsburg, Moravia, in 1849. He studied at Vienna University and took his medical degree in 1872. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He stayed in Vienna for his whole career.

Paschkis became an assistant at the university hospital. In 1883 he rose to privat-docent in pharmacology. He wrote many essays for medical journals. He also edited a handbook of dentistry. His books cover mercury treatment for syphilis and medical cosmetics. Another book set out the standard drugs of his day.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-perez-b-isaac-c:
Perez ben Isaac Cohen was a cabalist of the thirteenth century. Kaufmann Kohler and Philipp Bloch wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His surname Gerondi rests on a shaky guess by Jellinek. Even his full name is not fully certain. He lived toward the century's end.

One work is tied to this Perez with confidence. It is called Ma'areket ha-Elahut, the System of the Godhead. The book treats the order of the divine powers. It ranks among the early works of Kabbalah. The entry gives no place or date for its author.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-picart-bernard-:
Bernard Picart was a French engraver who settled in Amsterdam. He was born at Paris in 1673 and died in 1733. Joseph Jacobs and I. George Dobsevage wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Some thirteen hundred of his plates survive.

His Jewish fame rests on the Ceremonies des Juifs. That volume opened a vast survey of world religions. Its plates show Jewish worship with rare care and accuracy. Readers see the synagogue, the shofar, and the Passover meal. They see circumcision, weddings, and burial as well. They rank among the first such engravings ever made.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-poitiers-12228:
Poitiers is a French city, capital of the department of Vienne. Richard Gottheil and S. Kahn wrote its history for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Their account centers on the Jews of the town in the Middle Ages. It runs from attacks by Crusaders to final expulsion.

Crusaders harried the Jews of Poitiers in 1236, though the pope condemned the attacks. In 1240 Nathan ben Joseph debated the bishop in public. Alphonse de Poitiers expelled the Jews in 1249 and wiped out debts owed to them. Yet he later called a famed Jewish doctor to treat his eyes. Philip the Fair expelled all Jews from the city in 1296.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-puah-12428:
Puah was one of two midwives in the book of Exodus. Emil G. Hirsch and Schulim Ochser wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Pharaoh charged her and Shiphrah with a cruel task. They were to kill all Hebrew boys at birth. Both women are named in the first chapter of Exodus. Their act of defiance saved lives the king sought.

Philo may have linked her name to a like Hebrew word. That word means the red, in the sense of color. A dye plant bears a name close to hers in Arabic. A midrash on Exodus takes up her name as well. The article weighs these clues to who Puah was.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-raframi-ben-pap:
Raframi ben Papa was a Babylonian amora of the fourth century. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. In his youth Raframi studied under R. Hisda. He later led the school at Pumbedita after Rab Dimi.

The article notes sayings he passed on in Hisda's name. Those sayings cover both Jewish law and story-like teaching. It also gives two different death dates from old sources. Abraham ibn Daud gives 387, while Sherira Gaon gives 395. Readers get a brief record of a teacher whose own words survive through the Talmud.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ree-bernhard-ph:
Bernhard Philip Ree was a Danish editor and politician born on July 18, 1813. Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Aarhus in Jutland. He died there on November 13, 1868.

The article says he studied law, then turned to newspapers. In 1838 he edited the Aalborg Stiftstidende. He also published several magazines of his own. He joined Aalborg's council in 1844 and again in 1860. He served in the lower house from 1850 to 1854. There he urged selling the Danish West Indies to America. He later sat in the upper house. Illness forced him to resign in 1867.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rose-12828:
Rose is a subject entry in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia, written by Joseph Jacobs and Immanuel Löw. It traces every mention of the flower in Jewish writings, old and later. The rose never appears in the Bible itself, which the entry points out early.

Its first clear mention comes in Ecclesiasticus, and later texts name it more often. In the Targum and later readings, the rose often replaces the lily of Canticles. The entry lists wild kinds that grow in Palestine, Syria, Lebanon, and Sinai. It also recalls an old tradition of a rose bed in Jerusalem, kept since the prophets.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rueff-jules-129:
Jules Rueff was a French merchant and ship-owner born at Paris on February 16, 1854. Isidore Singer and Jacques Kahn wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Young, he turned to colonial affairs and navigation with energy.

In 1872 Rueff went to Indo-China, becoming a pioneer of French influence there. He planned the Saigon-Mytho railroad in Cochin-China as well. He founded the Messageries Fluviales, whose boats spread French trade along the Mekong. His company opened the first French counting-houses in Abyssinia, at Jibuti. From 1900 he administered the great dockyards at Saint-Nazaire.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rumania-10928:
Rumania is a kingdom of southern Europe, treated here for its Jewish history. Gotthard Deutsch, D. M. Hermalin, and Joseph Jacobs wrote the entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Its opening pages reach back to Roman times in Dacia.

Rumanian historians claim Jews lived there before Trajan's conquest of Dacia. A decree of 397 protected Dacian Jews and their synagogues, the entry notes. In the eighth century, Jewish Khazars reportedly entered Moldavia and Wallachia in arms. When Radu Negru founded a new realm about 1290, Jews followed him. They helped him set up his rule over the country.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-salkind-solomon:
Solomon ben Baruch Salkind was a Lithuanian Hebrew poet who taught at Wilna's rabbinical seminary. Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He died at Wilna on March 14, 1868.

Salkind's Shirim li-Shelomoh, from 1842, gathers poems in Hebrew verse. Most of them are adaptations from other languages into Hebrew dress. Two later collections, Kol Shelomoh and Shema Shelomoh, followed in 1858 and 1866. His Hebrew speeches stand in a volume of seminary addresses from 1864. That book was printed at the Russian government's own expense. Through them, Hebrew readers met foreign poetry in their own tongue.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-b-meir-r:
Samuel b. Meïr, called RaSHBaM, was a French Bible exegete of Ramerupt, near Troyes. Wilhelm Bacher and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born about 1085, he was Rashi's grandson and his pupil as well.

RaSHBaM began with homiletic reading, then moved toward the plain sense. He ranks among the first realistic exegetes of the Bible in his school. His commentaries cover the Pentateuch, the Prophets, Job, and the Five Scrolls. Notes of his hide inside the Ezra commentary long ascribed to Rashi. He is often named as a tosafist on the Talmud too.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schulman-samuel:
Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Samuel Schulman. He was an American rabbi. Schulman was born in Russia on February 14, 1865. His parents brought him to New York before his first birthday. He was educated in New York's public schools. He also studied at the College of the City of New York.

Schulman took his rabbinical diploma in Berlin. The Hochschule für die Wissenschaft des Judenthums granted it. He then held pulpits at Helena, Montana, and Kansas City, Missouri. In 1901 Temple Beth-El in New York elected him associate rabbi. When Dr. Kohler left for the Hebrew Union College, Schulman became rabbi. In 1904 the Jewish Theological Seminary gave him a doctorate of divinity.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-senses-the-five:
Five senses — sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch — form the subject here. Kaufmann Kohler and Isaac Broydé wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on them. The idea came from Aristotle, who taught that the soul perceives things through bodily organs. That teaching entered Jewish writing with Greek and Arab thought.

Saadia tried to show that the Bible itself names all five senses. Bahya linked the senses to Moses' commandments, sense by sense. Most medieval writers accepted five as the full count. A few added speech or movement as extra senses. The entry shows Jewish thinkers testing an old Greek idea against their own texts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shefar-am-calle:
Shefar'am is a place in Palestine about three hours from Haifa. Gotthard Deutsch and M. Franco wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. In the second century it sheltered the Sanhedrin for a time. Little is known of its early Jewish community's story.

No traveler, Jewish or Gentile, mentions the town for centuries. It sat off the main roads to Haifa and Tiberias. Around 1741 many Palestinian Jews settled there anew. Rabbi Hayyim Abulafia of Smyrna encouraged that settlement. Jews first farmed there, then turned to trade under heavy taxes. Their lands passed to Druses, then back again. The entry rescues a small town from near silence in the record.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-siblonot-13628:
Siblonot is the Talmudic term for gifts given to a bride before marriage. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Isaac Broydé wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the term. A bridegroom or his parents presented these gifts. Scholars dispute where the word itself comes from.

Some derive it from a Greek word for a token payment. Others link it to a Hebrew word meaning load, or presents. Talmudic teachers debated what the term covered in law. Did it mean all bridal gifts or only the first? Rabbinic law set rules for gifts if death or divorce intervened. Clothes worn out at her father's house need not be returned. Jewelry and lasting goods stood under different rules. The entry shows wedding gifts treated with legal care.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simhah-freudema:
Simhah Ephraim ben Gershon ha-Kohen, called Freudmann, was a rabbi in Belgrade. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Alexander Büchler wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born about 1622 and died in 1669. He followed his teacher Judah Lerma as rabbi at Belgrade.

In 1657 he published Sefer Shemot at Venice. That book dealt with how to spell Hebrew personal names. It also covered names of places and rivers in Asia and Europe. He became rabbi at Budapest in 1660, but left after two months. A ban on rabbis with kin in the city forced his return to Belgrade.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-soeira-samuel-a:
Samuel Abravanel Soeira, also called Samuel ben Israel, was born in Amsterdam in 1625. Joseph Jacobs and Israel Cohen wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was the son of Manasseh ben Israel. In 1654 he went to England on his father's behalf. He carried a petition to Cromwell for the readmission of Jews.

He is said to have received a doctor's degree from Oxford. Scholars later argued that the diploma was spurious. In 1655 he returned to Amsterdam to fetch his father. Manasseh came to London that October with his son. Samuel died in London in September 1657. His body was carried back to Holland for burial.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sosa-martin-alf:
Martin Alfonso de Sosa was a Portuguese envoy and governor of Goa. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He served in the middle of the sixteenth century. At Cranganore, near Cochin, he found bronze tablets with inscriptions. Cochin then had a large Jewish community of its own.

An old Jewish scholar said the tablets were in three tongues. They recorded privileges granted to the local Jews long before. He translated all the inscriptions into Hebrew at the time. They were later rendered into Portuguese as well. A Hebrew copy was held in New York in the 1850s. It was kept by a cantor of the Greene Street Synagogue.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stern-david-vis:
David de Stern was an English banker born in Frankfort-on-the-Main. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He came from a family that built banking houses across Europe. He died in London on January 19, 1877. His firm helped float loans for the Portuguese government.

In 1869 the King of Portugal made Stern a viscount. The title honored his firm's role in Portuguese loans. He sat on the Commission of Lieutenancy for London. He also served as a director of the Imperial Bank. He married a daughter of Aaron Asher Goldsmid. His son Sydney inherited the title and later became Baron Wandsworth. The short entry sketches a banker raised to foreign nobility.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-suspended-lette:
Four letters in the Hebrew Bible hang raised above the line. Crawford Howell Toy and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. One nun hangs in the book of Judges. Three ayin letters hang in Psalms and Job. The Talmud already mentions this scribal custom.

Why scribes suspended these letters is not fully clear. Rabbis read the Judges nun as hiding Moses' name. The text there calls Jonathan a grandson of Manasseh. Tradition said he was really Moses' grandson instead. Scribes spared Moses the shame by lifting the letter. Midrash reads one Psalm ayin out to change the sense. It turns a forest boar into a river or sea beast. That beast stands for Rome in the reading. The entry shows tiny marks carrying heavy interpretation.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-te-omim-frankel:
Baruch ben David Te'omim-Fränkel was a Galician rabbi and Talmudist. Solomon Schechter and A. Peiginsky wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. He served at Wisnicz and then at Leipnik in Moravia. His work falls in the 1800s' first half. He descended from Aryeh Löb Te'omim.

Fränkel won fame as a Talmudist in his region. His chief book, Baruk Ta'am, appeared at Lemberg in 1841. It holds his Talmudic dissertations in one volume. He also wrote notes to the Mishnah. Those notes entered the Lemberg Mishnah of 1862. His Talmud notes joined the Warsaw edition of 1859 to 1864. Readers still meet his glosses in those standard printings. The brief entry ties a name to two classic editions.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-todros-ben-kalo:
Todros ben Kalonymus was a French scholar and liturgical poet at Narbonne. Gotthard Deutsch and S. Mannheimer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He lived in the first half of the twelfth century. His father, Kalonymus the Great, was famed for learning and service. Kalonymus lived to the age of eighty.

A ten-year war over Narbonne's rule hurt the Jews badly. About two thousand Jews lived in the city then. Special war taxes were laid on them to fund the fight. Todros gave his own family in bondage for those taxes. He wrote Azharot, poems for the liturgy. His son Kalonymus bore the title Nasi. His nephew Todros ben Moses also appears in the record.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-troyes-hebrew-o:
Troyes, capital of Aube in France, had Jews as early as the tenth century. Isidore Singer and S. Kahn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. A responsum reached its community around the year 1000. Its Jews owned vineyards and other real estate. The counts of Champagne prized them as a revenue source.

Counts and kings later agreed to surrender each other's fugitive Jews. In March 1288 a ritual-murder charge struck Troyes. The Inquisition condemned thirteen Jews to the stake that April. An elegy by Jacob ben Judah preserves their names. Whole families died together in that burning. Troyes' Jews still paid the treasury large sums in 1301. Prosperity drew loans from lords and churchmen alike.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-valencia-14628:
Valencia, capital of its former kingdom in Spain, had a rich Jewish community under Moorish rule. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. James I of Aragon entered the conquered city in 1238. Its Jews met him with rabbis and delegates in procession. They presented him a roll of the Law in homage.

In reward for help in the conquest, James gave gifts. Some Jews received Moorish houses and city real estate. Royal secretaries and interpreters shared in those grants. Gold-workers, merchants, and money-changers were honored too. In 1239 James assigned the Jews a roomy quarter. Its bounds ran between named walls and gates. A high wall ringed the Juderia only in 1390.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-weil-karl-ritte:
Karl Weil, Ritter von Weil, was an Austrian journalist. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in Württemberg, in Germany. He died at Vienna on January 7, 1878. He studied law at Freiburg and took his degree in 1827. He then joined the Allgemeine Zeitung.

Weil reported from Paris for that paper until 1832. He edited papers in Stuttgart and Berlin next. In 1851 he moved to Vienna. There he served the Austrian government as a journalist. He retired in 1873 with a ministerial title. He took an active interest in Jewish affairs. He sat on the board of the Israelitische Allianz.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-will-or-testame:
A will is a legal act that disposes of property after death. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Lewis N. Dembitz wrote this entry. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. A will can be changed or revoked before death. Jewish law's usual substitute works differently. It is the deathbed gift of a sick person.

The Mishnah gives only scant notices of wills. Later authorities disagree widely on the details. One core question drives the debate. How far can an owner override the succession rules of Numbers? Can he cut the firstborn's double share from Deuteronomy? The entry works through these disputes with care.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wreath-15028:
Wreath, in old Jewish life, was a band of leaves worn as a sign of honor. Emil G. Hirsch and Judah David Eisenstein wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Rich brides and grooms wore crowns of gold and gems. The poor wore twists of roses, myrtle, and olive leaves.

The Mishnah names wreaths of vine twigs and ears of corn. When foes ringed Jerusalem, the rabbis banned crowns at feasts. They let plain flower wreaths pass at that time. One rabbi wore olive leaves at his own wedding feast. Oxen led to the altar wore olive wreaths on their horns. A new scholar wore a crown of the sage at his rite. The entry draws each fact from Talmud tales and rules.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yudan-ben-ishma:
Yudan ben Ishmael was a scholar of Palestine in the third century. Joseph Jacobs and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was most like a brother of Yannai ben Ishmael. He ruled on one point that touched all teachers of the Law.

That point asked if such teachers should be paid for their work. He said they should be paid for the time they lost. That time could have earned them cash at other work. He read a verse in Job as a sign of the Law. The Law is like water, he said in that note. Its words are given to each man by measure, he held. One man gets Bible, one Mishnah, one law, one tales.
jochelson-peoples-of-asiatic-russia-1928:
Waldemar Jochelson spent years in Siberia with the Jesup North Pacific Expedition, studying the native peoples of the far northeast. His 1928 survey gathers that work into one broad account of the peoples of Asiatic Russia, from the Yukaghir and Koryak to the Tungus groups.

Jochelson describes how each people lived: their hunting, fishing, homes, dress, and family life across a harsh land. He gives much space to shamanism, the spirit world, and the rites used against illness and bad luck. Because he recorded much of this before Soviet rule transformed the region, his survey preserves ways of life that soon vanished.
keightley-fairy-mythology-1828:
Thomas Keightley, an Irish writer and scholar, published The Fairy Mythology in 1828. The text here follows the enlarged edition of 1892. Keightley ranged across Europe comparing the fairy beliefs of many peoples, the first broad survey of its kind.

He sorts elves, dwarfs, trolls, and household spirits by country and by kind. Tales from Ireland, Germany, Scandinavia, and beyond sit side by side so their kinship shows. He also covers mermaids and other beings of the sea. The book helped found the study of folklore, and its tales still charm readers.
kellogg-briand-pact-1928:
In 1928, leading nations signed a short pact in Paris renouncing war as a tool of national policy. It took its name from its two sponsors, American Secretary of State Frank Kellogg and French Foreign Minister Aristide Briand. Germany, Japan, and the Soviet Union were among the early signers, and sixty-two nations joined in time.

The signers promised to settle all disputes by peaceful means and never to seek their aims through war. The pact carried no army and no penalties, and within a decade several signers were at war. Still, it wrote into law the idea that aggressive war is a crime, a principle later used at the Nuremberg trials.
larsen-quicksand-1928:
Nella Larsen published Quicksand in 1928, her first novel. Helga Crane is a young woman of mixed Danish and Black heritage. She teaches at a Black school in the South and feels stifled there. She moves to Chicago, then Harlem, then Copenhagen, always hoping the next place will fit.

In Denmark she is prized as exotic yet still feels like an outsider. Back in Harlem, she seeks meaning and makes choices that trap her in a hard marriage in the South. Larsen writes with cool clarity about race, sex, and belonging. The novel is now a classic of the Harlem Renaissance.
law-serious-call-1728:
William Law wrote A Serious Call to a Devout and Holy Life in 1728. Law was an English priest who gave up his post for his views. The book bids each Christian to live each day for God. It shaped John Wesley, George Whitefield, and the great church revolt of the age.

Law shows how prayer, work, food, and funds all fall under God's rule. He mocks half faith with tales of folk who pray well and live ill. His tone is strict, warm, and hard to shake off once read. The book stands as a peak of plain English works on the holy life.
lawrence-lady-chatterley-1928:
D. H. Lawrence wrote Lady Chatterley's Lover in Italy and published it privately in Florence in 1928. No regular British or American publisher would touch it. Lawrence rewrote the novel three times before settling on this final version, the complete Florence text.

Connie Chatterley's husband Clifford returns from the war paralyzed and sealed into his mind. Connie slowly withers in their great house until she begins an affair with the gamekeeper, Mellors. Lawrence treats their love as a cure for a dead, mechanical age. The book was banned for obscenity for decades, then became a famous test case for free publication in 1960.
le-grand-esclairsissement-de-la-pierre-p:
A French alchemical work of 1628 bears Nicolas Flamel's famous name. Its long title promises a great clarification of the philosophers' stone. Pierre Béraud published it, and Jean Blanchin engraved for it.

The dedication addresses a royal counselor at the Parlement of Paris. Its writer praises that lord's love of all the sciences. The book treats the transmutation of metals as its core subject. Flamel's legend as a successful alchemist sold many such works. This one shows his name still powerful two centuries after his death. Printers in 1628 still sold Flamel as a living authority. The dedication shows alchemy seeking noble protection at court.
lewis-man-who-knew-coolidge-1928:
Sinclair Lewis published The Man Who Knew Coolidge in 1928, a short comic novel built as a single endless monologue. Its speaker, Lowell Schmaltz, is a traveling salesman and proud clubman from Zenith, the same fictional city as Babbitt. Lewis called the book a pendant to Babbitt, its hero's booster cousin at full length.

Schmaltz buttonholes the reader with his great claim: he knew President Coolidge at college, slightly. Around that boast he pours out lodge talk, business creeds, Prohibition dodges, and opinions on everything in America. The comedy is in the voice itself, complacent, slangy, and utterly sure. Lewis catches a whole class talking in its sleep. The book is minor Lewis but perfect of its kind.
library-of-the-world-s-best-literature-a:
Warner and his associate editors built Volume Three of their world literature anthology. Their advisory council drew on professors of Hebrew, history, literature, and science. That breadth matched the set's aim: the best writing from ancient times onward. Charles Dudley Warner, a well-known American author, led the whole enterprise.

Inside, readers find selected passages and works arranged for browsing and study. The selections favor writings that had already won lasting reputations. Home readers could sample many literatures without owning hundreds of separate books. Today the volume documents both the classics themselves and Victorian taste in choosing them. Edward Holden, director of the Lick Observatory, joined the council from California. Cornell's Willard Fiske covered Germanic and Scandinavian literatures for the project.
lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-literat:
The August 1873 Lippincott's serves The New Hyperion's second part. Strahan calls this installment The Two Chickens. Margaret Howitt continues Our Home in the Tyrol. Sarah C. Hallowell's On the Church Steps runs five chapters.

W. E. Griffis takes readers inside Japan. William Black transforms his Princess of Thule in chapter twelve. Reginald Wynford tours deer-parks for the sporting reader. Fannie Feudge rambles among tropical fruits and flowers in part one. Glimpses of ghost-land and Lazarus's Afternoon poem add variety. Washington's birthplace in 1873 anchors the monthly gossip. Jason's Quest, by Charles Warren Stoddard, adds a four-part tale.
mckay-home-to-harlem-1928:
Claude McKay published Home to Harlem in 1928, his bestselling novel of Harlem nightlife and Black labor in prose. The landmark Harlem Renaissance novel follows Jake's return from war and wandering to the cabarets of Harlem in 1928. It was the first novel by a Black writer to reach the bestseller lists then.

Jake, a deserter from a labor battalion, comes home hungry for Harlem's music, food, and women of its nights. He loves Felice, loses her in a brawl, and searches the district's clubs and buffet flats for her. Ray, a Haitian waiter and writer, gives the pleasure chase a brooding, questioning second voice in the tale. McKay renders dialect, jazz, and street philosophy with a poet's ear and a radical's sympathy for workers. Du Bois scorned its cabaret focus, yet readers made it the Renaissance's popular breakthrough.
mead-coming-of-age-in-samoa-1928:
Margaret Mead went to Samoa as a young researcher and returned with Coming of Age in Samoa, published in 1928. Her study follows Samoan girls through adolescence, asking whether teenage turmoil is nature or culture. Custom, rank, and the religious regulation of youth shape the lives she watched on the island of Ta'u.

Mead's answer, that Samoan teens grew up with little of America's storm, made the book famous worldwide. It carried anthropology to a vast public and set off arguments that ran for decades. Few scholarly books have changed so many readers' picture of their own society.
nicholas-cusa-vision-of-god-salter-1928:
Emma Gurney Salter published her translation of Nicholas of Cusa's Vision of God in 1928, with an introduction by Evelyn Underhill. Cusa, a German cardinal and thinker, wrote De Visione Dei in 1453 for monks at Tegernsee. He sent them an icon of an all-seeing face with the book.

Cusa taught that God's gaze rests on each person wholly, and that opposites meet in God beyond reason's reach. His doctrine of learned ignorance held that knowing our ignorance is the start of wisdom. The short book blends prayer, logic, and mysticism. It bridges medieval devotion and Renaissance thought, and Salter's English made it a modern devotional classic.
odoric-journal-komroff-1928:
Friar Odoric of Pordenone wandered through Asia from 1318 to 1330 and dictated a journal of the trip on his return. Manuel Komroff included it in his 1928 volume on the contemporaries of Marco Polo. Odoric was a Franciscan, and his road ran from Persia to China and back by sea.

He reports pepper forests, strange customs, and the martyrdom of four friars in India. His Valley of Death passage, full of drums and terror, became famous. Marvels crowd his pages, yet much of his report checks out against other sources. Odoric rivals Polo as a witness to medieval Asia. Komroff's edition made his vivid voice easy for English readers to reach.
openalex-w1972654228:
M. Stucchi and a large European team built this earthquake catalogue. It appeared in the Journal of Seismology, dated 2012. The SHARE project aimed to harmonize seismic hazard in Europe. A single, uniform earthquake record was needed for that work. The catalogue covers the years 1000 to 1899.

National records used varied scales and uneven methods before. The team merged them into one parametric catalogue. Each quake gained shared measures of size and place. Hazard maps for engineers rest on such long records. Nine centuries of quakes deepen the sample greatly. The catalogue serves planners across the whole continent.
openalex-w2062529028:
Ana Requena-Mendez, Peter Chiodini, Zeno Bisoffi and colleagues reviewed lab diagnosis of strongyloidiasis. Their paper appeared in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2013. The disease is caused by a parasitic worm. Many infections cause no symptoms at all. Standard stool tests often miss the worm.

Blood tests help, but only specialist labs offer them. Better tests matter most for patients with weak immunity. The review searched several medical databases. It covered studies from 1960 to 2012. The authors compared old and new diagnostic methods. They also reviewed markers that show cure. Stool methods remain insensitive in their judgement. Antibody tests perform better but have limits. Clear guidance helps labs choose wisely.
openalex-w2066534928:
Benjamin Chi, Constantin Yiannoutsos, Andrew Westfall and colleagues searched for a shared rule for patients lost to HIV care. Their paper appeared in PLoS Medicine in 2011. Dropout threatens the success of HIV treatment programmes. Yet programmes defined loss to follow-up differently. A common rule would make results comparable.

The team analysed records from over a hundred facilities. The sites spanned Africa, Asia and Latin America. They tested different time gaps since last visits. Each rule was checked against later patient status. Rules that were too short mislabelled many patients. Rules that were too long missed true dropouts. The study identifies a threshold that performed best. Shared definitions help track programme quality fairly.
openalex-w2098082628:
Theo Vos, Ryan Barber, Brad Bell and the Global Burden of Disease collaborators measured illness and disability worldwide. Their paper appeared in The Lancet in 2015. Health policy needs current data on disease levels. The study covered 188 countries. It spanned the years 1990 to 2013.

The team estimated incidence and prevalence for 301 conditions. They also estimated years lived with disability. Tens of thousands of data sources fed the models. Methods were refined from the earlier 2010 study. More causes and after-effects were added this time. Injury coding and statistical models also improved. Results allow fair comparison across countries and years. They show where disability burdens are rising fastest.
openalex-w2121761828:
Luis Rosales and Jhon W. González published this theory study in Nanoscale Research Letters in 2013. They asked how electric current moves through two short, parallel ribbons of graphene, a single sheet of carbon atoms. The ribbons have armchair-shaped edges and connect to leads made of the same material.

Using a tight-binding model and Green function methods, the authors calculated the states available and the conductance of the ribbons. They also tested what a steady magnetic field pointing through the ribbons would do. The results show resonant tunneling and regular swings in transport as shape and field change. The ribbons flip between metal-like and semiconductor-like behavior in an interference pattern.
openalex-w2761329828:
Wen Ju, Alexander Bagger, and Guang-Ping Hao studied carbon catalysts for turning carbon dioxide into fuel in Nature Communications in 2017. An electric route could recycle waste CO2 using renewable power. Cheap catalysts are the bottleneck: noble metals work but cost too much. Carbons doped with metals and nitrogen look promising, yet how they work stayed unclear.

The team explored a whole family of these single-site catalysts, pairing lab tests with computer modeling. Earlier work suggested the metal centers are in fact crucial for producing carbon monoxide. Different metals steer the reaction toward different products, giving the study its selectivity map. Knowing which atomic sites do the work replaces trial-and-error design. The findings guide builders of CO2 electrolyzers toward ample materials. Such devices could one day turn emissions into feedstocks and fuels.
openalex-w2794465828:
Gaëlle Marteil, Adan Guerrero, and André F. Vieira lead a team studying centriole defects in cancer, in Nature Communications in 2018. Centrioles are tiny cylinders that organize the poles dividing cells use to split chromosomes. Healthy cells keep their number and length tightly controlled. Cancer cells often show too many centrosomes, a fault tied to scrambled chromosomes and poor prognosis.

The paper's title states its finding: centrioles grown over-long in cancer promote yet more centriole copies. Extra centrosomes then cause chromosomes to mis-segregate during division. That instability can fuel tumor growth and evolution. Cancer cells, unlike normal ones, survive these abnormal divisions instead of dying. Understanding how over-elongation starts may expose a weakness in cancer's tolerance for chaos. The work links a subtle structural flaw to a hallmark of aggressive tumors.
openalex-w2947686928:
Marcos Silva, Cristina Loures, Luan Alves, and colleagues wrote this 2019 review in the Journal of Biomedical Science. It summarizes risk factors for Alzheimer's disease and measures that may protect against it. Alzheimer's is the most common type of dementia, marked by a slow loss of memory and thinking skills.

The disease is tied to plaques of beta-amyloid protein and tangles of tau protein in the brain. The authors note that about seventy percent of risk is linked to genetics. Acquired factors that raise risk include blood vessel disease in the brain, diabetes, high blood pressure, obesity, and abnormal blood fats. Protective factors covered include cognitive reserve, physical activity, and diet.
openalex-w3015226328:
Antônio Ribeiro, Manoel Ribeiro, Gabriela Paixão, and colleagues published this study in Nature Communications in 2020. It trains a deep neural network to diagnose heart conditions from the standard twelve-lead electrocardiogram, or ECG. Automatic ECG reading is common, but the accuracy of older models limits its clinical use.

Deep networks have lately excelled at tasks like image and speech recognition, raising hopes for medical tests. Training them takes many labeled examples, which in medicine raises privacy and security concerns. The team built their model for the full twelve-lead tracing used in clinics worldwide. A reliable automatic reader could speed up screening and support doctors, above all where heart specialists are scarce.
openalex-w4318318928:
Andrew Collins, Peter Møller, Goran Gajski, and colleagues present a compendium of protocols for the comet assay, in Nature Protocols in 2023. The comet assay detects DNA damage inside single cells, from yeast to human. Under an electric field, broken DNA streams out of the nucleus like a comet tail. The method reveals strand breaks and several kinds of chemical damage to DNA bases.

Different samples need different handling, so one recipe does not fit all. The compendium gathers consensus protocols for many cell types, species, and damage types. Each aims to avoid adding damage during processing while keeping the test sensitive. The assay is already an official test for genetic harm in animal organs, and shared protocols strengthen its use in safety testing.
openalex-w4416899828:
Andrés Caraballo-Rodríguez, Andrés Cumsille, Sarolt Magyari, and colleagues measure how much chemistry still hides inside actinomycete bacteria. Their paper appeared in The Journal of Antibiotics in 2025. These bacteria gave medicine many of its natural-product drugs.

The team profiled nearly a thousand strains with mass spectrometry. They collected close to two million spectra. Only about one spectrum in eight matched a known molecule. The rest point to compounds nobody has described. The authors release the dataset as a public resource for mining microbial molecules. They prove its value by spotting a recently found family of peptides. Even in well-studied organisms, most natural products remain undiscovered.
openalex-w7204269128:
Dleice Kelly Damião Albuquerque led a Portuguese-language narrative review, published in Brazil in 2026, on the START protocol for sorting victims when an incident produces many casualties at once. START is a rapid triage method that ranks patients by urgency so scarce pre-hospital resources go where they save the most lives. The review drew on seven studies published between 2012 and 2026 from three databases, with attention to the nursing team's role and the organization of care flow.

The protocol supports fast triage, rational use of available resources, clear care priorities, and better organized assistance, the authors find. Correct use depends on continuing education and regular training. They conclude the method is indispensable for safer, faster decisions in mass casualty events.
openalex-w7204933428:
Sueli Teixeira Oliveira and Joaquim Agostinho de Santiago Neto released a Portuguese-language scoping review protocol in Brazil in 2026 on digital self-care in schooling. The COVID-19 pandemic accelerated digital tools in schools and exposed the need for teaching approaches to balanced, healthy tools use. Digital self-care means intentional methods for physical, psychological, and relational well-being while using tools, a topic still scattered across studies. The review maps teaching methods found from 2018 to 2025 across seven sources.

Using established scoping methodology, the authors set out to characterize the foundations, implementation formats, and effectiveness evidence of the methods found, and to identify contexts, audiences, plans, and knowledge gaps. The map is meant to guide future research on a theme schools now face daily.
openalex-w7206201828:
Ricardo Rosal dos Santos leads a team of eleven medical students reporting on outreach work early in their training in Brazil. Their 2026 experience report argues that university extension, where students serve the surrounding community, should begin at the start of medical school rather than later. The group, then in their third semester, carried out three actions in community settings.

Students ran rapid tests at a basic health unit, handed out an information folder at a school, and produced an educational video, shared by QR code, on preventing diabetic foot problems. The work let them practice health education while meeting real community needs. The authors conclude that early contact between students and society strengthens both medical formation and the bond joining teaching, health services, and community.
openalex-w7207688228:
Adriana Lucia Leal da Silva and three colleagues ask how high school kids feel about gym class in Brazil's state schools. Their study mixes past work with field work of their own. They used a form that probes inner and outer drives in gym class, first drawn up in the 1990s. The kids filled it in though their schools had scant gear and halls for the class.

Kids, the team finds, do prize the class. They credit it with gains in flesh and mind. They name health, a push to stay in sport, skill in games, and even a sharper mind in class. Some pulls on its worth, left half open in the study, still drag. The close calls for sound posts for gym staff and strong class craft, so the class can play its full part in school life.
openalex-w7208820628:
Rafael Alves de Oliveira and five colleagues report how a teaching initiation program helped distance-learning chemistry students gain real classroom practice in Brazil. The PIBID program places future teachers in schools, and this interdisciplinary subproject at a federal university worked with a state school in Mossoro, Rio Grande do Norte. Six scholarship students recorded their 2025 experience, which mixed active methods, teaching games, practical kinematics lessons, and guidance of student science projects.

The school results were concrete: students launched rockets past one hundred meters in national astronomy and rocket competitions, and science fair projects won state prizes. For the future teachers, being physically present in a school softened the classic weakness of distance training, building autonomy and confidence in the classroom. The authors conclude that joining PIBID, distance education, and interdisciplinary work strengthens science teaching in Brazil's interior.
openalex-w7208834428: Maria Clara Peres de Castelo Branco and colleagues write on long-acting monoclonal antibodies for preventing respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) disease in infants. The 2026 article, in Research, Society and Development, takes up efficacy, safety, and the effect on hospital stays and severe cases, as its title states. The hosted text available here is cut short before the abstract, so no findings can be reported from it.
openalex-w7212170228:
Eduardo Paes Barreto, Joao Ricardo da Silva Virginio, and Vitor de Souza Ferreira take up consent and data rights for people with mental or learning impairments in Brazil. The data law asks for a clear yes before a firm can use a person's data. But what is a fair yes from a person who may need help to weigh the choice? The trio read the constitution, the world treaty on disability rights, and Brazil's data and inclusion laws.

Old law too often swapped the person's will for a guard's. The new frame must not. It must back the person's own choice with real help, and with guards where risk runs high. The authors set terms for a valid yes: plain words, real aid to choose, and checks that fit the case. The goal is rights with both wings: free choice, and safe care.
openalex-w7213063928:
Dirchely Samara de Lima Farel reads a short tale by Clarice Lispector, a star of Brazil's prose. The tale, from 1959, tells of the world's least tall woman, found deep in the woods of Africa. A white scout finds her, takes her size, and gives her a name: Little Flower. Farel reads the tale with a cold eye on how such tales frame the found folk.

To size and name her, he finds, is to own her. In the scout's words she stops being the head of her own tale. She turns into a thing to be seen, a curio for French eyes. The prose wears the calm mask of science, but harm hides in the mask. Lispector, with wit and a light touch, peels it back. The tale asks its reader a hard ask: whose words get to say who a soul is?
openalex-w7213432728:
Eliane Regina de Souza Lima argues that cultural diversity and inclusion belong at the heart of the school course plan. Her 2026 article rests on a review of books, papers, and official papers. It connects curriculum choices to citizenship formation and equal opportunity.

Valuing diversity in the curriculum supports inclusion, the article finds. It also strengthens the fight against discriminatory practice at school. A curriculum alert to different social and cultural realities can build respect, fairness, and human rights awareness. Lima concludes that inclusive teaching and a sensitive curriculum help form students fully. School then becomes a place of coexistence, participation, and social change.
openalex-w7214808228:
Eros Andria Maliska Lovatel led a 2026 systematic review comparing two weight-loss drugs on body composition in adults with overweight or obesity. Semaglutide is highly effective for weight loss, but a large share of the weight lost can be lean mass, which harms metabolism and function. Bimagrumab, an antibody drug that blocks a growth-limiting receptor, is tested here as the alternative.

In the reviewed evidence, bimagrumab cut body fat by more than a fifth while meaningfully increasing lean mass. It aided mobility and quality of life, especially for people with type 2 diabetes at risk of muscle loss. Both drugs were moderately tolerated. The authors still advise pairing drug treatment with resistance exercise to protect muscle, above all alongside semaglutide. They present bimagrumab as the more promising option for preserving and building lean mass.
openalex-w7214985428:
Adgilma Shirlei da Conceição Gonzaga led a 2026 bibliographic study tracing the path from B. F. Skinner's radical behaviorism to applied behavior analysis, and what that path offers early childhood learning in special and inclusive education. Skinner argued that consequences change how likely a behavior is to recur, and he treated private events such as thoughts and feelings as behaviors under the same principles, not as exceptions.

Applied behavior analysis grew from those foundations, and the reviewed literature credits it with gains in communication, social skills, autonomy, and learning for young children. Benefits appear when strategies are built into teaching plans ethically, in context, and fitted to early childhood and each child. Joining these principles with Brazil's national curriculum and inclusive education commitments, the authors argue, widens the chance to build teaching that recognizes each child's singularity.
openalex-w7220952828:
Wendy Gabriela Soares de Melo Gomes and two co-authors charted hospital admissions for diabetes complications in the Brazilian state of Paraná from 2015 to 2025, in a 2026 study. Their data come from the public hospital information system of Brazil's national health service.

More than eighty thousand admissions were recorded over the eleven years, with no clear rise or fall in the yearly trend. Patients aged fifty and over made up about two thirds, and a little over two thousand admissions ended in death. The eastern macro-region held the largest share, while the total cost of admissions climbed by roughly three fifths. The authors urge stronger prevention of complications that should not need a hospital bed.
oppian-halieutica-cynegetica-mair-1928:
A. W. Mair translated Oppian, Colluthus, and Tryphiodorus for the Loeb series in 1928. Oppian wrote the Halieutica and Cynegetica around 180 CE. These didactic poems teach fishing and hunting in epic hexameters.

The Halieutica describes fish, their habits, and the arts of catching them. Sea creatures receive personalities, battles, and cunning in Oppian's telling. The Cynegetica turns to hounds, horses, and the hunting of wild beasts. Colluthus and Tryphiodorus add short mythological epics on Helen and Troy's fall. Mair's Loeb gives Greek facing English throughout. The ancient outdoors comes alive in verse here. Hunters and anglers of antiquity speak in these poems.
osborn-man-rises-to-parnassus-1928:
Henry Fairfield Osborn delivered these Princeton lectures in 1928 under the title Man Rises to Parnassus. The museum leader used them to state his mature view of human prehistory. He organized the past around what he called critical epochs.

Osborn promoted a dawn-man theory and looked to central Asia for human origins. Both ideas won influence in his lifetime and were later abandoned. The lectures show his gift for grand, readable synthesis. They also preserve the last strong statement of views that new fossils soon displaced. The lectures were printed for a general audience, not only for specialists.
petition-of-right-1628:
Parliament sent the Petition of Right to King Charles I in 1628, at a time of sharp conflict over royal power. Led by figures such as Edward Coke, members listed old rights they said the king had broken. They asked him to accept clear limits, not to grant new favors.

The petition protests taxes raised without consent, arrests without a stated cause, and soldiers lodged in private homes. It also objects to martial law used against civilians in peacetime. Charles agreed to it, then kept quarreling with Parliament anyway. Later generations treated the petition as a founding text of English liberty.
pillow-book-waley-1928:
Arthur Waley translated The Pillow-Book of Sei Shonagon into English in 1928, the first version to bring it to Western readers. Sei Shonagon, a lady of the Heian court around the year 1000, served the Empress Teishi in Kyoto. Her book is a classic of zuihitsu, the flowing miscellany of lists, scenes, and sharp opinions.

She lists things that quicken the heart, things that are hateful, and sparrows, clouds, and court gossip between. Her wit is quick and her eye for dress, weather, and folly is unmatched. Waley selected and arranged the material with a poet's tact. The Pillow-Book now stands beside The Tale of Genji as Heian Japan's gift to world letters.
plos-pbio-0020128:
Ying Wang, Michael Pierce, Lisa Schneper, and co-workers mapped sugar sensing in yeast in PLOS Biology in 2004. Yeast cells react to glucose, their favored food, through more than one signaling path. The team shows that the Ras proteins and a partner, Gpa2, run one branch of that system.

Having two branches for one signal looks wasteful, yet it gives the cell options. Each branch can tune a different part of the response, like growth rate or stored food use. The study sorts out which branch does what. Yeast sugar sensing is a basic model for nutrient signals in all cells, including human cells where the same logic links to diabetes research.
plos-pbio-0020328:
Patrick Eichenberger, Masaya Fujita, Shane T. Jensen, and their team charted gene use in a bacterium in PLOS Biology in 2004. When food runs out, Bacillus subtilis forms tough spores that can wait out hard times. One cell type in that process follows a set program of gene switching over several hours.

The authors mapped the program step by step, showing waves of genes turning on and off in order. Few systems let researchers watch a full development program in a single cell type this cleanly. The map is a reference for how timed gene programs work in general. It also matters for health, since spore formers include the germs behind anthrax and food poisoning.
plos-pone-0000028:
Aaron Seitz, Jose Nanez, Steve Holloway, and co-authors showed in 2006 that training one visual skill can speed up another. Perceptual learning is the sharpening of the senses with practice. Their subjects practiced judging motion, the direction things move. The surprise was what else improved: flicker perception, judging rapid blinking light, got faster too.

Transfer like that tells researchers the training changed something shared in the visual system, not just a narrow motion circuit. It bears on how the brain stays plastic in adults, and on training programs for people with weak vision. The study is a neat example of practice reshaping perception beyond the exact task practiced.
plos-pone-0000128:
Hiroshi Okabe, Sang-Hyun Lee, Janyaporn Phuchareon, and colleagues published this cancer cell study in PLOS ONE in 2006. It centers on cyclin D1, a protein that pushes cells to divide and that runs high in many cancers. The team examines how two players, FBXW8 and the MAPK pathway, control the breaking down of cyclin D1.

If a growth-driving protein is not cleared away on time, cells can keep dividing when they should stop. The authors report that FBXW8 and MAPK play a critical role in that cleanup. The finding names possible targets for drugs meant to slow cancer cell growth.
plos-pone-0000228:
Myriam Baratin, Sophie Roetynck, Bruno Pouvelle, and colleagues published this malaria immunology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Natural killer cells are immune cells that can sense red blood cells infected by Plasmodium falciparum, the malaria parasite. The authors dissect the roles of two molecules in that sensing: PfEMP1, a parasite protein on the infected cell, and ICAM-1, a docking protein.

How killer cells spot malaria-infected blood is a step toward using immunity against the parasite. The paper separates what each molecule contributes to recognition. That detail matters for vaccine and therapy ideas that try to help the innate immune system find infected cells sooner.
plos-pone-0000328:
Marie Suzan-Monti, Bernard La Scola, Lina Barrassi, and colleagues published this virology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Acanthamoeba polyphaga mimivirus is a giant virus that builds a volcano-like factory inside the amoeba it infects. The authors give an ultrastructural characterization of that factory, imaging its fine structure in detail.

Giant viruses blurred the line between virus and cell when they were discovered. Their factories are where new virus particles are assembled, on a scale visible in fine detail. The paper documents that structure, basic knowledge for a branch of virology that was then brand new.
plos-pone-0000428:
Jinn-Moon Yang and colleagues used computation to hunt for drug candidates against flaviviruses, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Flaviviruses include the causes of dengue, yellow fever, and West Nile disease. The team applied combinatorial computational approaches to identify tetracycline derivatives, variants of a familiar antibiotic family, that might inhibit these viruses.

Screening by computer first lets researchers test many molecules cheaply and carry only the promising ones into the lab. Starting from a known, tolerated drug family also shortens the road to treatment. The paper is an example of drug repurposing by design: mining old chemistry for new antiviral uses.
plos-pone-0000528:
Alexandra Winkeler and colleagues reviewed how light-activated switches are changing gene therapy. Their 2007 PLOS ONE paper was titled Switching on the Lights for Gene Therapy. Gene therapy delivers working genes to patients, but controlling when and where they act remains difficult. Light offers a switch that can be aimed in space and timed precisely.

Optically controlled systems pair light-sensitive proteins with therapeutic genes, so a clinician could activate treatment only in the diseased tissue. The paper surveys this strategy at an early stage. The idea later grew into a broader field of remote-controlled therapies, where external signals, not just light, direct what delivered genes do.
plos-pone-0000628:
Sarit Mizrachy-Schwartz, Nataly Kravchenko-Balasha, Hannah Ben-Bassat and colleagues studied energy use in cells transformed by HPV, the human papillomavirus. Their 2007 PLOS ONE article starts from cancer basics: growth signals go wrong and metabolism shifts. Cancer cells divide faster than normal cells. Reported work links their growth rates to higher metabolic flux during transformation.

The authors examine how energy-consuming pathways get optimized toward rapid growth in these cells. In plain terms, a fast-dividing cell must spend its fuel budget where growth needs it most. Mapping that spending could reveal weak points in transformed cells. Cancer metabolism was a rising field, and this study adds the HPV case to it.
plos-pone-0000728:
Thorsten Stoeck, Jennifer Kasper, John Bunge and colleagues surveyed tiny protists in Arctic waters and asked how they got there. The impact of climate on biodiversity is indisputable, and climate shifts over geological time must have shaped today's patterns. Their 2007 PLOS ONE study considers the paleoclimate record, the climate of the deep past, as a possible sculptor of modern Arctic diversity.

Protists are single-celled organisms that form the base of polar food webs. If ancient warm periods let lineages in, or cold ones pruned them, current diversity carries a climate fingerprint. The question matters as the Arctic warms again: its smallest residents may reorganize first.
plos-pone-0000828:
Victor Marinescu, Patricia A. Loomis, Svetlana Ehmann and colleagues studied how a stress-linked gene's message gets edited, in PLOS ONE in 2007. One effect of stressors such as chronic drug administration involves the transcription factor FosB. A sequence within its final exon comes to be recognized as intronic and is removed by alternative splicing. That removal shifts the reading frame and produces an early stop.

Their subject is how the protein PTB regulates retention of FosB intron 4. Keeping or cutting one segment changes which protein version a neuron makes. FosB is famous in addiction research, where its stable forms accumulate, so its splicing control is a mechanism worth pinning down.
plos-pone-0000928:
Jason Gioia, Shailaja Yerrapragada, Xiang Qin and colleagues read the genome of a hardy Bacillus strain from a spacecraft lab, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Bacillus spores shrug off ultraviolet light, radiation, peroxide and drying. This strain, SAFR-032, even survived the standard cleaning used at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.

Its genome holds a puzzle the authors call paradoxical: genes for DNA repair and peroxide resistance look conserved in odd ways. A germ that rides through spacecraft cleaning matters for planetary protection rules. Reading its genome shows which defenses make it so hard to kill. That knowledge feeds back into better cleaning for missions to other worlds.
plos-pone-0001028:
James Elser, Marcia Kyle, Marilyn Smith and colleagues applied ecological accounting to human cancer, in PLOS ONE in 2007. A growing tumor can be seen as an ecological and evolutionary system inside the body. Their growth rate hypothesis proposes that tumors demand extra phosphorus, the element rich in the nucleic acids a fast dividing cell must copy.

Biological stoichiometry tracks the balance of elements in living tissue. Applying it to cancer turns tumor growth into a budget problem: where does the phosphorus come from, and what limits it. A budget view could reveal weak points that pure genetics misses. It also links oncology to a mature field of ecology.
plos-pone-0001128:
People often give strangers more than they have to. Paul Zak, Angela Stanton, and Sheila Ahmadi set out to test one chemical suspect behind that generosity. Their 2007 PLOS ONE article looks at oxytocin, a hormone linked to trust and social bonding. Earlier work had hinted that empathy might drive generous acts.

The authors report, as their title states, that oxytocin increases generosity in humans. The study treats generosity as something with a biological mechanism, not just a moral choice. Findings like these feed into wider debates about how hormones shape everyday social behavior between strangers.
plos-pone-0001228:
Blood cells and the endothelial cells lining vessels are thought to descend from a common ancestor cell, the hemangioblast. Wei Weng, Erike Sukowati, and Guojun Sheng examined whether such cells truly exist in the chicken embryo, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. By the strict definition, a hemangioblast must be a single clonal precursor that divides to give both cell types. Its existence in the body was still debated.

Using a combination of mitotic labeling and observation, the authors test the claim in vivo. The question is foundational for developmental biology and for efforts to grow blood and vessels in the lab.
plos-pone-0001328:
Neurons never fire exactly the same way twice, and that change limits all information handling in the brain. Jan Grewe, Matti Weckström, and Martin Egelhaaf compared ways to gauge how reliable sensory coding is, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Different studies measure reliability with different approaches, and it is largely unclear how much the findings depend on the approach chosen.

The authors set information measures against discriminability measures as gauges of coding reliability. Their comparison is about method, aimed at sensory coding in general. Choosing the right reliability measure matters when neural codes are compared across animals or settings.
plos-pone-0001428:
Stephen Watt and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE methods paper on a new switch for yeast genes. Fission yeast is a work horse for gene studies. The switch in wide use needs more than 15 hours to turn a gene fully on. That slow pace blurs fast events. The team built a faster switch based on a food the yeast can sense.

Their switch turns genes on and off in a much shorter time. It is steered by uracil, a normal cell building block. A fast, clean switch lets labs catch brief gene effects as they happen. The tool should aid cell cycle and stress studies that hinge on timing.
plos-pone-0001528:
Andreas Rolfs and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE report on a large set of human gene clones. The set holds more than 7,000 fully checked clones that cover over 3,400 distinct human genes. Each clone holds the full protein coding part of a gene, ready for lab use. The team built them from a national gene stock set.

Clones come in two forms, with or without the stop signal at the end. That choice lets labs fuse genes to tags or leave them plain. A shared, checked set saves each lab from building its own. It speeds gene by gene tests across the field.
plos-pone-0001628:
Se-Jin Lee wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE research article on myostatin, a protein the body makes to limit how much skeletal muscle grows. Because myostatin holds muscle back, many groups want drugs that block it. Such drugs could help people with diseases that waste muscle away. Myostatin is made in a quiet, latent form and must be cut by other proteins to become active.

Lee used gene-based tests to ask which cuts matter for switching myostatin on. The full text lays out the genetic analysis, the forms of the protein that resulted, and what each change did to its activity. Pinning down how the protein is activated gives drug makers a clearer target. The paper is a single-author study of one step in a pathway of wide medical interest.
plos-pone-0001728:
Rick Dale, Jennifer Roche, Kristy Snyder, and their co-authors used hand movements to track learning in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Evidence increasingly shows action and cognition interact more richly than once assumed. Fast processes like movement may relate in orderly ways to slow ones like learning.

The team had people learn paired associates, linked word or symbol pairs, while recording the dynamics of their actions, such as mouse movements. Those movement patterns served as an index of how learning progressed. The full text gives the task, the movement measures, and how they tracked memory strength. Movement data is cheap and continuous, so it could give teachers and software a live readout of learning instead of just right and wrong answers.
plos-pone-0001828:
Silvia Miretti, Ilaria Roato, Riccardo Taulli, and their co-authors built a mouse model of bone cancer spread in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Osteosarcoma is lethal when metastatic after chemotherapy or surgery. Animal models are necessary to study its metastatic spread and to validate new therapies for systemic disease.

The team reports a syngeneic Balb/c mouse model of pulmonary metastasis from spontaneous osteosarcoma. It is monitored in vivo by luciferase imaging: the tumor cells glow, so spread can be watched in the living animal. The full text gives the model construction and imaging results. A trackable model lets drug tests measure metastasis directly instead of waiting for end-stage disease.
plos-pone-0001928:
Friedemann Paul and co-authors tested a cholesterol drug at high dose in multiple sclerosis, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Statins calm the immune system in some settings. Data from animal models, plus a small pilot study, hinted they might help in this illness too. The drug tested was atorvastatin, given by mouth at a high dose.

The team checked safety and tolerance first, and also tracked disease activity. The drug was given alone and, for some, alongside interferon-beta, a standard therapy. Trials staged this way show whether a cheap oral drug is safe enough to test for real benefit in larger groups of patients.
plos-pone-0002028:
Karen Yao and co-authors watched for a waking virus in patients on a strong immune drug, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The drug, natalizumab, works well in multiple sclerosis and kin disorders, but it was linked to a rare fatal brain infection by the JC virus. That surprise put doctors on alert for other dormant viruses.

The team report reactivation of human herpesvirus-6 in patients treated with natalizumab for multiple sclerosis. A second virus waking under the same drug widens the safety watch. Patients on such therapy may need checks for more than one hidden infection.
plos-pone-0002128:
Kevin Weinfurt and co-authors checked how well medical writers follow the rules on reporting money ties. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Telling readers about an author's financial interests is meant to protect trust in medical research. The team focused on papers about coronary stents, the small tubes used to hold heart arteries open.

They searched PubMed for stent papers published in 2006 and compared how the same authors reported their interests across papers. The study asks a simple question with real weight. When a study was funded or backed by a company, can doctors count on that note being there every time it should be?
plos-pone-0002228:
Tal Makovski, Gustavo Vázquez, and Yuhong Jiang studied what people learn while tracking moving objects, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Keeping track of several moving things at once is part of daily vision, from driving to team sports. The lab version, the multiple object tracking task, asks people to follow a subset of moving items among identical distractors.

The team examined visual learning inside that task: what the tracker picks up about the items and the scene while attention is busy. Their results show learning still happens under the strain of tracking. The work clarifies how much of a moving scene the mind records beyond the targets themselves.
plos-pone-0002328:
Weili Shen and co-authors fed diabetic rats a mix of nutrients and checked their muscle power plants, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Insulin resistance in skeletal muscle may be tied to having too few mitochondria, the cell's energy producers, with too little burning capacity. Whether raising mitochondrial number and function can improve insulin resistance was unknown.

The team used Goto-Kakizaki rats, a model of type 2 diabetes, and gave them a combination of nutriments. The mix improved mitochondrial biogenesis, the making of new mitochondria, and their function in muscle. The result supports the idea that feeding the power plants can ease a core defect of diabetes.
plos-pone-0002428:
Led by Dylla, a team of researchers published its study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Scott J. Dylla, Lucia Beviglia, In-Kyung Park, and others. Its subject is colorectal Cancer Stem Cells Are Enriched in Xenogeneic Tumors Following Chemotherapy. Patients generally die of cancer after the failure of current therapies to eliminate residual disease.

A subpopulation of tumor cells, termed cancer stem cells (CSC), appears uniquely able to fuel the growth of phenotypically and histologically diverse tumors. What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full.
plos-pone-0002528:
Research by Rotolo and co-authors came out in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Sabrina Rotolo, Simona Ceccarelli, Ferdinando Romano, and others. Its subject is silencing of Keratinocyte Growth Factor Receptor Restores 5-Fluorouracil and Tamoxifen Efficacy on Responsive Cancer Cells. Keratinocyte growth factor receptor (KGFR) is a splice variant of the FGFR2 gene expressed in epithelial cells.

Activation of KGFR is a key factor in the regulation of physiological processes in epithelial cells such as proliferation, differentiation and wound healing. Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. In short, the piece gives a clear, short route into a field that can seem hard to enter from the outside.
plos-pone-0002628:
Work by Kathleen H. Rubins and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was comparative analysis of viral gene expression programs during poxvirus infection: a transcriptional map of the vaccinia and monkeypox genomes. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Kathleen H. Rubins, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Poxviruses engage in a complex and intricate dialogue with host cells as part of their strategy for replication. The authors add a further point. However, relatively little molecular detail is available with which to understand the mechanisms behind this dialogue. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002728:
Work by Lise Aksglaede and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was forty years trends in timing of pubertal growth spurt in 157,000 danish school children. The catalog record names Lise Aksglaede first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Entering puberty is an important milestone in reproductive life and secular changes in the timing of puberty may be an important indicator of the. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002828:
Work by Bindee Kuriya and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008, dealing with quality of pharmaceutical industry press releases based on original research. Authorship is credited in the record to Bindee Kuriya and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Press releases are a popular vehicle to disseminate health information to the lay media. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002928:
Ángel Felicísimo, Jesús Muñoz and Jacob González-Solis argued in 2008 that ocean winds steer long aerial journeys. Global wind patterns shape how organisms, seeds, and particles disperse, which in turn affects colonizations, invasions, and spread of pathogens. How wind-driven movement actually unfolds had been hard to study.
