In PLOS ONE they show that surface winds over oceans drive the dynamics of transoceanic flights. That means wind maps can help predict where flying creatures and wind-borne material will land. Ecologists tracking invasions or disease spread across seas gain a practical forecasting aid. The full text gives methods, results, and references for readers who want to check each step.
plos-pone-0003028:
Morten Overgaard, Katrin Fehl, Kim Mouridsen and co-authors studied degraded conscious vision in a blindsight patient in 2008. Blindsight patients have damage to primary visual cortex. They can discriminate stimuli in their blind field above chance, yet report no visual awareness of them.

Most blindsight work uses single patients, as here. The PLOS ONE paper asks whether some faint seeing remains, framed as seeing without seeing. Careful tests of awareness grading matter, because a simple aware-or-not split may miss partial experience. The case informs debates on what consciousness adds to vision. Its full text, with tables and references, is openly available to any reader online.
plos-pone-0003128:
Mike H. Allsopp, Willem J. de Lange and Ruan Veldtman tackle how to put a fair price on insect pollination in this 2008 PLOS ONE study. Values for nature's goods and services can guide spending on conservation, but weak estimates can lead to poor choices. The authors propose the cost of replacing pollination by other means as a more exact way to value the service bees and other insects provide.

They lay out that replacement cost approach and why they judge it better than past estimates. Readers get a practical method for policy and farm planning. It helps show what would truly be lost if wild pollinators declined.
plos-pone-0003228:
Jason Munshi-South studies dispersal in the large treeshrew in this single-author 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Female-biased dispersal is predicted to occur in monogamous species due to local resource competition among females, but evidence for this association in mammals is scarce. The predicted link between such dispersal and monogamy may also be too simplistic, given that many pair-living species differ.

Working with Tupaia tana, a behaviorally monogamous mammal, the author examines female-biased dispersal and gene flow. Readers get a rare mammal test of a classic prediction. Field genetics like this can show whether theory built on birds and other groups holds for mammals.
plos-pone-0003328:
Sophie Beltran, Frank Cézilly and Jérôme Boissier test mate choice genetics in parasitic worms in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Correlational studies strongly suggest that both genetic similarity and heterozygosity can influence female mate choice. However, influence of each variable has usually been tested independently, although similarity and heterozygosity might be correlated. The team experimentally disentangled the two factors.

The title reports that genetic dissimilarity between mates, but not male heterozygosity, influences divorce in schistosomes. Readers see pair bonds in a parasite respond to genetic matching. Schistosomes live as male-female pairs in blood vessels, so mate switching has direct disease relevance.
plos-pone-0003428:
Joep P. M. Derikx and co-authors studied gut injury and repair in people in this 2008 paper. When blood flow to the intestine stops and returns, the lining gets hurt. This harm, called ischemia-reperfusion injury, follows events like aortic surgery. Animal studies had told only part of the story.

In human patients, the injured lining cells were shed quickly. Fresh lining then grew back over the gut surface fast. That rapid repair reversed much of the early damage. The finding gives surgeons a clearer picture of how the human gut heals.
plos-pone-0003528:
Pascal F. Egea, Johanna Napetschnig, and Peter Walter solved protein structures in this 2008 paper. The signal recognition particle grabs new proteins bound for membranes or export. It acts as those proteins emerge from the ribosome. Two proteins, SRP54 and SRP19, organize its RNA core.

The team worked with versions from Pyrococcus furiosus, a heat-loving microbe. Atomic structures show how the two proteins frame the core. The particle's design is conserved across all life. Such pictures reveal how the universal shipping machine is assembled. Heat-loving microbes give sturdy proteins that are easier to crystallize and read.
plos-pone-0003628:
Miriam Dyck, Maren Winbeck, Susanne Leiberg, and colleagues published this psychology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. It tests whether people read emotions in computer-made faces as well as in real ones. Virtual faces are now realistic enough to use as test material in emotion research.

Volunteers judged the feelings shown by natural faces and by virtual faces. The authors compared how well each type of face was read. The results show where digital faces work as stand-ins for real ones and where they fall short. That guidance matters for labs that use avatars in studies and therapy.
plos-pone-0003728:
Anahi Molla-Herman, Cedric Boularan, Rania Ghossoub, and colleagues published this cell study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Most cells carry a primary cilium, a thin sensing bristle built from the centrosome when the cell rests. It samples the cell's surroundings and helps run key processes.

The team tracked beta-arrestin2, a well-known signaling protein, to the centrosome and primary cilium. There it plays a part in controlling how cells proliferate. The placement links a classic signaling player to the organelle that senses the world outside the cell. That role puts the cilium at the heart of cell growth control.
plos-pone-0003828:
Hong Lu, Prabhu Patil, Marie-Anne Van Sluys, and colleagues published this plant bacteria study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Xanthomonas is a large genus of bacteria that cause disease on more than 392 plant species. Each strain shows marked loyalty to certain hosts and tissues. What decides that specificity was unknown.

The team studied how gene clusters tied to pathogenesis were acquired and evolved in these bacteria. They searched for candidate determinants of tissue specificity among the clusters. The work maps how plant pathogens assemble their weapon kits as they adapt to chosen hosts.
plos-pone-0003928:
Courtney B. Field, Kevin Johnston, Joseph S. Gati, and co-authors mapped a primate brain hub's connections in 2008. Brain wiring was usually traced by injecting chemicals and viewing tissue later. Those methods cannot be used while an animal is alive and scanned. The team wanted a live method for the superior colliculus.

They paired tiny electric stimulation of the hub with whole-brain fMRI scans. The scans showed which areas responded when the hub was zapped. That traced its connections without any chemical tracers. The method opens live wiring maps for other deep brain areas too.
plos-pone-0004028:
Tawee Chotpitayasunondh, Usa Thisyakorn, Chitsanu Pancharoen, and co-authors trialed a bird flu vaccine in children in 2008. H5N1 influenza has caused outbreaks in birds across several continents. Human infections, often in children, have been severe and deadly. Human-to-human spread stayed limited, but the threat remained.

Their PLOS ONE article tested two forms of an inactivated H5N1 vaccine. They measured safety plus antibody and cell-mediated immune responses. Children are a priority group for pandemic vaccine planning. Data in children cannot simply be assumed from adult trials. It was printed in PLOS ONE, where the full text stays free to read.
plos-pone-0004128:
Luca Beltrame and colleagues published this methods study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Microarrays measure the activity of thousands of genes at once, and labs have built up huge public stores of such data. Finding which stored experiments resemble each other has become a major challenge for researchers.

Instead of comparing single genes, the authors propose pathway signatures, patterns drawn from defined groups of genes that work together. They use these signatures as the basis for judging how similar two microarray experiments are. The approach gives scientists a practical way to search public data and spot links between studies done for different reasons.
plos-pone-0004228:
Juanita Bezuidenhout and colleagues published this tuberculosis study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Granulomas, balls of immune cells that wall off stubborn germs, are an essential defence against persistent infection. They can also damage the tissue they defend. The team asked whether HIV co-infection changes that balance in pleural tuberculosis, infection of the lung's lining.

They compared the look and cytokine profile of granulomas in patients with early HIV infection. They report increased expression of TNF-alpha and more necrosis, dead tissue, in those granulomas. The finding shows how HIV can make a defence structure more destructive.
plos-pone-0004328:
Richard Hunter and colleagues published this brain study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Kainate receptors are a class of glutamate receptors that modulate glutamate release and synaptic plasticity in the hippocampal formation, a memory centre. Earlier work had tied corticosteroids, the stress hormones, to the control of these receptors, and recent clinical work pointed the same way.

The team measured how stress and corticosteroids change the levels of kainate receptor subunit messenger RNA in the rat hippocampus. Which subunits rise or fall shapes how the memory centre behaves under stress. The study connects the hormone surge of a bad day to the wiring of memory.
plos-pone-0004428:
A gene variant tied to body fat may also raise the risk of death on its own, report Esther Zimmermann, Sofia Kring, Tina Berentzen, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. They studied a common variant in the FTO gene, known to be linked with greater fatness. The team wondered whether the variant drives sickness and death only through fatness itself.

To test that, they turned to records of Danish men examined for military service, a very large group. They tracked who carried the fat-linked form of the gene and what later happened to them. Their finding, stated in the title, is that the variant raises mortality even apart from fatness. That result warns against blaming weight alone for the gene's health effects.
plos-pone-0004528:
The blood fats of a blind mole rat that lives underground hold clues to life with little oxygen, report Nicola Nasser, Marielle Kaplan, Eviatar Nevo, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The animal is Spalax, the blind subterranean mole rat. It is adapted to air with swinging oxygen levels, and it can survive severe oxygen shortage and carbon dioxide build-up that would kill other mammals.

Life underground reshaped the animal's body and genes. The team profiled its lipid profile, the fats in its blood, and other serum traits. Comparing these with above-ground relatives shows how its chemistry was tuned for the dark and airless burrow. Such natural adaptations interest medicine, where oxygen shortage damages hearts and brains.
plos-pone-0004628:
Mice short of the trace mineral selenium suffer worse infection from the gut parasite Cryptosporidium parvum, show Chengmin Wang, Yanyun Wu, Jianhua Qin, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The parasite causes severe diarrhea. It is a grave risk for the young and for people with weak immune defenses.

How well a host resists this parasite tracks with how much selenium it gets. The team used mouse models with enough of the mineral and with too little of it. They studied the cell-based immune response in each group during infection. In the low group, infection came with a weak antioxidant system, the body's shield against chemical damage. The work links one trace nutrient to the fate of a common gut infection.
plos-pone-0004728:
Vanessa Almendro and colleagues studied how a cutting enzyme helps cancer cells resist a chemo drug, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The drug oxaliplatin works less well once tumors learn to resist it. The enzyme MMP7 has been tied to that loss of response, though the exact route was not fully clear.

MMP7 levels also predict outlook on their own in some cancers. The team traced cross talk between MMP7 and a death signal system in the cells. Their work suggests the enzyme helps cells dodge drug induced death. Blocking that help could restore drug response in some tumors.
plos-pone-0004828:
Sébastien Joucla and Blaise Yvert modeled improved focalization of electrical microstimulation using microelectrode arrays, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Extracellular stimulation of the central nervous system has been used for decades with fundamental and medical goals. Microelectrode arrays offer new possibilities for microstimulation, although focal activation remains difficult because current spreads to neighboring neurons and axons beyond the intended target zone.

Modeling shows how array configurations sharpen focus. Better focality improves prosthetics and brain mapping. Simulations guide electrode design before implantation. Precision matters for safety and function. These findings offer a firm starting point for the next round of testing. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field.
plos-pone-0004928:
Filamin A is a scaffold protein that helps give cells their shape. It links to many partner proteins. Mutations in it cause developmental disorders in humans. Fumihiko Nakamura and co-authors studied one of its partnerships in PLOS ONE in 2009. They solved the structure of the part that interacts with FilGAP. FilGAP helps control the cell's internal skeleton.

The structure covers the twenty-third repeat of filamin A. That repeat is the region that grips FilGAP. Comparing it with disease-linked mutations showed how the changes impair the grip. The work gives a molecular explanation for filamin A disorders. It shows how a broken handshake can disturb development.
plos-pone-0005028:
c-Rel is a control protein in immune cells. It keeps B cells alive and multiplying. Its persistent activation is tied to allergies and lymphomas. Wenzhi Tian and Hsiou-Chi Liou silenced it with RNA interference. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. The tests ran in living mice.

Silencing c-Rel led B cell tumor cells to die. It also suppressed the antigenic immune response in vivo. The protein is a linchpin for these cancers. Removing it hits tumor and immune response together. Silencing it could become a lymphoma therapy. The study also warns that the same move would calm normal immunity. Any treatment would need to balance those effects.
plos-pone-0005128:
Huntington's disease damages the brain progressively. A popular theory blamed a jammed protein-disposal system. That system is the ubiquitin-proteasome system. John Bett and colleagues tested the theory in PLOS ONE in 2009. They used the R6/2 transgenic mouse model of the disease. A glowing reporter, GFPu, shows whether the disposal system is backed up.

The reporter did not accumulate in the mice's neurons. The disposal system appears to keep working there. Inclusion bodies exist, yet the machinery runs. The negative result challenges a leading explanation. It redirects attention to other causes of neuron failure. Huntington's research has limited resources. Ruling out a wrong path is valuable work.
plos-pone-0005228:
Bacteria spread antibiotic resistance by moving genes between cells, and integrons are a major route for that traffic. An enzyme called IntI1 does the cutting and pasting that moves resistance genes into place. Dubois and colleagues studied how it works in PLOS ONE in 2009.

For class 1 integrons, the joining reaction needs IntI1 units to bind together cooperatively. The study also identified specific multi-unit forms that appear along the way. Details like these show how resistance genes hop between bacteria, and they may reveal weak points where the hopping could be slowed.
plos-pone-0005328:
Bacterial meningitis is an acute disease that kills quickly without early treatment. Culture tests that name the germ are sensitive but slow, and need large spinal fluid volumes. Himmelreich and colleagues offered a faster route in PLOS ONE in 2009, based on NMR spectroscopy.

The method reads metabolite profiles in cerebrospinal fluid plus the host's response pattern. Those fingerprints sort meningitis cases by cause far faster than culture. Speed matters here more than in most diseases, since each hour of delay raises the risk of death or brain damage. Brain fever of this kind can kill a child in a day, so a fluid test that gives an answer in hours. Not days, can be the gap between full health and lasting harm.
plos-pone-0005428:
Francis Robert and colleagues wrote a 2009 PLOS ONE study on cancer drugs and protein making in mice. Cells build proteins at a step where many growth signals meet. A mouse model of lymphoma lets workers test how a tumour's genes affect its response to drugs.

The team changed the speed of one late step in protein building and watched drug response change with it. Their work links growth signal pathways to whether cancer cells live or die under treatment. It suggests that tuning protein building could one day help make cancer drugs work better.
plos-pone-0005528:
Nadia Caccamo and co-authors compared T cells in tuberculosis patients in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. One arm of the immune system, CD8 T cells, helps hold the tuberculosis germ in check. Little was known about how good those cells are in people with hidden infection versus active disease.

The team tested CD8 cells that react to several germ proteins in both groups. Comparing the strength and quality of the responses shows what protection looks like. That can guide vaccine design toward the responses that keep infection hidden and harmless. Protection that lasts for years without illness is the goal that tuberculosis vaccines have long failed to reach.
plos-pone-0005628:
Kelly Nevin and co-authors studied bacteria that make electric current in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Geobacter bacteria can pass electrons to a solid surface outside the cell, in effect breathing metal. Thick films of them on electrodes produce current in microbial fuel cells.

The team read gene activity in films grown on anodes to find the parts that matter for high current. Parts on the outer surface of the cells proved essential. Knowing them helps engineers raise the power of fuel cells fed by waste. Fuel cells of this kind could treat wastewater while making power, which doubles their appeal.
plos-pone-0005728:
Nicolas Antoine-Moussiaux and colleagues hunted in 2009 for the cause of a sharp drop in white blood cells during a parasite infection. In mice infected with Trypanosoma evansi, the peak of parasites in blood matched the low point of white cells almost exactly. The team asked whether the parasite itself kills those cells.

They traced the effect to a protein of the parasite that sits outside its own cell sap. That protein triggers death in lymphocytes, the white cells that run immune defense, through a CD45-linked path. Killing the defenders is a neat trick for a parasite, and a target for blocking it.
plos-pone-0005828:
Fuyuki Tokumasu and co-authors studied red blood cells from people with two copies of the hemoglobin C variant in 2009. Hemoglobin C differs from normal by one amino acid swap, and it is less stable under oxidation. Cells carrying two copies hold more membrane-bound breakdown products.

The team measured how those changes alter the cell membrane's structure and surface charge. Stiffer, altered membranes change how the cells flow and how long they last. That explains part of the mild anemia seen in this condition. The work links a single letter change in a gene to whole-cell physics.
plos-pone-0005928:
Two kinds of T cell answer the call when tuberculosis bacteria invade. Truc Hoang, Anneline Nansen, Sugata Roy and colleagues compared them in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Both the CD8 and CD4 cells they tracked aim at TB10.4, a protein the bacteria make in large amounts, which allows a fair head-to-head test.

The team found clear contrasts in how the two cell types grow in number and in the traits they show after infection. Those contrasts shape how strong and how lasting the defense is. Knowing which cells do what helps vaccine builders choose the response they most need to raise against this stubborn germ.
plos-pone-0006028:
A compound called locostatin can stop cells from migrating, a fact that made it a tool for studying movement. Anne Shemon, Eva Eves, Matthew Clark and colleagues found a natural shield against it in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies RKIP, a protein that also brakes the Raf growth pathway, and its clash with locostatin.

The title states the shield: RKIP protects cells against locostatin's block on migration. Since locostatin was reported to bind RKIP itself, the pair's interaction needed careful sorting. The result clarifies what the tool compound really does, which matters for every study that has used it to probe how cells move and spread.
plos-pone-0006128:
Two cancer drivers hold hands on the cell surface. Keren Farin, Ayelet Di Segni, Adam Mor and colleagues mapped that handshake in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies the ErbB receptor tyrosine kinases and nucleolin, both major contributors to malignant transformation, which meet through the receptors' cytoplasmic tail inside the cell.

When both proteins are overabundant, the meeting drives the receptors into an active state. A structure-function analysis shows which parts of each partner the grip depends on. That detail turns a cancer alliance into a possible drug target, since a handshake with known fingers can, in time, be pried apart.
plos-pone-0006228:
Polyethylene is the world's most familiar plastic, yet the inner order of its bulk form has stayed disputed. Morteza Laridjani and Pierre Leboucher tackle that puzzle in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Images of the material in Fourier space show sharp lines laid over a hazy, diffuse background.

That mixed picture points to a complex internal structure, neither fully ordered nor fully random. The authors propose an intermediary structure that fits the data. Settling the structure helps explain the plastic's strength and flexibility. It also guides makers who tune those traits for products from pipes to packaging.
plos-pone-0006328:
Modern HIV therapy extends life, but lung complaints may not have faded with the virus suppressed. Patricia George and colleagues measured respiratory symptoms and airway obstruction in HIV-infected subjects in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Prevalence and risk factors in the era of highly active antiretroviral therapy were unknown.

The team evaluated symptoms and measured obstruction to identify the impact of therapy and other factors. Chronic lung problems matter more as patients live longer. Knowing who struggles to breathe guides screening and smoking advice. The study fills a gap in long-term HIV care.
plos-pone-0006428:
Olaia Martínez-Iglesias and co-authors explored thyroid hormones and cancer in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Loss of thyroid hormone receptors can give tumor cells an edge, they note. But how hormone levels themselves relate to human cancer has stayed a matter of debate. The team studied what happens when thyroid hormone levels run low.

Their title gives the result: hypothyroidism, the low-hormone state, makes tumors more invasive and helps spread to new sites. That finding sharpens a long argument about hormones and cancer growth. It suggests doctors should watch thyroid status in cancer care. It also opens new questions about how hormones restrain tumors.
plos-pone-0006528:
Nicholas Boulais, Ulysse Pereira, Nicolas Lebonvallet, and colleagues tested skin sensor cells in the lab for PLOS ONE in 2009. Merkel cells are involved in mechanoreception, the sense of touch and pressure. Several lines of evidence suggest they may also participate in skin disorders through release of neuropeptides. The authors ran an in vitro study of Merkel cells as putative regulatory cells in skin disorders.

Regulatory cells would help coordinate skin responses to injury and disease. Showing Merkel cells can release active signals strengthens that case. The work widens the job description of a cell known mainly for touch. It may inform research on itch, pain, and skin inflammation.
plos-pone-0006628:
Kieran Cooley, Orest Szczurko, Dan Perri, and colleagues ran a randomized trial of naturopathic care for anxiety in PLOS ONE in 2009. Anxiety is a serious personal health condition and represents a substantial burden to overall quality of life. Anxiety disorders also represent a significant cost to society. The trial tested naturopathic care against a control in a randomized controlled design.

Testing complementary care with a rigorous trial design is the only way to know if it works. Randomization protects against placebo and selection effects. Whatever the outcome, patients and practitioners gain evidence. The study is registered, adding transparency to a contested area.
plos-pone-0006728:
Robert J. Lake and co-authors examined a cut made in the Notch receptor inside living animals in PLOS ONE in 2009. Notch signaling guides development in many tissues. Before reaching the cell surface, the receptor is cut at a site called S1. That cut creates the standard two-part form of the receptor. It happens without any ligand binding first.

The team analyzed the S1 cleavage in vivo in the fruit fly. They asked what the cut means for Notch signaling in Drosophila. Their results clarify whether the cut is essential or incidental. The answer shapes how the whole Notch pathway is modeled. Notch errors underlie developmental disorders and cancers, so details matter.
plos-pone-0006828:
Sumathi Sivapalasingam and colleagues evaluated a cheaper viral load test for HIV care in Kenya in PLOS ONE in 2009. Monitoring viral load during antiretroviral therapy has a key advantage. It detects treatment failure before illness or resistance appears. Early detection prompts adherence counseling or a drug switch. Standard viral load tests are expensive for many clinics.

The team assessed a low-cost assay in HIV-infected adults. They checked how well it tracks treatment responses. A reliable cheap test could extend monitoring across Kenya. That would catch failing regimens years earlier than symptoms do. The evaluation supports wider, more equitable HIV care.
plos-pone-0006928:
Chantel Sloan, Angeline Andrew, Eric Duell, and others looked at ancestry in New Hampshire in PLOS ONE in 2009. Family roots can shape the genes of whole groups of people. That kind of pattern is well known in groups that live far apart. Less was known about fine patterns inside mixed American groups.

The team searched for these patterns without telling the computer what to find. Their work turned up a clear Eastern European signal in the sample. That shows even mixed groups in the United States carry roots that tests can spot. Health studies must allow for such hidden roots, or their results can mislead.
plos-pone-0007028:
Joseph Orgel, Aya Eid, Olga Antipova, and colleagues studied a collagen partner protein in PLOS ONE in 2009. Decorin is a classic small proteoglycan of the tissue matrix between cells. Its sugar chain helps stabilize the packing of collagen fibrils. Type I collagen is the main fibrillar collagen in vertebrates.

The team examined the decorin core protein, which they call decoron. Its shape matched the surface of collagen fibrils closely. That fit explains how decorin binds and organizes the fibrils. Orderly collagen underlies skin, tendon, and bone strength, so its organizers matter broadly.
plos-pone-0007128:
Paul Olivier, Romain Fontaine, Gauthier Loron, and colleagues tested melatonin in injured newborn rat brains in PLOS ONE in 2009. White matter damage is a serious risk in the developing brain. The team used a model where a uterine artery was tied, injuring one side. They also traced how melatonin acts on the oligodendrocyte lineage, the cells that build white matter.

Melatonin treatment promoted the maturation of those cells after injury. More mature oligodendrocytes mean better insulation for young nerve fibers. A safe, familiar hormone showing this effect is promising. It could lead to protection for premature infants at risk.
plos-pone-0007228:
Ni Shu, Yong Liu, Jun Li, and colleagues examined brain networks in people blind from early life in 2009. The layout of the cerebral anatomical network reflects how the human brain is organized. Graph theory now gives tools to measure large-scale networks of that kind in precise numerical terms.

The authors use diffusion tensor tractography to trace white matter connections. They compare network structure in early blindness with typical brains. They report an altered anatomical network. Their work shows how losing vision early can reshape the brain's wiring far beyond the visual areas themselves.
plos-pone-0007328:
Yuxi Feng, Yumei Wang, Oliver Stock, and colleagues studied retinal blood vessel loss linked to nerve damage in rats in 2009. Neuronal damage correlates with vascular dysfunction in diseased retinas. Mechanisms stayed controversial, partly for lack of models where vessel regression starts in mature retinal vessels alongside neuronal injury in the same eye.

The authors use rats with a defect in polycystin-2, a protein linked to kidney disease. They examine vasoregression in the retina of these animals. Their PLOS ONE model lets researchers separate vessel loss from developmental effects. That separation clarifies how nerve damage and vessel loss interact.
plos-pone-0007428:
Jônatas Abrahão and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on vaccinia virus outbreaks among cattle in Brazil. Vaccinia is a poxvirus once used in the smallpox vaccine campaign. Smallpox itself was declared wiped out in 1980, yet vaccinia keeps reappearing in Brazilian herds. How it travels from wildlife to cattle was an open ecological question.

The team investigated rodents that live around farms and houses as a possible bridge. Such peridomestic rodents move between wild habitats and barns, so they could carry the virus across that gap. Confirming their role would solve a missing piece of the outbreak puzzle. It would also tell farmers and health officials where control efforts should focus.
plos-pone-0007528:
Knut Rudi and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the microbes living in earthworm guts. How those communities are distributed across a host population is basic to understanding host-microbe relations. Feeding is a major disturbance for any gut community. The team tracked the worm gut microbiota across a population, before and after feeding. They asked how a meal reshapes the mix.

Feeding flipped the gut community from a varied state to a uniform one. Across the population, worms' guts converged on the same microbial mix after eating. A meal, in effect, resets the community to a shared pattern. That reset shows how strongly food intake steers gut ecology. The finding matters for soil science, since earthworms process so much earth. It also offers a simple model of gut community dynamics.
plos-pone-0007628:
Ketan Ghaghada and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on a new contrast agent for magnetic resonance imaging. Gadolinium-based agents make MRI scans clearer, and liposomal versions have drawn wide interest. Earlier designs packed the gadolinium chelates inside the liposome. That limited how the agent could be used and seen. The team built a nanoparticle agent designed to work in two imaging modes at once.

A dual-mode agent can serve as both a blood-pool tracer and a molecular imaging probe. One injection then yields two kinds of information. That efficiency matters for tracking disease and for watching where a drug carrier goes. Nanoparticles can also be aimed at specific tissues. The study is an engineering step toward scans that say more. Better contrast physics becomes better medicine when it reaches patients.
plos-pone-0007728:
Annie Demers and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It traces how the hunger hormone ghrelin talks to immune cells called macrophages. A receptor named PPARgamma sits at the center of that talk. PPARgamma also shapes blood vessel health and slows atherosclerosis, the hardening of arteries.

The team found a concerted interplay of kinases, enzymes that pass signals along. That interplay marks PPARgamma as a direct target of ghrelin signaling in macrophages. The result links appetite hormones to vessel inflammation. It suggests new ways to think about heart and metabolic disease.
plos-pone-0007828:
Lidziya Ulvenes and co-authors published a survey in PLOS ONE in 2009. It asks what Norwegian physicians know and think about evidence-based medicine. Evidence-based medicine, or EBM, grounds care in the best research available. The study posed five research questions.

Do doctors know EBM's three core aspects, and do they use its methods? What are their attitudes, and has EBM changed practice over ten years? The cross-sectional survey gives a national snapshot of the answers. Such snapshots help educators see where training takes hold. They also show where skepticism remains.
plos-pone-0007928:
Jun Zhang, Partha Niyogi, and Mary Sara McPeek offered a fresh math tool for ancestry work in PLOS ONE in 2009. For years the main tool was principal components analysis, a way to sum up how genes vary across places. Their paper tests a method built on Laplacian eigenfunctions instead.

The new method draws out the shape of population structure from gene data. It can recover maps of where groups live and how they moved, much as the older tool does, but from the geometry of the data itself. The authors show it works well, giving geneticists a second lens for large modern datasets.
plos-pone-0008028:
Vibha Gupta and colleagues solved the shape of an iron-storing protein from the tuberculosis germ in PLOS ONE in 2009. The protein, BfrA, holds iron the germ needs. Shapes like this guide the design of new drugs against a disease that badly needs them.

To solve the shape, the team used a common labeling trick that swaps in a heavy atom. The trick backfired in an instructive way: it cut the protein and knocked out its iron-holding core. The warning matters for any lab using the same trick on like proteins, lest they publish a shape the trick itself deformed.
plos-pone-0008128:
Laura De Marco and colleagues found hidden hepatitis C in people not picked for liver illness in PLOS ONE in 2009. Hidden, or occult, infection means the virus lives in liver and blood cells while standard blood tests find little or no trace. Enzyme readings often hint that something is wrong.

Finding such cases in an unselected group suggests hidden infection is more common than doctors assumed. Missed cases still damage the liver and can still spread the virus. The result argues for deeper testing when liver enzymes stay odd without a clear cause.
plos-pone-0008228:
Shih-Wei Wu, Maria F. Dal Martello, and Laurence T. Maloney studied movement planning in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Planning actions means dividing limited time and energy among steps. Most past research looked at single, isolated movements. Real actions, though, come in sequences where each step competes for time. The authors investigated how people allocate time across such sequences.

Their experiments showed that people do not always split time in the best possible way. The allocation was sub-optimal in systematic respects. Understanding those habits reveals how the brain plans under limits. It also matters for models of skilled movement and learning.
plos-pone-0008328:
Maxim Pilyugin and colleagues studied control of a histone chaperone in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Histone chaperones sit at the hub of networks that modify chromatin. The chaperone ASF1 handles histones H3 and H4 during DNA copying. Tousled-like kinases target ASF1 and are regulated by the cell cycle. Both proteins cooperate while chromatin is replicated.

The team showed phosphorylation by these kinases controls ASF1 levels. A phosphate tag thus sets how much chaperone the cell keeps. That control helps coordinate histone supply with DNA replication. The work adds a regulatory detail to genome duplication.
plos-pone-0008428:
Craig Nunemaker and co-authors reported in PLOS ONE in 2009 on islets from mouse pancreas. Islets are small groups of cells that make insulin. In past work, islets from one mouse pulsed in calcium and insulin in much the same way. Islets from a unlike mouse pulsed in a unlike way. The team called this pattern islet imprinting.

Here they test what shapes that pattern. They look at how the cells burn glucose, how the islets are built, and how alike the mice are in their genes. The study helps explain how insulin rhythms are set. That matters for work on blood sugar control.
plos-pone-0008528:
Michael Bruchas and co-authors link stress systems in mouse brains in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Stress has both rewarding and aversive motivational properties. Its adverse effects are well documented. Yet many mechanisms behind stress remain unclear and controversial. The team study a brain area called the basolateral amygdala. It helps process fear and anxiety. They focus on the CRF1 receptor, a stress signal receiver.

Activating CRF1 switches on the dynorphin and kappa opioid system in that area. That activation mediates anxiety-like behavior in the mice. The chain connects two stress systems once studied apart. It suggests a joint target for anxiety treatments.
plos-pone-0008628:
Barend Bronsvoort and co-authors evaluate sleeping sickness tests in western Kenya in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. African animal trypanosomiasis is caused by tsetse-transmitted protozoan parasites. Species include Trypanosoma vivax, congolense, and brucei. Two subspecies of T. brucei occur in East Africa, one infecting humans. No gold standard test exists to judge new diagnostics against. The team estimate sensitivity and specificity of two molecular protocols without one.

Their no-gold-standard method uses statistical modeling of combined test results. It yields accuracy figures for each protocol in field samples. Accurate animal diagnosis guides treatment and control of human risk too. The approach serves other diseases lacking a perfect reference test.
plos-pone-0008728:
William Reichmann, Elena Losina, George Seage, and colleagues compared two ways of asking personal questions. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study grew out of a trial on HIV testing in an emergency department. People answer sensitive questions more honestly in private. One option was a computer that reads questions aloud through headphones. The other was a plain pen-and-paper form.

Enrolled patients chose or were assigned a survey method. The team compared answer quality and missing data between methods. They also asked which method people preferred. The results guide clinics that need truthful answers about risk behavior without adding staff burden.
plos-pone-0008828:
Floriana Gargiulo, Sônia Ternes, Sylvie Huet, and colleagues built a tool that makes fake homes and fake families for computer models. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Models of towns, roads, and disease all need a set of homes to start with. The fake homes must look like real homes on a census form. If the start is wrong, the whole forecast can go wrong too. Their tool builds the set one step at a time.

Each step nudges the fake set closer to the real counts. Homes end up with the right mix of old, young, rich, and poor. Town planners can test new rules on these fake towns first. The tool helps any study that needs a stand-in for real people.
plos-pone-0008928:
Christoph Langer and colleagues tackled a common flaw in gene-silencing experiments in PLOS ONE in 2010. Their work used the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster, a stand-by of genetics labs. Silencing a gene with RNA interference can sometimes hit the wrong target and give false results. A rescue test, restoring the gene, is the standard way to check.

The team built rescue copies from a cousin species, Drosophila pseudoobscura, instead of the same fly. Because the cousin's gene differs slightly, it survives the silencing treatment and can restore the lost function. Living flies recovered when the matching rescue gene was added back. The trick gives labs a cleaner way to confirm that a silencing result is real.
plos-pone-0009028:
Raphaël Serduc and co-authors refined a hair-thin X-ray treatment for brain tumours, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Microbeam radiation therapy splits radiation into beams only micrometres wide. The beams come from a synchrotron, a machine that makes very bright X-rays. Normal brain vessels tolerate the striped pattern surprisingly well.

Crossing two sets of microbeams concentrates the dose where they interlace. Tumour tissue at the crossing gets a heavy dose; tissue elsewhere gets stripes of low dose. Precision like this could treat tumours that resist ordinary radiation. The work is preclinical, a step on the road toward human radiosurgery.
plos-pone-0009128:
Katherine Carr, Brian Janes, and Philip Hanna studied how anthrax spores wake up, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Bacillus anthracis spores sleep until nutrients tickle receptors in their inner membrane. Amino acids and purine nucleosides are the usual wake-up calls. A gene cluster called gerP was suspected of helping that meeting happen.

The team tested spores lacking parts of the gerP operon. Without it, germination and the outgrowth that follows faltered. GerP seems to ease the germinants' path to their receptors. Understanding spore wake-up calls matters for decontamination and biodefence.
plos-pone-0009228:
Narendranath Reddy Chintagari and co-authors published this lung study in PLOS ONE in 2010. It asks how lung cells release surfactant, the soapy film that keeps air sacs open. Without surfactant, the tiny sacs would stick shut at each breath. The release step itself was not fully understood.

The team focused on vacuolar ATPase, an enzyme that pumps acid into storage sacs called lamellar bodies. Those sacs hold surfactant inside alveolar type II cells. The authors show the pump controls release by setting the calcium level inside the sacs. That link connects acid, calcium, and the moment surfactant leaves the cell.
plos-pone-0009328:
Mukta Watve, Neelesh Dahanukar, and Milind Watve published this bacteria theory study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Plasmids are small DNA rings that live inside bacteria and copy themselves. All the genes controlling that copying sit on the plasmid itself. That raises a puzzle: a mutant plasmid that copies faster could cheat, yet low-copy plasmids persist stably.

The authors treat the plasmid population like a society with rules. They ask what social controls keep copy numbers low despite the cheater threat. Their argument borrows from sociobiology, where cooperation survives through policing and shared fate. The paper reframes a microbiology puzzle as a problem of group living.
plos-pone-0009428:
Mazhar Adli and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2010 on a key switch for inflammation. The switch is a protein called NF-kappaB. It is turned on by signals such as TNF, which comes from immune cells. Two partner proteins, named IKK alpha and IKK beta, help to turn the switch on.

The team asked what job each partner does in this well known pathway. They found that both partners play a real part in turning NF-kappaB on. The work helps explain how the cell starts an immune response step by step. It also points to parts of the switch that drug makers could aim at.
plos-pone-0009528:
Young Soo Han and Ozgur Ogut studied heart muscle fibers in rats in PLOS ONE in 2010. After a heart attack, blood flow stops and then returns. That stop and return, called ischemia and reperfusion, changes how the heart contracts. The changes happen in the tiny cycle by which muscle proteins grab and release each other. The team used a rat model to track that cycle.

They measured how the steps of the cycle shift after the insult. Each step helps set the force and speed of a heartbeat. A clear map of those shifts can guide smarter treatment for attack damage. It tells drug makers which step of the machinery is out of tune.
plos-pone-0009628:
Olalekan Uthman and colleagues reviewed the economics of male circumcision for HIV prevention in PLOS ONE in 2010. Three randomized trials had shown that circumcised men face lower risk of catching HIV through heterosexual sex. Policy makers in sub Saharan Africa then faced a money question. Does the procedure save enough future care costs to justify its price? The review gathered the economic studies on that question.

By weighing those studies together, the authors judged where circumcision gives good value. Cost effectiveness varied with setting, HIV rates, and the price of the procedure. The synthesis helps governments plan programs with limited funds. It turns a proven medical effect into a workable public health investment.
plos-pone-0009728:
Words for hand actions, like grasp or tear, may live partly in the hand itself. Victor Frak, Tatjana Nazir, and Michel Goyette tested that idea in PLOS ONE in 2010. They measured grip force while people processed manual action verbs.

Semantic representation is how the brain stores what a word means. The results place grip force inside that store for hand-action words. In other words, understanding a verb partly involves the muscles that would perform it. The finding supports embodied views of language, where meaning leans on the body. The setup was simple, but the result was telling.
plos-pone-0009828:
Sounds in speech often soften over time, a change linguists call lenition. Eftychia Eftychiou studied the routes that softening can take, using sound measurements. The acoustic study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. A hard stop sound may end up as a soft hiss or vanish.

An acoustic study measures the physical sound waves of speech. Lenition can weaken a strong consonant step by step toward a softer one. Mapping the routes shows which paths weakening actually follows. The work speaks to how languages change their sounds across generations. Lenition is one of the most common sound changes known.
plos-pone-0009928:
Seabirds hunting over vast oceans use every clue to find food, including each other. Henri Weimerskirch and colleagues showed that resting groups of birds act like signposts. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Food patches at sea are scattered and hard to find.

The signposts are compass rafts, groups of birds sitting on the water. Their heading, the direction the raft faces, indicates where food patches lie. Other birds read that social information and steer toward the patch. The finding shows how group life doubles as a navigation aid.
plos-pone-0010028:
The authors were Jingyu Liu, Marilee Morgan, Kent Hutchison, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study looked at DNA methylation across the whole genome. Methylation adds small chemical marks that can turn genes up or down. Earlier work had spotted sex differences at single genes only.

The team asked whether being male or female shifts those marks genome-wide. They also worked on how studies should account for sex when they scan so many sites. Getting that right matters, because a missed sex effect can distort gene studies of health and disease.
plos-pone-0010128:
Irene Frachon leads a 2010 PLOS ONE case-control study of a diabetes drug and heart valve damage. Benfluorex, used for overweight diabetic patients, is related to diet drugs withdrawn in nineteen ninety-seven for valve harm. Case reports had begun to link it to leaking heart valves.

At one French hospital, the team compared patients with unexplained leaking of the mitral valve against matched patients with explained leaks. Nineteen of twenty-seven unexplained cases had used benfluorex, against three of fifty-four controls, a strong statistical link even after adjusting for weight and diabetes. The study adds controlled evidence to warnings about the drug's heart risk.
plos-pone-0010228:
The authors were Kaushiki Mazumdar, Xavier Alvarez, Juan Borda, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study used monkeys that react to gluten like celiac patients do. Rhesus macaques with gluten sensitivity mirror human celiac disease in symptoms, tissue signs, and blood tests. The team also checked for antibodies to an enzyme tied to the human disease.

They visualized how a thirty-three residue peptide from gliadin, a wheat protein, crosses the gut wall. That peptide is a strong trigger of the celiac immune response. Watching it cross in a living model helps explain how a food fragment reaches the immune system.
plos-pone-0010328:
Erliyani Sartono, Ida Lisse, Elisabeth Terveer and colleagues reported a vaccine study from Guinea-Bissau in PLOS ONE in 2010. Babies there normally get oral polio vaccine at birth, given together with BCG, the tuberculosis vaccine. During two trials with small and normal birth-weight infants, polio vaccine ran out for some stretches. That gap was not planned, but it created a rare natural comparison.

Some infants got BCG alone, while others got both shots as usual. The team could thus ask whether the polio vaccine changed how babies responded to BCG. Vaccines can have side effects on the immune system beyond their target disease. A natural gap in supply let the authors measure one such effect without withholding care on purpose.
plos-pone-0010428:
Patrick Paladino, Susan Collins and Karen Mossman studied how a herpes virus protein dodges immunity in PLOS ONE in 2010. When viruses invade, a defender protein called IRF3 raises the alarm. Many viruses therefore attack IRF3 directly. Herpes simplex virus makes a protein, ICP0, whose effect on IRF3 was disputed. The team asked where in the cell ICP0 sits, since location may decide its power.

ICP0 kept in the nucleus behaved differently from ICP0 allowed into the cell body. Its address, in effect, dictated whether it could block the alarm. Settling that point clears up conflicting earlier reports. It also shows viruses tune not just their weapons but their placement. Immune evasion, here, is partly a matter of geography.
plos-pone-0010528:
Christophe Egles and colleagues found that blocking certain adhesion proteins slows skin healing in a human 3-D model in PLOS ONE in 2010. One adhesion protein, integrin alpha6beta4, also helps tumors grow and spread. That made it an attractive drug target in cancer. But the same protein anchors normal skin cells and guides their signaling. Blocking it might damage healing, a risk worth measuring first.

In the 3-D wound model, blocking antibodies delayed the skin sheet's regrowth. The model mimics human skin far better than flat cell layers. Safety signals from such models can redirect drug design early. A cancer target that breaks skin healing needs careful dosing or delivery. This study sounds that warning with human tissue.
plos-pone-0010628:
Philipp Bishay and colleagues studied a painkiller that works in an unusual way, in PLOS ONE in 2010. R-flurbiprofen eases pain but barely blocks the enzymes that most painkillers target. Its real mechanism had stayed unclear for years.

In rodents with nerve pain, the drug lowered the release of a stimulating chemical in the spinal cord. It also restored the body's own cannabis-like compounds, which calm pain signals. Both effects eased the animals' pain behavior. A painkiller that boosts natural calming systems, without heavy side effects, would be a welcome addition to nerve pain care.
plos-pone-0010728:
Chris Diehnelt and colleagues reversed the usual hunt for protein-binding molecules, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Drug discovery normally starts with vast libraries and screens them against a target protein. Most candidates fail, and the process is slow and costly for each new target.

Their backwards approach started from binding pieces and built outward. The method found tight-binding ligands for test proteins with far less screening. A cheaper route to binders matters because thousands of human proteins still lack any chemical handle. Handles are the first step toward drugs, sensors, and research tools alike.
plos-pone-0010828:
Megan Durr, Wojciech Mydlarz, Chunbo Shao and colleagues published this cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2010. They examined salivary gland tumors, a rare and varied group of cancers. The team measured chemical tags called methylation on the control regions of nineteen tumor suppressor genes, which normally help keep cell growth in check.

Samples came from tumor tissue and from normal parotid gland tissue, tested with a sensitive lab method that counts methylation levels. Salivary duct carcinoma stood out with far more methylation events than normal tissue, and patterns varied by gene and by tumor type. Durr and colleagues argue that such profiles could one day aid early detection and prognosis. For a cancer group with few markers, a measurable signature in tumor DNA is a useful lead.
plos-pone-0010928:
Saravanan Ayyadurai, Hubert Lepidi, Claude Nappez and co-authors published this plague study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Plague, caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, still kills people yearly in parts of Africa and is classed as a bioterrorism threat. Standard preventive antibiotics face resistant strains, so the team looked for a backup in an unlikely place: a cholesterol drug.

Lovastatin, already known to ease the symptoms of severe infection, was given to mice daily for six days before they were challenged with plague bacteria. Treated and untreated control groups let the authors judge whether pre-treatment changed survival and disease course. Ayyadurai and colleagues test the idea that a cheap, widely available statin could serve as extra protection after exposure. A positive result would matter most where resistant plague strains appear.
plos-pone-0011028:
Aamir Aslam, Hsien Chan, David Warrell and co-authors published this allergy immunotherapy study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Wasp venom immunotherapy gradually teaches allergic patients to tolerate stings, making it a rare human model of induced immune tolerance. Earlier work tracked T cell behavior indirectly; this team built tools to follow the exact T cells that recognize wasp venom.

They first mapped the dominant regions of Ves v 5, a major wasp venom protein, that T cells target, then identified the presenting molecule version that displays one key region. With that they could build tetramer reagents, molecular tags that latch onto matching T cells. Aslam and colleagues give tolerance research a tracking device: specific cells can now be counted and tested through treatment, revealing whether tolerance works by silencing, deleting, or converting them.
plos-pone-0011128:
Lanyon and Denham built computer models of a brain injury effect in PLOS ONE in 2010. After some strokes, a person may ignore one side of what they see, a state called visual neglect. The authors modeled how damaged attention systems could produce that loss.

Their models link the injury to changes in conscious seeing itself. In other words, the missing half is not an eye problem but an awareness problem. That insight helps explain test results from patients. It may also guide rehab that retrains attention rather than vision, a key point for stroke care.
plos-pone-0011228:
Djiane and Mlodzik studied a fruit fly protein in PLOS ONE in 2010. Fly tissues arrange their cells in neat patterns, a property called planar polarity. The team examined the fly version of a protein named GIPC and its effects on the cell motor myosin and on that tissue patterning.

The protein fine tuned motor based processes and polarity, yet flies developed without it. That makes it a modulator rather than an essential builder. Such fine tuners reveal how tissues polish their architecture. The finding informs developmental biology by separating core machinery from the controls that refine it.
plos-pone-0011328:
Anaïs Panosa and co-authors published a 2010 PLOS ONE study on Salmonella Typhimurium, a germ that causes food poisoning. They looked at a family of enzymes that build the raw material cells need to copy DNA. Salmonella carries three classes of these enzymes, and each class works best under different oxygen levels.

The team traced how the germ turns each class on and off and tested what each class does during infection. Their work shows the classes are not spare copies of one another. Each plays a distinct part when the germ makes a host sick. That split helps explain how Salmonella survives in varied places inside the body, and it points to enzymes that future drugs might block.
plos-pone-0011428:
Claudia Tam and colleagues tested in 2010 whether common gene variants raise blood sugar in Chinese adults. Three genes were in view: one tied to the sleep hormone melatonin, one to sugar sensing, and one to a key sugar-handling enzyme. All three had been linked to diabetes traits in other populations, but their effect in Chinese subjects needed direct testing.

Variants in all three genes tracked with higher fasting blood sugar and weaker function of insulin-making beta cells. The pattern was found in people without diabetes, so the genes nudge sugar upward long before disease begins. Population-specific checks like this one matter, since a variant that matters in one ancestry may be silent in another. The findings support earlier screening for people whose genes already push their sugar toward the danger zone.
plos-pone-0011528:
Sung-Wuk Jang and co-authors reported in 2010 a natural plant product with strong nerve-growth activity in mice. Compounds that make nerves grow, called neurotrophic agents, are prized because damaged nerves and degenerating brain cells badly need them, and nature produces few. The team tested deoxygedunin, a compound from a plant family known for bitter medicinal chemicals.

Deoxygedunin powerfully stimulated nerve growth in their mouse work, marking it as a genuine neurotrophic candidate rather than a weak hint. A small natural molecule that can be made and dosed is easier to develop than the protein growth factors the body uses, which are hard to deliver to the brain. The compound now deserves testing in models of nerve damage and degenerative disease. Even a partial success could seed a new drug family for conditions that currently have almost no regenerative options.
plos-pone-0011628:
Vasu Sheeba, Keri Fogle and Todd Holmes studied the fruit fly body clock in PLOS ONE in 2010. Small clock neurons called s-LNv are thought to be essential for daily rhythms, including the burst of activity flies show just before dawn. Large clock neurons, by contrast, affect arousal and sleep.

The authors disabled the small neurons and watched what happened to morning behaviour. Surprisingly, both dawn anticipation and a strong morning startle response persisted without them. The persistence reveals backup circuits in the clock network. Understanding that redundancy helps explain why daily rhythms are so hard to break.
plos-pone-0011728:
Maria do Carmo Costa and co-authors studied a disease protein's second job in muscle, in PLOS ONE in 2010. During muscle formation, many regulators are rapidly cleared by the cell's protein-recycling system. Ataxin-3, an enzyme in that system best known for a brain-wasting disease, is strongly expressed in mouse muscle, suggesting a role there.

The team found ataxin-3 helps steer young muscle cells toward maturity by adjusting levels of integrin subunits, the cell's grip proteins. That second job shows the protein's range extends well beyond the brain and may matter for muscle development generally.
plos-pone-0011828:
Rodney O'Connor and co-authors tested phone-type radio fields on three cell types, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Daily life now exposes people to many man-made fields that nature never made. Whether GSM radio fields upset calcium balance, a basic cell signal, was one sharp worry.

Exposure left calcium balance unchanged in human vessel-lining cells, in rat tumour cells and in rat brain neurons. The clear no-effect finding eases one narrow worry tied to mobile phone use. It does not settle all health questions, but it closes this one quite carefully and on firm ground.
plos-pone-0011928:
Kuan-Yu Lin and colleagues read in 2010 the small bits of RNA that plants use to fight a virus of bamboo. So-called satellite RNAs are tiny hangers-on that live only with the plant viruses they lean on. When a virus infects a plant, plant enzymes chop the virus RNA into small bits, and those bits guide the plant's next attacks on the invader.

The team made a full list of those small bits from the bamboo virus and from its satellites, across more than one host plant. The list shows which parts of the virus the plant aims at most. That map of the plant's fight-back helps explain why some cases stay mild while others, with satellites in tow, turn harsh.
plos-pone-0012028:
Franck Rapaport and Christina Leslie worked in 2010 on finding the recurring DNA gains and losses that mark cancers. Tumors accumulate copy number alterations, extra or missing chunks of genome, in bewildering variety. Yet across many tumors, some patterns repeat, and those repeats likely mark changes the cancer needs.

Their method determines which alteration patterns are genuinely frequent against the background of genomic instability. Separating drivers from noise is the central problem of cancer genomics, since unstable genomes generate plenty of innocent damage. Recurring patterns give drug researchers a shorter list of regions whose genes are worth testing as targets.
plos-pone-0012128:
Noa Levy, Assaf Pressman, and Ferdinando Mussa-Ivaldi studied how people adapt their arm movements in PLOS ONE in 2010. The brain learns to correct for steady forces that push a reaching hand off course, a classic setup in motor learning research. Here the twist was delay: the force pushing on the hand arrived late, based on how the hand had moved a moment before.

Volunteers practiced reaching while a device applied these delayed forces, and the team measured how their brains adjusted. Coping with late feedback is something the nervous system faces in real life, from tools to touch screens. The study shows the limits and tricks of that adjustment, informing both brain science and the design of machines people control.
plos-pone-0012228:
Shigeyuki Kanazawa, Toshihiro Fujiwara, Shinsuke Matsuzaki, and co-authors traced how a growth factor moves wound-healing cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Fibroblasts, the cells that rebuild damaged tissue, must both multiply and crawl into the wound, and the factor bFGF is known to drive both. The chain of signals by which it orders the crawling, however, was still unclear.

The team mapped a route running through three named signaling proteins that ends in the cell's movement machinery. Filling in that route explains how a single factor coordinates repair. It also offers points where creams or dressings might speed healing, a real need for the slow wounds of older and diabetic patients.
plos-pone-0012328:
Jun Yin, Si Hu, Wei Jiang, and co-authors studied clumping of a protective enzyme implicated in ALS, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The enzyme SOD1 normally disarms harmful oxygen radicals, but in the leading theory of its disease role, both mutant and normal copies can turn to damaging chemistry. Vitamin C, ascorbate, is abundant in nerve tissue and can drive such chemistry in the wrong company.

They found DNA itself can trigger the enzyme to aggregate in ascorbate's presence. Aggregates of this enzyme are a hallmark inside dying motor neurons. Each newly found trigger for clumping is a condition a future drug might prevent, and a warning that context decides whether an antioxidant protects or harms.
plos-pone-0012428:
Elodie Briefer, Fanny Rybak and Thierry Aubin tested how territorial animals treat strangers versus known neighbors, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Many territory holders attack strangers hard but go easy on familiar neighbors, a pattern called the dear enemy effect. The authors asked whether an unknown neighbor, heard but never met, counts as dear or as a stranger.

Their experiments show that familiarity with a neighbor's signals, not mere nearness, earns the gentler treatment. An unfamiliar neighbor was treated more like a threat. The distinction matters for understanding how animal neighborhoods stay stable and how new arrivals upset them, from birdsong contests to urban wildlife conflicts.
plos-pone-0012528:
István Kovács, Robin Palotai, Máté Szalay and colleagues presented a network mapping method called Community Landscapes, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Complex networks — from proteins to social graphs — organize into communities that overlap, and most methods force each node into just one box. A fast method that allows overlap and ranks key nodes was missing.

Their approach builds a landscape over the network where hills mark community centers, revealing hierarchy, key nodes, and likely dynamics at once. Overlapping modules fit real biology and real societies far better than rigid partitions. The tool is aimed at anyone mapping organized complexity, from cell pathways to the web.
plos-pone-0012628:
Figueira, Polikarpov, Veprintsev and co-authors measured how two gene switches bind on the same stretch of DNA. One switch is the thyroid hormone receptor, the other a factor called GATA2. Both act on the promoter of the TSH beta gene, which helps control thyroid hormone output.

Their 2010 binding studies tackle a puzzle: how switched-on receptors sometimes turn a gene down instead of up. Measuring how tightly each factor grips the DNA gives clues to that repression. The work adds detail to the basic rules of gene control by hormones.
plos-pone-0012728:
Lebouvier, Neunlist, Bruley des Varannes and co-authors tested whether a colon biopsy can reveal Parkinson's disease damage. The gut's own nerve network carries the same Lewy bodies and fibres seen in Parkinson's brains. Their 2010 study took small colon samples from patients and checked them for those marks.

They also compared the gut findings with each patient's symptoms. A gut biopsy is far easier and safer than brain sampling, so a reliable read would help diagnosis and research alike. The study tests how far that promise holds in practice.  Samples came from patients at several stages of disease.
plos-pone-0012828:
Lefevre, Gales, Olagnier and co-authors used diabetes-related drugs to shift gut immune cells and clear a yeast infection better. Obesity brings low-grade inflammation that feeds insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes. In that setting, Candida yeast in the gut becomes harder to control.

Their 2010 study found that PPAR gamma ligands switched gut macrophages from an M2b state to an M2a state. After the switch, the mice cleared intestinal Candida more effectively. Immune tuning by metabolic drugs is a two-way benefit worth clinical attention.  Gut yeast control is part of diabetes care more broadly.
plos-pone-0309628:
Kayumba and colleagues tracked side effects after COVID-19 vaccination in Congo in a 2026 study. Nearly five thousand people in Kinshasa were phoned over four weeks after vaccination during mass campaigns. About one in four reported some reaction after immunization.

Reaction rates differed by vaccine type and age, with older adults reporting fewer reactions and less fever. Active phone follow-up catches more events than passive reporting, which helps explain the rate. Steady safety watching like this supports public trust, the authors argue, and helps tailor future campaigns to groups more likely to react.
plos-pone-0335328:
Sanjiv Rampal and colleagues reviewed records of four hundred thirty-four patients whose diabetic foot infections led to amputation at a large hospital in central Malaysia. They asked what pushes a case from a minor amputation, at or below the knee, to a major one above it. Most patients arrived with advanced disease, and about seven in ten amputations were minor.

Two factors stood out as independent warnings of a major amputation: older age and a worse grade of foot damage on the standard Wagner scale. Each step up in damage grade sharply raised the odds. The lesson is about timing. Feet graded early and treated before damage deepens are far more likely to keep the leg, which argues for fast referral pathways in regions where diabetes is climbing.
plos-pone-0340628:
Babak Kamali Doust Azad and colleagues built software that counts prostate cancer cells automatically from photographs taken with ordinary mobile phone cameras. Manual counting under a microscope is slow and error-prone, and many labs lack high-end imaging gear. Their 2026 system first uses a neural network with a region-finding step to locate candidate areas in messy phone images, then applies classic image analysis to tally the cells.

In their evaluations the pipeline beat conventional manual counting on accuracy. Because it tolerates the clutter and uneven quality of phone photography, the authors present it as an accessible, scalable option for clinics and research labs with limited budgets.
plos-pone-0342628:
Jialu Wang and colleagues chart in 2026 liver cancer tied to metabolic risks across five East Asian countries over three decades. They drew death and disability figures from a global health database and split them by country, sex, and age. Forecasts then projected the pattern far into the future.

Mongolia had the highest rates for its population size, while China had the largest total counts. Burden fell in Japan and South Korea but rose elsewhere, and men and older people bore more of it everywhere. Gaps between countries are expected to widen, so the authors urge stronger action on metabolic risks.
plos-pone-0342728:
Mukesh Kumar Meena and colleagues enriched ordinary farmyard manure with a pinch of extra nutrients and tested it on Indian mustard grown in chalky soil. Indian mustard is a major oilseed, yet yields sag as soils tire. Field plots compared plain manure at a heavy rate with small amounts of fortified manure carrying sulfur, zinc, boron, and iron in several combinations.

A modest fortified dose, half the full nutrient rate folded into a small heap of manure, gave the best money return while lifting seed yield strongly. The full fortified rate pushed soil life hardest, raising microbial carbon and nitrogen and enzyme activity far above unfertilised soil. It sharply increased how much sulfur, zinc, iron, and boron plants could reach. The authors recommend fortified manure as a cheap soil revival strategy for semi-arid farms.
plos-pone-0344828:
Hui Yee Yeo, Nikki Turner, and co-authors published a 2026 protocol for mapping studies that ask the public what trade-offs they accept in measures against respiratory viruses. Masks, distancing, closures, and isolation only work when people accept them, and choice experiments can measure which features people value most. Evidence from those experiments, though, is scattered across diseases and methods.

As a protocol, the document describes the planned review rather than reporting results. The team will search three databases for choice experiments on influenza, COVID-19, and RSV measures, extract their designs and findings, and judge reporting quality with a dedicated checklist. A narrative summary is planned because studies are expected to differ widely. The finished map should guide both future preference studies and more acceptable control strategies.
plos-pone-0346328:
Mashal Shahzadi and co-authors tested bark from the Afghan ash tree as a possible diabetes treatment in 2026. The small tree grows in dry highlands and has a history in folk medicine, but hard evidence was thin.

Plant extracts were split into parts and checked for chemicals, then tested in dishes against enzymes that handle starch and sugar. The strongest part went to diabetic rats at two doses. It curbed the target enzymes and improved blood measures, and tissue checks followed. The results are early and from animals, yet they mark the bark as a lead worth careful follow-up.
plos-pone-0346628:
Yue Hu and colleagues took a full chemical scan of heart muscle from rats with epilepsy, hunting for shifts that might help explain sudden death in this disease. Such deaths are tied to the heart, but the chain of events is still not known. The scan reads hundreds of small molecules at once, and the team set the heart scans of sick rats next to those of healthy ones.

Clear gaps split the two sets of scans, and a short list of molecules stood out as changed the most. Those shifts point to the fuel and signal paths the sick heart seems to rewire. If the same marks show up in people, they could one day flag the patients at most risk, and the path map gives labs firm leads to test.
plos-pone-0347228:
Maryam Amini and colleagues study a protein that helps the eye's surface heal, in this 2026 PLOS ONE cell paper. In congenital aniridia, a rare disorder missing part of the iris, the cornea slowly clouds because its stem cell niche fails. The protein FABP5 runs low in these patients' cells, so the team knocked it down in cultured human limbal cells, with and without inflammatory triggers.

Losing FABP5 shifted key identity genes, weakening the master eye gene PAX6 and one keratin while raising another, and inflammation changed the picture further. The results position FABP5 as one link between the known genetic cause and the failing cornea, a possible handle for future treatment.
plos-pone-0347328:
Alice Plebe asks a simple question with wide consequences: do large language models have a built-in tendency to trust others? Her 2026 paper tested nineteen models in two ways. One used a questionnaire borrowed from human psychology. The other placed models in simulated situations where they had to decide whether to hand a task to someone else.

Every model claimed high trust on the questionnaire, which Plebe links to training that rewards agreeable answers. The simulations told a different story. Stronger models adjusted their choices when given clues about whether a partner was competent, while weaker ones handed over tasks almost blindly. Questionnaires alone, she argues, cannot reveal how these systems will actually behave.
plos-pone-0347428:
Zhiyi Zhang surveyed five hundred fashion design students at eighteen Chinese universities about learning with generative artificial intelligence. The 2026 study asks how different kinds of teacher support shape students' use of these tools, and whether that use builds creative skill and better coursework. Zhang tested the links with a statistical technique that maps chains of cause and effect.

Practical help, both technical and teaching-focused, predicted how much students used the tools, while emotional encouragement showed no direct link. Tool use in turn strengthened creative design ability, which then lifted learning outcomes. Most of the benefit of technical support travelled through this chain. Zhang advises schools to invest in hands-on guidance rather than cheerleading alone.
plos-pone-0347528:
Azrin Shah Abu Bakar and two co-workers asked two hundred state staff in Malaysia what helps them live well with long-term ills. The staff work in the town of Putrajaya. Book facts alone do not change how folk act. So the team weighed facts known, stance, and help from the crowd and the state.

Stance was the key link. It shaped good care on its own. It also passed on the force of facts known, which did not move acts by itself. Help from the crowd and the state lent its own push. The team says plans should work on stance and on crowd help, not just hand out facts.
plos-pone-0347828:
Rebecca H Correia, Andrew P Costa, and co-authors asked whether Ontario family doctors with extra training or a focused practice in elder care actually practice differently from their peers. Older adults depend heavily on family physicians, yet the payoff of added geriatric credentials was unproven. Their 2026 study matched two hundred thirty-two such physicians to more than nine hundred similar doctors and compared eleven accepted quality measures using health system data.

Most measures showed no meaningful difference. The specially trained group did more testing aligned with the national dementia consensus, but also prescribed more potentially inappropriate medicines and antipsychotics to older patients. The authors offer three readings: the training may change little, everyday practice constraints may swamp it, or the measures themselves may be too blunt to catch real differences.
plos-pone-0348028:
Guanxi Chen and Jiajun Chen study how city tourists come to feel like partners in creating their own trip's value, in this 2026 PLOS ONE tourism paper. They distinguish contact with government services from contact with local residents, and ask whether artificial intelligence tools, such as smart guides, change these relationships.

Survey analysis combined with a case-based method showed both kinds of interaction raised tourists' sense of empowerment, and empowerment, in turn, raised their wish to co-create experiences; neither interaction worked directly. AI tools strengthened the government path but not the resident path. Cities chasing engaged visitors, the study suggests, should empower tourists through services while keeping human contact human.
plos-pone-0348128:
Bora Lee, Soojin Im, and Sungho Won questioned whether the usual yardsticks for body weight, smoking, and blood fats sort people by death risk as well as sharper ones could. Loose definitions can mislead studies, so they tested refined measures in two large Korean health cohorts linked to death records, covering hundreds of thousands of people.

Their refinements split obesity by belly fat as well as body mass, scaled smoking exposure against age, and combined several fat ratios instead of single values. In the main analyses, underweight people carried higher death risk across all age groups. The authors argue that tidier definitions change who counts as high risk, which matters for both doctors counseling patients and researchers pooling health data.
plos-pone-0348228:
Important notice first: an earlier version of this study by Md Saiful Islam and three colleagues was retracted by PLOS One. The authors had found an error in their p-value math. Editors concluded that one conclusion, drawn from a large validation dataset, was incorrect. The journal invited this corrected and republished version, which is what this entry holds. The core method was judged sound.

The work itself tackles uncertainty in matching-based policy evaluation. When several matched pairs look equally good, different algorithms can yield different verdicts. The authors propose faster algorithms that test whether a causal conclusion survives all reasonable assignments. They validate the approach on California hospital data. Applied there, the Medicare readmission penalty programme showed no causal link to rises in readmissions at other hospitals. The scalable test lets analysts check big observational studies without prohibitive computing cost.
plos-pone-0348628:
Seokmin Kim and Christopher Searcy led a test of sea travel by plant seeds. Many island plants bear fleshy fruit. Can their seeds float on currents and stay alive? The team picked fourteen such species from Caribbean shores. They timed how long each fruit floats in salt water. They also traced more than a thousand drift buoys to map links between forty-four islands.

Float times ran from zero days to more than ninety. Species that floated longer did live on more islands. The best floater could cross the widest gap in the sea.
