Yet maps of currents failed to explain which islands hold which plants. Human use of the plants did a better job. The team calls for gene studies next.
plos-pone-0349028:
Corinna Leppin and colleagues fine-tuned the algorithms behind a phone-based quit-smoking coach that is meant to intervene at the exact moment a craving threatens. Thirty-seven quitters answered sixteen short check-ins a day for ten days, reporting mood, setting, cravings, and slips. The team then varied how many check-ins, how many predictors, and whose past data the prediction forests learned from.

Average accuracy was modest and swung wildly between people, with many setups falling below accepted minimums. Predicting actual slips worked better than predicting cravings. Fewer check-ins oddly improved slip prediction on one score while hurting craving prediction across the board, and trimming predictors cost almost nothing for slips. The authors say designers must balance nagging users against accuracy outcome by outcome, not chase a single setting.
plos-pone-0349128:
Riya Mukherjee and Chung-Ming Chang lined up a quarter century of osteoarthritis burden against the research world's response, asking whether science and translation keep pace with need. Osteoarthritis is a leading cause of disability worldwide. Their 2026 analysis merged global burden estimates from 1999 to 2023 with yearly counts of publications, experimental models, clinical trials, and funding drawn from major databases.

Disability from the disease roughly doubled while publication volume more than quadrupled, growing faster than burden. Trial starts, though, peaked in the late two thousands and have since declined, remaining a small slice of all papers. Human-relevant experimental work held a modest, steady share. The authors conclude the field publishes abundantly but translates thinly, and they frame the mismatch as a planning problem for funders.
plos-pone-0349328: Deuber and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE plan for the REVELIO pilot trial, run on a test track. Healthy adults who use cannabis for leisure will drive on a closed track in a planned trial. Sensors in the car will try to detect cannabis-impaired driving in real time. The single-centre trial uses random assignment and a control group. Roadside tools of this kind are a live policy question where cannabis is legal.
plos-pone-0349828:
Tran Le Hong Ngoc and colleagues tested a metal printing method that lays wire along part edges to focus heat where it helps most. Edge guided paths narrow heat damage and ease leftover stress versus standard wire arc printing. Printed steel samples were bent under standard tests, and a neural network learned to predict stress curves from process settings.

Best printed samples more than doubled the bend strength of plain base steel and beat typical standard prints, with far better strength per weight. Layer thickness mattered most among settings. The method even formed inner spiral channels while keeping heat controlled. Strong, light printed parts suit repair and custom metal work.
plos-pone-0350128:
Rana Muhammad Zahid Mushtaq and co-authors surveyed pharmacists across Pakistan about what keeps them well at work. Pharmacists carry heavy responsibility in stressful settings, and their well-being guards patient safety. Their 2026 study questioned five hundred sixty-four licensed pharmacists about job demands and control, how strongly they identified with their work, how they reshaped their own jobs, and their overall psychological well-being.

Job content itself showed no direct tie to well-being. Instead, two middle steps carried the effect: pharmacists who identified with their work, and those who actively crafted their jobs, reported better well-being. A chained path ran from job content through identity and crafting to well-being. The authors advise caution given some model limits, but suggest building professional identity and room to reshape tasks as practical levers.
plos-pone-0350328:
Yange Chen and co-authors adapted a light object detection model for finding key traffic elements in messy road scenes in 2026. Self driving and traffic systems miss small or partly hidden signs and vehicles, and heavy detectors are too slow for the roadside.

Their version of a compact detection family adds flexible convolution for odd shapes, a slimmer feature merging neck, and an attention step that mutes background clutter. On a road data set it missed far fewer objects and scored higher overall, while staying small and fast. Fewer missed road elements is a direct safety gain, not just a benchmark gain.
plos-pone-0350628:
Nosayba Al-Damook and colleagues mapped how lung and breast cancers rewire their fuel use in 2026. Tumors feed growth by changing metabolism, but each cancer type does so differently, and treatments rarely exploit those quirks.

Combining several public databases, the team compared three lung and breast cancer groups and a set of spread breast tumors. One lung type leaned on sugar burning, another mixed two routes, breast tumors favored building fats, and spread tumors stressed defense and recycling. Known drugs already touch some of the genes involved. The map points drug hunters toward weak spots specific to each cancer.
plos-pone-0350728:
Elisa Liberati and a team including senior psychiatrists describe a protocol for studying how MDMA works in therapy by giving it, carefully, to psychotherapists themselves. MDMA-assisted therapy shows strong trial results for post-traumatic stress, but its psychological mechanism is untheorized: trials measure brains and symptoms, not the felt, relational process. About twenty-five experienced psychoanalytic therapists will take two supervised doses and be interviewed before, during, and long after.

The interviews follow a phenomenological method, pressing on the texture of the experience and on how trained clinicians afterward understand what the drug does in a therapeutic relationship. As a protocol it reports no findings. The bet is that expert witnesses, people who both undergo the state and hold a theory of mind, can name mechanisms that symptom scales walk past.
plos-pone-0350828:
María Heredia-Torrejón and colleagues present a laboratory protocol for growing fibroblast cells from a skin sample the size of a pinhead, designed for children. Skin cells power research into genetic disease, but standard biopsies need stitches, anesthesia by injection, and wound care, a heavy ask of a child. Their method shrinks the punch to one millimeter across and simplifies every step around ordinary cell culture equipment.

Even from that speck of tissue, the team reports, primary fibroblast cultures establish reliably, and no complications have been reported so far. A smaller wound means less fear, no sutures, and samples that clinics can take during ordinary visits. For pediatric biobanks and rare-disease studies, where every donor family weighs burden against benefit, a near-painless protocol can be the difference between a sample and a refusal.
plos-pone-0350928:
Yang Yang, Bochun Lu, and Shimeng Wang surveyed more than a thousand Chinese college students in 2026 on exercise and coping with crisis. They asked whether moving more links to steadier coping, and whether looping negative thoughts and emotion habits carry that link.

Students reported activity, crisis coping styles, rumination, and two ways of handling feelings: reshaping thoughts and bottling expression. Activity tied to both healthy and unhealthy coping. Paths through rumination and emotion habits, including a chain of the two, helped explain the pattern. Campus programs, the authors suggest, should pair exercise with skills for handling thoughts and feelings, not treat sweat alone as the cure.
plos-pone-0351128:
Carlos Rivera and colleagues linked lab style sprint tests with match tracking in fourteen elite female field hockey players. Players ran six thirty metre sprints with short rests, while satellite trackers logged four top level matches within three weeks. Sprint speed, step rate, and step length were set beside match sprinting and high speed running loads.

Sprint speed in tests tracked match sprint distance, sprint pace, high speed running, and hard accelerations very strongly. Step rate also tracked those match loads, including top acceleration. Step length tracked nothing clearly. Coaches can read match readiness from simple repeated sprint speed and step rate tests, without waiting for match data.
plos-pone-0351328:
Bradley A Sheffield and co-authors mine a huge United States health record network for patients with progressive lung scarring who never receive the diagnosis code. The condition worsens steadily and anti-scarring drugs can slow it, yet coded prevalence looked far below earlier estimates. The team built three proxy definitions of increasing strictness from related lung diagnoses plus signs of progression, then compared coded and proxy patients on treatment and outcomes.

Coded cases were rare, while even the strictest proxy found many times more likely patients. Anti-scarring drug use was low everywhere, but far lower in proxy groups than in coded patients, who still went untreated most of the time. Sheffield and colleagues argue many Americans with this disease sit unrecognized and untreated inside ordinary records.
plos-pone-0351428:
Jianguang Song and five colleagues build a hybrid forecasting system for electricity demand in this 2026 study. Accurate load forecasts keep power grids stable and cheap to run. Demand curves are knotted and nonlinear, and standard optimisers get stuck in local traps. The team combined three deep learning networks that read time patterns differently. Their outputs were merged by weight. An improved parrot-inspired optimisation algorithm then tuned the system, with an error-correction step on top.

The combined model converged far faster than gradient descent training. It reached strong accuracy in about two hundred rounds, where the standard route needed well over three hundred. Final accuracy was higher too. On a British distribution network dataset, its long-term forecast errors were the lowest among rival methods. Extra machinery guarded against drifting weights and short-term bias. Grid operators gain a forecaster that learns quickly and stays honest over long horizons.
plos-pone-0351628:
Emmanuel Ahene and a large Ghanaian team built a solar-powered, camera-watching fish farm system meant to free small producers from grid power and constant manual checking. Fish farming in controlled ponds promises protein with less waste, but labor, electricity costs, and missed water problems kill margins and fish. Their system watches behavior and water, manages feeding and waste, and runs on sunlight, with learning software reading the camera feed.

Development ran from architecture to a complete working build, trained on custom video and sensor datasets from real ponds. Computer vision flags abnormal behavior and water trouble in real time, the events a farmer otherwise discovers too late. For regions where the grid is dear or unreliable, an autonomous, solar fish attendant is not a gadget but a route to making green aquaculture pay.
plos-pone-0352028:
Eugene Lee and Youngjoo Chae measured a gap that quietly drives returns in online clothing sales. A fabric feels one way in the hand. It looks another way on a screen. The team made plain and twill weaves at varied densities, weights, and thicknesses. True roughness came from atomic-level surface scans. Screen roughness came from the product images shoppers actually see.

Weave build decided the size of the gap. In plain weaves, a looser weft with a tighter warp photographed most honestly. In twills, heavier cloth with a looser weft did best. These are knobs a mill or a photo studio can turn. Teaching a flat image to tell the truth about touch has real value. It cuts returns, waste, and let-down at the door.
plos-pone-0352328:
Olivier Toubia and Jonah Berger argue that creative thinking depends not just on which ideas a person finds, but on the order in which the ideas arrive. Wandering far through memory wastes effort; moving in a tidy sequence may not. They built a short test that asks people to link concepts and scores how direct their path is, a quality they call circuitousness when it goes wrong.

Across five validation studies, people's path scores predicted creative performance better than older measures alone, and added information those measures missed. A straighter sequence through related ideas went with stronger creative work. If the test holds up, teachers and employers could spot creative thinkers with a quick exercise. The authors also note where the scoring tools still need sharpening before wide use.
plos-pone-0352428:
Arturo Octavio Gonzales-Rodriguez and co-authors examined whether the bacteria in a mother's breastmilk relate to her baby's anemia. Anemia is a widespread problem in rural Peru. Their 2026 study recruited forty-six mother and child pairs in the coastal town of Talara. It sequenced the bacterial DNA in milk samples. The children were grouped as healthy, iron-deficient anemic, or anemic for other reasons.

Two bacterial genera dominated nearly all samples. Milk from mothers of children with non-iron anemia carried a richer mix of bacteria. Milk tied to iron-deficiency anemia held more of a few genera, including Corynebacterium and Acinetobacter. It held somewhat fewer Streptococcus. The authors treat these patterns as early clues, not proof. They call for larger studies of how milk microbes and infant iron interact.
plos-pone-0353128:
Erika Yawata and four co-authors report this 2026 PLOS One hospital study of accidental hypothermia. In such patients, blood tests and scans often look like pancreas inflammation. The team reviewed nearly one hundred seventy cases at a Japanese critical care center. The cases spanned more than a decade. They asked when such findings truly matter. They also asked what blood level should prompt a detailed scan.

About one in five patients had raised pancreatic enzyme levels. Almost all patients with pancreas-like scan findings were in that group. The authors name an enzyme level above which scanning is worth weighing. A raised level alone, though, predicted scan findings poorly. Happily, no patient developed severe pancreas damage. None needed invasive care. Most recovered well with fluids and feeding support.
plos-pone-0353228:
Sen Yang and four colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One study comparing muscle strength in young men with and without obesity. Seventy-five university students, split between normal weight and obese groups, completed grip tests, maximal lifts, and machine-based strength tests at four joints. All measures were scaled to body weight, the fairest way to ask how much strength each person carries per unit of load.

By that measure the obese group was weaker on every single test, a pattern the authors call a strength-to-load imbalance. A variable-selection technique picked five predictors of grip strength, including several elbow and shoulder measures, and group membership itself remained a predictor even after joint strength was counted. The authors suggest grip strength could serve as a quick screen of overall muscle function in this population, pending larger studies.
plos-pone-0353528:
Yilmazer and colleagues tested vineyard fungicides on cabbage white butterflies in a 2026 study. Fungicides are sprayed often and assumed gentle on insects, yet proof is thin. Caterpillars met three common sprays either by eating treated leaves or by direct contact, and survival plus development were tracked.

Eating treated leaves did not raise deaths, though sulphur sprays lengthened the pupal stage and another spray shortened early growth. Direct contact caused clearer harm. Risk thus depends on how the insect meets the spray, not only on the chemical. Timing sprays to avoid direct hits on caterpillars could cut the hidden cost to helpful and harmless insects.
plos-pone-0353728:
Yinjie Huang and three colleagues published this 2026 machine learning paper on data that arrives as an endless stream. Such streams shift over time, and rare classes get swamped by common ones, so a fixed model quickly goes stale. Their design adds a reshaping layer to an online learning machine, plus a forgetting factor that lets old patterns fade.

A drift alarm based on balanced accuracy watches for change, and several of these learners vote together as an ensemble. Across nine artificial streams and two real ones, the system handled imbalance and shifting patterns better than rivals. Banks, sensors, and hospitals all depend on stream models that stay honest.
plos-pone-0354028:
Madelestin Melhan and colleagues modelled how heavy rain destabilises tropical hillsides in Pagar Alam, South Sumatra. Intense rain soaks near-surface soil, weakening the suction that helps hold slopes together. Their 2026 study used lab-measured soil properties and terrain-based slope shapes, testing both uniform and layered ground under simulated rainfall.

Safety margins fell fast once rain infiltrated. Steeper slopes lost more of their margin than gentler ones. Layered ground generally ended less stable than uniform ground, even though failure shapes looked similar. Melhan and colleagues say slope angle and hidden layering should both feature in local hazard maps, since either one can tip a hillside toward failure during long storms.
plos-pone-0354128:
Joao Manoel Rossi Neto and colleagues studied a tense drug question. It faces people waiting for a heart transplant. Their analysis appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. Many such patients survive on a drip of dobutamine. That drug helps the heart pump. Clinicians disagree about also giving beta-blocker pills. The two drugs pull in opposite directions.

The team looked back at fifty-three patients. All had tolerated both drugs for at least a month. Those who stayed on beta-blockers reached transplant far more often. They also died before surgery far less. The sample is small, and the authors urge caution. Still, the results argue for prospective trials.
plos-pone-0354728:
Arafat and colleagues, in a 2026 review, weigh whether blood tests can catch breast cancer early. Finding cancer sooner improves outcomes, but mammograms can miss tumors in dense breasts and can also raise false alarms. Two blood-based signals are candidates: tiny gene regulators called microRNAs, and patterns in blood fats and related chemicals.

The team gathered thirty-two studies with nearly seven thousand people, about half of them cancer cases, and pooled their accuracy figures. On average, the blood tests found most cancers while keeping false alarms moderate, and their combined scores looked strong. Results varied a fair amount between studies, which the authors probed with standard checks for bias and unevenness. They present these blood markers as a promising companion to imaging, not a replacement, and their pooled numbers give future test designers a benchmark to beat.
plos-pone-0354928: Grund, writing alone, published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on an age quirk in pro soccer. In youth sport, children born just after an age cutoff often gain an edge over younger teammates. Grund asks how strong that pattern is in pro football, how it differs from one country to the next, and how it has shifted over time. The work speaks to scouts and coaches who weigh birth dates when judging young talent.
plos-pone-0355228:
Alejandro Vázquez and co-authors test in 2026 whether a scale of psychological adjustment to a new culture works fairly for Latino caregivers in the United States. Caregivers of young people with emotional or behaviour problems answered in English or Spanish. The scale measures belonging and emotional attachment to each culture, and the team checked its structure and consistency.

Scores held together very well and pointed mainly to one overall dimension, though a two part split also appeared with heavy overlap. Crucially, the English and Spanish forms did not line up in the same structure, so comparing scores across languages needs care. The authors support cautious use as a short proxy measure.
plos-pone-0355628:
Kadek Surya Atmaja and co-authors pooled studies on blood sugar control and lung function in type 2 diabetes. The lung is not usually counted among diabetes target organs, yet tissue changes may quietly reduce breathing capacity. Their 2026 meta-analysis compared adults whose long-term sugar marker showed good versus poor control.

People with poor control blew out smaller air volumes on standard breathing tests. Both a one-second measure and a total capacity measure were clearly lower. The ratio between them, though, was slightly higher, which points to smaller lungs rather than blocked airways. Results were consistent across studies. The authors argue breathing checks deserve a place in diabetes care when control stays poor.
plos-pone-0355728:
Cole Baird Brookson and Ariel Greiner ask a blunt money question about coral reef rescue: when does planting new coral actually hold? Planting is popular, but reefs also face local harms such as overfishing and nutrient runoff on top of warming seas. The authors combine a math model of reef growth with records from real planting projects to find when planted coral can sustain thick cover on its own.

Healthy starting reefs with low seaweed and strong baby coral supply needed only modest planting to stay thick. As fishing and nutrient pressure rose, the planting needed grew steeply, past the point of practical use. Brookson and Greiner advise funders to cut local pressure first and plant second, or risk pouring coral into conditions where it cannot last.
plos-pone-0355828:
Qing Huang and colleagues compare in 2026 four Malaysian plant extracts for their power to guard cells against damage from oxidation. After standard lab tests picked the strongest extract, they studied it in nerve like cells and in formed muscle cells. They checked cell survival, damage to DNA, and markers tied to a cleanup process inside cells.

The winning extract came from a plant long used in folk practice, and it cut DNA damage without plainly harming the cells. Markers suggested the cleanup process became more active as dose rose. The authors present it as a candidate for more study, not as a proven treatment.
plos-pone-0356528:
Md Nahidul Alam led a team of five authors building a smart monitoring system for poultry farms, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Small farms in developing countries lose birds to heat stress and disease they cannot see coming. The team's internet-of-things system watches farm conditions in real time and flags trouble early.

Alam's sensors track the environment inside poultry sheds, sending alerts before flocks sicken. Early warning is the difference between treating a shed and losing it. Low cost is central to the design, since small farmers cannot buy pricey gear. The work shows how cheap connected sensors, well aimed, can protect both livelihoods and food supply in places where a lost flock means a lost income.
plos-pone-0356728:
Marianna Graziosi and colleagues report repeated attempts to reproduce three famous findings about awe, the feeling stirred by vast or beautiful scenes. Earlier studies had claimed that awe makes people see hidden purpose, act more generously, and feel better overall. The new team tried video, writing, and virtual reality inductions in online and lab settings, then ran three larger direct repeats of the original tasks.

The claimed effects generally failed to appear, in both the looser attempts and the larger, closer repeats. Graziosi and colleagues discuss whether online tools can stir real awe at all, and they offer guidance for future emotion research. Their report adds to a growing record that some celebrated emotion effects are weaker or less reliable than first claimed.
plos-pone-0357028:
Chenliang Zhao, Jianrong Xiong, and Yongxiang Li measured vitamin D in the blood of 131 hospitalized adults. They compared the readings with each patient's score on a standard fall risk scale. Their 2026 cross-sectional study sorted patients into low, moderate, and high fall risk. It asked which personal factors traveled with the highest-risk category. Most patients fell into that category.

Vitamin D ran lowest in the high-risk group. Each small rise in blood vitamin D came with lower odds of being classed high risk. That held even after accounting for other factors. Older age pushed risk the other way. Sex made no independent difference. Because the study captures one moment, it cannot show deficiency causes falls. The authors call for follow-up studies on whether correcting it helps.
plos-pone-0357628: Liu and four co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on where drones and air taxis might fly in cities. They used fluid-flow simulation, a method borrowed from wind engineering, to find low-altitude traffic corridors. Air at low height twists around buildings, so safe lanes must respect that flow. Early corridor maps could help cities plan drone routes before the skies get busy.
plos-pone-0357828:
Kyle A. Emery and coauthors published a 2026 ecology study in PLOS ONE on California's Northern Channel Islands, where waves wash seaweed and kelp onto sandy beaches. This washed-up material, called wrack, feeds crowds of small beach invertebrates, whose activity releases carbon dioxide as it rots. The team compared fourteen beaches that differed hugely in wrack cover, measuring the animals present and the gas escaping from the sand at the high-tide line.

Beaches with more wrack held richer, larger invertebrate communities, and carbon dioxide output rose strongly with wrack cover. The animals themselves accounted for about a tenth of beach emissions on average, though their share varied widely from beach to beach, and total consumer respiration differed fifty-fold between sites. Material drifting in from the sea, they conclude, powers this shoreline food web and its carbon processing, a link sea-level rise and coastal building threaten.
plos-pone-0358128:
Yoshiyuki Nishimiya studied gene signals on a plant virus, in a PLOS ONE paper from 2026. Tobacco mosaic virus is a classic lab virus with a well-known RNA genome. Nishimiya used cDNA analysis to detect bacterial gene expression elements carried on that viral RNA.

The work probes how gene-expression signals behave when placed on a viral RNA scaffold. Such basic questions matter for synthetic biology, where viruses are often used as delivery tools or production platforms. Knowing which bacterial signals still function in that setting helps engineers design more reliable systems. The study is small in scope but precise: one virus, one method, and a clear test of whether foreign signals are read as expected.
plos-pone-0358228:
Gang Ren leads a team of six asking why students keep using, or abandon, artificial intelligence learning devices, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The gadgets, tablets and robots carrying large language models, win easy first trials. Staying power is the real question. Surveying seven hundred twenty-six first year high school students with device experience, the team modeled how product features feed basic psychological needs, enjoyment, and the intention to continue.

Feeling related, connected through the device, drove enjoyment more strongly than any other link in the model. Warm friendliness in the device's manner showed the largest pull among the product features. Two expected links failed: feeling the device was personalized did not raise students' sense of autonomy, and fast responses did not build relatedness. Altogether the model explained about half of both enjoyment and the wish to continue. Designers are advised to engineer companionship, not just speed and tailoring.
plos-pone-0358428:
Jing Liu and Chaoqun Niu worked in 2026 on the printable silver paste used to draw fine conducting lines on a type of solar cell called TOPCon. The front side lines must be tall and narrow, a high aspect ratio, so they carry current well while shading as little of the cell as possible. The paste's organic vehicle, the liquid mixture that carries the silver particles through printing, largely decides whether those fine lines hold their shape.

The authors engineer that vehicle and study how its properties affect the printed lines. Small printing gains matter at factory scale, where a fraction more sunlight converted means large amounts of extra power across millions of panels. The study sits in the practical engineering that keeps solar costs falling.
plos-pone-0359528: Umar and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on a gene family in bread wheat. The genes, called ITPK, help make a signaling compound inside cells. The team searched the whole wheat genome to find every member of the family and then analyzed them. A full census of these genes gives breeders and biologists a map for work on growth and stress tolerance.
plos-pone-0359628:
Muhammad Bilal Riaz, A Zahra, and S A Mardan published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It examines PSR J0952–0607, a massive pulsar, a spinning neutron star heavier than most of its kind. The authors test the star's physical viability within a polytropic framework, a mathematical model of how pressure and density relate inside it.

Neutron stars pack more than the Sun's mass into a city-sized ball, and models must show such an object can exist without collapsing. Checking a record-heavy pulsar against a framework helps physicists judge which equations of matter are believable. Astrophysicists studying dense matter are the readers for this test.
plos-pone-0359728: Chang and one co-author published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on teamwork inside a semi-closed chat network. In urgent moments, knowledge sits with scattered experts who must be reached fast. The study examines how that know-how gets coordinated so it can be used in time. The lessons apply to crisis teams, hospitals, and firms where the right expert is online but hard to mobilize.
pmc-10767828:
Varadi, Bertoni, Magana, and co-authors report the 2024 state of the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database. The free database holds predicted shapes for proteins, the folded chains that do most work inside cells. By 2024 it covered well over two hundred million protein sequences.

The resource began in 2021 with a far smaller first release of predicted shapes. Its growth since then has reshaped how biologists plan experiments, since a good shape hints at what a protein does. The update explains the scale of coverage and why open access to these shapes speeds basic research worldwide.
pmc-13195228:
Kazim Sahin and Gozde Erek review chronic variable stress and a proposed supplement pairing in a 2026 article. Chronic variable stress, a lab model applying varied mild stressors unpredictably, mimics long-term human stress load. It overactivates stress hormones and drives oxidative damage, harming not just the brain but the gut-liver-brain axis, the network linking gut, liver, and brain.

The review gathers evidence that stress breaks gut barrier integrity, fattens the liver, disturbs iron handling, and fuels inflammation. A complex pairing magnesium with L-theanine, an amino acid from green tea, protected barriers and liver in animal studies, partly through metabolic regulators. Human data on the separate ingredients suggest calming and sleep benefits, supporting further study.
pmc-13195628:
Hamid Tahernia is first author on a 2026 case report described as the first known coexistence of plasma cell gingivitis and multiple sclerosis in one patient. Plasma cell gingivitis is a rare, benign gum inflammation packed with plasma cells, of uncertain cause. Multiple sclerosis is a chronic autoimmune disease damaging nerve insulation in the brain and spinal cord.

The patient was a twenty-six year old woman with nine years of stable, well-controlled multiple sclerosis, presenting with gum pain and spontaneous bleeding. Examination showed widespread red, swollen gums, and a biopsy confirmed dense plasma cell infiltration. Steroid mouthwash brought symptomatic improvement, and her multiple sclerosis stayed stable over six months of follow-up. Whether the pairing is shared immune pathways or coincidence remains open.
pmc-13196128:
Abdulkhalek Dakhel and colleagues report a 2026 study of a changed form of vimentin in the sick brain. Vimentin is a support protein inside cells. The team studied brains affected by Alzheimer disease and Parkinson disease, two illnesses where clumped proteins harm brain cells.

Using a special antibody called 84-1, they found a distinct vimentin pool that common tests miss. It formed deposits in harmed brain areas, often beside clumped proteins. The pool was mostly cut protein pieces in tough clumps. Levels were also high in spinal fluid from patients. Levels rose in human astrocytes, a type of brain support cell, exposed to harmful protein clumps. The form may serve as a marker or future drug target.
pmc-13197028:
Tadayuki Hashimoto and colleagues wrote a 2026 tutorial on hidden harms in medical teaching. Drug trials watch closely for side effects, yet teaching programs rarely get the same check. The authors argue that lessons and training can harm learners in ways that stay unseen.

They list twelve such harms with a tip to curb each. Examples include rising confidence without real skill, rewards that sap inner drive, and heavy content that overloads memory. Others cover safety that exists on paper only and overuse of AI tools that dulls thinking. The harms fall into three groups: in the learner, in the setting, and in study methods. Each tip aims to spot harm early.
pmc-13197628:
Shida Chen and colleagues wrote a 2026 review on stomach and bowel upset from metformin, a first-line diabetes drug. Nausea, diarrhea, belly pain, and bloating are common and often lead patients to quit a drug that works well. The review sorts causes into two groups to guide care.

First come fixable exposure factors: dose size, how fast the dose rises, pill type, taking it with food, kidney function, and other drugs. If symptoms persist, host factors come next, such as gut sensitivity, gut microbes, and bile handling. Fixing fixable factors first can spare needless drug stops. The authors offer a stepwise plan for clinic use.
pmc-13201528:
Many machines need three-phase power where only a single-phase supply exists, and a 2026 engineering article headed by Heba Abdellatif Nagi proposes a converter with fewer parts. The research article presents a single-phase to three-phase boost converter that drives motors while using only six controlled semiconductor switches.

The design pairs its switching layout with a simple sinusoidal pulse width modulation strategy instead of more complex space vector control. Fewer switches and passive parts should cut losses and improve current quality, the authors argue. They tested the circuit in MATLAB and Simulink simulations and then confirmed the results with a laboratory prototype run through a real-time controller.
pmc-13202028:
China bought insulin in bulk to cut diabetes costs, and a 2026 quasi-experimental study authored by Hongbin Yi evaluates what that policy did to prices, use, and spending. The research article analyzes the national volume-based procurement policy for insulin, introduced in May 2022, using quarterly hospital procurement data.

Data covered fifteen insulins from 761 public hospitals across thirty provinces, spanning late 2020 through 2023. After the policy began, winning-bid insulin prices fell by roughly half while procured volumes rose and total expenditure dropped substantially. Every insulin group showed significant price reductions, and the authors conclude centralized procurement improved affordability and use of insulin in China.
pmc-13202128:
Training may cut cancer recurrence risk, but delivering programs remotely raises practical questions, and a 2026 plan led by Gillian Jackson plans to study the delivery itself. The plan presents a mixed-methods process review embedded in CANFit, a feasibility trial of personalized remote physical activity support in England.

The trial serves people at high risk of breast, lung, or bowel cancer returning, using a basket design across the three cancers. The review will gather surveys, interviews, adherence logs, trainer diaries, and observations from participants and staff. Guided by an implementation guide, the team will judge acceptability, fidelity, reach, and sustainability, then refine how the program is meant to work.
pmc-13240928:
Hong Ngoc and colleagues in Ho Chi Minh City developed an edge-focused variant of wire arc additive manufacturing for steel parts. Guiding the arc along edges concentrates heat and narrows the damaged zone. Builds used CT38 steel with a standard filler wire. Three-point bending tests compared the new route against plain substrate and conventional printing.

Best builds more than doubled the substrate's flexural strength, beating typical conventional prints as well. Strength per unit mass rose about forty percent over the substrate. A neural network rebuilt full stress-strain curves from process settings with high fidelity. Layer thickness emerged as the single most influential parameter.
pmc-13241428:
Krause's team at Erlangen surveyed German-speaking transplant centers on readying leukemia and MDS patients for donor stem cells. Twenty-two centers replied across five typical clinical scenarios. Options ranged from transplanting immediately to bridging with chemotherapy first. Practice proved strikingly inconsistent between centers. The scenarios spanned newly found disease and disease that came back.

Two-thirds favored upfront transplantation for intermediate-risk MDS cases. For AML already in remission, most favored chemotherapy as the bridge. AML that came back split the field, with gentler agents and induction both defended. The authors call for prospective trials to settle the pathways.
pmc-13241528:
Khoshnoud's team in Tübingen asked which Parkinson's patients gain the most quality of life from deep brain stimulation. Outcomes after the procedure vary widely between patients. The team studied 130 surgical patients with a machine learning model that shows its reasoning. Inputs ranged from mood and motor scores to the exact lead position on imaging.

Three factors foretold real gains: younger age, heavier mood burden from the disease before surgery, and a specific lead spot. Leads sitting at the motor-associative border of the right subthalamic nucleus fared best. The model sorted patients fairly well on held-out data. The authors offer the cut-offs as aids for planning care patient by patient.
pmc-13242328:
Vieira and Vieira in Porto propose a mentoring cascade for radiology training. Senior trainees mentor junior trainees; juniors then guide students. The model maps onto the European training curriculum for radiology. Defined roles run from senior faculty down to first-year students.

Case talks, bedside teaching, research projects, and structured feedback fill each tier of it. Each level both learns and teaches. Teaching deepens the teacher's own skill while spreading the faculty load. Early student contact doubles as a draw into a specialty short on staff. The authors argue steady oversight, feedback, and review make the cascade last.
pmc-13242628:
Chan Cheah and co-authors ran an early-phase trial of a chemotherapy-free triplet for newly diagnosed, advanced follicular lymphoma. Their study appeared in HemaSphere in 2026. Fifty patients with high tumor burden received obinutuzumab, lenalidomide, and venetoclax in six induction cycles, with venetoclax dose levels tested along the way. Responders then moved to two years of maintenance antibody, and blood-based tumor DNA was tracked for residual disease.

Complete responses came in at eighty-six percent, and nearly all patients responded at least partly. Two years out, almost all patients were alive and free of progression in this follow-up window. Low white cell counts, diarrhea, and chest infections were the most common side effects. Clearing tumor DNA after just one cycle predicted a very high chance of staying negative. The authors present the regimen as a strong chemotherapy-free candidate now ready for larger comparison trials.
pmc-13245028:
Keith Fraser and colleagues modeled where yellow fever could ignite if an infected traveler carried it into three at-risk countries. Their study appeared in BMC Global and Public Health in 2026. Djibouti, Somalia, and Yemen are classed as potential or moderate risk, ringed by endemic regions. The team coupled a movement model, estimating imported cases, with a transmission model for what happens next, and multiplied the risks.

Three zones stand out: Yemen's western coast, Somali regions bordering Ethiopia and Kenya, and Djibouti City. In such places, a single imported infectious case carries better than even odds of sparking an outbreak, thanks to suitable climate and mosquito conditions. Elsewhere the combined risk runs lower but not zero. The authors urge surveillance systems to treat travel-linked fever as a possible introduction. The exercise is preparedness mathematics: knowing where sparks catch before one lands.
pmc-13247828:
Gezgin, Kabatas, and Kılıç used computer simulation to squeeze more power from paper-thin solar cells, in this 2026 RSC Advances study. Their device stacks an ultrathin copper indium gallium selenide absorber, barely four hundred nanometers thick, with standard partner layers. In the SCAPS-1D simulator they swept doping, defect densities, and band alignment to find what helps and what kills performance in such a thin cell.

Heavier acceptor doping strengthened the internal field and lifted efficiency, while interface and bulk defects caused severe recombination losses. The best band alignment sat at a slightly negative offset. Among candidate back-surface field layers, copper oxide won on its wide band gap and strong rear field, producing a simulated efficiency near forty percent in the model. The authors offer the design map to experimentalists building ultrathin cells.
pmc-13249528:
Zhang and co-authors ran a sixty-day transplant experiment on freshwater bacteria, reported in 2026. The question was what steers a microbial community's makeup over time: its own history, the chemistry around it, or new arrivals washing in. The team crossed three factors, swapping source communities between media and adding either normal or boosted immigration.

Early on, the arrival rate mattered most, with extra immigration enriching diversity. By day sixty, history dominated: communities from the same source stayed on distinct paths no matter where they lived or who arrived. The authors call this a priority effect, where early settlers lock in the future, and they argue it makes freshwater communities partly predictable from their past.
pmc-13249728:
Keno and co-authors warn that corn plants steal from their neighbors in breeding trials, in a 2026 Theoretical and Applied Genetics paper. Cash-strapped African breeding programs plant early hybrid trials in single rows, where each plot competes with the next for light, water, and nitrogen. Analyzing four hundred seventy-eight Ethiopian hybrids across six trials, the team modeled each genotype's direct worth and its effect on neighbors separately.

Both effects varied by site, and rankings shifted when competition was counted. Between a fifth and seventy percent of the top selections changed; under low nitrogen, the mismatch reached ninety percent. Ignoring competition, the authors argue, quietly slows genetic progress exactly where harvests need it most.
pmc-13249828:
Vogel and co-authors froze two insulin-blocking molecules in the act, in a 2026 Nature Communications study. Congenital hyperinsulinism makes the body release too much insulin, and one treatment idea is a molecule that jams the insulin receptor. The candidates each carry two arms, gripping the receptor's two insulin binding sites at once, and a sibling molecule with the arms swapped paradoxically activates the receptor instead.

Using cryo-electron microscopy, the team showed both blockers holding the receptor in its inactive shape, explaining why they block rather than trigger it. Subtle differences in how each touches the receptor also appeared. The authors say the pictures should guide safer next-generation blockers.
pmc-13249928:
Vraggalas and a European team found a splicing factor that shapes tomato fruit before it blooms, in a 2026 Plant Molecular Biology study. Splicing factors edit gene messages, and one called RS2Z36 is active in ovaries and very young fruit. Plants lacking it grew ovaries with altered patterning and produced smaller, elongated tomatoes.

Gene and protein readings in the mutant ovaries showed hundreds of messages spliced differently or switched in amount, including cell wall proteins that steer expansion. Mutant skins also deposited more of certain wall sugars. Because the cell shape changes were set before flowering, the authors place this splicing control at the very start of fruit formation.
pmc-13250028:
Zhou and co-authors demonstrated holograms that control light's polarization as well as its brightness, in a 2026 Discover Nano study. Ordinary holograms shape only intensity, wasting half the information light carries. Their surface stacks metal and insulator layers in tiny patterned cells, a standard structure that usually fails at visible wavelengths because the metal absorbs too much light.

An improved design algorithm, splitting the light field into parts, produced cells that steer both properties at once. In full-wave simulations under circularly polarized red light, the surface generated the intended vectorial holographic images. The authors present the work as a step toward compact displays and optical devices that use polarization as a working channel.
pmc-13250628:
Mark Kern and colleagues examine how ageing changes swallowing in this 2026 study. Swallowing links the throat and the upper food pipe in a timed sequence, but how that teamwork shifts in healthy older people had not been mapped in detail.

Thirty-three healthy volunteers were studied with pressure sensors, split into elderly and younger groups. The team found the food pipe's swallowing motion runs in four periods, from rising empty, to receiving the food, to pushing it down. The early periods differed clearly in older subjects, and a link between flow and squeeze strength seen in the young faded with age. Weak throat muscles may explain the change.
pmc-13250828:
Tsubasa Mikie and co-authors report a design shortcut for plastic electronics in this 2026 chemistry paper. Polymers that carry electric charge well usually need fused rings locked into the backbone, but this team reached high performance without any fused rings.

They tuned a feature called quinoid character, which controls how bond lengths alternate along the chain, by varying one building block's length. Stronger quinoid character evened out the bonds and let charge flow more freely along each chain. Test transistors carried both charge types at high speeds despite modest crystal order. The authors propose bond pattern tuning as a fresh design lever for organic electronics.
pmc-13251028:
Capucci and colleagues clarify a confusing blood marker in rabbits vaccinated or infected with hemorrhagic disease virus. Their 2026 Veterinary Research study combines two vaccination experiments with a three-month farm watch during an unexpected outbreak. Antibody readings in rabbits are widely used, but the IgA class was hard to interpret.

Vaccination alone produced only traces of IgA for a few weeks in about half the rabbits. A real oral challenge, by contrast, triggered a marked and rapid IgA rise in the animals. On the farm, steady IgA marked the oldest does, survivors of an earlier epidemic, and new positives appeared with the outbreak. The authors conclude that IgA works as a sign of reinfection rather than of vaccination.
pmc-13251328:
Lonergan and co-authors show that nitric oxide, a short-lived gas signal, rewrites the makeup of microbe weapons called phenazines. Their 2026 study uses a Pseudomonas microbe that gives off these germ-killing pigments to shape the area around it. Whether released compounds react with nitric oxide, and what follows, had been little studied.

Nitric oxide reacted with certain phenazines to form stable, distinct products with much weaker germ-killing action. A rival germ, Staphylococcus aureus, shrugged off the altered compounds in tests. Pseudomonas itself, though, died quickly when its own phenazines met nitric oxide, even with the rival present. The authors say this tuning of what microbes give off could steer which germs win inside the body.
pmc-13254428:
Sreeja Gandamsetty and co-authors test a heart tracing marker for early rhythm problems in a 2026 cohort study. They enrolled 196 patients with a first acute myocardial infarction, or heart attack, and tracked rhythm events within 48 hours. The marker is the Tp-e interval, the span from T wave peak to end on an ECG.

Rhythm problems occurred in 65.3 percent of patients, most often ventricular tachycardia. A longer Tp-e interval and higher Killip class, a severity grade, independently predicted these events. A cutoff of 98 milliseconds gave 77.3 percent sensitivity and 69 percent overall accuracy.
pmc-13257928:
Shawn A Thomas and co-authors wrote a 2026 United States public health report on drinking alcohol during pregnancy. Alcohol in pregnancy can harm birth outcomes and cause fetal alcohol spectrum disorders, and no amount is known to be safe. The team analyzed survey data from the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System for 2021 to 2024. It covered pregnant women aged eighteen to forty-nine across the United States.

In the past thirty days, 15.2 percent of pregnant women reported current drinking, 4.9 percent reported binge drinking, and 2.2 percent reported heavy drinking. Rates were higher among women who were not married and women with frequent mental distress. The authors suggest routine screening in clinics, plus community steps such as warning signs at sale points and alcohol taxes, to cut drinking in pregnancy.
pmc-13258128:
Sen Yang, Yi Liu, and Liping Xu wrote a 2026 tourism study of how food experiences shape what tourists do next. Their case was food tourism in Zibo, Shandong, China, a city whose food scene drove a strong post-epidemic tourism recovery. An online survey gathered 447 valid responses from tourists who had taken part. The authors used mental imagery theory, which holds that people rebuild sensory experiences in the mind, to model engagement behavior.

Food sensory experience, covering sight, smell, taste, and touch, had a significant positive effect on engagement. Its strongest effects were on feedback intention and revisit intention. Two factors carried the effect in parallel: food memory, the stored sensory record, and mental imagery, the active rebuilding of the experience. Imagery mattered more for recommending the place, while memory mattered more for wanting to return.
pmc-13259628:
Daphne Menssen and colleagues sketch a factory future for lab-grown cartilage. Damaged joint cartilage burdens millions, yet regenerative repairs stay costly, fiddly, and rarely reimbursed. Their 2026 review backs a modular fix: grow tiny cartilage balls, then assemble them into full implants.

Every production step, from freeing cells to forming and harvesting microtissues, has an automated version somewhere in the literature. Nobody has yet chained them into one cheap, compliant production line. The authors map the design choices that matter early, including automatic quality checks and cleaning. Building for scale from day one, they argue, decides whether patients ever benefit.
pmc-13261328:
Zhifu Kou and colleagues present a 2026 prospective cohort study of residential green space, genes, and irritable bowel syndrome. IBS is a chronic bowel disorder with recurring pain and changed bowel habits. Whether nearby greenery interacts with genetic risk was unexplored.

The study included 376,749 UK Biobank participants, with greenness measured by a satellite vegetation index. Over 11.73 years of follow-up, 7,091 new IBS cases were documented. Within a 1000 m buffer, each interquartile-range rise in greenness meant a 5% lower IBS risk. Greater distance to water was also linked to lower risk. The green-space benefit appeared only in high-genetic-risk people, who saw an 8% risk reduction. No interaction appeared for blue space. Physical activity partly explained the green-space link. The authors commend urban greening as a prevention strategy.
pmc-13262428:
Stephania T Miller and colleagues describe patient partnership in a diabetes trial in a 2026 journal article. The SISTER study tested self-care support for African American women with type 2 diabetes. A Patient Advisory Group of women with the condition joined the work from the start, in 2020, rather than only taking part as subjects.

Group members helped design the trial, shaping recruitment materials and the comparison group's content so it fit their culture. During the trial they aided community outreach, refined session topics, and guided COVID-19 safety rules. Later they helped interpret results and served as co-authors on papers. The authors present this record, drawn from meeting notes and reports, as a model for engaging groups often left out of research.
pmc-13262928:
Lena Jaki and co-authors show drug resistance hiding inside herpes viruses before any drug arrives. Aciclovir failures in immunocompromised patients emerge during long treatment, puzzling clinicians. Their 2026 study grows herpes simplex virus under drug pressure and reads whole genomes at extreme depth.

Resistance appeared within a single round of growth under aciclovir. The responsible mutations sat in two viral genes and, crucially, already existed in the untreated parent virus at vanishingly low frequencies. Repeated passaging of a clean rebuilt strain confirmed that rare variants swell under selection. Deep sequencing could flag resistance risk early, aiding drug stewardship.
pmc-13263328:
Corinna Patzina-Mehling and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on West Nile virus in mosquitoes across a small part of Berlin, Germany. West Nile virus spreads between birds and mosquitoes and can infect people. The team sampled mosquitoes at five sites within one square kilometer over the 2023 and 2024 seasons.

Infection rates reached nearly five percent in some samples, and risk varied sharply over short distances. Homes and cemeteries showed the highest monthly infection rates, while restored nature areas and a sponge city site, built to soak up rainwater, showed much lower ones. Mosquito numbers and species did not explain the pattern. The shape of each habitat and its bird community mattered more.
pmc-13263528:
Lennart Essmann and colleagues read a decade of Swiss hospital records for infections in and around the brain. Over twenty-three thousand cases of meningitis or encephalitis span twenty twelve to twenty twenty-one in their 2026 study of the whole country. Pathogens and outcomes split sharply by age.

Case counts climbed year by year until twenty nineteen, then dropped hard during the pandemic years. Meningitis from pneumococcus and enterovirus fell furthest, hinting that the same curbs blocked them too. Young children carried enterovirus and streptococcus, while patients over fifty hosted pneumococcus, listeria, and tick-borne viruses. Bacterial cases landed in the ICU and died far more often than viral ones.
pmc-13263928:
Chunmei Sun and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on growing a medicinal orchid, Dendrobium devonianum, on China fir trees in Yunnan, China. The orchid grows on other plants without harming them, and its stems are valued in herbal medicine. The team compared plants grown on dead tree frames with plants on living standing trees.

Dead frames produced thicker, longer, heavier stems, but plants there suffered far more rust and black spot disease. Living trees hosted richer root microbe communities, including groups linked to lower disease, and the orchids built up more flavonoids and polysaccharides, prized medicinal compounds. The authors conclude living-tree cultivation gives the better balance of disease resistance and medicinal quality.
pmc-13264428:
Sarvesh P Azgaonkar led a 2026 case report on a giant cystic neck tumor in a man in his 90s. The growth was a very rare skin gland cancer with a long name, SCACP for short. Such tumors can look like harmless cysts, which makes them hard to name and treat.

The swelling had grown for two years and filled the left half of his neck. A needle test gave no clear answer, and scans showed spread across both front and back parts of the neck. Surgeons removed it through the neck, and lab tests with three markers confirmed the rare cancer. The authors stress lab study of the tissue as the way to tell this growth from common cysts.
pmc-13264628:
Eman AbdElRhiem and colleagues wrote a 2026 chemistry study on slowing rust-like damage to brass in salty water. They used a sulfur compound called MBT, a known protective agent, plus tiny particles of two oxides. The question was which particle partner makes the protective film work best.

In salt water like seawater, MBT alone reached 97.4 percent protection at its best dose. Adding titanium oxide particles lifted protection to 98.2 percent, while silica particles gave 94 percent, below MBT alone at that dose. Tests showed MBT sticks to the brass surface on its own, forming a film. Computer models said the titanium partner binds most strongly and passes charge best. The authors credit the particle's electronic nature, not a simple barrier effect, for the gain.
pmc-13264928:
Sanxiu He and a large team published a 2026 study on a protein that helps a common lymphoma dodge the immune system. The cancer is diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, and up to 40 percent of patients relapse or resist standard therapy. The protein, HMGB2, is overproduced in this cancer, but its role was unclear.

The team found high HMGB2 marks a worse outlook. Cutting it back in cancer cells alone changed little in dishes, yet it slowed tumors in animals by reshaping the tumor surroundings. Cancer cells ship HMGB2 out in tiny bubbles, and it switches macrophages, immune cells in the tumor, into a calm state that eats fewer cancer cells. Blocking that chain restored macrophage eating and boosted a standard antibody drug. The authors name the chain as a drug target.
pmc-13267428:
Muhamed Baljevic and colleagues wrote a 2026 study of how suspected heart amyloidosis is worked up in United States practice. In this disease, stiff protein deposits build up in the heart. Two main types need different treatments, so sorting them fast and correctly matters. The team read electronic health records from 2017 to 2023.

They tracked three patient groups: about 1,650 with one type, about 1,050 with the other, and 59 with signs of both. Only about half to two-thirds got any targeted test within two years before diagnosis. Full protein testing, a key step, was done in well under half of each group. Heart specialists and general doctors led most workups. The authors urge wider awareness so patients are tested as guidelines advise.
pmc-13267628:
Yunli Li and a large team report a 2026 survey of a cat virus in captive giant pandas in China. Feline panleukopenia virus attacks meat-eating animals and can spill into rare species. The team tested 262 blood samples from 136 pandas at the Chengdu panda breeding base, collected between 2015 and 2023. They looked for antibodies, signs of past exposure.

About 57 percent of samples tested positive, and levels stayed high across the years. Young pandas and summer samples showed lower rates, which the team links to mother's antibodies and weaker virus survival in summer. Pandas with a past transfer between sites trended toward higher risk. Current vaccines seemed to raise weak responses. The authors urge tailored vaccines, tighter hygiene in risky seasons, and care with animal transfers.
pmc-13267928:
Shih-Chieh Lo and colleagues present a 2026 study of jaw-advancing mouthpieces for sleep apnea, watched during sleep endoscopy. These devices hold the lower jaw forward to keep the throat open. The team tested 75 adults under sedated sleep observation. They compared a standard edge-to-edge mouthpiece with a custom simulator pushed to maximum forward position.

The advanced device cleared full blockage at the soft palate in about 35 percent of cases where the standard one had not. It cleared blockage at the voice box flap in 80 percent during head turning. In a monitored subgroup it also cut apnea events and raised lowest blood oxygen. But it caused more blockage while breathing out, in 64 percent against 41 percent. The authors call this a trade-off needing longer study.
pmc-13269028:
Sayed Mortaza Fayez wrote a review article in 2026 surveying where nanomedicine, medicine built at a tiny scale, stands. The review looks at recent clinical gains, at blocks that slow new treatments, and at what may come next. Worked examples with numbers are used to show broad trends.

Those examples include 23 studies with 412 patients on uneven drug spread in tumors, and 847 clinical trials listed from 2010 to 2020. Fayez highlights early trial results in lung cancer, particles that act on tumors, and gold crystals tested for a nerve disease. The main claim is that such particles now act as treatments themselves, not just as carriers for drugs.
pmc-13269928:
Vikas Kumar Kushwaha and co-authors published a physics paper in 2026 simulating one active particle, an intruder, moving through a dense crowd of self-steering active particles. All particles see ahead and steer to avoid collisions, and each has a limited turning ability. Computer simulations tracked the intruder's speed in its chosen direction.

Steering around neighbors did not help the intruder; it actually slowed its directed speed. Progress depended instead on neighbors seeing the intruder and moving aside in time. The crowd's own collision avoidance spread particles more evenly than random, which eased the intruder's path. Speed and sideways wandering depended on turning limits, vision angle, and crowd density. The authors note uses for emergency staff moving through crowds.
pmc-13271128:
Sandip Patra and Aakash Nathani wrote a 2026 review on engineering nanocarriers, delivery vehicles built at tiny scale, to carry dopamine into the brain. Dopamine controls movement, thinking, and reward, and its loss drives Parkinson's disease, yet normal dopamine drugs cross into the brain poorly, break down fast, and can cause harm outside the brain.

The review surveys polymer particles, fat bubbles, branching carriers, inorganic particles, and cell-derived vesicles, weighing how each protects dopamine from damage and releases it in a controlled way. Polymer, lipid, and vesicle systems look most promising, they argue. They also cover nose-based delivery, receptor targeting, and hurdles of scale-up, long-term safety, and regulation.
pmc-13271328:
Jessie Schwartz is lead author of a 2026 study of HPV shots in community pharmacies in the United States. It is based on interviews. Human papillomavirus causes about 39,300 cancers a year nationally. Yet teenage shot rates lag. Pharmacies can give the shot to teens, but they are underused for it.

The team interviewed eleven pharmacy staff and thirteen parents of children aged nine to 17 in early 2021. They listed 31 current practices and 35 chances to improve. Staff named uneven vaccine checks, weak proactive advice, and split reminder systems. Parents valued ease of access and clear, short advice. Proposed fixes include standard scripts, prompts, bigger technician roles, and better follow-up.
pmc-13271428:
Zhen Wang is lead author of a 2026 journal article on whether a simple insulin sensitivity score can predict atrial fibrillation returning after radiofrequency ablation. Ablation is a heart procedure that burns tiny areas to fix rhythm. Insulin resistance, where the body responds poorly to insulin, helps drive this rhythm disorder. The score, called SPISE, estimates it from routine measures.

The study followed 529 patients aged 65 and older after ablation, and 175, or 33.1 percent, saw their fibrillation return. Higher SPISE scores linked to lower recurrence risk in the fully adjusted model, with a negative, curved relationship. The link held across subgroups split by sex, blood pressure, diabetes, and heart disease.
pmc-13273828:
Xu and colleagues use genetics to probe links between blood proteins, brain scans, and Alzheimer's disease. Their 2026 journal article applies Mendelian randomization in both directions. The method uses gene variants as natural experiments.

The team examined 1,633 plasma proteins for causal links to Alzheimer's risk. They also studied brain imaging measures. Twelve imaging metrics showed causal links. Imaging measures helped explain the protein results. They mediated 67 percent of one protective link. That link ran from the protein PTPRC to lower Alzheimer's risk. Mediation means the brain measures carried part of the effect. The authors say such chains may reveal drug targets.
pmc-13274128:
Aleksandra Strokach and a large team report a 2026 journal article linking gut bacteria to melanoma treatment response. Melanoma is an aggressive skin cancer, and immune checkpoint drugs help many patients but fail others. Gut microbes shape immune responses, so the team asked which bacteria track with success.

They combined a first Russian group of sixty-two patients with six published data sets, for 490 patients in seven cohorts. Analysis found 527 assembled bacterial genomes tied to outcome, 239 with response and 288 with non-response. Several Faecalibacterium species tracked with response, while Enterobacter ludwigii tracked with failure. Effects could flip within one species, so fine-level profiling matters.
pmc-13275628:
Sujin Kang and colleagues present a 2026 journal article tracing how heart and metabolic risks may reach the brain through body chemistry, using the long-running CARDIA cohort. They analyzed 606 participants aged forty-eight to sixty at the study's thirtieth year, profiling urine metabolites with two laboratory methods and brain scans in a 281-person subset. Structural equation models mapped paths from risk factors to thinking scores.

Higher fasting blood sugar was linked to worse cognition. Several amino acids, including valine, isoleucine, leucine, and phenylalanine, rose with fasting sugar, and valine and aminoadipic acid sat on the path between sugar and cognition. Tryptophan also correlated with both. A gut-related compound, indole-3-acetic acid, fell as blood pressure and sugar rose, while memory-area brain measures tracked waist size.
pmc-13276128: Jonna Hybelius and co-authors published a study of basic emotions in people with persistent physical symptoms receiving exposure therapy or lifestyle promotion in primary care. Their 2026 correction notice fixes errors in a paragraph on how stable emotion questionnaire answers were over time. The emotion surprise had wrong stability figures, and figures for shame were left out of a summary range. The corrected text reports surprise as far less stable than the other emotions and notes the team dropped it from later analysis. The original article has been corrected.
pmc-13276428:
Jianjun Li and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on forecasting the microclimate inside desert solar power plants. Panels change local heat, moisture, and dust, which affects both panel output and plant life underneath. Standard forecast tools struggle with the tangled space and time patterns at these sites.

Their model is a graph neural network, a method that learns from connected stations arranged as a network. Extra environmental inputs, such as surrounding weather data, feed in as covariates. The network predicts temperature, relative humidity, and airborne dust at fine detail across space and time. It beat conventional graph models in the team's experiments. Analyzing the extra inputs showed each contributed differently to the three forecasts. The authors aim to support day-to-day operations and maintenance planning at sandy solar stations.
pmc-13276528:
Yongjun Liao and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on tiny vesicles from spices that cut the hazards formed when meat cooks at high heat. Frying and grilling create heterocyclic amines and advanced glycation end products, compounds linked to cancer and inflammation. The team harvested exosome-like nanoparticles, natural plant nanovesicles, from six spices.

They tested the vesicles in air-fried beef patties. Horseradish vesicles worked best and broadest, cutting total amines by just over half and the glycation products by about half at the tested dose. They also mopped up free radicals best and slowed fat and protein oxidation more than the rest. Taste and texture stayed largely intact. Chemical profiling showed horseradish vesicles uniquely rich in mustard-oil precursors, which may trap harmful molecules two ways. The authors propose a clean-label strategy for the meat industry.
pmc-13280628:
Marriam Ahmed and colleagues wrote a 2026 review on exosomes in cancer. Exosomes are tiny sacs that cells release into blood and other fluids. They carry proteins and bits of gene code from the cell that made them. That cargo can show what is going on inside a tumor.

The review explains how these sacs form and how labs find and measure their proteins. It describes how the sacs can help tumors grow and can change how the immune system reacts. It also looks at ways to block or use those proteins as drug targets. The authors argue that exosome tests could one day make cancer care more exact and more personal.
pmc-13281328:
Candice Peart and colleagues described a youth project on loneliness in a 2026 paper from Australia. Loneliness is rising among young adults and can shadow health for years. The project, called a/part of the crowd, built a web response with young people, not just for them. It drew on one hundred twenty-eight short works sent in by people aged eighteen to twenty-five. The works spanned stories, poems, art, and music.

A twelve-member advisory group of young adults with lived experience guided the design. Five of them also served as paid co-researchers on the team. Their notes shaped the web space, outreach, and user tests. The group found that a steady coordinator kept the team linked and heard. Shared meetings, where all read the data together, built trust. The authors say deep roles, not token seats, made the work stronger.
pmc-13282128:
Evonne Zoe Younan and co-authors describe a 2026 case of advanced bile duct cancer treated with a complex liver operation. Bile duct cancer, called cholangiocarcinoma, is often deemed inoperable when it grows into nearby blood vessels. The patient was a seventy-one-year-old woman whose tumour had invaded the vessels at the liver gateway. The team removed the extended left side of her liver.

Rather than cutting all vessels at once, the surgeons rebuilt them one by one. They reconstructed the liver artery, the portal vein, and the large vein to the heart before removing the specimen in one piece. Keeping blood flowing lowered the risk of starving the liver of oxygen. She left hospital on day fourteen after a smooth recovery. Forty-four months later she remained well, with no sign of return on scans.
pmc-13282428:
Norio Tomita and co-authors present a 2026 exploratory trial on how hands-on therapies change a deep back tissue layer in people with chronic low back pain. The layer, the thoracolumbar fascia, may contribute to pain without a clear cause. Sixty participants were randomly assigned to acupuncture, chiropractic care, or a three-week waitlist. After waiting, the control group received massage, allowing a within-person second phase.

Quantitative ultrasound measured how the fascia slides and strains. Chiropractic care reduced the cumulative strain measure, while controls grew worse and acupuncture showed no clear change. Massage after the waitlist cut both strain measures strongly. Only chiropractic care improved a disability score, and strain changes did not track disability changes. A tissue structure measure detected no changes at all. The authors say ultrasound strain can capture short-term mechanical responses to some therapies, offering a biomarker for how such treatments work.
pmc-13283328:
A freshwater sponge from Brazil's Cerrado hosts microbes quite unlike the water around it, Carla Patricia Pereira Alves's group found in 2026. Sponges are among the oldest animals and host rich microbe partners. Freshwater sponge microbes are far less studied than marine sponge microbes.

Samples of Metania sponge and nearby water came from the Brazilian Cerrado. Gene tests found 17 phyla across bacteria and archaea in the samples. The sponge host held a distinct microbe mix from the water around it. Only about a quarter of taxa were shared between the two sets. Sponge microbes were rich in defense systems that block virus attack. Water microbes leaned toward traits for life in open conditions.
pmc-13283428:
Sean P Woytowitz and Charles Manchee present a 2026 case of repeated confusion in a man treated for blood cancer and mental illness. Altered mental state in cancer care often has many drivers at once. Sorting the main cause is vital to cut harm and recurrence.

The man was in his 60s with relapsed plasma cell cancer after stem cell transplant. Episodes arose during chemo combined with many psychiatric drugs at once. Brain scans ruled out structural or vessel causes for his episodes. Kidney function dipped mildly at times without a full metabolic crisis. Care improved after his drug list was simplified by the team. Team-based review is urged for such complex cases.
pmc-13283728:
Peeling cartilage inside the hip socket can worsen if left alone, and Leandro Calil De Lazari with colleagues evaluated a drilling method meant to heal it from behind in 2026. Their reverse approach drills from above the socket rim so the joint surface stays intact.

Forty patients had keyhole hip surgery with impingement repair plus the drilling step. Scores for hip function rose sharply and pain scores fell sharply by final checks. Bone angles improved after surgery in line with the impingement repair work. MRI follow-up ran for at least two years in every patient. Results support the method as a low-cost, cartilage-sparing option worth wider testing.
pmc-13284028:
A cilia gene runs higher in tissue from boys with undescended testis in a 2026 study by Sinan Kilic and colleagues. Testis descent failure has known hormone and mechanical angles, but genetic angles are thin. Hair-like cell structures guide many development steps in embryos.

Tissue came from 24 young patients and 24 matched controls during surgery. Five dynein heavy chain genes were measured against a standard reference gene. Only DNAH9 stood out, at over twice the level in patient tissue. Other genes shifted little and without statistical firmness in tests. Mean ages matched closely between groups, near two years old. Ciliary paths merit study.
pmc-13285528:
Do trusted evidence reviews rest in part on work by repeat fraudsters? Theint Moh Moh Zaw, James Heathers, and Gideon Meyerowitz-Katz check Cochrane reviews in a 2026 study. Cochrane sets high bars for rigor, yet its reviews may still hold studies from authors with long retraction lists. The team flagged authors with at least twenty-four retractions and traced their papers.

Of 9,323 reviews, eighty-one held or cited at least one suspect study, and thirty-two folded such work into pooled results. When reviews shut such studies out, stated grounds seldom named trust worries. Only a small share of the affected reviews ran checks on whether dropping bad work moved the verdict. The authors urge closer screening.
pmc-13285628:
Severe leaking eye vessels struck a 10-year-old boy with a rare body syndrome, Eiji Kishi and co-authors report in a 2026 case. Bardet-Biedl syndrome had already left him with fading retinas, weak kidneys, weight gain, and learning delay, and gene tests pinned paired faults in the BBS2 gene. He arrived with sight down to bare light sensing in both eyes.

Scans showed heavy fluid leakage, retinal lifting, and a bleed in the left eye, plus pressure climbing there from new vessel growth. Laser treatment, surgery on both eyes, and an injected growth blocker followed. A month on, sight stayed at light level, yet pressure sat controlled with drops. The authors tie the vessel harm to blocked retinal flow.
pmc-13285928:
Xiaping Yao and colleagues build a gel eye drop for dry eye disease in a 2026 formulation study. Quercetin, a plant compound, calms inflammation and fights oxidative stress, but it barely dissolves in water and washes off the eye fast. The team packed it into coated fat bubbles, then set those bubbles in a gum that turns to gel on the eye.

The finished gel held tiny, even particles and trapped most of the quercetin loaded into it. It clung to the eye surface far longer than the bubbles alone and raised drug levels in tears and eye tissues. In mice with induced dry eye, the gel restored tear flow, healed surface damage, and cut two key inflammation signals. Results matched a standard prescription drop, with no irritation seen, which marks the gel as a strong candidate.
pmc-13286328:
Kimbra Edwards and co-authors survey how patients feel about AI writing research documents in a 2026 questionnaire study. Drug firms increasingly draft plain-language trial summaries with generative tools, stirring questions about accuracy and trust. An online panel of 1,010 patients across the United States and Europe reported their familiarity with AI and how much human hand they want in such documents.

Nearly two thirds had used AI before, and three quarters called themselves somewhat or very familiar with it. Over half believed AI drafting would cut grammar and data errors. Yet trust cratered when documents came from AI alone and peaked for human-only writing, and 95% rated human review as important. Most also demanded open disclosure when AI helps write public documents, a transparency call the authors say firms cannot skip.
pmc-13286528:
Sergio M-Cam and colleagues compare game-based and plain versions of ear training for young adults in a 2026 cross-sectional comparison. Tone discrimination drills support hearing rehabilitation, but months of repetition bore younger users into quitting. Both systems delivered identical pure-tone tasks and scoring; only one wrapped them in dual-task game play. Eleven volunteers aged 18 to 30 tried each build and rated experience, usability, and engagement.

The game version won six of eleven questionnaire dimensions, sweeping focused attention, looks, reward, and novelty. Raw performance, though, refused to budge: response speed, accuracy, and combined scores matched between systems. Plain software held a slight usability edge, suggesting simpler screens still navigate easier. Gamified drills thus look safe for keeping users hooked without dulling the training itself, pending longer trials.
pmc-13287028: A short 2026 retraction notice from the editors and publisher of OncoTargets and Therapy withdraws a 2019 study of a long noncoding RNA in hemangioma cells.
