A third party raised concerns in 2024, and the journal's check found image panels from different treatment conditions looking unusually alike, plus blots overlapping with an unrelated group's earlier article. The authors did not answer the queries. The original article stays online, watermarked as retracted, to preserve the scholarly record.
pmc-13287328:
Emmanuel N Nkuruemma and co-authors reviewed 81 studies in 2026 on making levan, a fructose-based chain sugar with food, medical, and industrial uses. Output figures vary wildly between labs, partly because microbe choice, growing conditions, and reporting styles all differ.

The enzyme that builds levan, and where it sits in the cell, shapes both yield and chain size. Oxygen supply and sugar strength emerged as major but under-studied controls. Recovery steps use much energy and solvent and can damage product quality. The authors propose a shared engineering framework so future plants can scale up with standard measures and cleaner processing.
pmc-13289328:
Yilin Liu and colleagues describe a 2026 effort to make nattokinase in engineered bacteria and test its promise for obesity care. Nattokinase is an enzyme that breaks down blood clots and may help heart and metabolic health. Normal production gives low yields, which blocks wider medical and factory use of the enzyme.

The team rebuilt Bacillus subtilis with a strong always-on promoter and a glowing fusion tag to watch output live. Flask cultures reached activity far above older methods, and a fed-batch run in a 5-liter bioreactor pushed output higher still. Animal work then probed effects on fat metabolism and heart complications linked to obesity. Higher, cheaper supply could make trials and products far more practical.
pmc-13289528:
Lena Schemet and Sarah Friedrich-Welz present a 2026 simulation study on statistics after variable selection in Cox survival models. Cox models estimate how factors affect time to an event, but standard math assumes factors were fixed in advance. When data-driven selection picks factors first, naive follow-up results can mislead badly, and censoring adds more uncertainty.

The study tests several fixes after Lasso selection, including sample splitting, selection-aware methods, and a debiased approach. Each method targets a different question, so coverage, interval width, power, and error rates must be read with that target in mind. Simulations used realistic biomedical data patterns, plus a public survival dataset example. Findings guide analysts toward honest uncertainty after selection.
pmc-13290728:
AI has moved into the clinical skills classroom mostly as a virtual patient, Birpartap Thind and colleagues map in a 2026 scoping review. They collected implemented uses of AI in undergraduate medical clinical skills teaching from January 2022 through January 2026.

From 1,130 records, 39 studies qualified, and their uses sorted into eight themes. Large language model virtual patients and simulations dominated with 19 studies, followed by AI-augmented exam and simulation assessment at six. Robots, procedural trainers, documentation tools, and tutoring systems filled the rest, with publication activity bunching in 2024 and 2025. Nearly everywhere, AI played a supporting, formative role rather than replacing teachers. Thind and colleagues note that hard evidence on long-term learning impact is still thin and call for longitudinal evaluation to keep pace with adoption.
pmc-13290828:
Patients fresh from hernia repair preferred the stiffer belly support, Kryspin Mitura and colleagues report in a randomized cross-over study from 2026. Abdominal binders are routine after ventral hernia repair despite thin evidence, and clinicians worry semi-rigid corsets will be tolerated badly in the first days.

Twenty-three patients after open sublay repair of large hernias each wore an elastic binder and a semi-rigid corset for about three hours on day two or three. Self-rated health on a visual scale matched between devices, and no quality-of-life domain scored worse with the corset; usual activities and anxiety ratings even improved. About 70% preferred the corset, and nearly all would recommend it, against two-thirds for the binder. Mitura and colleagues say rigidity is no early barrier, though long-term adherence went untested.
pmc-13290928:
Gene-guided prescribing gets a cautious welcome inside early psychosis services, A. Jameson and colleagues report in a qualitative study from 2026. Pharmacogenomic testing could sharpen antipsychotic choice, but how it would land in Early Intervention in Psychosis teams, with patients and carers, was largely unexplored.

The team interviewed 12 service users and ran focus groups with 18 staff and 3 carers across three NHS sites. Stakeholders saw early psychosis care as a complex ecosystem and knew uneven amounts about genetic testing. Overall the test felt acceptable, much like routine medicines-safety checks. Support came with conditions: offer timing matters, communication must be clear, expectations must stay realistic, and the service must be funded well enough not to crowd out other therapy. The authors frame testing as a supportive extra, never the decider.
pmc-13291028:
What daily life feels like for people who cannot stop turning the same thoughts over is the subject of a 2026 qualitative study led by Aleš Oblak. Rumination is tied to distress, self-criticism, and the course of many mental disorders, yet accounts of the lived experience itself have stayed thin.

Fifty-one people from general and clinical groups gave 107 interviews covering 79 episodes, studied through close phenomenological methods that track body, space, time, feeling, and relationships. Rumination emerged as an effort to settle doubt and make meaning after everyday understanding breaks down. Episodes carried feelings of paralysis and emptiness, and a drift away from bodily, gut-level response toward pure thought, offering clinicians a richer picture to work from.
pmc-13291128:
A farm chemical caused rare brain poisoning in a 2026 case by Luye Wang and colleagues. The chemical is chloropicrin, a soil fumigant. It is known for harming eyes, lungs, and skin. Brain effects are almost never reported.

Their patient was a 53-year-old man. He lost clear awareness after exposure. Stroke, infection, and immune causes were ruled out. Brain scans looked largely normal. Brain wave tests backed the toxic brain diagnosis. Mild lung signs could not explain his state. Support care and high-pressure oxygen helped him gain ground. He went home after three weeks of care.
pmc-13291328:
Two toothpastes for sensitive teeth are compared in a 2026 trial led by Kohei Ishii. Sharp tooth pain starts in exposed dentin tubules. One paste held potassium nitrate alone. The other added aluminum lactate to the same base.

The trial held 127 people in three blinded groups. Pain scores were taken by touch and air blasts. Both real pastes beat the dummy paste from week two. Gains showed right after first brushing too. The combined paste edged ahead at set later checks. At eight weeks it won on both test types. Adding the second agent thus helps some users more.
pmc-13291528:
Nan Xu writes a 2026 letter questioning a claimed carbon sink in the Taklamakan Desert. A recent study praised tree planting at the desert edge. Green cover and plant activity rose there. Xu urges care before crediting a human-made sink.

The carbon trend carries an error bar as large as itself. Such a signal may not differ from zero at all. Other causes of greening were not ruled out. Watering, groundwater shifts, and carbon dioxide gains could all play a part. No untreated desert comparison was made. Bare sand also trades carbon gas without life. Heat and salt chemistry drive that dead exchange. Stronger proof is needed, Xu argues.
pmc-13292328:
Jared Omundo, with co-authors, reviews a 2026 youth mental health idea: Discovery Colleges, recovery-oriented learning spaces adapted from adult Recovery Colleges for young people. Youth services face soaring demand, staff shortages, and broken referral paths. The narrative review pulled together journal articles, program descriptions, and implementation reports on these colleges and kin initiatives.

Four strands define the model: recovery-focused learning fitted to development, ways of drawing young people into participation, effects on organizations and professions, and a seat spanning education, community, and clinical sectors. Framing help as shared learning rather than treatment alone is the core shift. The authors also name friction points around safeguarding, staying true to the model, funding, and joining up sectors. They call the concept promising but still lightly evidenced.
pmc-13293128:
Khalid Abu-Zeinah leads a 2026 chart review of Lyme arthritis, the joint swelling that can follow Lyme disease spread in the body. Most patients clear with antibiotics, yet some keep inflamed joints after the germ is gone.

Records covered 77 patients with lab-confirmed joint infection treated from 2004 to 2025, including 13 children. One swollen knee was the usual picture, while children had fever more often and higher white cell counts in joint fluid. Among adults, 41 recovered fully with antibiotics, while 19 kept inflamed joints afterward. Longer antibiotic courses in that group showed no clear benefit, urging care in drug use.
pmc-13293428:
Lauren Wakefield and colleagues build, in a 2026 study, a simulation tool to judge deer farm screening for chronic wasting disease. Farmed deer live close together and move often between sites, so this fatal brain disease can spread fast once it takes hold.

Testing only a few deer early on can easily miss infection, and a clean small sample does not prove a herd is free. The tool blends herd age data, movement records, and past test results to estimate the chance that screening would catch disease at each farm. Data from 23 Texas facilities show how agencies could aim checks where risk runs highest.
pmc-13293928:
Yonghao Li and coauthors lay out a 2026 trial protocol testing Guipi Mixture, a Chinese patent medicine, for early extra heartbeats called premature ventricular contractions. The trial targets heart-spleen deficiency syndrome and pairs the mixture with metoprolol, a standard drug whose single target and long-term risks limit it. Eighteen centers will enroll 200 people in a double-blind, placebo-controlled design.

Half get the mixture plus metoprolol and half get a dummy mixture plus metoprolol over 12 weeks. The main measure is change in 24-hour extra beat counts by week 8 on ambulatory monitoring. Quality of life, sleep, syndrome scores, and safety events are also tracked.
pmc-13294328:
Mohammed Naveez Valathoor and Anand Prem Rajan review a food germ's attack tools and drug shield through a One Health lens in 2026. Salmonella Typhimurium spreads among people, farm stock, food, and the wild. It causes gut illness and deep infection across the globe. Entry genes, needle pumps, sticky hairs, and slime mats power host entry and life inside cells.

Drug shield spreads by gene swaps and gene change, across key drug groups. Multi-drug strains now blunt first cures. The review weighs toll data, trends in India and beyond, current drugs, and vaccine hopes. Shared weak spots where attack and shield meet are the prize.
pmc-13294428:
Julien Dejean-Servieres and a large team re-read wrist scans for missed ligament anchor tears in a 2026 study. Foveal tears of the triangular fibrocartilage can drive ulnar wrist pain and joint looseness, yet first reports often skip them. Two blinded specialists reviewed 149 arthro-CT scans and compared fresh reads with first reports, clinic notes, and surgery.

Fresh review found cartilage complex tears in 59% of patients. Forty-five tears had been underreported, 89% of them ulnar and most at the foveal bundle in the reported shares. Complete ulnar tears tied strongly to pain and looseness. Twelve patients had surgery, and review agreed with operative findings even where first reports were negative.
pmc-13295028:
Fei Yuan and colleagues model how a resting iron mass shapes blast furnace hearth safety in a 2026 study. The hearth holds molten iron under harsh heat, and lining erosion there can end a furnace's life. A partly floating coke mass, called the deadman, influences heat, flow, and wear inside.

A three-dimensional model linked heat flow, liquid movement, carbon transport, iron freezing, and material stress for a locally eroded hearth. Raising the deadman float height and keeping its base size and slope low encouraged a protective frozen iron layer and eased stress. A rounded base beat a flat base on layer thickness, stress, and carbon loss.
pmc-13295728:
Na Ri Seo and colleagues compare two dental implants in fake bone models in a 2026 study. How tightly an implant screws in matters most where bone is weak or support is missing. The KS 3 design was set against the established TSIII design in three standardised setups.

Models mimicked weak bone, a fresh tooth socket with reduced support, and the hollow upper jaw sinus area. The newer implant reached higher peak and final screwing forces in the weak and socket models. Sinus results shifted with leftover bone height and drilling style. The authors stress the findings show bench behaviour only, not proof of better patient outcomes.
pmc-13295828:
Betül Dikkanoğlu Demirok and colleagues group lupus patients by symptom pattern in a 2026 study. Lupus varies hugely between people, making outlook hard to judge at diagnosis. Records of 199 patients at one Turkish university clinic were clustered at diagnosis and again at the last visit.

Three groups appeared at diagnosis: joint-led, kidney and blood-led, and skin-led patterns. At the last visit, after a median 168 months of follow-up, a fourth mixed group carried the heaviest organ damage scores. Skin-led patients faced about double the odds of drifting into that poor-outlook group. Death rates did not differ between groups, so the clusters mainly warn about damage ahead.
pmc-13297228:
Marya K. Kolokolova and colleagues develop, in 2026, a quick fluorescence test for 4-chlorophenoxyacetic acid, a growth regulator and herbicide ingredient needing environmental monitoring. Their antibody-based assay runs in fifteen minutes and detects the chemical at very low levels across a wide range.

Open water samples spiked with known amounts returned near-complete recoveries. The hard part is a close chemical cousin that fools the antibody, so two fixes are offered. One runs paired tests and solves both levels with maths. The other strips the cousin out first on a capture column. Both routes worked in the study.
pmc-13298928:
Putting a primary care doctor inside the sickle cell clinic sharply raised preventive care, report Sherraine Della-Moretta and colleagues in a 2026 cohort study. At one tertiary center, 174 of 388 adults with sickle cell disease saw an internist embedded full-time in the hematology team between 2020 and 2025.

Those patients were far more likely to receive cervical cancer screening, depression screening, and tetanus vaccination, with odds ratios up to 7.97, and also scored better on sickle-specific care such as eye exams and urine protein checks. Outpatient visits rose from 2.7 to 4.2 per year while admissions drifted down without reaching significance. The authors credit coordinated, outpatient-focused management.
pmc-13301028:
Long cast as a bone vitamin, vitamin D also steers the immune system, Sandesh Shende and Jaishriram Rathored argue in a 2026 narrative review. Searching five databases, they gather mechanistic, population, and clinical work on vitamin D as an immuno-endocrine modulator in autoimmune and infectious disease.

Through its receptor, the vitamin switches on antimicrobial peptides, steadies macrophages and natural killer cells, and favors tolerogenic dendritic cells that calm adaptive responses. Trial results, however, swing widely with starting vitamin D levels, dose schedules, genes, and the disease in question. The authors call for sharper randomized trials to find who truly benefits and at what dose.
pmc-13301928:
Two pills may beat three for clearing stomach bacteria, Nikolay Georgiev and colleagues find in a 2026 meta-analysis of Helicobacter pylori treatment. Five randomized trials with 1,363 adults compared vonoprazan plus amoxicillin against the classic clarithromycin-based triple therapy. Resistance has been eroding the older regimen for years, setting up the contest.

Dual therapy cleared the infection more often, with a risk ratio of 1.17 in favor of the two-drug arm and low disagreement between trials. Stronger, steadier acid control from vonoprazan likely props up amoxicillin's killing power. The authors still want larger, well-built trials before dual therapy takes the first-line crown, and safety data remain thinner than efficacy data.
pmc-13303428:
Joseline Jiménez-Venegas leads a 2026 systematic review of bacteria that tolerate or clean up toxic metals in mining settings. Industrial activity releases metals such as cadmium, chromium, copper, iron, lead, and zinc into soil and water.

Following PRISMA guidance, the team searched Web of Science and Scopus for work from 2000 to 2025. Some bacterial families tolerated high metal levels in alkaline sites, while genera such as Acidithiobacillus worked actively in acid sites through leaching, settling, or uptake. Bacillus subtilis and Acidithiobacillus ferrooxidans both tolerated metals and removed them well. Mixed methods across studies mean standard lab tests are needed before wide field use.
pmc-13303828:
Raluca Rilla heads a 2026 commentary warning that online behavior studies are being distorted by participants who quietly use large language models. Paid survey platforms promise genuine human answers, yet audits now find frequent model use by respondents.

Three forms of contamination are set out: partial help from a model, full hand-off of the task, and spillover effects beyond single answers. Together they skew samples, bias conclusions, and spark a costly methods arms race. Countermeasures are proposed at three levels, covering researcher habits, platform responsibility, and shared community adjustment to protect study quality.
pmc-13304128:
Yufeng Liu and co-authors hunt brewing microbes that make a smoky aroma compound in a 2026 screening study. The compound, 4-ethylguaiacol, gives fermented foods and Baijiu liquor prized woody and spicy notes.

Isolates from Baijiu pit mud yielded a Bacillus coagulans strain, JN11, that produced the aroma in sorghum juice. Its key enzyme gene was copied and grown in lab bacteria for testing. The enzyme worked best at mild acidity and moderate heat, liked one starting acid far above others, and gained activity with iron while zinc blocked it. Shape modeling hints why the favored acid fits so well.
pmc-13305428:
Kabir Brar leads a 2026 scoping synthesis of ticks and their germs in Australian wildlife. Ticks bite wildlife, farm animals, and people, yet records for unique Australian fauna remain scattered across a century of reports.

Studies from 1940 to March 2024 yielded 133 usable records across three major databases. Fifty tick species were found on 160 wildlife hosts, mostly marsupials such as bandicoots, wallabies, and possums. Germ records stayed thin and mostly showed mere presence rather than proven spread. Sampling favored the east, and deeper germ screening plus unified health surveillance are called for in future work.
pmc-13305728:
Keyan Gao mapped eight years of publishing on fatty liver disease and muscle loss in a 2026 bibliometric study covering 2012 to 2025. English articles and reviews were drawn from two large databases, giving 701 distinct papers for analysis.

Output grew fast, averaging 36.6% per year in the authors' count, with China, South Korea and the United States as the main network. Topics moved from basic mechanisms toward risk prediction, lifestyle steps and combined metabolic care. Topic modelling found three rising themes, while cohort evidence linked low muscle mass or weak function to higher risk of liver disease starting or worsening.
pmc-13306028:
Leyla Kaya built a new family of carbazole ester compounds as possible diabetes drugs in a 2026 chemistry study. Starting alcohols were reacted with varied acid chlorides to give ten single esters and ten double esters for testing.

Most compounds blocked alpha-amylase only weakly but hit alpha-glucosidase more strongly and selectively in lab assays. The strongest compound reached an IC50 of 22.79 µM in the reported figure, beating the standard drug acarbose on that measure. Computer docking explored how the molecules fit the target enzyme, supporting further work on this selective group.
pmc-13306528:
Abigail Chari mapped uneven child undernutrition across Ethiopia in a 2026 spatial study. Survey data from the 2019 national demographic and health round were joined to local boundaries and analysed at village cluster level.

Children in northern and north-eastern clusters faced higher undernutrition than elsewhere on the thematic maps. Dryness, rainfall, skilled health worker supply, location and mothers' schooling each shaped rates in the reported model. Neighbouring clusters also influenced each other, with clear spillover for stunting, wasting and overall undernutrition, so the authors urge targeted resources for underserved areas. The team calls for joint action on food, care and school for young girls and boys.
pmc-13308728:
Rano K Sinuraya and co-authors review in 2026 fair access blocks for vaccines and screening in low and middle income lands, where gains in cover have not reached all groups alike. Their search drew on PubMed and Scopus, with screening proof drawn mostly from cervical and HPV linked programmes.

Blocks stacked at home, town, clinic, and state levels, from poverty and travel cost to stigma and thin staffing in clinics. Vaccine work faced cold chain faults and drive based delivery, while screening faced repeat trips and weak follow up chains. Rural folk, poor homes, women, migrants, and disabled people bore the brunt. Strong front line care and fair data use anchor the fix list.
pmc-13308828:
Héléna Vassilieff and co-authors mine in 2026 plant genomes for fossil virus bits that trace the deep past of the Caulimoviridae, the sole double strand DNA virus family of plants. They scanned 93 genomes across all main land plant groups and found 47,135 such bits in 75 of the genomes.

The bits fell into 71 groups, and 35 of those groups had never been named before this scan. One old branch sat only in a Gondwanan conifer family, which hints at very deep roots for the clan. Family trees of virus and host lined up well, which backs shared splitting as the main driver of spread over vast time.
pmc-13310828:
Isabella Monteiro Carvalho led a 2026 study comparing a urine infecting germ found in patients and in a polluted bay in Brazil. Staphylococcus saprophyticus causes many urine infections, yet its life outside clinics is little known. The team asked if bay strains carry the same risky traits as clinic strains.

Forty strains were tested, split evenly between clinic and bay sources. Gene patterns and harm traits looked alike across sources. Bay strains resisted many drugs, formed biofilms, and harmed test larvae much like clinic strains. A virus that attacks germs killed many strains and broke biofilms. Watch of dirty coastal water is warranted.
pmc-13310928:
Janka Pecuchová and colleagues release a dataset of student software models with smart feedback in a 2026 paper. Students in a software course built UML diagrams, and a large language model gave written feedback in Slovak. The set lets scholars test automated grading in a non English, technical class.

Files hold 112 student records, 448 feedback notes, and 700 raw XML reports from a design tool. Each record links the model, feedback, scores, grades, student ratings of helpfulness, and human ratings. Prompt drafts and scoring rules are shared for repeat tests. Work in the 2024 to 2025 school year at a university in Nitra grounds the set.
pmc-13311028:
Xing Lin and co-authors build a physics simulation for magnetic touch sensors in a 2026 study. Touch feedback guides fine robot assembly when sight is blocked, and magnetic sensors are fast and compact. A lack of true to life simulation blocks training of robot policies, so a joint frame was built.

Soft material bending is modeled with a particle method at fine scale on modest hardware. A masked learning model compresses touch point clouds by over 88 percent of size while keeping shape error tiny. A mapping model then projects real signals into the simulated space. Mapped forms kept contact shape and aligned domains well for later real use.
pmc-13311128:
Alysson Fellipe Costa Telles led a 2026 gene study on long COVID in Brazilian health workers. Long COVID has many causes, and gene variants in a virus entry helper gene may shape risk. Two variants were tested against illness reports in a self report survey with mouth cell gene checks.

Workers totaled 363 in number from mixed clinic roles. For long COVID overall, only clinical traits such as symptom load and severity mattered. For brain fog, the top named symptom, women and young adults were most at risk, and one variant showed a link in select models. The other variant showed no link. Case control work must clarify the fog link.
pmc-13311328:
Simon Østergaard and colleagues, in 2026, share a case where an invasive Ureaplasma infection copied the look of returning lymphoma. The germ usually lives quietly in the urinary tract but can turn invasive when immunity is weak.

The patient had finished chemoimmunotherapy for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and stayed in remission. A growing, tissue-eating sore on the scrotum and belly wall looked like cancer spread, yet standard cultures found nothing. Gene-based microbe scanning named Ureaplasma urealyticum as the cause. Two antibiotics given over a long course cleared the infection fully. Early gene testing could spare such patients needless cancer workups.
pmc-13311628:
Anhong Li and co-authors set out a 2026 trial protocol to find the right dose of oliceridine, a newer opioid, for keeping patients still and cough-free during bronchoscopy under remimazolam sedation.

The single-center trial will enroll adults aged 18 to 65 having painless flexible bronchoscopy. Each patient gets oliceridine first, then a set dose of remimazolam. The starting oliceridine dose is 40 micrograms per kilogram, moved up or down in steps based on the prior patient's response, with men and women tracked apart. Middle and high effective doses will be estimated for each sex, alongside safety events.
pmc-13311928:
Jie Qiao, Qing Kou, and Ji Qiu present a 2026 study pairing engineered macrophages with a CD47-blocking antibody against ovarian cancer. The macrophages carry a receptor that homes to HER2 on tumor cells.

Cell tests showed the engineered macrophages found and killed HER2-positive ovarian cancer cells. Adding the CD47 antibody boosted their eating of tumor cells, pushed them toward an inflammatory mode, and raised their signal output. In mice bearing human tumors, the pair shrank tumor burden more than single treatments. Blocking the don't-eat-me signal, it seems, frees the engineered cells to work harder.
pmc-13312528:
Jessica T. Jacobs and Jacob C. Nordman present a 2026 hypothesis-driven review linking early life stress to lifelong aggression through changes in synapse structure. Stress early in life is a major risk factor for reactive aggression that can outlast the original hardship by decades. The machinery that locks the change into the brain was poorly defined.

The authors gather clinical, postmortem, imaging, and animal evidence around NMDA receptor-dependent structural plasticity in aggression circuits, centered on the pathway from the medial amygdala to the ventromedial hypothalamus. Animal work suggests stress adds dendritic spines and excitatory synapses there, placed where they drive firing hardest, which would raise circuit excitability and lower the bar for aggressive outbursts. The review closes by weighing two approved NMDA blockers, ketamine and memantine, as candidate tools against this rewiring.
pmc-13312828:
Hao Liu and colleagues report, in a 2026 study, the first complete mitochondrial genome of the fly Helina trivittata. Its genus is one of the largest in the house fly family, with 683 known species. Yet mitochondrial sequences existed for only two of them, leaving the group's family tree resting on thin genetic evidence.

The genome runs 18,959 base pairs and holds the standard set of 37 mitochondrial genes, with adenine and thymine making up 82.01 percent of its letters. Family tree analysis supported the subfamily Phaoniinae as a single natural group. It placed Helina as the closest relative of the genus Phaonia, a relationship once blurred when Helina was treated as a mere synonym of Phaonia. Specimens came from Inner Mongolia, China. The authors offer the sequence as a reference for future evolutionary and classification work on the family.
pmc-13312928:
Shamsun Nahar and colleagues report a 2026 mouse study showing how two common genetic changes team up to make endometrial cancer aggressive. Endometrioid endometrial cancer is usually caught early with a good outlook, but late-stage disease kills most patients. Tumors carrying both PTEN loss and CTNNB1 mutation are known to fare worst without anyone knowing exactly why.

The team engineered mice whose uteruses lacked Pten, carried a stabilized Ctnnb1, or both. Double-mutant mice died sooner than single mutants and developed invasive, metastatic cancer, with muscle-wall invasion already present at four weeks of age. Gene profiling showed WNT, PI3K/AKT, Hedgehog, and epithelial-mesenchymal transition programs switched on together, and tissue staining confirmed the transition's hallmarks. The authors present the pair as a synergistic engine of early invasion and spread.
pmc-13315528:
NGA Mulyantini S․S․ and colleagues fed broiler chickens in 2026 with diets where soybean meal was partly swapped for cricket nymph meal and moringa leaf meal. Two hundred forty day-old broilers were split into four diets, with the swap replacing 10, 20, or 30 percent of the soybean share using a three-to-one blend.

Birds on the 10 and 20 percent swaps gained more weight than controls, while the 30 percent group grew less despite eating more. Carcass weight and thigh yield also rose at the two lower swaps. Protein and organic matter digestibility fell at higher swap levels, marking a practical limit for the blend.
pmc-13316228:
Auguste Vadisiute and colleagues deleted the release gene Snap25 in 2026 in selected mouse brain cells to study how long synaptic silence reshapes glial support cells in aging. Blocking transmitter release in layer 5 cortex cells and dentate granule cells let them watch glial change across connected regions and the spinal cord.

Silenced cortex zones showed strong astrocyte reactivity and more microglia, while downstream targets such as the superior colliculus and CA3 showed marked microglial remodeling and synaptic change, and CA1 changed mildly. In the spinal cord microglia fell while astrocytes rose. Aging amplified the glial responses.
pmc-13316628:
Ana Costa-Ribeiro and colleagues compared, in a 2026 food safety study, fast ways to find Vibrio parahaemolyticus, a germ that causes illness from raw or undercooked seafood, in mussels. Since shellfish spoil fast, same-day answers carry real value for sellers and inspectors.

Three digital PCR machines were set against standard gene tests and a rapid loop method, all after the enrichment steps of the official standard. After the first enrichment, gene testing could find about 15 germ units per 25 grams, while digital systems read negative despite faint signals; a second enrichment improved all methods. Among growth plates, one brand proved most specific. Sample preparation, the authors stress, decides success more than machine sensitivity alone.
pmc-13317828:
Tingting Hu and colleagues follow, in a 2026 community cohort study, whether thyroid hormone levels predict early muscle-loss obesity in people whose thyroid tests sit in the normal range. The condition pairs shrinking muscle with deep belly fat, a risky blend in aging adults.

A total of 1,280 residents over forty were recruited in 2013 to 2014 and rechecked about two years later, with MRI belly fat and body composition measures. Those starting in the highest third of free T3 hormone levels faced notably higher risk of the combined condition, with a risk ratio of 1.82 against the lowest third in the adjusted model. Rising hormone levels over time also tracked with new cases. Normal range, they note, does not mean no effect.
pmc-13318928:
Shujing Hu and co-authors report a 2026 study of two blood indices in older adults with depression, with or without obstructive sleep apnoea. One index blends inflammation, triglycerides, and glucose. The other counts immune cells from routine blood tests. Both are cheap and quick to calculate.

The sample held 52 patients with both conditions and 108 with depression alone. The combined group had higher body mass and more men. Their glucose, triglycerides, and inflammation markers all ran higher. Immune cell ratios and the inflammation index were also raised. Modelling linked male sex and higher values on both indices to having sleep apnoea. The authors propose the pair as helpful flags in depressed older patients.
pmc-13319028:
Shijiao Cao presents a 2026 study of how a university's spread of disciplines relates to PhD student research output. The sample covers 1,418 accounting dissertations sent to Chinese universities between 1999 and 2022. Cao builds a new measure of university-level disciplinary diversity. Poisson models control for student, supervisor, and institution factors.

A simple model showed a negative overall link between diversity and productivity. Closer analysis showed an upside-down U shape instead. Moderate diversity helped output, and richer universities gained from more of it. Harm clustered where fields were lopsided or sprawled into unrelated areas. Students at diverse universities did more cross-discipline work with greater impact. The author argues for keeping healthy diversity without chasing breadth for its own sake.
pmc-13320028:
Dunja Scheepmaker and co-authors compare ways to prepare cartilage for joint repair in a 2026 lab study. Chopped own cartilage offers a cheap one step fix for worn joint patches, but chopping may kill cells and cut new tissue growth. Hand chopping, scope guided chopping, freed cell clusters, and freed lone cells were grown side by side for four weeks.

At day 28 lone cells and cell clusters stayed alive at rates above nine in ten in the counts reported, while scope chopped bits lived least well of all. Freed cells also laid down more of the springy filler that gives cartilage its bounce, while chopped bits lost ground. Loose bits from real surgery varied wildly in weight and cell content, which flags quality risks.
pmc-13320228:
Pritpal Singh and co-authors present a hands on workflow for mapping proteins in tissue in a 2026 methods article. Protein maps that keep place intact show where each protein sits in cells and tissue, which can reveal new disease signs. Full start to finish workflows that stay open, repeatable, and easy to steer have been scarce, so a boxed step pipeline was built.

Steps cover cell outlining, grouping of like cells with optional batch fixes, checks of groups on the image, and clear displays of cell types. A form based screen lets users run or tune each step with a click. Trials on healthy tonsil and bowel cancer tissue, stained for dozens of proteins at once, showed the flow in action.
pmc-13321028:
R Ibusuki and colleagues examine gene faults that blunt a lung cancer drug in a 2026 study. Patients had advanced lung adenocarcinoma with EGFR faults and received first line osimertinib. Faults in TP53 often go with worse outcomes, but the effect of one class, gain-of-function faults, on drug resistance was unknown.

Gene profiling of pre-treatment tumours from 140 patients found TP53 faults in 45.7 percent overall, with gain-of-function faults in 13.6 percent of patients in the cohort. Time without disease growth was far shorter with gain-of-function faults, at a median of 12.0 months against 31.4 months for those without TP53 faults in the study. Gene activity scans pointed to raised ephrin signalling in that group.
pmc-13322928:
Jie Yang and co-authors review how liver immune cells talk to each other in autoimmune hepatitis, in a 2026 article on disease origins and drug discovery. This chronic liver disease is rising in frequency, and its tangled causes make treatment hard.

Focus falls on faulty activation in dendritic cells, macrophages and T and B cells, plus signal exchange among liver cells, bile duct cells and immune cells. Viewing the disease as a regulatory network, rather than a single faulty molecule, opens new drug targets. The authors survey drugs now in use, compounds in development and candidate agents, weigh the limits of current care, and judge how far network-based targets might carry future treatment.
pmc-13323028:
Hanan M Al Kadri leads a review of inducing labour when a baby is suspected to be very large, published in 2026. Macrosomia, set at a birth weight of 4,000 grams or more, raises risks such as caesarean birth, shoulder dystocia and nerve injury, and guidance on timing remains unsettled.

Searching four databases to December 2023, the team pooled 13 studies with 4,442 women, mixing trials and observational work. Induction did not change caesarean rates against waiting, in a pooled estimate centred near no difference. Further outcomes covered shoulder dystocia, low Apgar scores and brachial plexus palsy, split by study design. The authors call for clearer shared decision-making until stronger guidance exists.
pmc-13325628:
Can Zhang and colleagues feed yeast nucleotides to weaned kittens to test growth and immune effects in a 2026 animal study. Young cats face stress at weaning, and nucleotides support gut and immune tissue.

Sixteen four-month-old kittens were split into plain feed and feed with 0.03 percent yeast nucleotides for 42 days. The supplemented group showed higher blood protein, albumin, and creatinine readings. Digestion of dry matter, organic matter, and protein all improved over controls. Growth hormone, IGF-1, and antibody levels for IgG, IgA, and IgM rose sharply. Gut microbe balance shifted too, with Sellimonas and Acutalibacter gaining ground. The additive looks useful for kitten diets.
pmc-13326028:
Yu Luo and colleagues use vesicles from dental pulp stem cells against oral cancer in a 2026 study. Oral squamous cell carcinoma kills about half of patients within five years and often returns after treatment.

Vesicles harvested from inside the stem cells slowed tumor growth in dishes and in animals. Treated cancer cells divided less, invaded less, and died more. The vesicles carried the tumor suppressor PTEN into cancer cells, damping the PI3K, AKT, and mTOR growth pathway. Pairing them with the autophagy blocker 3-methyladenine deepened the effect and stressed mitochondria. The authors pitch the vesicles as a safe, scalable option worth clinical study.
pmc-13326128:
Lisa-Maria Rosenthal and colleagues analyze the heart transplant waitlist for children in Germany in a 2026 registry study. Most waitlist data come from North America, leaving European outcomes less clear.

The registry held 780 candidates listed between 2006 and 2020. Transplants reached 56.5 percent of children, while 17.9 percent died waiting and 7.8 percent recovered enough to leave the list. Mean waiting time was 197 days, longest for ages 1 to 10. Death risk ran highest in children under 2 with diagnoses other than dilated cardiomyopathy. Recovery clustered in infants under 1 year. Wider use of ABO-mismatched grafts is proposed.
pmc-13328328:
Mengdie Hu and co-authors define a gut frailty pattern in chronic heart failure in a 2026 study. Among 270 patients, gut frailty meant a symptom rating score of at least 3, and the team hunted clinical drivers plus microbe signatures in a balanced subgroup of sixty. Diet stood out sharply in the modeling.

A meat-rich diet independently raised gut frailty odds, with an odds ratio of 3.995 in the adjusted model, while vegetarian adherence lowered them, at 0.148 in the same model. Frail guts held far fewer microbe types, lost short-chain fatty acid producers such as Faecalibacterium, and gained potential troublemakers, with microbe chemistry shifting toward stress handling. Food and microbe care may ease this hidden burden.
pmc-13329128:
Richard W. Willy and co-authors validate a running watch with an accelerometer as a tool for estimating the impact forces runners absorb, without a laboratory treadmill. Their 2026 cross-sectional study first tests eighteen trained runners on an instrumented treadmill across a range of speeds, comparing watch estimates against the treadmill's force measurements.

The published estimation equation systematically underestimated peak vertical ground reaction force by about a tenth. A corrected equation derived from that data was then tested in ten fresh runners. The corrected version showed excellent agreement with the treadmill, with trivial bias and errors of only a few percent. Estimates of cumulative weighted damage per kilometre, a measure relevant to bone stress injury, were likewise accurate. The authors provide an online calculator and suggest the methods could monitor training load in runners at risk of bone stress injuries.
pmc-13329328:
Mokunfayo O Fajemisin and colleagues present a 2026 protocol for a trial of a video aid for end-of-life talks after injury. Each year many older adults enter hospital after trauma, yet talks about life-sustaining care and code status often fall short. The single-centre randomised trial, called ADVISE, will test a video conversation aid against usual care.

Eligible patients are trauma patients aged 65 or older admitted after injury, with some groups excluded, such as people already under do-not-resuscitate orders. The main outcome is change in code status. Other outcomes cover views of resuscitation, knowledge, conflict over choices, and days free of hospital or intensive care. The pilot aims to estimate benefit and guide wider use.
pmc-13329728:
P. Sreejindeth and T. Padmavathy propose Eco-FinOps, a system for cutting cloud cost and energy waste, in a 2026 article. Dashboards need constant watching, while deep learning tools need costly graphics chips and hide their logic. The proposed system runs on standard processors and aims to act on its own with clear reasons.

It links live usage data, cause-mapping methods, and effect checks to split real demand swings from waste. A prime target is idle servers that use little processor power yet hold much memory. Language tools then draft fix scripts that people can audit. On five fault tests from Alibaba cluster data, scores for precision and recall were high in the reported results. Cause checks cut false alarms sharply.
pmc-13330528:
Yuan Xu and colleagues compare how surgical teachers and trainees rate core skills in China in a 2026 study. Surveys ran in March 2025 across three training bases in Guizhou, covering 100 skill items in five fields. In total, 42 faculty and 68 residents gave valid replies, rating how vital each item seemed.

Agreement ran high for general surgery and neurosurgery items in the reported results. Half of the orthopaedic items split the groups, with trainees rating them higher. On life monitoring and resuscitation items, faculty gave top scores while trainees scored lower. Overall agreement was weak. Both groups backed stronger training in records and patient talk. Skill lists need joint review, the authors argue.
pmc-13331428:
Amir Molaie and Jeffrey L. Saver write a 2026 commentary on biomarker use in stroke clot removal choices. They aim to fix a growing mix-up between two biomarker kinds in patients with large vessel block and large damaged cores. One kind forecasts outcome whatever the treatment. The other kind changes how much a treatment helps.

Core volume acts as the first kind: bigger cores mean worse outlook in all groups, the authors argue. Penumbra measures and mismatch ratios act as the second kind, marking who gains from removal. Graphs in the piece show the split in plain form. Treating a forecast marker as a selection marker can mislead trial reading and bedside calls, they warn.
pmc-13333528:
Xiangjian Fang and co-authors present a trick in 2026 for extracting motion from still pictures of tumors: RNA velocity calculated from spatial transcriptomics. Standard velocity needs counts of fresh and mature RNA that spatial platforms do not provide, and without them researchers can map where melanoma cells sit but not where they are heading.

The framework substitutes geography for chemistry. It treats nuclear transcripts as the fresh, unspliced pool and cytoplasmic ones as the mature pool, then feeds the pair into the scVelo dynamical model. Applied to melanoma tissue maps, it reconstructed tumor cell progression paths and the differentiation routes of T cells, and it flagged cluster-specific dynamic genes. Those genes tied to patient prognosis and networked into protein clusters rich in immune pathways. The authors offer the method as a bridge between spatial biology and transcriptional dynamics, usable on the spatial datasets laboratories already hold.
pmc-13333628:
A French version of the Sport Psychological Safety Inventory gets its validation in a 2026 study by Véronique Boudreault and co-authors. Psychological safety affects athlete wellbeing and lasting performance, but measurement tools have mostly existed in English.

The team surveyed 210 French-speaking elite youth athletes aged 14 to 25 across many sports in 2024. Factor analysis confirmed the original three-part structure: low self-stigma, mental health literacy, and a mentally healthy environment. Scores lined up with wellbeing and coach relationship quality in expected directions, and ran opposite to reports of interpersonal violence in sport. Boys and girls answered the scale in comparable ways. The validated French tool lets researchers and sport bodies measure psychological safety in francophone settings.
pmc-13334228:
Saket Shrotri and Vinita Gowda studied flower color morphs of a nocturnal ginger, Curcuma caulina, from India's Western Ghats in a 2026 field study. Color variants within a species may differ in more than looks, and the pair asked whether nectar, pollinator visits, and breeding compatibility split along morph lines.

Three dominant morphs were compared for nectar energy, hawkmoth visitation, cross-compatibility, and fruit and seed output. The common green-red morph offers low-energy nectar, draws few visits, and cannot self-pollinate, yet achieves the highest female reproductive success. The rare red-white morph shows the opposite pattern on every trait but reproduces less. Path analysis found nectar, visitation, compatibility, and abundance jointly explaining reproductive success, overturning any simple story that showier rewards win.
pmc-13334428:
Fawzia Omer Alubthane reviewed in full generative AI's effects on university students' higher-order thinking in a 2026 article, asking whether these tools amplify minds or substitute for them. The review used PRISMA 2020 guidance.

Eighty-nine peer-reviewed articles from 2024 to 2026, drawn from Web of Science and Scopus, were summed up in words. Positive cognitive outcomes showed in 40.4 percent of studies, and 23.6 percent found mixed or conditional effects. ChatGPT dominated the work looked at, and over half the studies used no defined teaching strategy. Over-reliance was the leading risk, named in 33.7 percent of studies, ahead of lost analysis autonomy and cognitive offloading. Alubthane concludes AI boosts thinking under guided teaching and replaces it under unguided use.
pmc-13336228:
Iven Giovanna Trindade Lino and co-authors told of training workshops that introduced telenursing for chronic disease follow-up in Brazilian primary care in a 2026 experience report. Remote nursing follow-up for hypertension and diabetes grew during the pandemic, but teams needed preparation.

The work ran from May to July 2021: the team surveyed how care was then delivered, discussed what telenursing could add, built tools, and tested the technology. Sixteen nurses joined. They saw telenursing's potential while flagging scarce time, staff, and infrastructure as limits. Jointly they produced a patient suitability and risk form, a visit script, and a care plan. The report concludes workshops work as training, and that ongoing training underpins practice changes of this kind.
pmc-13336828:
Wenxuan Zheng leads a 2026 team turning the plant compound quercetin into a stroke nanomedicine. After a blocked brain vessel reopens, power units in neurons leak harmful oxygen species and their own DNA, sparking inflammation. Quercetin naturally sticks to the outer membrane of those power units, a trait the team used as a homing device.

Joined with iron, quercetin self-builds into tiny particles with two enzyme-like actions that clear harmful oxygen species in sequence. In a rodent stroke model the particles crossed the damaged blood-brain barrier and reached neuron power units. They steadied the units, stopped DNA leakage, calmed immune activation, and improved recovery. Natural products may hide targeting skills worth building into medicines.
pmc-13337428:
Thales M. H. Dourado and co-authors test whether a hormone receptor starts alcohol's early damage to heart and kidney in a 2026 rat study. Ethanol sparks oxidative stress through NADPH oxidase, and mineralocorticoid receptors mediate some of alcohol's pro-oxidant effects. Male rats drank ethanol for five weeks, with or without a receptor blocker.

Blocking the receptor stopped rises in fat oxidation damage and superoxide in the heart ventricle and kidney cortex. It also prevented a hydrogen peroxide rise seen only in kidney tissue and erased ethanol-driven increases in thromboxane and prostaglandin signals. The findings place this receptor at the opening steps of alcohol-related cardiorenal injury, nominating it as an early intervention point.
pmc-13337628:
Corinne M Hohl leads a large 2026 team announcing the Canadian Emergency Department Research Network, built to fix slow, split-up emergency research. Emergency doctors treat unsorted, fast-changing cases, often with thin evidence, and paperwork barriers have blocked timely national data collection, above all in crises. The network grows out of a prior COVID-19 collaboration.

Data sharing and membership deals, privacy approvals, and shared governance are already in place. A standard, privacy-approved platform will gather shared-format data from member departments, including rural and remote sites, with cleaning, checks, and linkage to official records. Study committees set each project's outcomes and methods. The same data can serve quality improvement and surveillance, speeding evidence when the next crisis hits.
pmc-13339028:
Carsten Strobel and a large team improve graphene hot-electron transistors for fast electronics in a 2026 study. An atom-thin graphene base promises very fast switching, but weak injection limited earlier devices. Tuning the emitter and base stack was the lever used here.

A silica and graphene stack reached a record current gain of 42 in the reported measurements. A molybdenum disulfide and graphene stack pushed output near 2000 A per square centimeter as reported, also a record. Cutoff speeds approached 1 GHz even before full tuning. Results narrow the terahertz gap from the electronics side, pointing toward faster nano devices.
pmc-13339228:
Baraa J. Abdelghne and an undergraduate team test plant extracts on worm movement in a 2026 study. Plants make chemicals that affect animal nerves to deter feeding, yet common products are rarely tested this way. Cannabis, ginger, pepper tree, saffron, and tobacco extracts faced Caenorhabditis elegans worms.

Worms placed at plate centers chose between extract and solvent zones. Only tobacco strongly repelled the worms in the reported tests, while the other extracts showed no clear effect. The work came from a teaching laboratory course, giving students research training. Results single out tobacco chemistry for deeper study of nerve and behavior effects.
pmc-13339828:
Mizuhiro Kominato and colleagues catch a fleeting water dimer ion form in gas in a 2026 spectroscopy study. The hemibonded form of two water molecules sharing charge had been seen only inside helium droplets before. Ultraviolet and visible spectra of small water cluster ions were recorded.

A charge resonance band matching the hemibonded form appeared for the two-water ion as reported. Three-water clusters were measured alongside for contrast. Electronic spectra thus become a sensitive test for this elusive structure. Confirming it in plain gas sharpens models of radiation damage in water, where such ions appear first.
pmc-13340028:
Giovanni Milani and colleagues test two adhesion genes in a toxin-producing E. coli strain from raw milk cheese in a 2026 study. Some dangerous strains lack the classic attachment locus yet still infect people. Their alternative island, LAA, carries hes and sisA genes.

Mutants missing toxin genes, the hes-sisA pair, or both were built by recombineering. Wax moth larvae measured virulence, while cell and film tests measured sticking and biofilm. Deleting hes-sisA lowered larval death, biofilm, and attachment to intestinal cells clearly as reported. The pair likely helps colonization and persistence, marking a target for control.
pmc-13341428:
Other illnesses weigh heavily on life quality in Ménière's disease, in a 2026 cross-sectional study by Zhongbao Zhang and colleagues. The single-center analysis covered 473 patients, collecting their conditions alongside anxiety, depression, and disease-specific quality of life scores.

Hypertension appeared in 49.0% of patients, sleep disorders in 36.6%, and diabetes in 28.8%, while clear anxiety and depression symptoms showed in over half. Average quality of life score was 43.62 on the disease questionnaire. Hypertension correlated most strongly with worse quality of life at r = −0.521. Treating the ear condition alone, the authors imply, misses much of the burden.
pmc-13341528:
Food knowledge and eating confidence cluster together in liver cancer patients, in a 2026 survey by Ziang Liu and colleagues. The cross-sectional study recruited 456 patients from three tertiary hospitals between April and October 2025, using questionnaires on nutrition literacy, diet self-efficacy, fatigue, and social support.

Latent profile analysis found two groups: a low literacy, low confidence profile covering 47.37% of patients, and a high-high profile covering 52.63%. Attempts to split profiles by gender failed because the subgroups grew too small for stable solutions. Nearly half of patients thus face treatment with weak nutrition skills, a clear target for dietitian support.
pmc-13341928:
Knee loads while walking shift with age, sex, and activity, in a 2026 cross-sectional study by Hanna Zadoń and colleagues. Motion and force data fed a musculoskeletal model that computed internal knee reaction forces across the gait cycle, compared across age bands and activity levels.

Inactive people showed higher forces mid-stance, significantly in young women and in both sexes aged 46 to 65. Men exceeded women only in some age groups and early stance. Older walkers shifted peak loading earlier in foot contact, suggesting compensatory strategy changes. Joint loading analyses that ignore who is walking, the authors argue, miss where the stress actually lands.
pmc-13343128:
Madhuri Tribhuvan and Shashikant N Phatke write a 2026 letter commenting on a broiler chicken study that compared several zinc sources for uptake and growth. The original work used a depletion-repletion model plus a floor-pen trial, and the letter writers praise that design while raising points that could sharpen its reading.

Bone zinc, they note, shows exposure but not whether bones actually grow stronger, since no strength or structure tests were done. Mixed diets also strayed from target zinc levels, which could skew uptake rankings, and added phytase in all feeds may have freed extra zinc on its own. Broader farm validation, they argue, would firm up claims for organic zinc products.
pmc-13343228:
Chris Packer and co-authors profile the hydrosol of Utah juniper in a 2026 lab study, testing its chemistry and biological effects. The scented water left from juniper processing had barely been characterized, so the team measured its phenolic makeup and ran antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antibacterial assays in vitro.

Chromatography found naringenin as the only measurable flavonoid, a sparse profile typical of hydrosols. The liquid showed antioxidant activity and mildly slowed both COX-1 and COX-2 enzymes, with stronger effects at higher doses, yet produced no antibacterial zones under the method used. The authors call for cell and safety models to judge whether the hydrosol holds real bioactive promise.
pmc-13343728:
Steve Kevin Njouonkep Sime and co-authors examine whether metabolic syndrome changes how older adults move between frailty states, in both directions. Frailty is dynamic, yet most research treats metabolic risk as a one-way driver. Their 2026 study uses the Whitehall II cohort of British civil servants, with 4,750 participants followed for just under seven years on average.

At baseline most participants were robust, about a third pre-frail, and 36.9 percent had metabolic syndrome. Recovery transitions were commoner than deteriorations at every stage. Overall, metabolic syndrome was not significantly associated with moving between states. One component stood out: abdominal obesity raised the hazard of slipping from robust to early pre-frailty by twenty-seven percent. The authors conclude the syndrome as a whole matters less than specific components, and that frailty trajectories can improve as well as worsen.
pmc-13343928:
Luisa Nardini and co-authors show that gut bacteria can blunt insecticide power in malaria mosquitoes, in a 2026 study. Antibiotic feeding stripped the gut flora of susceptible Anopheles strains, yet the treated mosquitoes oddly survived the insecticide deltamethrin far better, with tolerance rising over 50 percent.

Blocking the mosquitoes' P450 detox enzymes erased the effect, tying tolerance to that system. Antibiotics cleared most gut tenants but let one Aeromonas type bloom, and seeding that microbe alone into untreated mosquitoes copied the tolerance. In Africa, where self-medication with antibiotics is common, the authors warn, gut disruption could quietly erode bed net and spraying programs built on insecticides.
pmc-13347328:
Gökhan Akarca and co-authors test magnetic fields on bread yeast, in a food study from 2026. Cultures of Saccharomyces cerevisiae were exposed at 180, 240. 300 microtesla strengths, then used for dough and bread that were checked for acidity, water activity, texture, rising, pore size, and acid content.

The middle strength stood out, with treated yeast giving bread at a pH value of 4.35 and the highest levels of several organic acids in the reported measures. Doughs from treated cultures felt softer while finished breads rose more and held larger pores, and sourdough cultures shifted more than commercial ones. The authors propose field treatment as a cheap way to lift bread quality.
pmc-13349928:
Zhen Zhang and colleagues reported a fatal case in 2026 of severe skin destruction, toxic epidermal necrolysis, after treatment with a new PD-1 blocking drug, pucotenlimab. Their patient, a man aged 67 with stage IIIB lung adenocarcinoma, had finished chest radiotherapy before immunotherapy.

Seven days after a single dose, scattered red spots spread fast until about 80 percent of his skin surface detached. Scores used at readmission predicted a death risk above 90 percent, and immune testing showed sharply lowered PD-1 on T cells with raised interleukin-6. Steroids, immunoglobulin, and intensive support did not save him. The case alerts clinicians to a rare but deadly reaction.
pmc-13351128:
Yestle Kim and colleagues traced how fatty liver disease progresses to end-stage liver disease in United States adults in a 2026 records and claims study. Among 49,983 patients with the inflamed form of the disease, a third already had advanced liver damage at first record.

Of those without it, 15.9 percent progressed, with a median of just 10.6 months to the first severe event, most often decompensated cirrhosis. Use of non-invasive tests around diagnosis, predictors of decline, hospital use, and costs were all mapped. Such speed of progression argues for finding and treating these patients far earlier than current practice manages.
pmc-13352628:
S. Zappalà and colleagues study mixing at the molybdenum and silica interface during graphene growth in 2026. Pairing graphene with metal layers suits electronics and optics, but heat during growth can blur the boundary. Graphene was grown by vapour deposition on a flat 35 nm molybdenum film and on tiny molybdenum patterns, both over a 1.6 micrometre silica layer.

On flat film, growth formed molybdenum-silicon and molybdenum-carbon phases and about 15 graphene layers. Patterned metal balled up instead, yielding only about 5 layers. Mixing ran one way on flat film but many ways in small patterns, losing carbon and gaining silicon. Below a critical size, evenness collapses, so layout size must enter device design.
pmc-13354028:
Ayubu E Mashambo leads a 2026 case report on severe malnutrition in a young adult with tangled causes. A 24-year-old woman had failed to gain weight for over 10 years despite adequate intake, with worsening leg weakness, body-wide swelling, delayed puberty, and no periods. Repeated hospital stays and feeding plans failed to reverse her decline.

Deep checks found Helicobacter pylori gastritis with micronutrient gaps, plus a hidden psoas abscess driving strong inflammation. Eradication therapy, surgical drainage, antibiotics, and structured feeding followed. She then gained weight steadily, swelling cleared, mobility returned, and periods began. The case shows hidden infection can quietly anchor severe malnutrition.
pmc-13355528:
Simonetta Genovesi and co-authors stage a 2026 pro-and-con debate on stroke prevention for dialysis patients with atrial fibrillation, an irregular heartbeat that raises stroke risk. These patients were left out of the big drug trials, so whether blood thinners help or harm them is unclear. One side favors thinners or a heart closure procedure for carefully chosen patients.

The other side notes that many studies show no clear stroke gain from thinners but clearly more major bleeding, plus possible harm to blood vessels. Both sides agree that choices must be personal, made with the patient, and that large, well-powered trials comparing thinners, closure, and no treatment are badly needed.
pmc-13356728:
Akin A Adio and co-authors studied in 2026 how post-traumatic stress disorder shapes recovery after arthroscopic rotator cuff repair. PTSD can alter pain sensing and raise substance risks, yet its effect after this common shoulder surgery was unclear. Using a large health network, they matched 2,262 patients with PTSD to the same number without it on health and demographic traits.

At ninety days, medical complications and opioid prescription counts did not differ. But patients with PTSD visited emergency departments more, at about 17 versus 11 percent, and had more sleep disorders. By two years, cannabis use disorder was nearly three times as common. The authors stress tending to mental health factors in recovery.
pmc-13356928:
Sweta Shrivastava and co-authors present a 2026 case series of six women treated for ectopic pregnancy at a hospital in western India. An ectopic pregnancy grows outside the womb and can burst, causing life-threatening bleeding. The series spanned three burst tube pregnancies, one intact tube pregnancy, one pregnancy in a horn of the womb, and one early tube miscarriage.

One unstable patient needed open surgery, while the other five had keyhole surgery guided by symptoms, blood tests, and ultrasound. Five recovered smoothly; one developed kidney injury after surgery but recovered with intensive team care. The authors stress early diagnosis, tailored surgery, and close watch after the operation.
pmc-13358428:
Isobel set out a perspective in 2026 on what trauma and violence informed research should mean for mental health nursing studies and service evaluations. Guides for trauma informed research are growing, and they stress safety, trust, choice, teamwork, and empowerment when working with people likely to have lived through trauma. Isobel argues the lens must widen to violence in its structural form, the slow harm done by systems that disadvantage people.

Being trauma and violence informed, in this account, means applying care principles in every contact with participants and data. Also weighing how a study's design, measures, and findings can compound harm. Research holds power over whose knowledge counts, and evaluations can repeat the very inequities they study. The piece calls for steady reflection at each decision point, informed by how trauma and violence cause and sustain distress, so nursing research supports recovery rather than adding to the burden.
pmc-13358828:
Kerui Cen and co-authors apply a math tool to COVID-19 case curves in a 2026 study. Epidemic waves rise and fall at several speeds at once, and standard methods can blur the timing of policy effects. The team used adaptive Fourier decomposition, a method that splits a wavy signal into clean layers, on daily case data from Washington, D.C.

They checked the city's case series against official records, then matched the layers' turning points with the dates of public health measures. A second test on London data checked whether the method holds elsewhere. Sharper timing pictures could help officials judge which measures truly bent the curve in past outbreaks.
pmc-13359528:
Ki Ju Cho and co-authors review a family of proteins as drug targets in thyroid cancer in a 2026 paper. Thyroid cancer is the most common hormone gland cancer and is rising fast. Most cases are curable, but some stop responding to standard care or turn highly aggressive. The seven sirtuin proteins help control cell stress and energy, and each can either feed or fight tumors.

The review maps what each sirtuin does in this cancer and gathers new links to immune control and to ferroptosis, an iron-driven cell death. The authors propose pairing sirtuin drugs with existing treatments and flag which ideas are ready for early patient testing.
pmc-13359628:
Camilo Jubino Londoño and Binhai Zheng review the scar that forms after spinal cord injury in a 2026 paper. At the injury site, a fibrotic scar grows at the core, ringed by a second scar from support cells. The fibrotic part was long overlooked. It seals the wound and limits further damage, yet its persistence can block nerve fibers from regrowing.

The review traces how this scar builds over weeks, which cells and signals drive it, and how it interacts with its neighbors. New treatments aim to soften the scar without losing its protection. The authors close with the open questions that must be answered before such treatments reach patients.
pmc-13360128:
Tzu-Chin Yang and co-authors present a 2026 computer system that spots tuberculosis on chest X-rays. Reading these X-rays is hard, and expert marking of each sore spot is slow and costly. Their system, called CPM-XNet, learns from whole images without needing those detailed marks. A special mask in the system guides it to weigh the lung area while still seeing the full picture.

The team tested the system on hospital images and on public data sets. It beat similar models trained on plain, unmarked images, and one main setup gave steadier, stronger scores across repeat runs. Tests that removed one part at a time showed the mask did most of the work. The authors say the system is a promising first step, but it needs checks across more hospitals before clinic use.
pmc-13360228:
Jacopo Lanari and co-authors report 14 years of experience using heat to destroy liver tumors that spread from other cancers. The cancers were not colorectal; they included breast cancer, gut stromal tumors, and pancreatic cancer, eight types in all. The team treated 138 patients with microwave ablation, which cooks tumor tissue with heat. The heat probe went in through a small cut or through the skin.

The treatment proved safe, with few major problems and short hospital stays. Survival differed a lot by which cancer the tumors came from. Patients treated through the small-cut route lived longer than those treated through the skin. The results help doctors judge when this gentle option suits patients who cannot have surgery.
pmc-13360328:
Rohmah and colleagues rank forms of talk therapy for poor sleep in teens. The therapy, called CBT-I, can come in more than one form. It may be face to face, in a group, by phone app, or on the web. The team pooled twenty-two trials. They used a method that ranks all forms at once. Web-based therapy came out on top for most gains.

Teens on web therapy slept about half an hour more each night. They fell asleep faster and slept more soundly. Their sleep problem scores fell too. Time awake in the night did not change much. The team backs web therapy as a first choice in school and clinic care.
pmc-13360728:
Regina Mikheeva and co-authors mapped big genome changes in a famous cancer cell line in a 2026 study. HCT116, a colon cancer line, is a workhorse for drug testing and cell studies. Its small gene typos are well known, but its large DNA rearrangements and copy changes are not. The team read several samples of the line with long-read Nanopore sequencing, including samples from a public database.

They found over 22,000 large rearrangements shared across the samples. Most of the big duplicated and deleted stretches were confirmed on a second check. The team also sorted which changes were common and which were unique to one sample. The map warns lab workers that this standard line varies more than many assume, which matters when results must repeat.
pmc-13360928:
Jorge F Beltrán and co-authors tracked protein changes in salmon cells fighting a kidney disease germ in a 2026 study. The germ, Renibacterium salmoninarum, lives inside fish immune cells and is hard to study at the protein level. The team infected a salmon macrophage-like cell line and sampled it across 48 hours. A scanning method counted thousands of proteins without labels.

Of about 6,800 proteins tracked, more than 2,200 shifted in amount after infection at some point. The changes showed how the host cell reshapes itself early in the fight. The team also tested whether classic cell-death paths switch on broadly. Maps like this can reveal weak points of the germ and guide vaccines or treatments for a disease that costs salmon farms dearly.
pmc-13361528:
Dilinare Abdurehman and co-authors used artificial intelligence to test a food plant against diabetic kidney disease in a 2026 study. This kidney damage is a heavy burden of diabetes, driven by inflammation and scarring. The plant, Coreopsis tinctoria, is edible and rich in polyphenols, but how it might help was unclear. The team combined network pharmacology with machine learning to rank its active compounds.

A learning model trained on millions of compound and target pairs predicted how 36 plant polyphenols interact with disease genes. The top 100 targets were grouped into pathways. Promising paths were then checked in rats made diabetic by a high-fat diet and a drug. Blending computation with animal proof can speed the search for food-based aids against this disease.
pmc-13361828:
Peipei Zhang and co-authors studied a hormone's effect on sheep egg maturation in a 2026 paper. Growing eggs well in the lab is a gateway to making embryos outside the body. Anti-Müllerian hormone, made by cells around the egg, normally reins in early follicle growth. The team added the hormone to lab cultures of sheep eggs and watched many quality traits.

They tracked cell activity, the movement of granules that prepare the egg, its inner skeleton, and its power plants. Single-cell gene reading added a deep view of egg development. A mid dose improved the share of eggs that matured and kept key structures in their normal pattern. Knowing the right dose helps farms and labs raise embryo production in sheep breeding programs.
pmc-13362328:
Lianlen Joy Go Distor and co-authors review a calcium channel that links cancer and heart rhythm trouble in a 2026 paper. Heart disease and cancer are the world's top killers, and many cancer drugs raise the risk of heart damage and arrhythmias. The channel, CaV1.3, lets calcium into heart cells and helps set the heartbeat's pace in its natural pacemaker. In several cancers, the same channel helps tumors grow, move, and resist therapy.

Cancer treatment stresses, such as oxidative damage, inflammation, and low oxygen, can reshape how much of this channel is made and how it behaves. Those shifts disturb the heart's resting rhythm and favor arrhythmias. The authors map this two-way link so oncologists and cardiologists can anticipate rhythm trouble in survivors.
pmc-13363928:
Alessandra Iannuzzi and a large team present a 2026 field study on whether water stress shortens telomeres in grapevines, the protective caps on chromosomes that also serve as aging markers in animals. Aglianico vines grew under rainfed or carefully limited irrigation in a real vineyard. The team joined leaf water measures, drone vegetation reads, and berry chemistry with a DNA test for telomere length across the season.

Rainfed vines were thirstier and loaded more stress compounds in their berries. Telomeres shrank over the season in both groups, but ended shorter in the rainfed vines, with paired checks backing the gap. The authors call the proof early, yet they propose telomere length as a fresh lens on how field stress ages vines.
pmc-13364228:
Larissa Carvalho Ferreira and Katia Viana Xavier present a 2026 study hunting Florida farm fungi that can fight celery early blight, a leaf spot disease that makes celery unsellable. They collected 48 fungi from leaves and soils near celery fields and screened each against the blight fungus in dishes, then moved the best performer into greenhouse plants.

Twelve isolates cut the pathogen's growth by more than half, spanning five fungal groups, and leaf-born isolates proved strongest over time. Two Mucor isolates led the screen, and one of them, Mucor nidicola KX3187, also suppressed the disease on living plants. The authors call the work a first step toward a biological spray for celery growers.
pmc-13369628: Temiz and Kargin published a correction in 2026 to their study of how copper and zinc oxide nanoparticles affect antioxidant defenses in the brains of male Swiss albino mice. The first author's name was misspelled in the article and its running headers, and the corrected spelling now stands in the record. Figures one and two are also replaced with full versions, covering brain antioxidant enzyme activity and damage markers in mice dosed orally for fourteen days at several nanoparticle levels. The journal record has been updated.
pmc-13371028:
Santosh Mahalik and co-workers test in 2026 how well a scan sign and a liver bit check call bile duct lack in sick new borns. The ill scars the bile tubes shut and needs fast knife care for best odds. The team reads 34 young babes with yellow skin at one big site.

All babes get a sound scan with flow read, a glow scan, and a liver bit read by a set score. A dye test in the op room is the gold call. Marks for each test come from that match. The pilot sets the base for a wide test of cheap calls.
pmc-13374628:
Bernier and colleagues test whether HIV-related stigma pushes people with HIV toward heavier drinking, and whether depression carries that effect, in 2026 behavioral health research. The cross-sectional study drew 331 participants with unhealthy alcohol use from two intervention trials, one for chronic pain and one for physical inactivity, both burdens in HIV care. Participants averaged 47.9 years of age; 51.4 percent were African American and 16.6 percent were women in the combined sample analyzed.

Stigma was associated with alcohol-related consequences across the combined sample, with significant indirect effects running through depressive symptoms. The fuller pattern, stigma tied to drinking severity and daily drinks via depression, appeared only among participants in the chronic pain trial. No trial-specific effects emerged in the inactivity trial sample. Bernier argues depression is a pathway worth treating in its own right, and that chronic pain may amplify how stigma translates into alcohol involvement for people with HIV.
pmc-13375528:
Pratley and colleagues test whether an antibody that blocks myostatin can preserve muscle during weight loss driven by tirzepatide, in the 2026 phase 2 EMBRAZE trial. Incretin drugs such as tirzepatide cut weight powerfully, but a share of the loss is lean mass, which can harm strength and function. Apitegromab inhibits activation of myostatin, a protein that restrains muscle growth. The double-blind trial randomized 102 adults with overweight or obesity, half to tirzepatide plus apitegromab and half to tirzepatide plus placebo.
