Yan He and co-authors reviewed in 2021 efforts to treat cancer by targeting the PI3K/Akt signaling pathway. This pathway helps govern cell growth, survival, and metabolism, and it is switched on abnormally in many cancers, helping tumors arise and progress. Because it has many connected nodes, examining the signals above and below it can reveal the full picture of its influence.

The review maps those upstream triggers and downstream effects, then surveys drugs aimed at different points along the route. It weighs the successes and the side effects that have limited this class of medicines so far. For drug developers, the pathway remains one of the richest and most frustrating targets in oncology.
podcast-joerogan-7-IOCUCDL28:
Episode 377 of the Joe Rogan Experience catches Duncan Trussell in the show's early, wild years. Trussell, a comedian with a mystic streak, was already a core member of Rogan's circle. The young show had fewer rules then, and this visit shows it.

The talk jumps between psychedelic stories, jokes about the self, and sudden deep turns on love and death. Trussell's free, riffing style fills the room, and Rogan matches his energy. Listeners who know Trussell's later, calmer work will hear the rawer version here, a snapshot of podcasting before the format grew polished.
podcast-tuckercarlson-qk3I6xi7c28:
Tucker Carlson sits with Donald Trump and asks him flat out what truly happened to Jeffrey Epstein. The episode title is built on that one exchange. Carlson puts the question that hangs over the whole case.

Trump gives his answer on the death and the files in his own words. Carlson presses on what the public still does not know. The clip of the clash is the heart of the episode. Listeners can hear the exchange whole, not cut into bits by the press. The library keeps the talk as a record of that rare, blunt moment.
procopius-wars-gothic-3-dewing-1928:
The History of the Wars of Procopius ends with books seven and eight, in H. B. Dewing's Loeb volume of 1928. Totila's Goths still hold Italy, and Justinian sends the eunuch general Narses with a great army to finish the war. Procopius brings his vast work to its close.

Narses crushes Totila at Taginae and ends the Gothic kingdom at Mons Lactarius. The last book sweeps wider, to Persia, the Danube, and the Slavs pressing the frontier. Italy lies saved and ruined at once, its cities emptied by twenty years of war. Procopius is the chief witness of the whole reconquest. His final books ask what the victory was worth.
raphael-manual-of-astrology-1828:
Raphael was the pen name of Robert Cross Smith, a London astrologer whose Manual of Astrology, or Book of the Stars, appeared in 1828. Astrology had sunk to almanac level in England, and Raphael set out to raise it. His manual became the founding text of the nineteenth-century astrological revival.

He teaches chart casting, nativities, and the judgment of daily questions in a brisk, popular style meant for self-taught readers. His almanacs and guides sold the art back to a Regency public that had nearly forgotten it. Every later English astrological writer worked in a market Raphael reopened.
russell-sceptical-essays-1928:
Sceptical Essays, published in 1928, collects Russell's shorter pieces applying rational doubt to religion, morals, politics, and everyday belief. His prescription is in the first essay: when the experts disagree, the non-expert does well to doubt.

Essay by essay he examines free thought, the dangers of propaganda, and the harm done by good intentions armed with power. Russell writes as a public teacher, witty and exact, refusing every comfortable fog. The targets change with the years, but the method never dates. These essays show the most famous skeptic of the century at his most readable and most humane.
schleiermacher-christian-faith-1928:
The Christian Faith, in the translation by H R Mackintosh and J S Stewart of 1928, is Friedrich Schleiermacher's Der christliche Glaube of 1821 to 1822. The English version is complete, and it carries the magnum opus of liberal Protestant theology. Schleiermacher spent a life preaching and teaching at Berlin, and this book gathers his whole system of doctrine.

His key phrase is the feeling of absolute dependence, the heart's sense of resting wholly on God. Every doctrine, from creation to the church to last things, is traced to that feeling in the believer's life. Critics call the system vast, subtle, and hard to storm. It still anchors the study of modern theology.
senior-two-lectures-population-1828:
Senior's Two Lectures on Population, delivered at Oxford in 1828, give his answer to Malthus on the great question of the age. Malthus had taught that population grows faster than food, so misery must check the numbers. Senior grants the race between mouths and loaves but disputes the finish.

He adds the check Malthus slighted: prudence. As people grow more decent in their wants, Senior argues, they delay marriage and limit families to protect their standard of life. The desire for improvement can thus outrun the pressure of numbers. The lectures soften the gloomy science with common sense and were praised for their humanity. They include his exchange with Malthus himself, who answered in letters printed with the lectures. The old classical school appears here at its most humane.
smith-rabia-the-mystic-1928:
Margaret Smith wrote the first Western study of Rabi'a al-Adawiyya, the slave girl of Basra who became the first great woman saint of Islam. Her book appeared from Cambridge in 1928. Rabi'a died in 801, famed for a love of God that asked no heaven and feared no hell.

Smith gathers the tales and sayings of Rabi'a from the Arabic sources and sets her among her fellow saints. She treats the women of early Islam and the growth of Sufi teaching on divine love. Rabi'a's lamp, her donkey, and her blunt prayers come alive in the telling. The book founded the study of women in Sufism in the West.
spence-mysteries-britain-1928:
Lewis Spence, a Scots writer on myth and folk lore, wrote this survey of the hidden rites of Britain in 1928. He had spent years on the myths of many lands. Here he turned to the isle he knew best and its deep past.

Spence walked from the druids to the great stone rings and the lore of old shrines. He held that a native rite line ran through British life from the far past. Some claims go past the proof, but the book sums up his case in one place.
spengler-decline-west-vol-2-1928:
Oswald Spengler's The Decline of the West, Volume 2, appears in Atkinson's translation of 1928. Subtitled Perspectives of World-History, the volume completes Spengler's work. He turns to the state, money, and the destiny of peoples. Democracy, in his account, yields to money power and then to Caesarism, rule by strong men.

Spengler surveys cities, classes, and religions across his eight great cultures. The West's final phase, he predicts, will be an age of empire and engineering without new art. Many reject his fatalism; few ignore his sweep. The two volumes form a vast, gloomy system. They remain essential for the study of historical pessimism between the wars.
spr-proceedings-vol36-1926-1928:
Volume thirty six gathers parts ninety seven through one hundred three, spanning 1926 to 1928. Seven parts in one binding close the run of Proceedings held here. The Society for Psychical Research had published since 1882, testing wonders by committee rule. Telepathy, apparitions, and trance mediumship fill these last parts as they filled the first.

Sittings, surveys, and spontaneous cases stand reported with the old care. The archive these volumes build is the primary record of the evidential debate to 1930. No verdict ends it; the files simply stand open. Volume thirty six completes the set on this shelf. Readers can now cross the whole span in order.
summers-vampire-kith-kin-1928:
Montague Summers gave the vampire its first full study in 1928. The Vampire: His Kith and Kin draws on lore from all over the world. Summers was a priest who took the old tales in full earnest. He treats the vampire as a true foe of man and God.

Tales from Greece, Slav lands, and the far East fill the book. He sorts the kinds of the undead and tells how men fought them. Church law, trial tales, and folk rites all get a place. The book set the base for all grave study of the vampire since.
the-project-gutenberg-encyclopedia-volum: This Gutenberg encyclopedia volume gathers knowledge A to entries. It digitized learning. The Tower library holds the full text. It alphabetized world. Volumes grew. Knowledge spread. Readers learned. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
thompson-epic-of-gilgamish-1928:
R. Campbell Thompson published The Epic of Gilgamish at Oxford's Clarendon Press in 1928. He spells the hero Gilgamish throughout, following his reading of the tablets. Thompson, a British Museum Assyriologist, made his verse translation from a fresh collation of the cuneiform tablets in London.

Gilgamesh, king of Uruk, loses his friend Enkidu and journeys past death's waters seeking eternal life. He returns with a story, a plant lost to a snake, and hard wisdom about fame. Thompson renders the epic in English hexameters meant to echo its stride. His version was the standard interwar English Gilgamesh. Readers met in it the oldest epic hero whose tale survives.
tob-10228:
James Legge's translation presents the Tao Teh King in eighty-one brief chapters under the name Lao Tzu. Legge was a pioneering Victorian translator of Chinese classics. The verses urge rulers and readers alike to govern by not forcing things against their nature.

Yield like water, desire little, and let people and events follow their own course: that counsel repeats in cryptic, compressed lines. Chinese thought on power and humility has drawn on these chapters for two millennia. English readers of Legge's version meet the text in formal Victorian dress, which can feel distant, yet the paradoxes still cut against ambition and control.
tob-10628:
Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri, a blind Syrian poet who died over a thousand years ago, filled his Diwan with rhymed meditations on fate and folly. He was a skeptic in a religious age. His verses distrust clerics, pity the credulous, and urge doing no harm to any living thing; he himself lived as a strict vegetarian.

Poems in the collection turn over death, hypocrisy, ambition, and the vanity of sects that kill over doctrine. The voice is bleak and brilliant at once, funny in its contempt and tender toward animals and outcasts. English readers meet a freethinker from the medieval Arab world who sounds startlingly modern.
tob-10828:
Annie Besant edited the posthumous third volume of The Secret Doctrine from H. P. Blavatsky's remaining papers. Its subjects shift from cosmic theory toward occult practice and esoteric history. Because Blavatsky did not live to shape it, the volume is more fragmentary than the first two books of the set.

Loose papers on hidden teachings, initiates, and disputed points of doctrine read like notes from a workshop rather than a finished system. Scholars debate how much reflects Blavatsky's final intentions. V1 evidence directs the volume to committed students of Theosophy rather than beginners; newcomers should start with her Key to Theosophy and return here for depth.
tob-13328:
Valmiki, the sage poet of ancient India, composed the Ramayana, one of the two great Sanskrit epics. R. T. H. Griffith turned it into English verse in the nineteenth century. The epic holds a central place in Hindu life and art across Asia.

Prince Rama is exiled to the forest with his wife Sita and his brother Lakshmana. When the demon king Ravana steals Sita away to Lanka, Rama allies with the monkey host and wages war to win her back. The seven books join high adventure to dharma, the law of duty that Rama's life displays in full.
tob-4028:
Immanuel Kant published the Critique of Pure Reason in 1781, asking what reason can and cannot know. His answer reshaped philosophy: we know things as they appear to us, never things in themselves, because space, time, and causality are forms our own mind imposes on experience. Kant called the shift his Copernican revolution in thought.

God, freedom, and immortality fall outside theoretical proof, though they return as needs of moral life. The prose is formidable, architected like a cathedral, and readers should expect slow going. Two centuries of argument later, the Critique remains the mountain modern philosophy is still climbing or deliberately circling.
tob-4128:
Mead's 1896 Pistis Sophia, translated from the Coptic, gave modern readers their first full Gnostic gospel. The risen Savior teaches his disciples for years after the resurrection, the text claims, and at its heart stands Pistis Sophia, Faith-Wisdom, a fallen power who repents through the aeons.

Her thirteen repentances, sung as psalms, plead for rescue from the rulers of darkness. Jesus answers with readings of psalms and odes as coded accounts of her fall. The cosmology is vast and strange. Verified from the 1919 edition, Mead's version introduced Gnosticism to the modern world and still opens the subject.
tob-9028:
Augustine of Hippo wrote The City of God across the years after Rome's sack in 410, and Marcus Dods's translation presents volume one here. Pagans charged that Christians had caused the disaster by abandoning the old gods. Augustine answers that Rome's gods failed long before Christ, and that Rome's own vices, celebrated by its historians, rotted it from within.

From that defense grows his larger vision of two cities, earthly and divine, contending through history toward judgment. The first volume handles Rome's religion and early calamities in detail. Few books have taught the West to think historically as this one did; volume one lays the foundation stone by stone.
troilus-and-cressida-pg1528: The Trojan War stripped of glory fills this edition of Shakespeare's bitter satire: Achilles sulks in his tent, the Greek chiefs bicker like clerks, and Cressida's vows melt at the first temptation. Thersites the jester speaks the play's truth, that heroism is folly. His most cynical work, and his most modern.
un-ga-res-28:
Ruined towns and dead farms fill the opening of Resolution 28, passed by the General Assembly on 2 February 1946. The war of aggression, it says, had smashed vast areas of member states on a scale never seen. The hurt lands held near half the people of the world. Their loss cut world trade, drove living standards down, and in some places wiped out normal work and trade in full.

To make good the ruin, the text argues, vast sums of new capital goods must flow into the smashed areas. Left alone, most states could not rebuild at the speed the task demands. The vote set out the case for the great aid flows that soon reshaped the postwar world.
un-ga-res-a-69-28:
New tools of talk and trade can serve peace or harm it, and Resolution A/69/28, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session, weighs that edge. The vote stands in a chain that goes back to 1998, on the role of science and skill in world safety. States had long agreed that the fruits of science have two faces: they can serve plain, civil ends, or be bent to war.

Great strides in data tools and long-range talk are noted with care. In that growth, the Assembly sees the widest chance for good: for the spread of wealth, health, and free ties between peoples. The task it sets is to guard the civil path of such tools, while curbing their use as arms.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 28, adopted on 2 February 1946, named the rebuilding of war-wrecked member countries a grave and pressing task. The Assembly noted that lands holding near half the world's people had suffered damage on a scale never seen before. Living standards, health, and output were badly cut. World trade was thrown off course.

Full rebuilding, the text held, would take vast sums of new plant and goods. The hurt countries could not supply them alone. The Assembly set the matter for deep study by its Second Committee. That was for the second part of the first session. It asked the Economic and Social Council to take it up at once as well.

Resolution 69/28 of the General Assembly deals with information and telecommunications in international security — in current terms, state behavior in cyberspace. The Assembly notes both the gains of new information technologies and the danger in them. They may be used against states' infrastructure, or for criminal and terrorist ends. It welcomes the work of its Group of Governmental Experts on norms of responsible state behavior and confidence-building. It tells the group to continue studying threats and how international law applies. It invites member states to keep submitting their views.
un-sc-res-1028: Acting formally, the Security Council produced the decision numbered 1028, catalogued under 1995. Such texts can call for cease-fires, set up missions, impose duties, or settle points of UN procedure and membership. Its value lies in the primary wording: the decision as adopted, kept through the Wikisource transcription of the record. No summary replaces it; the record itself is the content of the entry.
un-sc-res-128:
Lebanon charged in 1958 that the United Arab Republic was interfering in its internal affairs. Resolution 128, adopted on 11 June 1958, came after the Council heard Lebanon's charges and the reply of the United Arab Republic. The vote was ten to none, with the Soviet Union abstaining, though the heading also calls the vote unanimous.

The Council decides to send an observation group to Lebanon at once. Its job is to make sure there is no illegal movement of people, arms, or other supplies across the Lebanese borders. The Secretary-General is given power to take the steps needed to send the group, and the group must keep the Council informed through him.
un-sc-res-1328:
UNDOF's six-month rhythm on the Golan Heights rolled on in late 2000. On 27 November 2000 the Security Council renewed the force until 31 May 2001. The Secretary-General had reported on it ten days earlier. The Council also restated its standards for the health of peacekeepers. The mission's terms stayed exactly as before.

The parties had to carry out resolution 338 without delay. The Secretary-General owed a closing report on the term. It would track events and measures taken toward 338. UNDOF's observers manned the line drawn after the 1973 war. Their quiet patrols had become a fixture of the Israel-Syria frontier.
un-sc-res-1428:
UNIFIL's mandate in southern Lebanon came up again in July 2002. On 30 July 2002 the Security Council extended the force for six months. The new term ran until 31 January 2003. The Secretary-General had recommended the renewal in his July report. He was also reshaping the force to match conditions on the ground. The Council backed that reconfiguration work.

The text recalls that Israel had withdrawn in line with resolution 425. Lebanon's return of authority to the south remained a goal. The Council restated Lebanon's sovereignty and territorial integrity. It also repeated the call for calm along the withdrawal line. The force's size was being trimmed as its tasks shifted to observation.
un-sc-res-1528:
Côte d'Ivoire is the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1528, adopted on 27 February 2004. The Forces Nouvelles had returned to the unity government under the Linas-Marcoussis deal. Talks on disarmament had begun. The country's economy was sinking, with harm across the region. The president and West African states both asked for a full peacekeeping operation.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council creates the United Nations Operation in Côte d'Ivoire, UNOCI, for twelve months from 4 April 2004. Up to 6,240 troops and 350 civilian police will watch the cease-fire and guard disarmament sites. The mission will protect civilians, back elections planned for 2005, and help restore state authority. French forces keep their supporting role for the same year.
un-sc-res-1628:
The Congo mission received a one-month extension in September 2005. On 30 September 2005 the Security Council kept MONUC until 31 October 2005. The mandate stayed as set by four earlier resolutions. All of them had been adopted under Chapter VII. The Council restated the Congo's sovereignty and borders. It also restated its readiness to back the peace process. The country was then preparing its first free elections in decades.

The short term bridged a planning gap. A larger mandate with election support was being drafted. The Council stayed actively seized of the matter. MONUC was already one of the largest peace operations in the world. Its final shape for the election period came with the next renewal.
un-sc-res-1728:
Cyprus again comes before the Council in United Nations Security Council Resolution 1728. The Council adopted it on 15 December 2006. The Green Line stayed calm, and mine clearing in the buffer zone was moving ahead. Yet trust between the two communities stayed low, and an 8 July deal had stalled.

The text extends the United Nations Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus, called UNFICYP, until 15 June 2007. It presses both sides to carry out the July deal and finish groundwork for full talks. It calls on the Turkish Cypriot side to restore the old military position at Strovilia. The Secretary-General had to report back by 1 June 2007.
un-sc-res-1828:
Action on Darfur came with Resolution 1828, adopted on 31 July 2008. One year into the joint African Union and United Nations mission, UNAMID, safety in Darfur had grown worse. Attacks on civilians and aid workers went on. The World Court prosecutor had just asked for an arrest warrant for Sudan's president.

The text extends the mandate of UNAMID for twelve months, to 31 July 2009. It urges a fast build-up, with eighty per cent of the force in place by the end of 2008. Sudan must drop all blocks on the mission's movement and work. All sides are told to stop attacks and agree to a firm, lasting cease-fire.
un-sc-res-1928:
North Korea's nuclear and missile programs kept a sanctions panel at work in 2010. On 7 June 2010 the Security Council extended that panel for a year. The Panel of Experts helps enforce the sanctions set after North Korea's nuclear tests. Its mandate now ran until 12 June 2011. The panel had sent an interim report in 2009 and a final one in May 2010.

The panel owed a midterm report by 12 November 2010. A final report would come before the mandate ended. The Council urged all states and United Nations bodies to cooperate with it. Sharing facts on sanctions breaches mattered most. The text treats weapons proliferation as a standing threat to peace.
un-sc-res-228:
A large Israeli raid into Jordan drew censure from the Security Council on 25 November 1966. The attack had struck the southern Hebron area on 13 November 1966. The Secretary-General's statement of 16 November and report of 18 November laid out the facts. The Council found a large-scale, carefully planned military action on Jordanian territory by Israel's armed forces.

The Council deplored the loss of life and the heavy damage to property. It censured Israel for the action, which broke the United Nations Charter and the Israel-Jordan General Armistice Agreement. Israel was told plainly that military reprisals cannot be tolerated. If they were repeated, the Council would have to weigh further and more effective steps under the Charter to stop them. The Secretary-General was asked to keep watch on the situation and report as needed. The raid, on the village of Samu, was the largest Israeli operation since 1956.
un-sc-res-2728:
Gaza occupied the Council on 25 March 2024, when it adopted Resolution 2728 on Gaza. Months of war had left the Gaza Strip in a catastrophic state. Civilians lacked food, water, and medical care at any real scale. Egypt, Qatar, and the United States were pressing for a halt to the fighting and freedom for hostages.

The Council demands an immediate ceasefire for the month of Ramadan, respected by all parties. That pause should lead to a lasting, sustainable ceasefire. All hostages must be freed at once and without conditions. Barriers to aid at scale must come down across the whole Strip. The text also recalls that taking hostages breaks international law.
un-sc-res-28: Members of the Council adopted Resolution 28 on Greece on 6 August 1947 by ten votes to none, with one abstention. Rival drafts on the Greek question had left the Council stuck. The Council sets up a small sub-committee for the job. It is made of the delegations that had put forward proposals or changes. Their task is to test whether a fresh draft can win broad support. The sub-committee must report its findings on 11 August 1947. The text does nothing else.
un-sc-res-328:
Southern Rhodesia's raids on Zambia drew a broad rebuke on 10 March 1973. A special mission sent under resolution 326 (1973) had reported on the border crisis. South Africa refused to pull its military and armed forces out of Southern Rhodesia, defying resolutions 277 (1970) and 326 (1973). Britain, as the administering power, held the main duty to end the illegal minority regime.

The Council backed the mission's findings in full. Rhodesia's recent acts of provocation and aggression against Zambia had raised the tension, it declared. The only real answer lay in the people of Zimbabwe winning self-determination and independence. South Africa was strongly condemned for keeping its forces in place, and the demand for their instant withdrawal was repeated. The Rhodesia sanctions committee was told to speed its work. The Council urged Britain to call a national constitutional conference at once, so majority rule could follow.
un-sc-res-428: Council action recorded as Resolution 428 appears in this catalog under the year 1976. Formal decisions of this sort guide UN staff, peacekeeping forces, and governments in the years that follow. What is preserved is the exact formal wording, transcribed on English Wikisource from the official record of the Council. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci: Security Council resolution 1028, adopted unanimously on 8 December 1995, briefly extends the mandate of UNAMIR, the United Nations Assistance Mission for Rwanda. The Council had considered the Secretary-General's report of 1 December 1995 on the mission. It extends the mandate only until 12 December 1995. That is a four-day bridge while it decides the mission's future. It decides to remain actively seized of the situation in Rwanda.

Security Council resolution 128, adopted on 11 June 1958, answers Lebanon's charge that the United Arab Republic was interfering in its internal affairs. The Council had heard both sides. It decides to send an observation group to Lebanon urgently. The group is to make sure there is no illegal infiltration of men or supply of arms or other material across the Lebanese borders. The Council authorizes the Secretary-General to take the steps needed. It asks the group to keep it informed through him.

Some summaries file Resolution 1328 under Western Sahara, but the text concerns the Golan Heights. It passed unanimously on 27 November 2000. Members had just reviewed the Secretary-General's report of 17 November. The subject was the UN Disengagement Observer Force. That force monitors the separation zone between Israeli and Syrian troops.

The mandate was extended by six months, to 31 May 2001. The Council again urged both parties to put Resolution 338 of 1973 into effect. That older resolution links the observer mission to a negotiated Middle East peace. A further report from the Secretary-General was requested for the end of the period.

Half a year more for the Lebanon watch came in the summer of 2002. Beirut asked for it in a note dated 9 July. The chief's report of 12 July backed the plea. He also set out a leaner shape for the force. Resolution 1428 passed with no dissent on 30 July 2002.

UNIFIL's term ran to 31 January 2003. The chief had to press on with the reshape. Troop states and Beirut would be brought into the talks. Lebanon won praise for steps to rule its south once more. Its army's spread there was cheered. All sides had to honor the Blue Line in full. Acts of force drew blame. Breaches by air, sea, and land were called grave. Praise flowed for the force's mine work and for a new aid group backing it.

Côte d'Ivoire gets a UN peacekeeping operation in Resolution 1528, adopted unanimously on 27 February 2004. The Linas-Marcoussis Agreement had set a peace path, the Forces Nouvelles had rejoined the government, and a disarmament programme was agreed. Côte d'Ivoire's president and ECOWAS had both asked the Council to turn the small MINUCI mission into a full operation.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council establishes the United Nations Operation in Côte d'Ivoire, UNOCI, for 12 months from 4 April 2004, with up to 6,240 military personnel and 350 civilian police. UNOCI must monitor the ceasefire, support disarmament and demobilization, guard surrendered weapons, protect civilians under imminent threat, help restore state authority and policing, and assist preparations for the 2005 presidential election. It may use all necessary means. French forces are authorized for the same period to support UNOCI and protect civilians in their areas.

Resolution 1628, adopted on 30 September 2005, keeps a large peacekeeping mission in place for one more month. The mission is MONUC, deployed in the Democratic Republic of the Congo during the country's fragile move from civil war toward elections. The Council restated its respect for Congo's sovereignty and its support for peace and national reconciliation.

The single decision extends MONUC's mandate, set out in several earlier resolutions and backed by Chapter VII authority, until 31 October 2005. A one-month rollover of this kind usually signals that a bigger decision on the mission's size and tasks is still being negotiated. The Council closed by keeping the Congo question formally on its agenda.

Cyprus stays calm but divided in Resolution 1728, adopted on 15 December 2006. An 8 July agreement had set out shared ground: the present state of affairs was not acceptable, and a bicommunal, bizonal federation with political equality was the goal. Lack of trust had blocked every step since. Mine clearing in the buffer zone was moving ahead, and the zone might be mine-free within two years.

The Council gives full support to the UN Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus, UNFICYP, and extends its mandate until 15 June 2007. It calls on the Turkish Cypriot side and Turkish forces to restore the earlier military position at Strovilia. It backs active talks between the two communities to finish the groundwork so full negotiations can restart. It also welcomes peaceful crossings between north and south and urges more crossing points, including at Ledra Street. A report is due by 1 June 2007.

Darfur's hybrid peacekeeping force is renewed by Resolution 1828, adopted on 31 July 2008. A year after UNAMID's creation, security and humanitarian conditions had worsened and deployment lagged. The Council also noted the African Union's concerns about what might follow the International Criminal Court Prosecutor's application of 14 July 2008, and said it would consider those matters further.

The Council extends UNAMID for twelve months, to 31 July 2009. It presses for fast deployment of the heavy support package and the troops, police, and helicopters still missing, aiming for 80 percent deployment by 31 December 2008. It demands that Sudan honour the Status of Forces Agreement and remove all obstacles. It demands that all sides end attacks and commit to a permanent ceasefire. It also demands that they join talks under the new joint mediator. Reports are due every 60 days.

North Korea's sanctions sleuths gained another year in 2010. On 7 June, the Council adopted Resolution 1928. It acted under Chapter VII. The sanctions were built by Resolutions 1718 and 1874, after Pyongyang's nuclear tests. A Panel of Experts tracked how states evaded them. Its late 2009 and May 2010 reports lay before the Council.

The text extends the panel's mandate to 12 June 2011. Deadlines are set for its mid-term and final reports. All states and UN bodies must help the panel in full. Sharing word on how the sanctions are carried out matters most. The panel's reports became the public record of the North's buying webs.

Resolution 2028, adopted on 21 December 2011, renews the Golan observer force against the backdrop of Syria's spreading unrest. The Secretary-General's November report on UNDOF noted that evolving conditions in the region could affect how the force works. The Council repeated its grave concern at the May and June incidents in the force's area that had endangered the ceasefire dating to 1974.

UNDOF's mandate was extended for six months, to June 2012. Both parties were called on to respect the disengagement agreement, avoid breaches of the ceasefire and the separation area, and cooperate fully with the force. The text also welcomed UNDOF's work applying the UN policy of zero tolerance for sexual abuse by its own staff.

Resolution 228, adopted on 25 November 1966 by fourteen votes to none with one abstention, censures Israel for a large raid into Jordan. On 13 November Israeli forces had struck the southern Hebron area, in the village of Samu, in an operation the Council found large-scale and carefully planned. The Secretary-General had reported on the attack, and both Jordan and Israel addressed the Council.

The Council deplored the loss of life and heavy property damage. It censured Israel for violating both the Charter and the Israel-Jordan armistice agreement. And it put Israel on notice: military reprisals cannot be tolerated, and if repeated, the Council would have to weigh stronger steps of its own.

Gaza's war draws a ceasefire demand in Resolution 2728, adopted on 25 March 2024. The humanitarian situation in the Gaza Strip was catastrophic, hostages were still held, and Egypt, Qatar, and the United States were mediating for a halt to hostilities, hostage releases, and more aid. The Muslim holy month of Ramadan was under way.

The Council demands an immediate ceasefire for the month of Ramadan, respected by all parties, leading to a lasting sustainable ceasefire. It also demands the immediate and unconditional release of all hostages and humanitarian access to meet their medical and other needs, and reminds all sides of their duties toward people they detain. It stresses the urgent need to expand aid flows across the whole Gaza Strip, protect civilians, and lift all barriers to delivering humanitarian assistance at scale.

Greece sat near the top of the Council's worries in 1947. A civil war was beginning there. Rival proposals on the Greek question crowded the table. Resolution 28, adopted on 6 August 1947, tried to break the logjam. Ten members voted yes. The Soviet Union abstained.

The text creates a small drafting group. Delegations that had offered proposals or amendments would staff it. Its job was to find common ground. If a single new draft could win approval, the group would recommend it. The deadline was tight: report back by 11 August 1947. The device shows the Council negotiating with itself before confronting the crisis outside.

Resolution 328, adopted on 10 March 1973 by thirteen votes to none with two abstentions, follows a fact-finding trip to Zambia. A special mission created in February had reported on Rhodesian and South African pressure along Zambia's borders. Zambia's ambassador addressed the Council again. At issue was Pretoria's refusal to pull its military and police out of Southern Rhodesia, where they propped up the illegal regime.

The Council endorsed the special mission's assessment and conclusions. It treated South Africa's defiance of earlier demands as a serious challenge to its authority. Britain, as the administering power, was reminded that ending the illegal regime and transferring power to Zimbabwe's people on majority rule was primarily its responsibility.

South African forces raided Angola in May 1978, killing many people, including Namibian refugees living there. Angola brought the attack to the Council two days later. It had done the same after an earlier invasion, condemned in Resolution 387. A leader of the Namibian liberation movement also addressed the Council. Resolution 428 was adopted unanimously on 6 May 1978.

The Council strongly condemned South Africa's armed invasion. It was a clear violation of Angola's sovereignty and territory. The Council also condemned the use of Namibia as a springboard for the attacks. South Africa held Namibia in illegal occupation at the time. All South African forces had to withdraw from Angola at once, without conditions. The occupation of Namibia itself had to end without delay.

Membership for a new African state is the whole business of Resolution 828, adopted on 26 May 1993. The Security Council had examined Eritrea's application for admission to the United Nations, filed as document S/25793. Eritrea had just confirmed its separation from Ethiopia through a referendum, and its leaders sought a seat among member states.

The Council's answer fills only a few lines: it recommends that the General Assembly admit Eritrea. Admission works that way under the UN Charter, since the Assembly can seat a new member only after the Council recommends it. The short text marks the moment Eritrea joined the world body as an independent country along the Red Sea.
woolf-orlando-1928:
Virginia Woolf published Orlando in 1928 and called it a biography, though it breaks every rule of the form. Woolf wrote it as a playful love letter to her friend Vita Sackville-West, whose family home and ancestors fill its pages. It became her best-selling book during her life.

Orlando begins as a young Elizabethan nobleman and lives on for three hundred years. Partway through, in Constantinople, Orlando sleeps for days and wakes as a woman. The story sweeps through the Great Frost, Augustan coffeehouses, and Victorian damp to reach 1928. Woolf mocks biography, history, and gender itself with delight. Beneath the jokes sits a serious portrait of a writer's inner life.
yeats-tower-1928:
W. B. Yeats published The Tower in 1928, a book of poems written in his sixties. Yeats had bought and restored a Norman tower in Ireland as his home. Sailing to Byzantium opens the book with an old man's wish for a soul made like art. The title poem broods on age, memory, and imagination.

Meditations in Time of Civil War reflects on violence in Ireland after independence. Other poems address friends, ancestors, and the poet's own past loves. The style is grand, bitter, and full of strong images. Critics often call The Tower his finest single volume. It shows a great poet facing old age without flinching.
